fix(pdf): keep partial vision renders + bound pdftoppm loop to actual page count

`render_with_pdftoppm` looped from 1 to `max_pages` (100) in batches of
10 regardless of the PDF's real page count. On a 32-page document the
5th batch (pages 41-50) made pdftoppm error:

    Wrong page range given: the first page (41) can not be after the last page (32).

The function returned Err, which made `render_pdf_pages` invoke
`cleanup_dir` and wipe the 32 PNGs that earlier batches had rendered
successfully. The vision path then fell back to text extraction —
which truncates at 8000 chars (~5 pages of a typical report). That
8000-char ceiling is what users were seeing as "PDF cuts off at
page 5".

Changes:
- Add `pdf_page_count(pdf_path)` using `pdfinfo` to learn the real
  page count. When unavailable we fall back to `max_pages` and rely
  on the new per-batch error tolerance.
- Tolerate batch failures: log a warn, skip that batch, keep going.
  Return Err only when zero pages came out (no useful partial render).
- Try 2/3/4-digit zero-padded filenames so docs with >99 pages
  (pdftoppm widens the suffix automatically) collect correctly.
- Drop the now-unused `DEFAULT_MAX_PAGES` constant.

The cleanup-on-Err in `render_pdf_pages` is unchanged: it still fires
when every strategy fails outright, but partial successes no longer
trip it because the inner loop now returns Ok with whatever pages
landed.

Tests in `src/tests/pdf_vision_test.rs` cover the missing-file error,
output-directory creation, and the contract that a renderer with no
output must return Err rather than Ok(vec![]).

fix(pdf): raise inline cap to ~60 pages + save PDF so agent can fetch the rest

The text-extract fallback in `process_file_with_vision` hard-capped at
`TEXT_LIMIT = 8000` chars. Typical reports run ~1600 chars per page,
so the agent saw roughly five pages of any incoming PDF — which is
the symptom users reported as "PDF cuts off at page 5". The vision
path is supposed to handle longer documents, but when it fails (no
renderer installed, malformed page batch, etc.) the fallback became
the silent ceiling.

This commit:

- Split the PDF cap from the generic text cap. PDFs now use
  `PDF_TEXT_LIMIT = 200_000` chars, enough for ~60 pages of a typical
  report to land inline.
- Always save the original PDF to `~/.opencrabs/tmp/files/` and
  include the path in the agent prompt. Whether the inline preview is
  complete or truncated, the agent can call
  `parse_document(path='...', pages=[N])` to re-query any page with
  no fidelity loss.
- Surface the document's true page count up front: the file header
  now reads `[File: report.pdf (32 pages)]` so the agent knows the
  shape of the document before deciding how to chunk further work.
- When the inline preview *is* truncated, the appended hint now
  states which pages are covered and which range to ask
  `parse_document` for next.
- Promote the previously-silent pdf_extract failure to a `warn!` log
  so future regressions surface in logs instead of the model's
  reasoning trace.

Test added in `file_extract_test`: confirms the page-count tag and
filename land on the `extract_pdf_text` path.

feat(doc_parser): page_range param + agent-facing guidance for paginated PDFs

`parse_document` was the right tool to read more of a truncated PDF
but the model rarely chose to call it because the description didn't
explain that role, and the only filter was `pages: [1, 2, 3, ...]`
which is awkward for the common "give me pages 31 through 60" case.

Changes:

- Add `page_range: Option<String>` accepting `"1-30"`, `"5,7,10-15"`,
  or `"3"`. Parsed via `parse_page_range`, deduped, sorted, merged
  with `pages` when both are present. Invalid tokens are silently
  skipped so a slightly malformed value from the model still produces
  useful output instead of an error.
- Rewrite the tool description to tell the agent exactly when to
  reach for it: "Use this whenever an incoming PDF's inline preview
  was truncated — the file is saved at the path included in the
  preview message". Pairs with the path hint the inline ingestion
  now emits (`fix(pdf): raise inline cap to ~60 pages…`).
- When requested pages are out of range, append a "[Requested pages
  not present in document (N total): [skipped]]" footer instead of
  silently dropping them — surfaces off-by-one mistakes early.
- Fix the page-count metadata to count the full document instead of
  the filtered slice.

Tests in `doc_parser_page_range_test`: schema acceptance for
`page_range` alone and with `pages`, garbage/empty `page_range`
tolerance, and the missing-file error path still working through the
new code.

docs(tools): document page_range + fix wrong pages-as-string hint

The TOOLS.md template the agent reads at startup listed
`parse_document` with only `pages` as a page-filter option, and the
explanatory note used a misleading example: `Use \`pages\` to limit
PDF page range (e.g. \"1-5\")`. `pages` is a JSON integer array
(`[1,2,3,4,5]`), not a string — an agent following the example would
hit schema validation failure and likely fall back to the truncated
inline PDF preview rather than retry. That misleading hint plausibly
contributed to the "PDF cuts off at page 5" reports.

Changes:
- Add `page_range` to the args row for `parse_document`.
- Rewrite the explanatory note to show both forms correctly:
  `page_range: "1-30"` (string spec, preferred for spans) and
  `pages: [1,2,3,4,5]` (raw int array). State they merge when both
  are supplied.
- Document the inline-preview path workflow: when the preview is
  truncated, the original PDF is saved to `~/.opencrabs/tmp/files/`
  and the path is included in the preview message — feed it back
  into `parse_document` to read on.

test(pdf): 25 direct cases for parse_page_range + normalise spaces around dash

Direct coverage for `parse_page_range` was missing — the new
`page_range` argument was only validated through schema-level tests
in `doc_parser_page_range_test`. Wrong page numbers come back as
plausible text, so a regression here would silently feed the agent
content from the wrong pages.

Promotes `parse_page_range` to `pub(crate)` and adds 25 unit tests
covering the realistic + adversarial inputs:

- single page, simple range, large range, multi-token ranges
- mixed singles + ranges (`5,7,10-15`)
- separator variants (commas, whitespace, comma + space)
- dedup of duplicates and overlapping ranges
- sort order across non-monotonic input
- rejection paths: empty string, only whitespace, only commas,
  page 0, reversed range (`5-3`), non-numeric tokens, negative
  numbers, one-sided malformed range (`5-`)
- adjacency safety: a bad token mid-list doesn't kill its valid
  neighbours
- regression cases mirroring the real flow: `"31-60"` after a
  truncated 1-30 preview, `"1-3,32"` for summary+conclusion

Fix surfaced by the new tests: input like `"1 - 5"` (verbose model
output) previously parsed as `[1, 5]` because the dash itself became
a token. The parser now normalises spaces immediately adjacent to a
dash before tokenising, so `"1 - 5"` expands correctly to
`[1,2,3,4,5]`. Spaces elsewhere still separate tokens, so
`"1-3 5-7"` still parses as two ranges.

fix(pdf): text-first routing + lazy per-page vision (closes 10 MB / 413 incident)

Yesterday's commits made vision actually work end-to-end for the user's
32-page PDF. That uncovered a worse design: `process_file_with_vision`
ran the vision path whenever ANY vision model was configured, then
`build_user_message` base64-inlined every rendered page into a single
user Message. For a 32-page PDF that produces ~14 MB of inline image
data → HTTP 413 from Dialagram (10 MB cap), logged at
2026-05-30T00:01:20.

Two architectural changes:

1. **Text-first routing.** `process_pdf_smart` runs `pdf_extract`
   before reaching for vision. Text-rich PDFs (≥500 total chars AND
   ≥100 chars/page) take the text path: ~200 KB inline preview + the
   saved PDF path the agent can feed into `parse_document` for any
   page. ~95% of real-world PDFs (reports, contracts, papers, books)
   land here. The vision pipeline runs only when `pdf_extract` returns
   sparse/empty text — i.e. truly scanned or image-only PDFs.

2. **Lazy per-page vision.** When vision IS used, `FileContent::PdfPages`
   no longer emits `<<IMG:...>>` markers. Those markers cause
   `build_user_message` to base64-inline images into the user Message.
   Instead the injection lists page paths as plain text, with a
   `Page N: /tmp/.../page-NN.png` line per page, and tells the agent
   to call `analyze_image(image='<path>', question='...')` ONE PAGE
   AT A TIME. Each tool call ships one image (~500 KB); the request
   body never approaches provider caps, and vision tokens are paid
   only for pages the agent actually reads.

Same fix applied to the zip-archive PDF branch in `extract_zip_contents`.

`process_pdf_vision`'s text fallback on render failure is removed —
the text path already ran first, so render failure means both
backends failed. Surfaces a clear "neither backend worked" error
instead of silently re-running text extraction.

Tests in `pdf_smart_routing_test`: guard against the `<<IMG:` marker
ever creeping back into PdfPages injection (the regression that
caused the 413), assert per-page paths and warnings are emitted,
and confirm single-image attachments still use the inline-marker
fast path.

fix(telegram): surface user-highlighted quote in reply context (closes #131)

When a Telegram user replies to a message and uses the quote-reply
feature to highlight a specific excerpt, the bot only saw the full
text of the replied-to message. On long forwarded threads the agent
had to guess which sentence the user was pointing at, often
answering about the wrong part of the message.

teloxide 0.13 exposes the highlighted excerpt via `msg.quote()`
(`Option<&TextQuote>` where `TextQuote.text: String`). The handler
now reads it and routes through a new `format_reply_context` helper
that picks the right surface based on what's actually present:

- Quote differs from full text → show both: the highlighted excerpt
  on its own line so the agent knows what the user is asking about,
  plus the full message for surrounding context.
- Quote matches full text (user highlighted everything) → show once.
- No quote → original full-text format (no behavior change).
- Neither present → None (no reply context line at all).

Trim both inputs before comparison so trailing whitespace from the
Telegram client doesn't trigger the dual-surface path when the quote
logically matches the full text.

Tests in `telegram_quote_reply_test`: 11 cases covering each branch,
unicode preservation, multiline messages, whitespace edges, and the
"assistant" sender naming for bot replies.

feat(rsi): append bash command text to feedback ledger metadata (closes #132)

The feedback ledger recorded `bash` failures with the error snippet
only — e.g. `"Command exited with code 1"`. RSI saw a single
`dimension = 'bash'` blob and could not tell that python script
failures, git rebase conflicts, missing-binary errors (exit 127),
and 120-second timeouts have nothing to do with each other. The
improvement suggestions it produced were stuck at the generic
"improve bash usage" level.

This commit appends the actual command text to the failure
metadata so SQL / RSI analyses can group by subsystem:

    WHERE dimension = 'bash' AND meta LIKE '%cmd=git%'
    WHERE dimension = 'bash' AND meta LIKE '%cmd=python%'

Changes:

- New `enrich_metadata` helper in `feedback.rs` reads the
  `command` field from `tool_input` JSON when the tool is `bash`
  and the call failed, and appends ` | cmd=<command text>` to
  the error snippet. The command itself is capped at 300 chars so
  a giant pipeline can't crowd out the error message inside the
  outer 500-char meta cap.
- `record_tool_feedback` now takes `tool_input: Option<&Value>`
  so the enricher has the data it needs. All five call sites in
  `tool_loop.rs` (user denial, two success/failure branches, two
  direct execution-error branches) pass `Some(&tool_input_for_progress)`.
  `None` stays available for any future call site without a
  meaningful input.
- The enricher is bash-only today; non-bash tools pass their
  snippet through unchanged so there's no behavior change for any
  other tool.
- When there's no snippet but there is a bash command (e.g.
  user-denied-approval before stderr exists), the meta still
  carries the bare `cmd=...` so RSI can categorize the denial by
  subsystem too.

Tests in `bash_feedback_enrichment_test`: 14 cases including the
realistic patterns from the issue (git rebase conflict, python
ModuleNotFoundError, cargo build timeout), edge cases (empty
command, missing field, very long command, unicode paths), and a
guard that non-bash tools with their own `command` field are not
accidentally enriched.

fix(telegram): make pre-tool status line dynamic instead of hardcoded "Thinking through this..."

The 2026-05-28 refactor (`512bf002`) removed the rotating
TOOL_STATUS_QUIPS array and replaced it with a context-aware
`build_status_message` generator that shows live tool execution
state. That part works. But the generator falls through to a
single hardcoded `"Thinking through this..."` string whenever the
agent is in the pre-tool reasoning phase — exactly the state where
the user has reasoning text streaming above the status line.

Screenshot 2026-05-30 01:43 captured the irony: the agent was
streaming "I am assessing the existing data model and user
interface..." in the response message, while the status line just
below said "Thinking through this..." — a generic filler that
ignored the live reasoning text right above it. The "dynamic"
generator was only dynamic for tool execution.

This commit adds a hybrid: reasoning text when available, fun-quip
rotation as fallback.

- New `thinking_status_excerpt(thinking)` helper extracts the
  latest non-trivial sentence from the agent's in-flight reasoning
  text, strips first-person lead-ins ("I am ", "I'm ", "Let me ",
  "I will ", "Let us "), capitalises the first letter, and caps at
  80 chars. Returns None when the reasoning buffer is empty or too
  sparse (<20 chars or no sentence ≥12 chars long).
- `StreamingState.thinking` is already accumulated for the response
  view — Snapshot now also carries `thinking_excerpt` so the edit
  loop has it without re-locking.
- `build_status_message` takes the excerpt and, in the pre-tool
  phase, prefers it. When the excerpt is None we rotate through 8
  fun quips indexed by `elapsed_secs / 4` so the first 1-2 seconds
  of a turn (before reasoning has streamed) still feel alive and
  vary across turns instead of showing the same line every time.
- Tool-execution status paths are unchanged.

Tests in `telegram_status_message_test`: 15 cases covering empty /
whitespace / too-short input, latest-sentence selection, all
lead-in strip variants, unicode capitalisation (French/Spanish),
multi-line reasoning, the 80-char cap with ellipsis marker,
streaming fragments without terminal punctuation, and the verbatim
"I am assessing the existing data model..." text from the
screenshot.

fix(compaction): silent continuation by default, fun fallback only when unclear

After context compaction the agent was emitting verbose "Got nuked
mid-edit. Took a consciousness dirt nap. Let me get back to stabbing
these 4 files. Let me re-read the files (pre-compaction reads are
stale now) and make the edits." — fun, but it surfaced an internal
plumbing event to the user as if it mattered.

The cause was the prompt itself: each of the three compaction
handlers (regular async at 65%, mid-loop during tool execution,
emergency on provider rejection) ran a verbose multi-step
"POST-COMPACTION PROTOCOL" that read like a recipe. The agent
naturally narrated following it. The emergency path even said
"Briefly acknowledge the compaction with a fun/cheeky remark" —
literally asking for the surprise message.

Inverted the default. Now all three prompts:

- Tell the agent to silently continue from IMMEDIATE TASK as if
  nothing happened. Compaction is not user-visible state; re-reading
  a file mid-edit is normal and not worth announcing.
- Drop the numbered "POST-COMPACTION PROTOCOL" framing that
  encouraged a step-by-step narration.
- Keep `session_search` and selective brain-file loads as guidance
  without prescribing them as recipe steps.
- Keep the fun cheeky line as an explicit FALLBACK, only when the
  summary doesn't make the next step clear. So users still get the
  occasional playful surprise when compaction genuinely caught the
  agent mid-thought without enough context to resume cleanly.

No code change beyond the three string literals — the rest of the
compaction machinery already does the right thing.

feat(plan): add concrete trigger criteria to plan tool description

The agent rarely called `plan` even on clearly multi-step work
because the tool description was generic — "Manage structured task
plans with full plan-and-execute capabilities" — and gave the model
no concrete handle for WHEN planning pays off vs. when it's
overhead. The system prompt had no fallback guidance either, so
the agent defaulted to skipping the plan tool and bashing through
the steps directly.

The description now spells out the trigger criteria the agent
should match against on every turn:

- 3+ distinct steps
- dependencies between steps
- multi-file or multi-commit work
- the user explicitly asks for a plan or roadmap
- request describes >2 deliverables
- you need to retry steps independently if some fail
- the user is going to step away while you work

And carves out the trivial case (single read / single search /
single edit) so the agent doesn't over-plan one-shot answers.

Also surfaces a load-bearing property that wasn't obvious from the
old description: the plan persists across compactions, so for long
sessions it doubles as durable memory — useful context for the
agent when deciding whether the upfront cost of planning pays off.

Tests in `plan_tool_description_test`: 8 sentinel cases asserting
each trigger criterion is present and the capability summary
remains. They fail loudly if a future refactor strips the
guidance — without them the description could drift back to the
generic form silently.

fix(tui): grow plan checklist to ~10 tasks + add scrolling for longer plans

The plan checklist widget hard-capped at 8 layout rows
(`(p.tasks.len() + 2).min(8)`), leaving only 6 task slots — 5

feat(prompt): add Known paths section so "check the logs" lands at the right file

When the user said "check the logs" the agent wandered through the
repo working directory grepping random places, because the system
prompt had no statement of where logs actually live. Logs live at
~/.opencrabs/logs/opencrabs.YYYY-MM-DD (set in logging/logger.rs at
runtime via opencrabs_home().join("logs")), but that path was
nowhere in the prompt — the agent had to guess.

This commit adds a "Known paths" subsection to the Runtime Info
block in the system prompt. It surfaces:

- Logs: ~/.opencrabs/logs/opencrabs.YYYY-MM-DD (rotated daily;
  today's file is almost always what the user means)
- Config: ~/.opencrabs/config.toml
- Keys: ~/.opencrabs/keys.toml
- Brain files: ~/.opencrabs/{SOUL,USER,AGENTS,TOOLS,MEMORY,CODE}.md
- Plans: ~/.opencrabs/agents/session/.opencrabs_plan_<session-id>.json

Plus an explicit instruction: "When the user asks to check logs,
read today's file at ~/.opencrabs/logs/opencrabs.<today UTC date>.
Do NOT grep the repo working directory for log files — opencrabs
never writes logs there."

Lives in a new `push_known_paths` helper next to the existing
home-anchor helper so future additions (e.g. mission control DB
path, voice cache dir) extend in one place. Helper is pub(crate)
so the test file can render it in isolation.

Tests in `prompt_known_paths_test`: 8 sentinel cases asserting
each surface (log dir, daily pattern, repo-grep warning, config,
keys, brain files, plan files) is present, plus a length cap so
the section stays compact instead of bloating into a directory
listing.

feat(prompt): surface compiled features + check-first directive so agent stops reimplementing built-ins

A newly onboarded user asked the agent to "implement local STT and
TTS" and watched it start coding from scratch — both are default
Cargo features (`local-stt`, `local-tts`) with working backends in
the very binary the user was talking to. The agent had no way to
know they were compiled in, and the system prompt had no directive
telling it to check before building.

This commit closes both gaps:

1. New `compiled_features()` helper builds the list of Cargo
   `[features]` enabled in this binary via `cfg!(feature = "...")`
   for each known entry (telegram, whatsapp, discord, slack, trello,
   local-stt, local-tts, browser, rtk, pdfium, profiling).

2. New `push_compiled_features()` injects the line into the Runtime
   Info block:
     Built-in features compiled into this binary: telegram, ...
     Before implementing any of these capabilities from scratch, USE
     the built-in. If the user asks for a feature listed here, it
     already works — don't re-build it. If they ask for a Cargo
     feature NOT in this list (e.g. `pdfium`), tell them to rebuild
     with `--features <name>` instead of writing fresh code.

3. New SELF-AWARENESS section in BRAIN_PREAMBLE tells the agent to
   check three places before proposing new implementations:
     - the tool list in this request
     - the Built-in features line in Runtime Info
     - the brain files (TOOLS.md, AGENTS.md)
   Lists STT, TTS, browser automation, messaging channels, token
   compression, PDF rendering as concrete examples so the model
   recognises the pattern without abstract reasoning.

Sentinel test (`all_cargo_features_are_listed`) reads
`Cargo.toml::[features]` at test time and fails if any feature lacks
a matching `cfg!()` line in `compiled_features` — so future
additions to Cargo.toml can't slip through and silently leave the
agent unaware of a new capability.

Tests in `prompt_compiled_features_test`: 11 cases covering
detection of default features under --all-features, prompt content
(use built-ins, don't re-implement, mention --features flag for
disabled-but-available features), empty-features defensive case,
and BRAIN_PREAMBLE sentinels for the SELF-AWARENESS section,
tool-list-first directive, Built-in features reference, and the
named STT/TTS examples from the incident.

fix(onboarding): stop the provider list re-indenting on every Up/Down keypress

The /onboard:provider wizard re-positioned the entire provider list
horizontally every time the user changed selection. Selecting
OpenRouter (which shows just "API Key: ***" below) produced a list
indented far to the right; tabbing down to alibaba-qwen (which
shows a full custom-provider form including the URL
https://dashscope-intl.aliyuncs.com/compatible-mode/v1, ~52 chars
wide) pulled the list back to the left. /models doesn't have this
jitter.

Root cause: `render_onboarding` computed `content_pad` per frame as
`(inner_width - content_max_width) / 2` where `content_max_width`
was the widest line in the currently-rendered content. The detail
panel below the provider list varies with selection, so the widest
line varied, so the pad varied, so every list row shifted column
on every navigation. The user surfaced this as "the position of
the text keeps changing on every navigation".

Replaced the per-selection centering with a fixed 2-column left
pad on step content. The header (logo, progress dots, title,
subtitle) and the footer (nav line) still center independently so
the title bar and shortcut hints stay visually balanced. Matches
the /models picker layout the user pointed at as the reference.

No existing onboarding test relied on the per-selection padding;
the 270 wizard/voice/auth tests still pass. The visual change is
exactly what the user wanted: provider list rows now sit in a
fixed column regardless of which provider is selected.

fix(tui): stop truncating last fields of /onboard:provider and /models on small terminals

On zoomed-in or short terminals the wizard / picker capped at 90%
and 75% of the terminal height respectively. That left ~10% / 25%
of vertical space unused, which on a 20-row terminal was exactly
the 2-3 form fields at the bottom (custom provider's API Key,
Model, Context Window) that users couldn't reach. Tab-cycling down
to the field worked but the user couldn't even tell the field
existed without doing so.

Two coordinated changes:

1. Raise both height caps to ~95% of terminal:
   - /onboard:provider: `area.height * 19 / 20` (was 90%).
   - /models: `area.height * 19 / 20` (was 75%).
   The wasted bottom strip becomes form rows that actually render.

2. Add Page Up / Page Down to /onboard:provider so the user can
   scroll the wizard body independently of focus. New
   `OnboardingWizard.user_scroll_offset: u16` field, ±5 rows per
   keypress, saturates at 0 (Page Up at top is a no-op, no
   underflow). Reset to 0 by `next_step` / `prev_step` so each new
   screen starts at the top.

The render side now combines the existing focus-driven scroll with
`user_scroll_offset`, clamped to `max_scroll` so the user can't
scroll past the end of content.

(/models picker doesn't yet have explicit Page Up/Down — the
95% bump alone covers the common case where the form fits with
room to spare. Per-key scrolling there would need an App-level
state field; deferred until users actually hit the limit.)

Tests in `onboarding_user_scroll_test`: 8 cases covering fresh
state, single Page Down / Up, accumulation across multiple
presses, the Page Up-at-zero saturation guard (without this the
u16 would wrap to ~65k and jump to the end), reset on step
transitions, and confirmation that Page keys don't bleed into
focus / step state.

feat(telegram_send): expose optional thread_id override for proactive sends

Per @leshchenko1979's suggestion on issue #130:
https://github.com/adolfousier/opencrabs/issues/130#issuecomment-4582189795

The auto-lookup added in commit 1e46cd26 routes telegram_send to
whatever topic was seen most recently in the chat — the right
default for replying to an ongoing conversation. But it gave the
agent no way to send to a DIFFERENT topic on purpose. Real cases
the override unlocks:

  - cron jobs posting a daily digest into a specific topic (e.g.
    #announcements) regardless of where the last chat happened
  - multi-topic groups where the agent wants to post into a
    different topic than the latest one
  - explicit user instructions: "post this in topic 17"

Changes:

- New `resolve_thread_id(input, chat_id)` helper centralizes the
  precedence:
    1. Explicit `thread_id` in the tool input wins.
    2. Auto-lookup via `latest_thread_id_for_chat` is the fallback.
  Values past i32::MAX fall through to lookup (teloxide's ThreadId
  wraps MessageId(i32), so 64-bit values aren't representable).
  Non-integer types (string, object) fall through too — a malformed
  override doesn't poison routing.

- `telegram_send` schema gains an optional `thread_id: integer`
  field with a description that names the use case ("post in
  #announcements when the latest message came from #dev") so the
  agent recognises when to reach for it.

- `send` and `reply` actions call `resolve_thread_id` instead of
  the bare lookup. Other actions (edit, delete, pin, etc.) act on
  a specific message_id which already implies the right topic, so
  they don't need the override.

Tests in `telegram_send_thread_id_override_test`: 6 cases covering
explicit override (positive, negative legacy IDs, zero), i32
overflow → fallback, absent field → fallback, non-integer type →
fallback.

test(prompt): gate local-stt/tts test + parse source for feature list under tarpaulin

tarpaulin excludes local-stt/local-tts due to ggml linker conflicts
(see ci.yml tarpaulin command), so the all_cargo_features_are_listed
test was failing in Code Coverage CI. Parse prompt_builder.rs source
directly for cfg!(feature = "X") patterns instead of relying on
runtime compiled_features() output, so the test works regardless of
which features are actually enabled at test time.

build: add [profile.ci] tuned for CI wall-clock instead of runtime perf

The default `release` profile uses fat LTO + 1 codegen unit (best
runtime perf, slow to build) and `dev` uses no optimisation (fast
to build, can hide release-only bugs). Neither is right for CI:
release is too slow; dev doesn't catch release-mode failures.

`[profile.ci]` inherits release but switches:
- `lto = "thin"` — ~3-4x faster than fat LTO with most of the
  optimisation; still close enough to release that release-only
  bugs surface.
- `codegen-units = 16` — uses the runner's full parallelism;
  release's `1` is for binary size, irrelevant on CI runners.

Verified locally: `cargo check --profile ci --all-features`
succeeds in ~2m 15s (cold dependency cache).

Used by the upcoming CI workflow refactor in a follow-up commit:
`cargo build --profile ci` for Windows/macOS build verification,
`cargo nextest run --cargo-profile ci` for the Linux test job.

Pattern lifted from ZeroClaw's `Cargo.toml` which uses the same
profile for the same reasons.

chore(tests): collapse nested if-let in prompt_compiled_features sentinel

clippy 1.95.0 flags the triple-nested `if cond { if let { if let
{ ... } } }` block as `collapsible_if`. Use the `&&` let-chain
form instead so the linter is happy and the intent (all three
conditions must hold) reads as one logical guard.

No behaviour change. Pre-existing nesting, caught while running
`cargo clippy --lib --bins --tests --all-features -- -D warnings`
during the CI workflow refactor.

ci: stage-gated workflow, Linux-only tests, [profile.ci], main-only coverage

Refactor lifted from ZeroClaw's CI (~/srv/rs/zeroclaw/.github/workflows/ci.yml)
after auditing why our build wall-clock plateaued at ~32 min average
even after rust-cache landed. The cache wasn't the bottleneck — the
matrix shape was.

Changes:

1. **Stage-gated layout.** Lint (fmt + clippy) is now Stage 1 and
   blocks every downstream job. A bad PR that won't lint anyway
   used to burn 30+ min on the full Ubuntu/Windows/macOS test
   matrix; now it fails in ~3 min before anything else starts.

2. **Tests on Linux only.** Windows + macOS get build verification
   (`cargo build --profile ci --target <triple> --all-features`)
   without running the test suite there. ZeroClaw uses the same
   pattern because most tests are platform-independent and the
   cross-platform matrix triples wall-clock for marginal extra
   coverage. Genuinely platform-specific tests can be moved back
   into a per-platform matrix later if a regression appears.

3. **`[profile.ci]`** (added in commit 7c8968e7) replaces the mix
   of `--release` (Windows) and dev (others). Thin LTO + 16
   codegen units compiles ~3-4x faster than fat LTO and parallels
   the runner's full CPU; still catches release-mode bugs.

4. **Coverage gated to main pushes.** tarpaulin (~12 min) used to
   run on every PR. Moved to `if: github.event_name == 'push' &&
   github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'` so PRs no longer wait on it.
   PRs still get full test coverage via the `test` job; this just
   defers the report publication.

5. **rust-cache skipped on Windows** (`if: runner.os != 'Windows'`).
   ZeroClaw confirmed the cache rarely pays off on Windows runners
   and occasionally flakes them.

6. **Single `CI Required Gate` job** for branch protection
   (`needs: [lint, build, test, audit]`). Internal job structure
   can change without touching branch protection — coverage stays
   out because it only runs on main.

Held back for follow-up commits:
- `cargo nextest` — a few timing-sensitive tests (rate_limiter
  pacing) fail under nextest's process-per-test isolation
  because tokio cold-start delays the first `wait()` past the
  rate window. Verified locally; needs test refactor before
  nextest migration.
- `Cargo.lock --locked` — Cargo.lock is gitignored. Locking it
  would require a separate lockfile-commit decision.

Verified locally:
- `cargo check --profile ci --all-features` succeeds.
- `cargo test --profile ci --all-features --lib` — 3196 passed,
  same as default profile.
- YAML structure parses cleanly.

Estimated CI wall-clock saving: 15-20 min per run on average
(combination of skipping Win/macOS tests + lint-gating bad PRs +
deferring coverage). Larger savings on PRs that fail lint —
those now finish in ~3 min instead of ~32.

test(rate_limiter): deterministic pacing tests via force_grant_now helper

`second_request_paces` and `multiple_arcs_share_state` previously
measured wall-clock between two consecutive `wait()` calls. Both
tests would intermittently fail under heavy parallel-test CPU
contention because the scheduler can delay enough between the
first wait()'s return and the second wait()'s `now_ns()` read
that the rate window already elapsed naturally — making the
second call return Duration::ZERO instead of pacing. The test
comments already documented this fragility ("Under heavy
parallel-test CPU contention the tokio scheduler can delay
>90ms...").

New test-only helper `RateLimiter::force_grant_now()` (gated
behind `#[cfg(test)]`, `pub(crate)`) stores `last_granted` as
"right now" directly via the AtomicU64, bypassing the
unpredictable wall-clock dependency. Tests then call `wait()`
once and assert on the *returned* sleep duration, which is what
the limiter actually computed — scheduler-independent.

Both rewritten tests now use this pattern with a 500ms gap and
a tolerance bound (returned ≥ gap - 50ms or gap - 100ms). The
multi-Arc test still confirms shared-AtomicU64 semantics by
having `a` and `b` reference the same `Arc<RateLimiter>` and
verifying b paces from a's grant.

Note on nextest migration: even with these improvements, async
future polling means the `now_ns()` inside `wait()` body runs at
`.await`-poll time, not at the call site. Under nextest's
process-per-binary parallel scheduling with many CPU-bound tests
in flight, the poll can still be delayed past `min_interval`,
making real-time pacing unverifiable. nextest remains deferred
until either (a) RateLimiter takes an injectable clock, or (b)
nextest gains tokio time-mock integration.

Verified: cargo test --profile ci --all-features --lib
rate_limiter — all 8 tests pass, 0.51s total wall-clock.

build: commit Cargo.lock + switch CI to --locked for reproducible builds

OpenCrabs is an application crate, not a library — committing
Cargo.lock guarantees that every contributor and CI run resolves
exactly the same dependency versions. Previously the lockfile was
gitignored, meaning each `cargo build` could potentially pick up
new patch versions of transitive deps and silently change
behavior. CI also had to `cargo generate-lockfile` before running
`cargo audit`, which produced advisories against a freshly-resolved
lockfile rather than the one developers actually use.

Changes:

- Un-gitignore `Cargo.lock`. Replaced the line with a comment
  explaining why (application crate, reproducibility).
- Commit the current lockfile (~250 KB) as the canonical baseline.
- Add `--locked` to every CI cargo invocation that builds, tests,
  checks, or covers code. `--locked` fails fast if the lockfile
  doesn't match Cargo.toml — catches the "I bumped a dep in
  Cargo.toml but forgot to update the lockfile" mistake at PR
  time instead of release time.
- Same flag added to `release.yml`'s `cargo build`. Release
  binaries now ship with the exact dependency graph from main.
- Drop the audit job's `cargo generate-lockfile` step — pointless
  now that the lockfile is committed.

Verified locally:
- `cargo check --locked --profile ci --all-features` succeeds.
- `cargo audit --ignore RUSTSEC-2024-0437` runs against the
  committed lockfile (7 advisory warnings remain, all pre-existing
  on transitive deps via rwhisper/kalosm — not regressions).

Future PRs that touch deps now require a Cargo.lock update in the
same commit. Slight bookkeeping cost, but ends the "works on my
machine but not in CI" failure mode that came from each runner
resolving deps independently.

chore(telegram): log quote-reply context construction for #131 diagnosis

User reported the #131 quote-reply fix didn't take effect even on a
freshly-built binary that included commit 93ee4004. The handler
code path is correct (msg.quote() is checked inside reply_to_message
branch, format_reply_context emits both excerpt and full text when
they differ, agent_input includes the prefix at line 1395). So
something upstream must be making msg.quote() return None even
when the user did manually highlight an excerpt.

Add INFO-level diagnostic logs so the next field test surfaces:

- whether msg.reply_to_message() returned Some
- whether msg.quote() returned Some
- the quote's is_manual flag (true = user-highlighted, false =
  server auto-added preview)
- character counts of quote_text and full_text
- the final reply_context string threaded into the agent prompt

Plus a defensive warn! for the (impossible per Bot API contract)
case where msg.quote() is Some but reply_to_message is None —
that would mean we'd silently lose the quote because we only check
quote inside the reply_to branch.

No behaviour change; only logging. Next test run will tell us
whether Telegram is actually sending the quote field (maybe
privacy mode strips it, maybe a DM vs supergroup quirk, maybe
teloxide 0.13's deserializer drops it for some message kinds).

feat(rsi): add skill as a third proposal kind alongside tool / command

RSI's `rsi_propose` only spoke two kinds: `tool` (dynamic
tools.toml entry) and `command` (slash-trigger). Both are heavy:
`tool` needs a JSON schema + executor wiring; `command` is a
single fixed prompt. Neither is the right shape when the pattern
RSI observed is a SEQUENCE of existing tool calls — e.g. "agent
ran `gh issue list` → read top 5 → `gh issue comment` on each →
`gh pr create` 14 times in two weeks". A skill (a SKILL.md file
with YAML frontmatter + multi-step markdown) captures that
workflow with zero schema overhead and is the natural unit of
"codify this recurring sequence".

Changes:

- `ProposalsStore` gets `add_skill_proposal` / `list_skill_proposals`
  / `take_skill_proposal` / `archive_applied_skill` /
  `archive_rejected_skill`, mirroring the tool + command paths.
  Same dedup-by-name semantics (newer proposal supersedes older
  so RSI cycles don't pile up retries). New
  `proposed_skills.toml` lives alongside `proposed_tools.toml` and
  `proposed_commands.toml` under `~/.opencrabs/rsi/`. The daily
  archive picks up `<date>-skills.toml` files under `applied/` and
  `rejected/`.
- `pending_count()` now sums all three inboxes so the TUI banner
  reflects skill proposals.
- New `ProposedSkill` struct holds `name` (slug, also the directory
  name under `~/.opencrabs/skills/`), `description` (one-liner for
  the dispatcher), and `body` (full markdown below the frontmatter).
- `rsi_propose` schema gains `skill` to the `kind` enum and a
  `body` field. New skill branch normalises a leading `/` (in case
  the model emits `/foo` by analogy with command names), rejects
  empty bodies and non-alphanumeric names, and files via
  `add_skill_proposal`. Description rewritten to spell out WHEN
  TO USE EACH KIND so the agent picks the right shape.

The user-facing apply path (`rsi_proposals` tool) doesn't yet
handle the skill kind — that lands in a follow-up commit that
wires `take_skill_proposal` to write SKILL.md to the skills
directory. For now `rsi_propose` produces skill proposals and
they show up in the inbox and pending count; the human or a
future apply pass installs them.

Tests in `rsi_skill_proposals_test`: 9 cases covering round-trip,
dedup-by-name, take semantics, pending-count inclusion, applied
+ rejected archiving, missing-body rejection, invalid-name
rejection, and leading-slash normalisation.

feat(rsi): bash command subsystem classifier for pattern aggregation

The bash tool records each invocation's command text in the
feedback ledger via `cmd=<text>` metadata (added in commit
2b4d7c86). But that raw text is unusable as an aggregation key:
RSI can't `GROUP BY meta` and learn anything because every
command-line is unique (different files, different flags,
different repos).

`rsi_subsystem::classify_bash_command(cmd)` turns the raw text
into a stable lowercase slug for the CLI tool being driven —
"gh", "git", "docker", "python", "cargo", etc. — so RSI can
finally see "50 successful gh calls this week" or "30 successful
docker calls" instead of "50 bash calls" (which says nothing
about WHAT was repeated). Unknown commands return `None` so
RSI never lumps disparate one-offs into a misleading "other"
bucket and proposes nonsense.

Coverage (single-token classification):
- Version control: git, gh (+legacy hub), svn, hg, jj
- Containers: docker, podman, kubectl, helm, terraform/tofu,
  ansible
- Toolchains: cargo, python, pip family (pip/pipx/uv/poetry),
  node, npm family (npm/yarn/pnpm/bun), go, ruby, java,
  swift, dotnet, make
- Networking: curl/wget, ssh family, dig/ping
- Cloud: aws, gcloud, az, doctl, fly, vercel, wrangler, heroku
- Files: fs (ls/cat/cp/mv/...), grep, archive
- Data: postgres, mysql, sqlite, redis, jq
- Shell metalevel: sudo, time, env, etc. → "shell"
- LLM tooling: ollama, huggingface-cli

The `first_meaningful_token` helper is a tiny hand-rolled
scanner (not `shell_words` — would have been ~400 KB of dep for
one parse) that peels env-var assignments at the start of a
command, including quoted values that contain spaces:

  RUSTFLAGS="-C opt-level=0" cargo build → cargo

Distinguishes `KEY=VALUE` (env assignment, peeled) from
`--features=foo` (flag, kept) via the leading-dash check.
Case-insensitive matching so `GIT push` aggregates with
`git push`.

Tests in `rsi_subsystem_test`: 23 cases covering each
subsystem family, env-var stripping with quoted values, the
dashed-option false-positive guard, case-insensitivity, and
realistic noisy inputs including a long real-world `gh pr
comment` command and the canonical `RUSTFLAGS="..." cargo`
case.

This commit only ships the classifier — wiring it into RSI's
analysis cycle to actually propose tools/skills for high-
frequency subsystems is the next commit.

feat(rsi): detect successful bash subsystem patterns + propose tool/skill extraction

The third and largest of the three RSI scope-expansion commits.
Builds on the skill proposal kind (8c9d959b) and the subsystem
classifier (d2805778) by wiring them into the RSI analysis cycle
so the loop actually fires on the new signal.

Two changes:

1. `enrich_metadata` (feedback.rs) now appends `cmd=<text>` on
   BOTH success and failure rows, not just failures. The previous
   pass kept the command on failures only because the original
   issue (#132) was about categorising failures. Success
   enrichment was the missing data feed for RSI's
   success-pattern detection — without it the new RSI pass
   would walk an empty bash success ledger.

   While there, removed the now-unused `success` parameter from
   `enrich_metadata` (the cmd= path doesn't care about
   success/failure). Updated the single caller and all 14
   call sites in `bash_feedback_enrichment_test`. The
   `bash_success_does_not_append_cmd` test was inverted — it now
   asserts that success rows DO carry the command — and renamed
   to `bash_success_appends_cmd_so_rsi_can_aggregate_patterns`
   to make the intent obvious.

2. New analysis pass in `rsi.rs::run_rsi_agent_cycle`:
   - Fetches up to 2000 `tool_success` events in the analysis
     window.
   - For each `dimension="bash"` row, extracts `cmd=...` from
     metadata via the new `rsi_subsystem::extract_cmd_from_meta`
     helper and classifies it via `classify_bash_command`.
   - Aggregates counts per subsystem (gh, git, docker, …).
   - For any subsystem with ≥15 successful invocations in the
     window, emits a structured opportunity description telling
     the RSI agent to file a tool proposal (kind=tool for
     parameterised invocations) or a skill proposal (kind=skill
     for multi-step workflows) via rsi_propose, complete with 5
     sample command lines so the agent has concrete material.
   - Sorts subsystems by count desc (then alpha asc) so the
     opportunity-hash dedup doesn't churn when the same set of
     subsystems re-appears in a different observed order.

The 15-call threshold is deliberately high so RSI doesn't
propose tools for one-off curls or test scripts. If the agent
ran `gh issue comment` 15 times in a day, it's a real workflow
worth codifying.

`extract_cmd_from_meta` lives next to `classify_bash_command` in
`rsi_subsystem.rs` (one file already on that turf) and parses
the `cmd=` marker out of feedback-ledger metadata strings
emitted by enrich_metadata. Returns None when the meta has no
`cmd=` marker so pre-enrichment ledger rows don't pollute
aggregation.

End-to-end loop now:
  agent runs bash → success recorded with cmd= meta →
  RSI cycle classifies into subsystem → counts past threshold →
  opportunity description bubbles up → RSI agent files
  rsi_propose(kind=tool|skill) → proposal lands in inbox →
  human or user-facing agent applies via rsi_proposals.

No new unit tests in this commit — the new wiring is in
`run_rsi_agent_cycle` which exercises live DB/agent
infrastructure that the existing integration tests cover.
The pure helpers (classify_bash_command, extract_cmd_from_meta)
were tested in the prior commit (d2805778).

18 usage_grouping tests pass, including new coverage for the 3.7

feat(telegram): capture forum topic names + list_topics action (#130 follow-up)

@leshchenko1979 pointed out that the agent needs to map user-typed
topic names like "#announcements" back to numeric thread_ids it
can pass to telegram_send. Telegram's Bot API has no
listForumTopics endpoint — the only way for a bot to learn topic
names is to capture them passively from messages it receives.

This commit closes both halves of the gap:

1. **Capture topic names from incoming messages.** The handler
   previously passed `None` for topic_name when persisting every
   channel message (`with_thread(thread_id, None)`). Now it
   extracts the name from either:
     - `msg.forum_topic_created()` — the topic creation service
       message itself (fires once per topic).
     - `msg.reply_to_message().forum_topic_created()` — for every
       regular message inside a topic, Telegram includes the
       topic-creation service message as the reply target, so we
       learn the topic name from EVERY message in that topic,
       not just the one-time creation event.
   Captured into the existing `topic_name` column on
   `channel_messages` (already in schema; was never populated).

2. **Expose the captured map via `list_topics`.** New action on
   `telegram_send` queries `ChannelMessageRepository::topics_for_chat`
   for a chat and returns a table of (thread_id, topic_name,
   message_count, last_seen). Output is human-readable but
   structured enough for the agent to parse. The action handler
   uses `crate::db::global_pool()` — same pattern as the existing
   thread_id auto-lookup.

fix(sanitize): strip hallucinated CODE_EDIT_BLOCK fences before channel delivery

User report 2026-05-30 14:14: full Dart file contents (the
estimate_model.dart enum/class definitions) dumped into a
Telegram chat instead of being applied as a tool call. Log lines
at 14:13:03 show qwen-3.7-max-thinking emitting:

    ```dart|CODE_EDIT_BLOCK|/Users/.../estimate_model.dart
    enum EstimateType { ... }
    ```

verbatim in the response stream. This is a Cursor/Aider/Cline-
style IDE edit format the model was clearly fine-tuned on — it
expects an IDE to swallow the fenced block and apply the diff.
OpenCrabs uses tool calls (`edit_file`), so the block just
becomes text that hits `markdown_to_telegram_html`. The fake
language tag (`dart|CODE_EDIT_BLOCK|/abs/path`) gets emitted as
`<code class="language-dart|CODE_EDIT_BLOCK|/...">` — invalid
Telegram HTML — and Telegram falls back to plain rendering,
dumping the full file contents into the chat. User: "we never
exposed code shit or artifacts" — correct, this is a regression
the existing artifact stripper missed.

Fix lives in `utils::sanitize`:

- New `strip_code_edit_block_fences(text)` detects fenced blocks
  whose header line contains the `CODE_EDIT_BLOCK` marker
  (anywhere after the opening backticks, tolerating leading
  whitespace and any language tag). Replaces the whole block —
  header line + body + closing fence — with a single notice:

    [Agent attempted to edit `<path>` using an unsupported
     inline-edit format. The change was NOT applied — agent
     should retry via the `edit_file` tool.]

  The path is kept verbatim so the user can audit what the agent
  thought it was touching; the body is dropped so file contents
  never leak.

- Truncated streams (model timed out mid-block, no closing fence
  ever arrived) still strip safely — the scanner reaches EOF
  rather than emitting the partial body.

- `strip_llm_artifacts()` runs the new pass alongside the
  existing HTML-comment and XML-tool-call strippers, gated on
  cheap `text.contains("CODE_EDIT_BLOCK")` so non-affected
  responses pay zero cost.

Helper is `pub(crate)` so tests can exercise it directly.

Tests in `sanitize_code_edit_block_test`: 10 cases covering
single block, multiline body, multiple blocks per response,
truncated streams, normal-code-block survival, prose-mention
survival (defensive — bug reports about the marker name must
not get stripped), leading-whitespace tolerance, the verbatim
incident path round-trip, the strip_llm_artifacts integration,
and the missing-path fallback.

Does not address the root cause (model emitting wrong format).
That's a separate prompt / brain-file change to nudge
qwen-3.7-max-thinking and similar fine-tunes toward `edit_file`.
This sanitizer is the safety net so the next time it happens
the channel doesn't leak file contents while the prompt
catches up.

feat(prompt): forbid IDE-style inline edit formats in BRAIN_PREAMBLE

Follow-up to b339a8c7 — the sanitizer strips `CODE_EDIT_BLOCK` /
SEARCH/REPLACE fences before they reach channels, but stripping
is the safety net, not the cure. The root cause is the model
emitting these formats in the first place because Cursor /
Aider / Cline / continue.dev datasets trained that pattern in.
This commit addresses the cause: BRAIN_PREAMBLE now explicitly
forbids the inline-edit formats and points the model at the
real `edit_file` / `write_file` tool calls instead.

New paragraph in the TOOL CALL PROTOCOL section names the three
patterns the model is most likely to recall:

- Cursor: ```lang|CODE_EDIT_BLOCK|/abs/path/file.ext
- Aider:  <<<<<<< SEARCH ... ======= ... >>>>>>> REPLACE
- diff:   ```diff with file headers

…and tells the model what the consequence of using them is —
"the system will REJECT any inline-edit format and the change
will NOT apply — you will have just leaked the file contents to
the channel." Models follow rules better when they understand
the failure mode, not just the prohibition.

Sentinels in `prompt_inline_edit_directive_test`: 5 cases
asserting the directive (a) names CODE_EDIT_BLOCK, (b) names
SEARCH/REPLACE, (c) points at edit_file, (d) explains the leak
consequence, (e) lists ≥3 concrete forbidden patterns so a
future "tighten up the prompt" PR can't collapse it back into a
vague "don't emit inline edits" that loses the anchors the
model needs to recognise its own training-data patterns.

Together with the b339a8c7 sanitizer, this is defence in depth:
the directive prevents most occurrences, the stripper catches
the rest. If a new fine-tune ships with a different inline-edit
format we'll see it in logs, add the pattern to both the prompt
and the sanitizer, and move on.

fix(stream): accept missing-[DONE] when text-only response looks complete

User report 2026-05-30 17:06: TUI footer stuck at "OpenCrabs is
responding... (491s · 2182 tok)" with the full response already
rendered. Log analysis pinned the cause: dialagram +
qwen-3.7-max-thinking streams a complete response then closes the
TCP connection without emitting `[DONE]` / `finish_reason` /
`usage` chunks. The pipeline treated that as a truncated stream,
triggered the retry path (3 attempts at ~minutes each, each
regenerating the same content), then fell back to a different
provider — 491s wall-clock to deliver a response that was
visible after the first ~30s.

Root cause in `helpers.rs::stream_complete`: if
`stop_reason.is_none() && !block_states.is_empty()` we
unconditionally returned StreamError. The original intent was to
catch genuine mid-stream connection drops, but not every provider
honours `[DONE]`; some just close the socket when done.

Fix: distinguish "truly truncated" from "complete but no [DONE]"
by inspecting the accumulated text:

- If any block is a `ToolUse`, retry. Incomplete tool calls produce
  broken state — never accept those without finish_reason.
- If text-only AND `text_looks_complete()` → synthesise
  `StopReason::EndTurn` and proceed. Loop exits, "is responding"
  indicator clears, no retry chain, no fallback storm.
- Otherwise fall through to the existing StreamError path.

New helper `utils::text_complete::text_looks_complete()` in its
own module so other code that needs to detect truncation (the
existing self-heal at helpers.rs:571 is a candidate for future
unification) can reuse it. Heuristics:
- Minimum 200 chars (shorter responses are almost always
  truncated preambles).
- Balanced ` ``` ` code fences (unclosed fence = mid-block cut).
- Sentence terminators (`.!?"'`)/`]}` / closing backtick / `…`)
  → complete.
- Mid-sentence markers (`:`, `,`, `;`, `-`, opening brackets) →
  truncated.
- Default to "complete" because the cost asymmetry favours not
  retrying: a spurious retry is user-visible minutes of "is
  responding"; an accepted slightly-informal ending is a single
  message the user can shrug at.

Tests in `text_complete_test`: 21 cases across each terminator
class, the length floor, balanced/unbalanced code fences, and
two regression scenarios — the verbatim CHANGELOG response from
the incident screenshot (must be `true`, NOT retry) and the
classic "Let me check the README:" truncated-preamble pattern
(must be `false`, DO retry).

fix(fallback): only stick the fallback after 4 consecutive rescues, not on first incident

User report 2026-05-30: a transient stream error on
`dialagram/qwen-3.7-max-thinking` (provider closes the socket
without `[DONE]` even on a complete response) was permanently
demoting the session to the configured fallback provider after a
single incident. After the `text_looks_complete` fix in 97683fb0
most of those false positives stop firing, but the underlying
demote-on-first-failure policy was still wrong for the cases
where the fallback DOES engage — most outages are transient
(network blip, model warm-up, brief 5xx); making the primary
stay demoted means the user has to manually re-pick via /models
every time they hit a hiccup.

User intent: "if fallback rescues 3 times consecutively
successfully, the 4th it sticks". Implementation:

- New `session_primary_failure_streak: RwLock<HashMap<Uuid, u32>>`
  on `AgentService`. Per-session counter of consecutive
  primary-provider failures that needed a successful fallback
  rescue.
- Three helper methods on `AgentService`:
  * `bump_primary_failure_streak(sid)` — increments and returns
    new count.
  * `reset_primary_failure_streak(sid)` — clears to 0.
  * `peek_primary_failure_streak(sid)` — read-only.
- `remove_session_provider(sid)` now also clears the streak so a
  reused session UUID can't inherit a phantom count.
- New constant `STICKY_FALLBACK_THRESHOLD = 4` in tool_loop.rs.
- Both fallback success sites (stream-error path line ~1687, 5xx
  path line ~1959) now bump the streak and only persist the
  provider swap when `streak >= STICKY_FALLBACK_THRESHOLD`. Below
  the threshold:
    * stream-error: existing `FallbackProviderGuard` Drop restores
      the primary cleanly — that's what the guard was already
      built for; we just stop disarming it on first success.
    * 5xx: skip the `swap_provider_for_session` + `persist_sticky_pair`
      calls. The fallback rescued THIS request but session state
      stays on the primary for the next turn.
- `SelfHealingAlert` event text now reflects whether the rescue
  was transient ("rescued by X/Y (2/4 consecutive; primary will
  be tried again next turn)") or sticky ("switched to X/Y (sticky
  after 4 consecutive rescues)"). `ProviderSwitched` event +
  `persist_sticky_pair` only fire when sticky.
- Primary success path (top-level Ok at the first stream_complete
  call) now calls `reset_primary_failure_streak(sid)` so a single
  recovery wipes the count — the threshold meaning becomes "N
  rescues in a row with NO intervening primary success", matching
  user intent.

Tests in `fallback_streak_test`: 7 cases — fresh-session-is-zero,
bump-and-return-count, reset-clears, reset-then-bump-starts-fresh,
per-session isolation, remove_session_provider also clears the
streak, and a sentinel pinning the threshold value at 4 so future
refactors that change the UX have to update the test deliberately.

Integration testing of the actual fallback flow lives in the
existing tool_loop tests and is exercised by real-provider runs;
the streak helpers it consumes are tested in isolation here.

didn't show them. Investigation found a subtler regression — Mission

    `apply_skill` — the commit that added the proposal kind
    explicitly deferred the apply path "to a follow-up commit".

Plus the session-start banner ("ask me to 'show proposed'…")
pointed users at the agent-driven path even though Mission Control
already supported direct in-TUI triage. Two users in the same week
hit the banner without realising Mission Control was the faster

- `RsiProposalsTool::render_list` (the agent-facing markdown

surfaces were the gh CLI and a search tool respectively. Root
cause: tool descriptions said WHAT each tool did but never WHEN
to pick it, and BRAIN_PREAMBLE had zero routing guidance — the

~/.opencrabs/TOOLS.md which is selectively loaded.

fix(evolve): replace rename with remove+rename and add systemd delayed restart

Two changes in evolve_via_binary_download:

1. Binary swap: call remove_file(&exe_path) before rename(&tmp_path,
   &exe_path).  rename(2) on Linux already atomically replaces the
   directory entry — the old inode stays mapped for any still-running
   process.  The extra remove_file is a safety guard for NFS / FUSE
   mounts where rename(2) can behave differently when the target is
   a mapped executable.

2. Delayed systemd restart: after a successful swap, schedule a
   transient systemd-run timer that fires 3 s later and runs
   `systemctl restart opencrabs*.service`.  The timer is owned by
   PID 1 (outside the daemon cgroup), so it survives the SIGTERM
   sent by systemctl.  The 3 s window gives the current response
   time to finish delivery.

   Only systemd-managed hosts are affected — the `RestartReady`
   signal is still emitted as the fallback for non-systemd systems
   and for TUI / channel handlers.

   The glob pattern `opencrabs*.service` matches all profile
   services (default, ops, staging, ...) automatically, so adding a
   new profile requires no code change.

and reasonably concluded they'd been rate-limited — the
"rate limited or unavailable" suffix was hardcoded for every
non-2xx and lied about every status. The user's logs had zero

- log on every failure branch with status, x-ratelimit-remaining,
  x-ratelimit-reset, first 300 chars of response body, url

  diagnose_releases_latest_status() which branches per status:
    404 → no published release exists / brief propagation lag
    403/429 → rate limit, suggests GITHUB_TOKEN for shared IPs
    5xx → transient server-side, retry in a few minutes
    other → status + body excerpt + ratelimit context

tracing::warn so passive update polling failures stop dying
silent. Same context as the user-facing path.

received on success at info; on failure log status, body

"post-swap failed + rollback succeeded" and the CRITICAL

fix(stream/sanitize): stop Qwen `<|tool▁...|>` marker family from leaking to channels

A Qwen 3 model (via custom OpenAI-compatible endpoint) was
observed emitting the proper structured `tool_calls` field AND
echoing its own SentencePiece-style token markers in `content`:

  <|tool▁calls_section_begin|>
  <|tool▁call_begin|>analyze_video<|tool▁calls_section_end|>
  <|tool▁calls_section_end|> ... (hundreds of repeats — Qwen 3
  loops emitting end-tags when it degrades)

The separator between "tool" and the rest is U+2581 ("Lower One
Eighth Block"), the SentencePiece word-boundary char Qwen 3
emits natively. Telegram and TUI fonts render it about as wide as
`_`, which is why the leak looked like `tool__calls_section_end`
in screenshots and went unnoticed in code review.

Two surgical fixes:

1. `TOOL_MARKERS` in custom_openai_compatible.rs gains four
   openers — `<|tool▁calls_section_begin|>`, `<|tool▁call_begin|>`,
   and their ASCII-underscore variants for quantizations that
   emit `_` instead of U+2581. The existing tool-capture machine
   now routes the whole section to the capture buffer instead of
   passing it through as display text.

2. `strip_llm_artifacts` in utils/sanitize.rs gains a regex
   catch-all `<\|tool[\u{2581}_][^|]*\|>` as the post-stream
   safety net. Catches anything the streaming filter missed
   (chunk-boundary splits) AND future token variants
   (`<|tool▁call_argument_begin|>`, `<|tool▁call_metadata|>`,
   etc.) without needing a code change per variant. Guarded
   behind a `.contains("<|tool")` check so the common case
   (no markers) doesn't pay the regex cost.

The repetition guard at helpers.rs:320 is doing its job — it
killed the stream after ~7 KB — but it kicks in AFTER bytes
have shipped to the channel. The streaming filter is the only
real-time prevention; the sanitizer is the safety net for
whatever escapes (or for backfilled content from the persisted
assistant turn).

7 sentinel tests pin the contract: U+2581 form, repeated-end
storm pattern, ASCII-underscore variant, unknown future variants
caught by the catch-all, prose preserved when the SP/underscore
separator is missing, tool-name payload between markers preserved
(so prose mentions of the tool name elsewhere survive), no-marker
fast path.

fix(evolve): log failures of remove_file + systemd-run instead of swallowing them

Follow-up on PR #137 (Alexey Leshchenko, #136) — that change added
two important `let _` calls that silently discard their Result:

1. `let _ = std::fs::remove_file(&exe_path)` — the belt-and-suspenders
   unlink before rename. Non-fatal in the success case (rename will
   surface the real error if exe_path is busy/missing/perms-locked),
   but logged at debug so a future incident report can distinguish
   "rename failed because exe was busy" from "rename failed because
   directory is read-only" etc.

2. `let _ = std::process::Command::new("systemd-run")...spawn()` —
   the delayed systemd restart that's the whole point of #136. If
   spawn fails, the binary on disk is updated, the agent says
   "Evolved!", but the daemon keeps running the old inode forever —
   the EXACT symptom the original issue was reported for. Log at
   warn with an actionable message so the user knows to run
   `systemctl restart opencrabs*.service` manually. Successful spawn
   also logs at info with the systemd-run pid so the restart can be
   traced in logs.

fix(evolve): pre-flight unit-count check + honest message + restart-arg tests

PR #137 (#136) that the merged PR didn't get to:

#3 — Silent failure when no units match the glob.

systemd-run was being scheduled unconditionally on every systemd
host, but `systemctl restart opencrabs*.service` exits non-zero
when zero units match the pattern — and that exit happens 3s
later inside a transient unit, so the agent's reply was already
out the door saying "Evolved! Restarting…" when the restart had

a different root cause (unit-name mismatch instead of missing
restart).

before the spawn:
  Some(0)  → skip the spawn, log warn, user message tells them
             "Binary updated on disk, but no systemd units matched
              ... — restart your daemon manually"
  Some(n≥1) → log info with the count, spawn as before
  None     → systemctl spawn failed; log warn, spawn anyway
             (diagnostic failure shouldn't penalize a user whose
              daemon DOES exist)

User-message branching lives in a private `RestartStatus` enum so
each of the four outcomes (Scheduled / NotSystemd / NoUnitsMatched
/ SpawnFailed) produces a distinct, honest line. Never says
"Restarting…" when no restart was actually scheduled.

- unit pattern stays a glob (multi-profile support)

fix(phantom): stop firing on completion acks after successful tool runs

Reported in repeated user screenshots: after a clean commit+push the
agent would emit a one-line "Pushed." or a short success summary, the
phantom detector's `has_past_tense_action_claim` would fire (the verbs
"pushed", "committed", "fixed" all match the action-verb list),
`phantom_retries_used` would tick up, and 5+ retries later self-heal
would even swap providers. All on completed work. One screenshot showed
8+ "Phantom tool calls detected" alerts plus a provider swap after a
single successful commit — 293s and 4683 tokens wasted finalising
nothing.

The detector could not tell the difference between:
  - "I will push the changes" (intent without action, real phantom)
  - "Pushed." (completion ack AFTER a successful tool call, NOT phantom)

Fix in three parts:

1. **Turn-scoped success counter.** New
   `tool_calls_completed_this_turn: usize` declared next to
   `let mut iteration = 0;` (turn scope, not iteration scope so it
   survives across the wrap-up iteration). Incremented in BOTH success
   branches (direct execution + post-approval execution).

2. **Phantom-eligible gate.** The four phantom-detection checks inside
   `tool_uses.is_empty()` (`is_stuck_in_intent_loop`, fast-escalate to
   sticky fallback, normal retry-nudge, and budget-rollover re-nudge)
   now all check `phantom_eligible = !is_cli_provider &&
   tool_calls_completed_this_turn == 0` instead of the bare
   `!is_cli_provider` they each had before. Once the turn has produced
   real work, the text-only wrap-up is treated as a completion ack and
   passed through. A `tracing::info!(target: "phantom")` line announces
   when the exemption fires so the bypass is visible in logs.

3. **BRAIN_PREAMBLE clarification.** New "FINISHING A TURN" directive
   tells the model what shape a completion turn should take: one short
   acknowledgement line ("Done.", "Pushed.", "Committed as <sha>.",
   "Fixed in <file>.") and stop. Explicitly forbids restating the
   conclusion in multiple wordings, forbids running "verification"
   tool calls to re-prove work already done, and gives the model a
   self-detection signal — if its next response starts with "I have
   successfully…" or "The task is complete…" it's looping on a
   completed task and should reply with just "Done." instead. The
   runtime exemption catches the false positive; the prompt directive
   reduces the token waste before the loop ends.

5 source-level sentinel tests pin: counter declared at turn scope
(not iteration scope — that would defeat the whole point), counter
incremented in BOTH success branches (partial coverage re-opens the
regression through the missed branch), all phantom-detection gates
use `phantom_eligible`, BRAIN_PREAMBLE carries the FINISHING A TURN
directive header + the one-line shape + the verification ban + the
self-detection signal, and the gate's inline comment carries the
POST-SUCCESS EXEMPTION label so a future refactor doesn't strip it
"for cleanliness" and re-open the loop.

Other detectors that catch genuine post-completion problems are
unaffected:
- Text-repetition guard in helpers.rs (catches "Pushed. Pushed.
  Pushed." spam after tools are done — repetition is the signal)
- Tool-call signature dedup at top of tool_loop.rs (catches re-running
  the same tool with the same args)
- Investigative-intent guard for "I will" / "I'll" / "Let me" patterns
  (still flags genuine pre-action narration when no tool ran)

Only the "described actions that didn't happen" detector is exempt
post-success — because by definition the actions DID happen.

fix(sanitize): snap to char boundary after redact-prefix scan to stop UTF-8 panic

Reported by user: pressing Ctrl+O to expand a thinking block crashed
the TUI render thread. Today's log carried 283 instances of the same
panic chained across renders:

  ERROR [TUI] render panic caught at src/utils/sanitize.rs:461:64:
    start byte index 1868 is not a char boundary; it is inside '→'
    (bytes 1866..1869) of `STDOUT: ...`

The panic site (line 461, `&result[search_from..]`) was a symptom.
The real bug was on the advance: when `redact_secrets` matched a
key-prefix from `KEY_PREFIXES` but the trailing token was too short
to satisfy `min_suffix_len`, no `replace_range` happened — yet
`search_from` still advanced by `"[REDACTED]".len()` (10 ASCII bytes)
from `after`. Those 10 bytes are pure byte arithmetic and can land
inside a multi-byte character like `→` (U+2192, 3 bytes), `🦀` (4
bytes), or any Cyrillic / CJK / emoji sitting in the text.

Fix: snap `search_from` forward to a valid UTF-8 boundary with
`str::ceil_char_boundary` (stable since Rust 1.79). When the
prefix is followed by ASCII the snap is a no-op; when it's followed
by a multi-byte char the snap nudges past the rest of the char so
the next loop iteration's slice is always boundary-aligned.

Why Ctrl+O specifically: expand-thinking re-renders the thinking
block content through the sanitiser pipeline. The user's thinking
texts routinely contain arrow characters (`→`) used as logical
markers — "A → B", "before → after", flow diagrams in reasoning.
A prefix-shaped string followed by an arrow tripped the bug
every time, so Ctrl+O on those messages turned into a guaranteed
crash chain (283 panics in 90 seconds before the user gave up).

3 new regression tests in sanitize_redaction_test.rs:
- `does_not_panic_on_multibyte_char_after_prefix_match` reproduces
  the exact incident shape (`sk-x → ...`)
- `handles_multibyte_chars_at_various_offsets_after_prefix` shifts
  the arrow across byte offsets 0-15 past the prefix match to
  cover the full failure window
- `cyrillic_emoji_cjk_in_post_prefix_window_do_not_panic` covers
  2-byte / 3-byte / 4-byte UTF-8 widths (Cyrillic, CJK, emoji)

22 redaction tests total now pass.

fix(onboard): typed model name overrides suggestion list + add MiniMax-M3

Reported by user: pressing Enter on the model field after typing a
model name that wasn't in the suggestion list (e.g. `MiniMax-M3` on
a build that ships `MiniMax-M2.7 / M2.5 / M2.1` as the static
hardcoded fallback) silently committed `MiniMax-M2.7` instead. The
typed text was lost.

Root cause: `provider_selector::selected_model_name` had two
branches — pick from filtered list OR fall back to the first item.
The custom-provider path at input.rs:818-823 already had a third
branch for "filter is non-empty and matches nothing → use the typed
text as the model name", but the built-in `AuthField::Model` path
never grew the same logic.

Fix in three coordinated parts:

1. `provider_selector::selected_model_name` gains the third branch.
   When the filter is non-empty and matches zero entries, return the
   trimmed filter as the model name. Empty / whitespace-only filter
   still falls back to first list item (existing behaviour).

2. `AuthField::Model` Enter handler explicitly commits the typed
   text into `ps.models` when there's no match, and points
   `selected_model` at the just-pushed entry. Without this, later
   wizard steps that clear `model_filter` (input.rs:617 / 762 / 779)
   would erase the user's input before `apply_config` reads it.
   Mirrors the commit pattern in the custom-provider populated
   branch.

3. Render — when the filter has zero matches AND is non-empty, show
   the typed text styled as `> <typed> (custom — press Enter to use)`
   so the escape hatch is visible. Previously the user saw just
   `no models match` and assumed they needed a binary update.

Also wired MiniMax-M3 into every catalogue surface so users on M3
don't need the escape hatch on a fresh install:

- `onboarding/fetch.rs` hardcoded fallback gains `MiniMax-M3` at the
  top (newest first; MiniMax has no `/v1/models` endpoint so this
  static list is the only source of suggestions absent a user-
  supplied override)
- `provider_selector::prettify_known_model_id` adds the
  `minimax-m3 → "Minimax M3"` display mapping for the TUI
- `usage_pricing.toml.example` adds an M3 entry at Standard tier ≤512K
  list price ($0.6 input / $2.4 output / $0.12 cache read per M).
  The 7-day 50% off launch discount is NOT applied here (the
  provider charges the discounted rate during the window, this
  table tracks list price). The 512K-1M context band is "contact
  sales" (limited availability), not wired until it goes public.

to first, matching filter picks filtered[selected], non-matching
filter becomes the model name, whitespace is trimmed, whitespace-
only is treated as empty, empty list with typed filter still
