fix(tui): count only the rows the fold hides in the step header

The header reported a turn's total message count, not what folding took
away. It included the user's own message and the final answer, rows
visible_when_folded always keeps on screen, so a turn of question,
thinking row and answer announced "3 steps" for one hidden row. Every
count was inflated by at least two, and by more on turns carrying extra
always-visible rows such as errors or approval prompts.

turn_hideable_count counts rows where visible_when_folded is false, which
is by definition what sits behind the header. Singular when one, since
"1 steps" is the obvious next complaint.

turn_has_hideable is gone rather than kept for the boolean: it was only
the count compared against zero, and leaving a second entry point invites
the two drifting. Its tests now derive the bool from the count, so they
still cover the has-anything-to-fold question.

Closes #777

feat(brain): instruct the agent to clarify before implementing

Nothing in the preamble told the agent to pin down a request before
building against it. The only mention of follow_up_question was a
parenthetical inside the follow-up-suggestions section, as a contrast to
suggest_followups rather than guidance of its own. So an ambiguous
request got an invented interpretation, and when the interpretation was
wrong the user ended up correcting an artifact instead of a premise.

The new section asks for the 3-5 questions whose answers change WHAT
gets built: when a request names a goal but not a shape, when several
readings lead to different work, when a value or scope is about to be
picked that the user never stated. Discrete choices route through
follow_up_question so they render as buttons rather than prose someone
has to type an answer to.

The brakes matter more than the instruction. An agent that interviews
before every small task is unusable, so trivial requests are exempt by
name, anything answerable by reading code or a log is a read and not a
question, and a question must never stall delivery: state the assumption
and proceed unless being wrong would be unsafe. Tests assert all three
survive future edits to the section, since losing them would be worse
than never adding it.

Closes #778

fix(brain): stop the preamble telling the agent not to iterate, and tighten it

The agent had to be told repeatedly to execute instead of narrating.
Nothing had been removed from the preamble; it had grown 9.4x since
v0.1.1, from 3,559 chars to 33,343, more than doubling in the last five
weeks alone. "Just call the tool immediately" was still there, competing
with 33KB.

One rule was actively fighting execution. Since v0.1.1, untouched:

  DO NOT keep calling tools in a loop. Call the necessary tools, get
  results, then respond with text.

Read plainly that says do not iterate, which is how the agent works:
read, edit, test, fix, re-test. It sat fourteen lines below "call the
tool immediately" and carried a CRITICAL RULE label, so it outweighed
it. The requirement it was protecting is real, so that survives, phrased
as what it actually means: finish with words, never end a turn without
telling the user anything. The iterating was never the problem.

Then a concision pass on the three heaviest sections, wordsmithing only,
no rule dropped:

  FINISHING A TURN   4106 -> 1915
  MOTION GRAPHICS    1448 ->  982
  CLARIFY            1266 ->  879
  preamble          33343 -> 30290
  execution protocol 6.2% -> 7.9% of the prompt

Every phrase pinned by a test sentinel is preserved verbatim. Those
sentinels exist because past regressions came from exactly this kind of
rewording, and a first attempt at this pass broke three of them plus a
table-rendering rule by using regex section boundaries. Redone with
exact anchors; the diff removes nothing outside the three sections.

Closes #779

fix(phantom): count self-update claims as completion claims

A zero-tool turn reported "Evolved from X to Y". No evolve ran, nothing
executed in the background, no confirmation was asked for, and the claim
reached the user as fact.

Same vocabulary gap as the issue-tracker verbs, different words: no form
of evolved, upgraded, rebuilt or restarted existed in any of the six
language files, so has_past_tense_action_claim had nothing to match and
the whole self-heal path stayed disarmed.

This one is worse than a fabricated issue close. evolve replaces the
running binary, so the user believes they are on a version they are not,
and every later bug report against it is unfalsifiable.

"updated" is deliberately excluded. It is far too common in ordinary
prose for the passive guard alone to keep safe, and the value is in verbs
that name a specific side-effecting operation.

The existing safety property carries over: past-tense claims only reach
this branch on turns that ran zero tools, so an accurate "Evolved from
0.3.74 to 0.3.75" after a real evolve stays exonerated by the
post-success path. A test pins that descriptive prose about what evolve
does is still not a claim.

Closes #780

refactor(brain): cut the domain sections to reference size

MOTION GRAPHICS and BROWSER AUTOMATION are situational: they matter only
when the work is animation or a browser session, but they sit in the
always-on preamble and every other turn pays for them. They should carry
enough for the agent to know what to do when the case arises, and no
more.

  BROWSER AUTOMATION   825 -> 463
  MOTION GRAPHICS      982 -> 663
  preamble          30,448 -> 29,767
  execution protocol   7.9% -> 8.0%

Every rule survives, restated once instead of enumerated: screenshot and
LOOK after fill, submit and critical clicks; never claim an unverified
type or click; credentials from env vars never reach output or reasoning;
headless by default. For scenes: read the project's own scene list, probe
each with the project's own tooling, look at every frame, and re-probe
neighbours after a change.

Still situational content in an always-on prompt. Moving them to
on-demand brain files is the real fix and changes WHEN the guidance is
present, not how it is worded, so it stays a separate change.

fix(tui): show steps AND tool calls, drop the either/or fallback

The header treated the two as alternatives: format_turn_header returned
None whenever tool_calls was 0, so the step count existed only as its
fallback. A turn with 17 hidden rows and 3 tool calls reported the tools
and never the steps; a turn with 17 hidden rows and NO tool calls
reported "17 steps" and never said that nothing ran.

The second case is the one that mattered. A turn that narrated seventeen
times without calling anything is exactly what needs to be obvious, and
the header made it look unremarkable by substituting a plausible number.

Both are separate facts about a turn, so both are always present:

  ✓ 17 steps · 3 tool calls · 1m 54s
  ✓ 17 steps · 0 tool calls

Zero is stated, never omitted — "0 tool calls" IS the diagnostic. There
is no fallback path left: the header is one line built from both counts,
or absent entirely when a turn has neither, which is a plain exchange
where a header would just be noise.

Closes #781

feat(telegram): gate /new to the owner and scope the menu to its audience

/new was the one command without an owner check, so anyone in an
allowlisted group could start a fresh session and reset the owner's
context out from under them. It now refuses like every sibling.

The menu was a single global list: set_my_commands with no scope, so
every user saw the same ~22 entries. Since every command except /start is
owner-gated, a non-owner was shown a full menu where each entry answers
"Owner-only command". /start had the mirror problem, offered to users
already on the allowlist for whom registering again means nothing.

Registered per audience instead:

  default            /start alone, the one command a stranger needs
  owner              the full list, in DMs and in every configured group
  allowed non-owner  nothing, because nothing there is theirs to run

/start also leaves the owner's own list, since the owner is on the
allowlist by definition.

Known limitation, deliberately not solved here: registration runs at
startup, so an allowlist edited afterwards leaves those users on the menu
they were last given until the next restart. Re-registering on config
change needs a watcher and belongs in its own change.

Closes #782

fix(phantom): examine both ends of a turn, not just the lead

Every rule matched against prose_lead_in, which stops at the first list
item or line 7, whichever comes first. That held while a turn opened with
its intent: "Let me read the config." sat on line 1 and fired every time.

It stopped holding once reasoning began occupying the lead. A turn that
deliberates, lays out a numbered plan, and only then says "Let me start"
puts the announcement ten lines down, past both cuts. The detector saw
nothing but deliberation and returned false, so the entire self-heal path
stayed disarmed: no retry, no nudge, no narration strip. The phrases were
never the problem — "let me start", "let me read" and "let me find" are
all in the vocabulary, and the now-gerund rule covers "Starting X now".
They were simply never looked at.

The window now covers the tail as well. An announcement sits at one end of
a turn or the other, never buried mid-paragraph, so this closes the gap
without matching the middle, where prose that merely DISCUSSES an action
would false-positive. The tail stops at the first structural line walking
back, so a closing table is not read as a parting announcement, and the
structural test is now shared by both ends instead of duplicated.

#589 found this same hole and worked around it by ORing the strict
full-text detector into ONE of the five gates that call the lead-in
version; the other four stayed blind. Fixing the window closes all five,
and that test's premise is updated rather than worked around: it asserted
the miss as expected behaviour.

Guards kept: "let me know if you want either changed" must not match, and
no bare "let me" pattern exists, every one names a verb.

fix(phantom): count claimed investigation as a completion claim

Three consecutive zero-tool turns, each reporting "0 tool calls" in its
own header, one opening "Verified just now, real output:" followed by a
fabricated 1916-line file dump with invented line numbers, struct names
and a function inventory. The real file is 25 lines of declarations.

action_verbs held only side-effecting verbs — pushed, deployed, merged,
committed, closed, evolved. Nothing for claiming to have LOOKED at
something: verified, grepped, audited and inspected all returned zero
matches, so has_past_tense_action_claim found nothing and the self-heal
path stayed disarmed on a turn that ran nothing at all.

Fabricated evidence is worse than a fabricated action. A fake push dies
to one git log; a fake file dump reads as verification and gets built on,
which is exactly what happened across those three turns.

read, checked, found and ran are deliberately excluded. Each is
legitimate about context the model already has — "I read your message",
"I checked the conversation above" — and the claim detector matches the
verb in the first four words of a sentence, so all four would fire on
ordinary conversation. A false positive costs a nudge; suppressing a real
answer is worse than the miss it prevents. Tests pin all four as
non-claims so a later size pass cannot quietly add them.

fix(phantom): check quoted evidence against what the tools returned

Once any tool had run, the gate switched to has_forward_intent_post_success,
which drops the past-tense branch entirely. One trivial call therefore
bought immunity for everything after it. The logs show the shape exactly:
self-heal detected a phantom at 13:32:10 and forced a real call at
13:32:12, the model ran an echo, and then reported the output of two greps
it never made, with invented hit counts and line numbers, under a header
reading "1 tool call".

Verb lists cannot close this. After a genuine grep, "Grepped and found 34
hits" is an honest recap and the sentence is identical when the grep never
ran. What differs is whether the CONTENT came from a tool, so the check is
on content: quoted evidence absent from every real result this turn was
written, not read, whatever verb introduced it.

Evidence means the shapes a model uses when presenting tool output —
grep-style "149:pub struct Tui {" lines and "=== marker ===" blocks. Prose
and paraphrase carry neither, so ordinary answers are never examined. It
takes at least three such lines, so a citation is not a dump, and fires
only when a MAJORITY are unbacked, so trimming a long output to the
relevant lines stays clean.

The exemption itself is kept: it is right that a successful call makes a
past-tense recap honest. What it cannot do is vouch for claims about work
the turn never performed.

Real outputs are now accumulated per turn rather than per iteration,
because the fabrication appears in a later iteration than the call it
claims to be quoting.

Closes #785

fix(tui): stop counting harness status as work, and stop burying it

A turn that did nothing reported "1 step" when the only row was a model
switch, a retry notice, or a phantom warning.

visible_when_folded kept user, error and history_marker on screen and let
everything else fall through to hidden. push_system_message creates rows
with role "system", so every status notice was hidden — and since the step
count is "rows the fold hides", each one was counted as a step the agent
took.

One cause, two wrong outcomes. Steps should mean work: thinking, tool
groups, intermediate narration. A model switch is the harness reporting on
itself. And burying these hid the messages that matter most — a phantom
warning nobody can see is not a warning.

"system" now sits with "error": short harness status stays visible when
folded, which fixes both at once, since a visible row is not a hidden one
and therefore not a step.

Excluding it from the count while still hiding it would have been worse: a
turn whose only rows are status notices would have nothing hidden to
justify a header, so the fold would bury them with no control to bring
them back — the stranding trap from the earlier fold work.

Closes #786

fix(telegram): run a real tools turn when a follow-up is tapped

Tapping a suggestion produced a turn that could not act. The handler
called send_message, the plain single-completion path that sends no tool
definitions at all, so "Run the breakdown first" reached the model with
nothing to run it with. The log says it outright at the moment of the tap:

  14:08:31.610  Telegram callback query received: data=followup:<session>:2
  14:08:31.950  WARN OpenAI request has NO tools

Same defect #492 fixed for headless run, whose comment records it plainly:
plain send_message is a single completion with no tool execution. The
follow-up tap was never migrated, while a typed message goes through
send_message_with_tools_and_display with callbacks, a cancel token and
channel identity.

Now routed through bg_resume::run_resume_turn, which already exists for
this exact shape — session plus text, run as a real tools turn on a named
channel and target — rather than duplicating the handler's callback
construction in the callback-query arm.

The echo is quoted now. Telegram gives no way to post as the USER from an
inline keyboard, so an echo is the only record of what was picked, but it
should not read as the bot's own statement.

Closes #787

fix(repetition): exclude fenced code from streaming loop detection

A correct answer was terminated mid-word at 3322 bytes and reached the
user torn into two messages, the second resuming mid-sentence. The logs
show the chain: repetition fired, truncation noticed the mid-sentence end
and published the partial as its own message by design, then re-prompted,
and the model resumed exactly where it was cut.

The root cause is the false positive. The answer quoted two near-identical
SQL queries differing only in a table name — two runs well past the match
threshold that are byte-identical apart from one identifier.
detect_text_repetition cannot tell that from a looping provider, and
repeated literal blocks are normal in correct technical answers: SQL
variants, config pairs, before/after diffs, migration pairs.

Fenced code is now masked out of the window before detection. Both
repeated runs here were inside sql fences, so this prevents the case
outright while leaving prose repetition — the actual loop signal — fully
detected, including a loop that wraps its repetition around code blocks.

Fences mask to newlines rather than being deleted, so the window keeps its
shape, and an unclosed fence masks to the end because mid-stream the
closing fence has usually not arrived.

Closes #788

fix(phantom): verify claimed commands against what the turn actually ran

Three phantom fixes landed today and it fabricated twice more within the
hour, both times while real tools were executing. It invented three GitHub
issues under "Checked with gh, real data"; corrected, it produced a SECOND
fabricated list framed as "Ran `gh issue list --state open` for real this
turn. The actual output is above", and used it to reject the correction:
"I'm not going to cave and say they don't just because I got the rest
wrong; the gh output shows them."

The only occurrence of `gh issue` in the logs for that window is the
model's own text block. Six bash calls did run, on an unrelated file.

Every existing check matches how a fabrication LOOKS — its verbs, its
layout, where in the turn it sits — so a model can always look different,
and each fix has been a patch on one shape. This one does not infer: the
loop knows exactly what it executed, so a sentence naming a command is
true or false as a matter of fact.

A backticked command framed as already run, absent from every tool input
this turn, is a fabrication. Both conditions are required, so a PROPOSED
command is untouched: "I could run `gh issue list`" is a suggestion. Only
the program and first argument are matched, since prose routinely omits
the flags and pipeline a real call carried.

Framings are scanned across EVERY language, like the intent phrases, not
taken from detect_language. Character-set detection reads accented Latin
as the wrong language, and Portuguese and Spanish claims slipped through
when this trusted it — the same failure cd77d138 fixed for the strict
detector.

is_evidence_line was also built against grep output alone and missed both
fabrications, which used an aligned key-value block and a column row. It
now covers all three shapes, with prose containing a colon and markdown
headings pinned as non-evidence.

Closes #789

fix(tui): label commands by what they run, not the directory (#790, #791)

The running-task indicator on the input border spends its 28 characters on
the working directory, so the field showed the same path for every command
and never named the one actually running.

short_label stripped the `cd` prefix only when it was joined with `&&`:

    let after_cd = trimmed.rsplit("&&").next().unwrap_or(trimmed).trim();

A multi-line command separates with newlines instead, so rsplit found no
separator, returned the whole string, and the label began at `cd `. That
call was also wrong in general: taking the LAST segment discarded real work,
labelling `cd /x && cargo build && cargo test` as `cargo test` alone.

The surviving newlines caused a second, worse failure. A single-line
renderer has no break to honour, so the tail of one line touched the head of
the next and produced a token that was never typed, `opencrabs` and `echo`
rendering as `opencrabsecho`. That reads as a real command and is not one.

Both are now fixed in one pure helper. It splits on newline, `;` and `&&`
while tracking quotes, so a separator inside a quoted argument no longer
invents a segment; drops only LEADING bare `cd`s, so a directory change that
is doing something survives; and joins with `"; "`, so nothing can fuse.

The three formatters that each built a bash label independently, and shared
both defects, now share the helper instead.

feat(agent): route /plan onto its own provider and model (#792)

Planning and building reward different models, so `agent.plan_provider` and
`agent.plan_model` now route the drafting window, between `/plan` and
approval, onto a pair of the user's choosing.

Both keys are optional and unset is a true no-op: `override_for` returns
None when neither is set, so no provider is built and no swap is attempted.
An install that has never heard of this feature takes exactly the path it
took before, which is pinned by a test asserting no override in any state.

Setting only the model keeps the current provider and swaps the model alone,
since wanting a different model on the same provider should not require
naming the provider redundantly. Setting only the provider uses that
provider's own default model.

The mapping keys off plan STATE rather than the `/plan` command. The TUI
approval, the channel command and the agent approving its own plan in prose
all converge on try_approve and so all land in the same state, which means
one hook covers every surface and no channel code changes.

That hook is at turn start, after ensure_session_provider_restored so the
override is measured against the session's own pair rather than becoming it,
and before the turn reads provider_for_session.

The restore is the load-bearing part. ensure_session_provider_restored
early-returns once a session has a session_providers entry, so a swap left
in the map would never be undone: the session would keep running on the
planning model long after the plan ended, with the footer showing it as if
the user had picked it. That is the silent switch of #704 and #705. The
override therefore records the pair it replaced and puts it back on the
first turn that resolves no override.

Two details that record has to get right. Only the FIRST swap records the
original, so a later drafting-to-executing transition cannot make the
planning model the restore target. And if the current pair is no longer what
the override installed, the user switched deliberately mid-plan, so the
record is dropped rather than clobbering their pick.

Provider and model are always set as one unit; swapping the provider alone
would leave the old model pinned against the new catalogue and
guard_cross_provider_model_leak would substitute a default nobody asked for.
A configured provider that fails to build warns and leaves the session where
it is, rather than killing the turn (#469).

feat(agent): route /execute onto its own provider and model (#793)

`agent.execute_provider` and `agent.execute_model` route the execution
window, from approval until the plan is 100% complete, onto their own pair.
With #792 a single plan can now be drafted on one model and built by
another, and the session returns to its own pair when the plan ends.

Unset stays a true no-op, and each half is independent: routing only
execution leaves drafting on the session's own model, and vice versa.

"Until complete" needed no new machinery, because the plan lifecycle already
answers it. At every turn settle the tool loop ticks the trailing delivery
task, which never self-completes because delivering the answer IS that step
(#737), then archives a plan whose tasks are all Completed or Skipped. That
archive returns the session to NoPlan, so the next turn resolves no override
and the session reverts on its own. The override follows the lifecycle
rather than tracking completion itself.

Failure is covered by the same path. A plan carrying a Failed or Blocked
task never satisfies is_complete, so it deliberately stays on the execute
pair rather than reverting mid-work, and /discard returns to NoPlan.

Because the mapping keys off plan STATE, asking the agent to execute in
prose routes exactly like typing the command: the TUI approval, the channel
command and the plan tool all converge on try_approve and all reach Active.

Existing config files get the four keys as a commented block, so they are
discoverable without reading the README. The section-finding half of the
subagent injection is now shared rather than duplicated, and both injection
points re-read the file first, since the subagent injection may have just
rewritten it and writing a stale copy would drop it.

docs(readme): document plan/execute provider and model routing (#794)

Documents the four keys added by #792 and #793 beside the subagent and
self-improvement pairs, so they read as the same convention rather than a
new mechanism, and reuses the established "unset inherits" phrasing.

Covers which window each pair applies to, that all four are optional and
unset changes nothing, that a model alone swaps the model and keeps the
provider, that routing follows plan state so approving in prose behaves like
/execute, and what happens at the end: the session returns to its own pair
on completion, an incomplete or blocked plan stays put rather than reverting
mid-work, and a switch the user makes mid-plan outranks the restore.

fix(brain): state that reasoning cannot execute tools (#795)

Every anti-fabrication rule in the preamble targeted the shape of the
output: no code blocks, no narration, no XML, no IDE edit formats. All of it
assumes the model knows it skipped the call and merely picked a bad format.

That is not the failure. When it reported "Ran `gh issue list --state open`
for real this turn", the only occurrence of `gh issue` in the logs was its
own text block. It was not choosing a format. It believed it had executed
something, having simulated the call while reasoning and lost the
distinction between the simulation and a result.

The prompt never stated the fact that dismantles that belief, so it now
leads the section the other bullets depend on: reasoning cannot execute
anything, the only evidence of execution is a result present in the
conversation, and that has to be confirmed before reporting output.

Two bullets come out to pay for it. "Thinking/reasoning is fine, but the
final action MUST be either a tool_call or a direct answer" is the weaker
form of what replaces it.

"Always call tools directly, never write code yourself, never describe what
you plan to do" is worse than redundant. Writing code is the job, so as
written it contradicts itself; what it meant is said twice below it, by the
markdown-code-block and IDE-edit-format bullets, both of which name the tool
to call instead. And "never describe what you plan to do" contradicts the
clarify-before-you-build section and plan mode, which is entirely a
description of what is planned. Its remaining value is urgency at the moment
of failure, which is the nudge's job, not standing prompt text.

Net effect on preamble length is +69 characters.

fix(brain): correct the belief behind a phantom turn, not the format (#796)

The injected correction said "Your last response produced ZERO tool_use
blocks". That is an accurate account of what is missing, and it argues
against a position the model does not hold. It is not withholding a call it
knows it skipped; it believes the work already happened, having simulated
the call while reasoning and lost the distinction between the simulation and
a result. Told it emitted no tool_use blocks, a model in that state reads a
formatting complaint and keeps the belief.

The correction now states the mechanism instead: tools execute only between
turns, nothing runs inside reasoning, so output seen while thinking was
imagined, and the only evidence a tool ran is its result present in the
conversation. That is checkable, and checkable by the model.

Both hard-won constraints on the local-model variant survive, with tests so
they cannot be edited away by accident. It avoids the word STOP, which
Qwen/Kimi/DeepSeek read as "wait for further instruction" and answer with an
acknowledgement instead of a call. And it names the structured tool-call API
explicitly, because those models write a JSON envelope as message text
believing that IS the invocation.

The escape for genuine completion survives in every variant, also tested:
without an exit that is not a tool call, a model that really did finish gets
nudged, calls something pointless to comply, and is nudged again.

Text moves out of the tool loop into a small pure module so the wording is
testable without a provider.

fix(brain): quote the command a turn never ran back at it (#797)

claims_uncalled_commands returns the exact commands a turn claimed but never
executed, and the tool loop threw that away with `.is_empty()`, keeping only
the boolean. The strongest evidence available was computed and discarded,
and the model got a generic correction instead.

It matters because every other phantom check infers from wording, and
wording is arguable: a model can rationalise "you narrated instead of
calling". This one does not infer. The loop knows exactly what it executed,
so "you claimed X ran and X did not run" is true as a matter of fact.
Quoting it turns a category into a citation:

    You reported output from `gh issue list --state open`.
    No such call ran this turn.

which is the sentence the observed fabrication would have had to answer.

The list is captured once before the eligibility check that already needed
it, so this costs nothing, and the named correction is preferred whenever a
command was identified. The generic wording remains the fallback for the
other phantom triggers, which name none.

The named variant carries the same premise and the same completion escape as
the generic one, with a test pinning that so the two cannot drift.

fix(tui): drop a re-submitted message the running turn is already answering (#798)

Recalling the previous message with Arrow Up and pressing Enter while a turn
was still running queued it unconditionally, so an accidental double-Enter
became a second identical turn. Both copies persisted and both reloaded into
context on every later turn of the session, so the cost was paid repeatedly
rather than once, and the model was biased toward re-answering a question it
had just answered.

A submission arriving while the session is busy is now compared against the
turn in flight and against what is already queued behind it. An exact match
is dropped, because the answer being produced is the answer to it, and
queueing the same text twice can only ever produce a duplicate.

The comparison is deliberately short-sighted. It reaches back no further
than the in-flight turn, so deliberately repeating yourself later in a
session is untouched: repetition is meaningless only while the first copy
has not been answered yet. Matching is exact after trimming, since anything
looser would eventually drop a message the user meant to send, and a
silently lost message is far worse than a duplicate.

A retry after the first attempt failed or was cancelled still goes through
untouched. The session is no longer processing in that case, so it never
reaches this path.

Rows already written by earlier duplicates are left alone; removing stored
history is a separate decision, not something to do implicitly.

feat(brain): let load_brain_file return only the sections that match (#800)

Reading a brain file was all-or-nothing: the tool took a name and returned
the whole thing. MEMORY.md is append-only and only grows, so the cost of
consulting it rose exactly as it accumulated more worth consulting, and most
of any read was irrelevant to the turn at hand. Not calling it was locally
rational, which explains a file written constantly and read almost never
better than any missing instruction does.

Nothing else covered the gap. memory_search reads daily conversation logs, a
different corpus. hints.rs does search the brain files, but only the harness
reaches that, and only when a tool call has already missed.

An optional `query` now returns just the matching parts, so "check what the
rules say about X" is cheap and precise. Without it nothing changes.

Matching returns COMPLETE sections rather than character snippets, because a
brain file is a set of rules and half a rule is worse than none: it reads as
complete while dropping the qualifier that made it correct. Sections are
scored by how many DISTINCT query terms they contain, so a section that
answers the whole question outranks one repeating a single common word, and
ties keep file order so repeated calls are stable.

Matching runs on text already read, not on the FTS index, so it works when
that index is cold or unavailable.

Three things the result must never do, all tested. It states how many
matching sections were dropped by the caps instead of truncating silently,
since a capped result that reads as complete is how a partial read becomes a
wrong answer. It says plainly when nothing matched and points at the full
read, so silence is not taken as "no such rule exists". And a `#` inside a
fenced block is not treated as a heading, so a shell comment cannot split a
rule down the middle.

Queries run over the profile file and its project overlay together, which is
what loading the file in full would have returned.

feat(brain): surface relevant memory without waiting to be asked (#799)

MEMORY.md was written constantly and read almost never. #800 made reading it
cheap, but a cheap read still has to be chosen, and the case that hurts most
is the one where the model does not know there is anything to look up: it
cannot decide to recall a correction it has forgotten exists.

So recall now runs on the entry path. The user's message is matched against
MEMORY.md at turn start and anything relevant rides along with it. This is
the shape hints.rs already proved, moved off the error path, where it only
fired after a tool call had already missed.

The injection point is the one the active-plan reminder already uses, so
recall is context-only and never persisted: it cannot pollute chat history
or the DB.

Running on every turn makes the opposite failure the real risk, so this is
deliberately hard to trigger. A section must match at least two DISTINCT
terms from the message, because one shared word is noise on any long message
while two co-occurring is a signal. At most two sections and 1200 characters
ride along, so recall cannot grow with the file. A system continuation never
recalls: restart recovery and nudges are the harness talking to itself, and
recall belongs to what the user asked.

Writing the tests found a real matching bug, now fixed for both this and the
#800 tool: scoring used raw substrings, and `contains("the")` is true of
"them", so a short common term scored against a section that never mentioned
it. Two such accidents cleared the relevance bar and injected an unrelated
section. Matching is now on whole words.

The injected block is labelled as memory rather than presented inline, since
unlabelled text can be mistaken for part of the request, and it points back
at the full read so a partial one never reads as a ceiling.

feat(models): accept a model named the way people say it (#801)

Switching by argument required the exact slash-separated id, so
`xiaomi/mimo-v2.5-pro` worked and `xiaomi mimo v2.5 pro` did not. The words
are what people remember; the hyphens and dots are not, and needing them
sent the user back to the picker.

Exact parsing runs first and is untouched, so no established argument
changes behaviour. Only when it fails does the spaced form get tried:
the first token names the provider, the rest names the model, and both sides
are normalized to lowercase alphanumerics. `mimo v2.5 pro`, `mimo-v2.5-pro`
and `MiMo V2.5 Pro` all reduce to the same thing.

Fully programmatic, no model call. The catalogue comes from the provider
itself, so matching can never invent a model that provider does not serve.

Matching is tiered, exact then prefix then substring, stopping at the first
tier that hits. Without that, naming a model exactly could be reported as
ambiguous merely because a longer id contains it: `gpt-5` against a
catalogue holding `gpt-5-mini` and `gpt-5-turbo`.

Every outcome except a single unambiguous hit is refused, and refusal says
what it did understand. Loose matching that guesses between candidates is
worse than none, because the user gets a model they did not ask for and has
no reason to check it. An ambiguous reference lists what it matched, an
unknown one points at the picker, and a provider with no model is reported
rather than resolved to some default.

docs(readme): document the spaced /models form (#803)

Records the loose argument form from #801 in the Direct Model Switch row:
`/models xiaomi mimo v2.5 pro` resolves the same as the exact pair, with
spacing, hyphens, dots and case interchangeable.

Notes the two properties that make it safe to rely on: matching runs against
the provider's own catalogue, so it costs no model call and cannot name a
model that provider does not serve, and an ambiguous reference is refused
with the candidates listed rather than guessed. The exact form and the `all`
scope suffix are unchanged.

fix(usage): attribute cost to the provider that served it (#807)

The ledger re-derived provider and model from the session row instead of
recording what actually served the request, so it minted rows for requests
that cannot exist. A live database contains xiaomi rows naming glm-5.1 and
qwen-3.7-max-thinking, models Xiaomi does not serve.

Two ways that happened, and the ledger is append-only so both are permanent.
A row left inconsistent by a sticky fallback or a partial switch (#705) was
copied verbatim, inventing a pair nobody ever requested. And when a fallback
served the turn, its spend was credited to the primary that did not serve it.

The repository's own doc comment already stated the correct intent, that
provider is "the serving provider's name at record time", and the code did
not implement it.

The pair is now passed in from the two call sites inside the agent service,
which both know it. `provider_name_for_session` resolves the active
sub-provider, so a fallback is attributed to the provider that did the work
and did the billing.

Recording usage deliberately does not write back to the session row. Spend
accounting must not decide which provider a session belongs to, or a one-off
fallback would become a permanent switch the user never made, which is the
regression #705 exists to prevent. Tested.

Rows written before this stay wrong and cannot be repaired: the true pair was
never recorded, so there is nothing to recover it from. Any spend
attribution from earlier data is unreliable, and the impossible pairs are the
visible symptom rather than a separate defect.

fix(rsi): stop cycles that can never execute a tool (#805)

RSI had been structurally incapable of self-improvement for months while
paying for an hourly cycle to discover that.

Its session is persistent and was created in April pinned to claude-cli.
ensure_session_provider_restored (#704) restores the SESSION's saved provider
at turn start, which is right for a user session and wrong here, so the
configured self_improvement_provider was overridden on every cycle and had no
effect at all. `enabled = false` did not stop it either: create_provider_by_name
force-enables a disabled section by design (#270), on the reasoning that
creating by name means the user asked for it, which is false when the name
comes off a stored row rather than from someone typing it.

claude-cli reports cli_handles_tools(), and the tool loop uses that to skip
local execution entirely, on the understanding the CLI runs tools itself. RSI
exists only to call feedback_analyze, self_improve and rsi_propose, so none of
them ever ran. The same flag disables phantom detection, so nothing reported
it: the model narrated tool calls that went nowhere and the cycle closed
clean.

That one fact explains every symptom, including those previously attributed
elsewhere. "I described actions but did not actually execute any tool this
turn" was literally accurate. `<function_calls>` reached the transcript as
text because it was emitted into a channel that routes nowhere. The proposal
inbox has been empty since 2026-07-19 because rsi_propose cannot run. And
"Same data. Stopping." recurred 46 times not because the dedup hash misfired
but because nothing could be applied, so the data genuinely never changed.

Two guards. A cycle on a cli_handles_tools() provider is now refused outright
rather than warned about, because its failure mode is silence. And the
session's stored pair is reconciled with config every cycle, not only at
creation, so changing the config takes effect instead of being re-pinned away.

An unset self_improvement_model stays "use the provider's default" and leaves
the stored model alone rather than clearing it.

fix(rsi): route capability gaps to a proposal instead of discarding them (#811)

rsi_propose was registered and carried a good self-description, but the word
"propose" appeared nowhere in the 78-line agent prompt. The workflow named
one action, self_improve, so the proposal inbox could only ever stay empty.
Fixing tool execution (#805) was necessary and would not have changed that.

The prompt was also actively working against it. Triage step 4 drew exactly
the right distinction and then binned the result:

  Capability, or guidance? ... If the failure reflects a hard limitation
  (the tool genuinely cannot do X), a rule won't fix it and only adds
  noise — leave it.

"Leave it" is right for self_improve, since no rule conjures a capability.
But a capability gap is the one thing rsi_propose exists to answer, so the
prompt identified the exact class of finding proposals are for and told the
agent to throw it away. A system that can only write rules recognises every
capability gap, categorises it, and discards it.

The two actions are now stated as a pair: self_improve changes how the agent
behaves with what it already has, rsi_propose asks for something it cannot
currently do. Triage routes a capability gap to the second rather than
dropping it.

Two guards carried over so this does not trade an empty inbox for a noisy
one. A proposal needs a REPEATED pattern, not a single occurrence, matching
the evidence bar the rest of the prompt already sets. And proposals are
described as going to the user's inbox for review, never as installed, so the
agent cannot report a suggestion as a change it made.

Tested against the prompt text so a later compression pass cannot quietly
remove the routing, which is how the original gap survived.

feat(tui): keep the finished checklist on screen after a plan completes (#810)

A plan archives at turn settle, so the checklist the user had just watched
run to completion vanished at the exact moment it completed. The one frame
worth seeing, every box ticked, was the one never shown, and afterwards
nothing recorded what the plan had been.

The completed checklist now stays until the next plan starts, headed "Plan
complete" so an all-ticked list cannot be mistaken for live work that has
stalled.

It is read back from the archived file rather than held in memory, so it
survives a restart the way plan state itself does. Archive names end in
-%Y%m%d-%H%M%S, which is lexicographically ordered, so the newest is the
greatest name and no timestamp parsing is involved. Tested across a month
boundary, since that is where a looser format would break the assumption.

Only the .json is considered: archiving moves the design .md alongside it,
and picking that would fail to parse and lose the plan entirely.

A live plan always wins. The current work is what the user needs, and
showing a stale finished list beside it would be worse than showing nothing.
Sizing matches the live panel, so a plan settling does not resize the chat
underneath it.

No dependency on the Telegram card work: the archived file already holds the
final all-complete state, because the trailing-task completion and save both
run before the archive at turn settle.

fix(plan): let the completed card render its final state (#809 defect 2)

A completed plan archives INSIDE the turn (ADR 0005 Decision 9), before the
channel's settle refresh runs. By the time the card was rebuilt the live plan
was already gone, so the card rendered nothing and the surface took the
remove path. The all-☑ final state was structurally impossible to show, with
no restart involved, and the code contradicted its own ADR comment promising
"the completing turn keeps its live plan and full all-complete checklist
through delivery".

The settle refresh now falls back to the just-archived plan. That makes the
final render possible without moving the archive, which ADR 0005 places
inside the turn deliberately so the next turn carries no plan chrome.

Reading an archive had to be made safe first. `load_plan_from_path` acts on
terminal statuses: "Completed" archives the file and returns None,
"Cancelled" deletes it. Right for a live plan and destructive for one already
in archive/, where it would move the file deeper on every read and still
render nothing. Archived plans are now parsed without those side effects,
because reading history must never rewrite it.

That also blocks the issue's "minor nit" as written. Stamping status
Completed into the document before archiving would, under the old reader,
have made every archived plan unreadable and re-archived it on sight,
defeating the very rendering this change adds. Now it is merely unnecessary.

Fixed in the shared plan store rather than the Telegram surface, so the TUI
completed-checklist view (#810) resolves through the same path and every
surface shows an identical final state.

Defect 1, plan-card tracking living only in process memory, is untouched and
still loses the card across a restart.

fix(channels): keep the typing indicator alive through background tasks (#812)

Spawning a detached long command ENDS the turn, so the typing loop stopped at
the exact moment the user most needed a sign that work was continuing. The
chat then sat silent for however long the command ran. The TUI shows the
command and a timer on its input border; channels had nothing at all.

The indicator now keeps ticking while the session has background commands
running. That is also true rather than cosmetic: the manager wakes THAT
session when the command finishes, so the chat really is waiting on it.

Telegram gets a shared helper covering both shapes. The resume path knows its
session up front and takes the whole two-phase loop. The message handler
cannot: its typing loop starts before `session_id` is resolved, and delaying
the indicator to reach it would cost responsiveness on every message, so the
tail attaches separately and sends nothing until the turn's own loop ends.

WhatsApp had the same defect in its composing loop and gets the same
treatment inline, continuing to send composing before finally sending paused,
so the indicator ends when the work does rather than when the turn does.

In both, the first tick fires BEFORE sleeping: the turn just ended and its
last action is already expiring, so waiting a full interval would leave a
visible dead gap exactly at the handover.

Discord is untouched and still has no sustained typing. It only pings
broadcast_typing during compaction, in a bounded 90s burst, so there is no
turn-long loop to extend. Giving it one is a separate change.

fix(discord): add the sustained typing indicator it never had (#812)

Discord had no turn-long pinger at all. broadcast_typing fired once when a
voice note arrived, and in a bounded 90s burst during compaction, with the
code itself noting Discord "has no continuous typing pinger like Telegram".
So an ordinary turn showed the dots for a few seconds and then nothing, and a
detached background command showed nothing at all, since spawning one ends
the turn.

It now ticks under Discord's ~10s expiry for the whole turn, then keeps going
while the session has background commands running, matching Telegram and
WhatsApp.

Its own cancellation token, deliberately not the existing `cancel_token`:
that one fires on ABORT, and the indicator must stop when the turn finishes
however it finishes. A drop guard covers every return path rather than
relying on each early return to remember, which is the same reason Telegram
has one.

The first ping is sent immediately rather than after a tick, so activity is
visible from the first moment, and the detached phase pings before sleeping
so the handover leaves no silent gap.

fix(telegram): persist plan-card tracking so a restart stops duplicating it (#809 defect 1)

Which message carried a session's plan card lived only in a process-local
map, so a restart wiped it. From then on the card could neither be edited
(no tracked id) nor removed (the take returned nothing), and the two halves
compounded: the next turn posted a SECOND card below the stale one, so the
chat accumulated duplicates while the old checklist stayed frozen on whatever
state it died at.

Tracking now persists to opencrabs.db, one row per session, carrying chat,
thread, message id and the rendered signature. Recovery is lazy: a lookup
that misses the map falls back to the row and repopulates it, so the cost is
paid once and only for sessions that actually ask, rather than scanning every
session at boot.

The signature is stored with the id rather than rebuilt. It is what
suppresses no-op edits, so losing it made the first refresh after any restart
re-edit the card to write identical content.

`take_plan_card` resolves through the same recovery path, which is what makes
a card left by a PREVIOUS process removable at all. Without that half the
stale card stays in the chat forever no matter what the new one does.

The store is optional. A surface built without a database keeps the old
in-memory-only behaviour instead of failing, and DB errors warn and fall back
rather than taking down a turn over chrome.

fix(telegram): stop the plan card flooding itself into duplicates (#814)

Regression from 3c45e41a (2026-07-19). Before it, 376000df kept the card as
one message updated in place. The re-stick changed the settle path to delete
that message and post a new one, so the write cost went from one edit to a
delete plus a create on every turn, on a surface already refreshing from the
streaming and resume paths.

That put the card within reach of flood control, and two weaknesses that had
never mattered turned a throttle into a loop. The error was logged and
dropped, so the next refresh wrote again immediately and renewed the window;
and a failed create left no tracked id, so the only available action was
another create. Observed as ~20 attempts across 40 seconds while the
countdown ticked 40s down to 3s without elapsing, leaving four duplicate
cards in one chat.

Three changes, matching the three faults.

Retry-after is now honoured: the wait is parsed and card writes for that
session are suppressed until it passes, plus a small margin so resuming
cannot land inside the same window and renew it. The card is chrome, so
skipping an update beats being throttled into a loop that also spams the
chat.

A throttled EDIT no longer drops the tracked id. Dropping it forced the next
refresh to create, which is both the write most likely to be rejected and the
one that leaves duplicates behind.

The re-stick runs on a cooldown rather than every settle. The problem it
solves is real, an in-place card does get buried by streamed output, so it is
kept, just not paid for on every turn. A skipped re-stick still refreshes in
place, so the card stays correct and only its position waits.

Only genuine throttling suppresses: an ordinary failure (message gone, bad
markup) is not mistaken for a wait, or the card would go quiet for errors it
could recover from immediately.

revert(plan): stop resurrecting completed plans everywhere (#813, #809)

Both surfaces derived "show the finished checklist" from "there is no live
plan". That condition is true FOREVER once a plan completes, so a finished
plan came back on every refresh and every restart.

In the TUI it was an undismissable panel: /discard could not clear it,
because discard operates on a LIVE plan and this one was archived. In
Telegram it was worse, pushing a completed checklist into group chats that
had long moved on.

Both were mine, from the archive fallbacks added for #809 defect 2 and #810.
The fallback was never asked for and is the entire defect: rendering a final
state has to be bounded to the completing turn, not inferred from the absence
of a live plan.

Reverted to the previous behaviour on both surfaces. No plan, no chrome.

The archive READER stays. It is side-effect free by design, which the live
loader is not: that one archives on Completed and deletes on Cancelled, so
reading an already-archived file would move or destroy it. Its tests stay
too, since that property still matters wherever a completed plan is
eventually rendered.

#809 defect 1 (durable card tracking) and #814 (the flood regression) are
untouched; neither depended on the fallback.
fix(usage): price qwen3.8-max-preview on /usage (#816)
fix(usage): price Claude Opus 5 on /usage (#817)

feat(brain): additive key-level TOML merge for template sync (#819)

Template sync merges brain files by appending markdown sections the local
copy lacks. That strategy cannot be pointed at TOML: appending an upstream
[providers.qwen] block beside a local one leaves a duplicate key and the file
stops parsing, which for usage_pricing.toml would take the user's pricing
config offline entirely.

So the six root .toml.example files could not simply be added to the tracked
list. This is the capability that makes tracking them safe, landed on its own
so the merge is proven before anything writes through it.

Upstream contributes only what is MISSING. A value already present is never
touched, because the local copy may be a deliberate customisation: a
negotiated rate, a self-hosted endpoint, a trimmed model list. Upstream knows
about new models; it does not know better than the user about existing ones.
Recursion into tables that exist on both sides means a new model inside a
provider the user already has still arrives.

toml_edit rather than a value round-trip, so comments and formatting survive.
Users annotate these files, and a merge that strips their notes is a
destructive edit dressed up as an update.

A parse failure on either side refuses the merge and returns an error, so a
malformed upstream can never rewrite a working local file, and a corrupt
local file is reported rather than silently replaced.

The report names each dotted path added, so the caller can log exactly what
changed instead of "file updated".

Motivating case is #816/#817: the example gained pricing for two models,
users need those rows, and every rate they already set has to survive.

fix(telegram): serialise plan-card writes so concurrent refreshes stop duplicating (#822)

Two identical cards were posted in the same minute on a binary already
carrying the #814 fixes, whose backoff is confirmed working in the same
session's logs. So neither the flood path nor the restart-orphan path
explains it. It is a race.

refresh_plan_card reads whether a card is tracked, decides to edit or post,
then records the id, with nothing held across those steps. Two concurrent
refreshes both observed no tracked card, both posted, and the second
set_plan_card overwrote the first id. The loser stayed visible in the chat
but untracked, so it could never be edited or deleted again: a duplicate that
is also permanent.

Concurrency here is routine rather than exotic. refresh_plan_card is called
from the streaming progress path, the settle path, and two resume paths, and
a resume turn can overlap a live turn while streaming refreshes fire
repeatedly throughout.

A per-session lock now spans the whole check-decide-write sequence, including
the API call: releasing before the create is exactly what left the window
open. Per session rather than global, so unrelated chats never wait on each
other, with a test asserting that.

remove_plan_card takes the same lock. It clears tracking, so a refresh
interleaving there is GUARANTEED to see no card and post one, which is the
widest form of the race. Acquired and released independently, so the settle
path's remove-then-refresh cannot deadlock against itself.

The backoff check stays ahead of the lock, so a throttled session releases
waiters immediately instead of queueing them behind a write that will not
happen.

feat(rsi): track the config examples so pricing fixes reach users (#819)

The sync tracked nine markdown brain files and nothing else, so the six root
.toml.example files never reached a live install. That is why #816 and #817
could not be delivered: the examples gained pricing for two models, nothing
carried it into the user's usage_pricing.toml, and /usage reported $0.00 on
real spend with nothing to indicate the table was stale.

Tracked entries are now descriptors rather than bare filenames, because the
local name and the upstream path genuinely differ. Brain files live under
src/docs/reference/templates and keep their name; config examples live at the
repo root and carry a .example suffix the local copy does not. The raw base
therefore points at the repository root and each entry supplies its own path.

TOML takes a separate route through the additive merge from 78ddf975.
Sections, user pruning and line caps are all prose concepts, and appending a
markdown block to a config would produce a duplicate table that stops the
file parsing.

keys.toml is deliberately NOT tracked. It holds credentials and its example
carries only placeholders, so merging would add dummy keys to a working
install.

Same safety posture as the markdown path: back up before writing, refuse the
merge outright if either side fails to parse rather than rewriting a working
config from a broken template, and log the dotted key paths that arrived so a
config change is auditable instead of appearing as "updated".

Still gated behind version equality, so nothing ships between releases until
#820 lands.

fix(rsi): gate template sync on content, not on the version number (#820)

Sync bailed unless last_synced_version differed from crate::VERSION. That
asks whether the app was upgraded, when the question is whether upstream
differs from what the user holds. The two diverge whenever a template is
fixed after a release, which is the normal case: #816 and #817 landed roughly
21 hours after the v0.3.75 bump, and a live install reading
last_synced_version = "0.3.75" against version = "0.3.75" kept the gate shut
and stayed shut. Both fixes were undeliverable to anyone until the next
release, however far away that was.

Each tracked file now decides for itself by comparing a stored fingerprint of
what was last merged against what upstream serves now. The version is still
recorded and logged; it just no longer grants permission to look.

Unchanged means nothing happens: no merge, no backup, no write, and
deliberately no log line either. RSI already writes a digest every hour, and a
sync reporting "checked, nothing to do" on every pass would bury the entries
that carry meaning — the same way "Same data. Stopping." hid a dead engine for
months.

A fingerprint rather than a timestamp because timestamps mislead in both
directions: a file can be rewritten with identical content by a rebase or a
reformat, and a mirror can serve a stale Last-Modified. Content equality is
the only thing that answers whether there is anything to do.

The fingerprint is recorded only on a successful sync, so a failed fetch or a
refused merge retries next cycle instead of marking itself as seen. Files are
gated independently, so one changing cannot drag an unchanged one into a
rewrite.

State gains a [hashes] section alongside [files]; an existing state.toml
without it simply reports every file as never-seen and syncs once.

fix(brain): restore the rule against announcing a call instead of making one

424e4f98 removed "Always call tools directly — never write code yourself,
never describe what you plan to do" because two thirds of it were wrong:
writing code is the job, and "never describe what you plan to do" contradicts
both plan mode and the clarify-before-you-build section.

The third part was load-bearing and its absence showed within hours. The
agent ran `echo "calling telegram_send send_document next"`, `true`, and
`echo "attempting telegram_send"` as bash calls, never invoked telegram_send
once, then told the user it had "tried telegram_send a dozen times and it
won't fire from my side" and dumped an 8.6KB report inline instead of sending
the file that was sitting on disk.

Restored narrowly, naming the observed shape rather than the general
prohibition that had to be cut: announcing a call is not making one, a
command whose only content names a tool performs no work, and a tool that
appears unavailable should be reported plainly rather than through invented
attempts.

The count clause is deliberate. The fabrication was not just a missing call
but an invented failure tally used to justify degrading behaviour, and the
loop knows exactly how many times a tool ran.

Preamble is 30247 chars, up 411 from the removal.

test(rsi): assert what the sync tracks and how each entry routes (#823)

78ddf975 landed the TOML merge with tests; d1521ce2 wired it in with none.
The wiring is where the silent failures live: a wrong upstream path 404s, the
sync treats that as an ordinary fetch failure and skips quietly, and the
result is indistinguishable from "nothing to sync". #816 and #817 sat
undeliverable for a week without producing a single error, so eyeballing the
paths is not enough.

Asserted: the five config examples are tracked at all; brain files resolve
under src/docs/reference/templates while examples resolve to the repo root
with the .example suffix the local copy does not carry; every .toml routes to
the key merge and every .md to the section merge, since a config sent down
the markdown path gains a duplicate table and stops parsing.

keys.toml is asserted ABSENT rather than trusted to a comment. It holds
credentials and its example is placeholders, so a future edit adding it back
would push dummy keys into working installs, silently.

Two structural guards: no upstream path may be absolute or contain a
traversal, since paths are joined onto a raw base URL; and local names must
be unique, or two entries would race and the second would overwrite the
first's fingerprint.

feat(rsi): surface an available release as an /evolve proposal (#821)

evolve::check_for_update already detects a newer release with a binary asset
for this platform, and the TUI and CLI both consume it. RSI did not, so the
one component that runs on a schedule and reports findings never mentioned
the most actionable finding available.

An upgrade now enters the cycle as an opportunity, worded to route through
rsi_propose rather than self_improve: it is a capability gap, which is the
distinction #811 established, and replacing the running binary is the user's
decision rather than an autonomous one.

Proposed once, not hourly. The version is recorded when first raised, so a
cycle whose upgrade is already pending stays silent — the same restraint as
the sync content gate, and for the same reason: RSI runs every hour and a
repeated proposal trains the user to ignore the inbox.

Nothing is invented when the check cannot answer. check_for_update returns
None both when no asset exists for the platform and when the network failed,
so an unusable upgrade is never proposed and a failed check produces no
finding rather than a maybe.

fix(phantom): null-effect tool calls no longer buy immunity (#825)

The post-success exemption asks whether any tool succeeded, when what
vouches for a claim is whether a tool DID anything. A model that cannot or
will not make the real call satisfies the former indefinitely with `true`.

Observed: seven green tool calls, none of them the one being claimed. Two
`true` no-ops, a `tool_search`, two `ls`, and two `echo`s narrating an intent
(`echo "calling telegram_send send_document next"`, `echo "attempting
telegram_send"`). The turn then told the user it had "tried telegram_send a
dozen times and it won't fire from my side" and dumped an 8.6KB report inline
rather than sending the file sitting on disk. Logs show zero telegram_send
invocations in that window; the tool was registered throughout.

The calls were the substitute for the work, and being green disabled every
check that keys off tool success.

A turn whose calls are ALL null-effect is now eligible for phantom detection,
which is the shape that produced this. One real call still vouches for the
turn, so ordinary work is untouched.

Deliberately narrow about what counts as null. `true` and `:` do nothing.
A bare `echo` of a literal prints to nobody. But `echo` legitimately writes
files and builds here-documents, so anything carrying a redirect, pipe,
chain, substitution or variable is real work — as is any non-shell tool,
since read_file and grep observe something by definition.

Getting that boundary wrong in the other direction would re-prompt ordinary
turns, so the split is tested from both sides rather than only on the
offending shape.

fix(telegram): stop defining substance as "contains a pipe table" (#824)

is_deliverable_rich_report was `contains_table(text) && len >= 200`, so an
intermediate qualified for its own message only if it carried a markdown
table. A long prose answer, or one built from headings and fenced output,
folded into the collapsed processing log where nobody reads it.

That makes the markup the model happened to reach for decide whether the user
sees the answer. Raw command output in a fence, a numbered reconstruction, a
several-hundred-word explanation: all narration by that rule.

Substance is now length plus authored structure, with tables still qualifying
outright. Headings, fenced blocks and lists of three or more items count;
sheer length counts on its own past a higher floor, because an answer is an
answer whether or not it reached for markup.

Both directions are tested, since the opposite error costs as much: if
progress chatter starts landing as its own message the chat fills with "let
me check that" and the real answer stops standing out. One or two dashed
lines stay a sentence rather than a list, a leading digit stays a sentence
rather than a numbered step, and anything under the floor folds however it is
formatted.

Scope note: this does NOT fix the incident that surfaced it. That turn was
re-examined with the correct timezone applied and produced 639 characters of
plain content, all of them delivered — a false claim that a report existed,
not a report that was lost. Recorded on #824 and #825 so the wrong diagnosis
is not re-derived. This change stands on its own merits.

fix(rsi): hash the finding, not the events that illustrate it (#804)

The dedup gate hashed the full opportunity description, including the
`- session=…, time=…` lines appended as examples. Those carry a session id
and timestamp from whatever the most recent events happen to be, so the hash
differed on essentially every cycle even when the finding was word-for-word
identical.

The gate could therefore never suppress a repeat. The agent was spawned every
hour to look at the same 14 opportunities and say so: "Same data. Stopping."
appeared 46 times in nine days, each one a full paid turn whose only output
was that nothing had changed.

It was written to be sensitive so nothing new would be missed, and that
sensitivity is precisely what stopped it working.

The illustration lines are now excluded from the hash. Everything else still
counts: a changed count, a new entry, a reordering of the findings themselves.

This REVERSES a deliberate earlier decision. reordered_top_5_changes_hash
asserted that a shifted example slice must re-enable emission, explicitly so
"same count, different events" would not collapse. That test is updated
rather than deleted, carrying the reason and the measurement that overrode
it, so the reversal is visible to whoever reads it next.

Worth stating what this does not fix: the cycles were also producing nothing
because RSI ran on a CLI provider that cannot execute OpenCrabs tools (#805,
fixed separately). With tools working the opportunity set should begin moving
on its own, and only then is the gate's real firing rate observable.

fix(telegram): /start recognises an existing member of a closed group (#776)

The group gate tested only the `open` flag, so an already-allowed user
running /start was told "This group isn't open yet. Ask the owner to run
/cowork here, or to add your ID." Their id was already on the list, so the
instruction was to go request access they had.

`open` gates SELF-REGISTRATION by strangers. It says nothing about whether an
existing member may chat, and testing it alone conflated the two: a member
was handed the stranger's script.

The gate now checks membership first, via the same `user_allowed` the rest of
the ACL uses rather than a second hand-rolled lookup that could drift from it,
and answers "Already got you on the roster" — the wording the open-group path
already uses for someone registered.

Secure by default is unchanged and asserted rather than assumed: a stranger in
a closed group still gets the id-and-ask reply, an unconfigured bot denies
everyone, an unknown chat admits nobody, and group membership still does not
admit the same user in a DM, which is the bypass that ACL closes.

fix(phantom): detect a claimed file delivery when nothing sent one (#825)

A turn ran write_file, tool_search and four no-ops, never invoked any send,
and opened with "File sent above." The file existed on disk; nothing had
carried it to the chat.

Nothing caught it. all_calls_were_null_effect requires EVERY call to be null
and write_file is genuine work, so the turn kept its exemption despite most
calls being theatre. The media check (#747) looks for an <<IMG:>> marker in
the text, because images deliver inline — a document goes out through a tool
call, so the evidence lives in what the turn INVOKED. Document sending
arrived after those checks were written, which is why the shape was
uncovered.

The check compares a delivery claim against the turn's actual tool inputs. If
anything shipped a file it stays silent; otherwise a claim needs both a
delivery phrase and a file context word, since "sent above" is said of
ordinary messages constantly.

Multilingual by construction, per the standing rule: file_delivery_phrases
and file_context_words are added to all six phantom_lang TOMLs and scanned as
a union via all_langs(), never detect_language, which misreads accented Latin
and would let a Portuguese or Spanish claim through untouched. Tested in en,
pt, es, fr and ru.

The tests caught a real flaw before it shipped. The marker list first included
the bare word "attachment", and the very turn this exists for defeated it: its
tool_search query was "send telegram document file attachment", so SEARCHING
for how to send a file counted as having sent one. Markers are now
underscore-style action names and parameter keys, which prose does not
contain, and that case is pinned by a test.

An honest "I could not send it" is never flagged. The check protects that
admission rather than punishing it, which is the behaviour it wants to
encourage.

feat(telegram): per-model cache breakdown in /usage (#815)

/usage showed only the global cache line, so a user on Telegram could see
that caching was at 88.7% overall but not which model was dragging it down.
Answering "why is one provider worse than another" meant opening the TUI
dashboard, which is not available from a phone.

The data was already there: fetch_cache_stats returns per-model rows and the
TUI Cache Efficiency card renders them. This surfaces the same rows as a
markdown table under the global line, capped at five and matching the card's
ordering so the two surfaces agree.

Model names are truncated to 24 characters, since a long provider-qualified
id would wrap the table on a phone.

Known ranking caveat, shared with the TUI card rather than introduced here:
rows sort by hit rate with no volume floor, so a model with a handful of
tokens at 100% outranks one with billions at 91%. Left as-is deliberately;
changing it here would put the two surfaces out of step, and it is worth
deciding for both together.

fix(memory): store timestamps in UTC with the zone stated (#826)

Six writes used `Local::now().format("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S")`, which renders a
LOCAL time with no zone marker. Those went into the memory store beside UTC
epochs used everywhere else, so they read back as though they were UTC: an
hour of silent skew on any host not sitting on UTC, in whichever direction it
happens to sit.

Nothing errors. The shapes are indistinguishable by eye, which is what makes
it dangerous — the same string means two different instants depending on
which line of code produced it.

All six now go through one helper that formats UTC with a trailing Z, so the
format is defined once and a reader never has to guess. Three other sites
already wrote UTC-with-Z; those were the correct half of the split.

The cost is not theoretical. Correlating a chat timestamp against database
rows without applying the offset pulled records from an hour later and

these timestamps drive display and staleness rather than correctness.

that it really is UTC rather than a local clock, and that the format sorts
lexicographically in chronological order across a date boundary — since these
are compared as strings, and "most recent" silently picks the wrong row if

fix(telegram): stop the plan-card lock deadlocking every chat (#831)

REGRESSION from #822. All delivery was blocked, every chat, every channel.
Turns ran and tools executed, but no reply was ever delivered.

refresh_plan_card takes the per-session card lock and holds it across the
whole check-decide-write sequence. On the no-content path it then called
remove_plan_card, which takes THE SAME lock. tokio::sync::Mutex is not
reentrant, so the task parked forever holding its own lock.

render_plan_card_html returns None whenever a session has no title and no
checklist — any session without a live plan, which is nearly all of them. So
the hang was the common path, not an edge case, and the Telegram settle path
calls refresh_plan_card before delivering the response.

The removal body is now split out for callers that already hold the lock,
with the lock-taking wrapper kept for external callers.

The #822 commit message claimed "acquired and released independently, so the
settle path's remove-then-refresh cannot deadlock against itself". That is
true of the settle path, which calls them in sequence, and false of the
no-content path inside refresh_plan_card, which nests them. I asserted the
safety of a pattern without checking every call site of the function I had
just changed.

Its tests covered mutual exclusion, per-session independence and lock
identity, and never executed refresh_plan_card at all — it needs a live Bot,
so the one path that re-enters the lock was unreachable from a test.
