revert(telegram): stop delivering the agent's working-out to chat

Reverts 3ecc8c2a. It widened is_deliverable_rich_report from "contains a
pipe table" to "has headings, fenced blocks, three or more list items, or is
long prose". The agent's own intermediate reasoning has exactly those shapes,
so it began landing in group chats as standalone messages.

Nobody asked for it. It was justified by #824, whose premise I later
disproved myself — the report in question was never written, it was a false
claim — and I kept the change anyway arguing it stood on its own merits.

Back to requiring a table, which is what shipped for months without leaking.

fix(telegram): stop the flow block posting a new message every tick

open_flow's contract is "send the open processing-log message for the FIRST
time; subsequent entries merely edit this message in place". Nothing enforced
it. append_tool_group guarded at its own call site, but the chrome tick calls
open_flow directly on every activity update, so a long turn posted a fresh
block per tick.

That stayed invisible while the flow block carried plan title, prose and
checklist — the duplicate content was wrong but at least looked like content.
Once all three moved to the persistent card, the only thing left to render
was the elapsed time, and the chat filled with timer-only bubbles seconds
apart: 0:01, 0:01, 0:01.

The guard now lives in open_flow itself, so every caller is covered rather
than each having to remember. Already open means refresh in place, which is
what the doc comment promised all along.

The lock is released before awaiting: holding a std MutexGuard across the
refresh made the future non-Send.

fix(telegram): drop an echoed plan title from the response (#837)

The plan reminder shows the model `📋 Plan: "{title}"` every turn and the
model opens its reply by repeating it, directly under the card that already
renders the title. The user sees it twice, in two messages.

Fixed at both ends: the reminder now tells the model not to repeat it, and
delivery drops it when it does. The instruction alone is not enough — a rule
in the prompt loses often enough that the filter has to exist too.

Four problems with the in-flight version this replaces.

It would have missed the reported case. The reminder injects `📋 Plan: "…"`,
and the matcher trimmed only `#`, `*` and `~` — not the emoji, not the
`Plan:` label, not the quotes. An echo of the reminder's OWN formatting, the
likeliest echo there is, never matched. Both sides are now normalized, and the
whole first line must reduce to the title, so a sentence that merely mentions
it is left alone.

It only stripped for Active plans. #621 folded title and prose into the card
in both Editing and Active, so every plan still being drafted kept the
duplicate. Both states now.

The reminder claimed "the plan card is already shown above your message".
`format_plan_reminder` is shared context: TUI, CLI, Discord and WhatsApp have
no card, so the model was told one exists that does not, and might suppress a
title the user never sees rendered anywhere. Reworded surface-neutrally.

And it loaded the plan from disk inside the matcher, so the matching could
not be tested without a session on disk, and none was written. The matcher is
now pure and takes the title, with 9 tests covering the reminder's shapes,
markdown headings and emphasis, an unrelated opening, a mention mid-sentence,
a title appearing later, an empty title, and a different plan's title.

The reminder keeps the title itself: the model needs to know which plan it is
executing, and removing it to prevent an echo would trade a display bug for
lost grounding.

fix(phantom): catch a claim of having played or launched something

A zero-tool turn replied "Played it. Your notification.mp3 is alive and well,
sounds like a proper alert." It ran nothing. Challenged with "you did not
execute any tool call", it then ran afplay and said "There, actually played
it this time."

The turn was eligible — zero tool calls — but no detector matched the text.
action_verbs has grown by patching whatever the last fabrication exposed:
deploys, then issue-tracker actions, then self-update, then investigation.
None of it covered running something on the user's own machine, so "played"
was not a verb the system knew.

Adds the playback and launch family to all six phantom_lang TOMLs.

Known gap, asserted rather than hidden: action_verbs are deliberately gated
to the DETECTED language, because short single words carry real
cross-language collision risk, unlike the multi-word intent phrases scanned
across all languages. detect_language misreads accented Latin, so the
Portuguese and Spanish verbs are present but never consulted. A test pins
that as current behaviour and says what to do when it changes, instead of
leaving a passing suite implying coverage that does not exist.

Widening the gating would import exactly the collision risk that comment
warns about, so it needs its own change and its own evidence.

Also asserts the honest cases stay clean: offering to play something, and
ordinary prose about a file, are never flagged.

fix(telegram): gate flush_intermediates like the streaming path (#838)

An audit reply arrived twice, two minutes apart: once as a numbered list,
once as the same content in a table. The log showed
`sent_intermediates count=1` alongside the final response, so an intermediate
had been sent as its own message.

There are two delivery paths and only one was gated. The streaming loop
checks is_deliverable_rich_report before promoting an intermediate — the #582
rule that it must carry a table and clear a length floor. flush_intermediates
sent everything queued, with no check anywhere in it. Its own doc notes it
runs from the resume and follow-up paths, so any turn routed through those
dumped its working-out verbatim.

So "an intermediate needs a table to earn its own message" was only ever true
for one of the two ways an intermediate reaches a chat.

Calls the shared function rather than restating its rule, so the two cannot
drift apart again — which is exactly how this survived: reverting the
streaming classifier was expected to stop the duplicate, the binary was
rebuilt, and it persisted, because the revert addressed the gated path.

Worth recording why it took two attempts. `sent_intermediates count=1` was
read as proof the streaming classifier had promoted the message, without
first checking which code path increments that counter. Both do.

The dedup in delivery.rs cannot cover this: it strips a final response
overlapping a sent intermediate by comparing normalized text, and a bullet
list against a table carrying the same meaning share almost no bytes.

Registration was gated on the ACL having rejected the user. An open group

Global allowed_users are admins in every group, so their per-member menu
must be cleared wherever they are members. Nothing records which groups

invalid-id error, which was warned four times per group across nine

and its neighbour misdated.

fix(rsi): cap rule size and allow a narrow consolidation path (#857, #858)

RSI wrote rules as paragraphs into files that are always loaded, so every
byte is paid on every turn of every channel, permanently. One application
added 1,329 bytes; 645 of 722 improvements target AGENTS.md or SOUL.md.
An apply is now capped at 600 characters and rejected over it, with the
rejection saying to tighten the rule rather than split it in two.

It also could not consolidate. Rewording a rule shorter is a shrink, and
append-only rejects shrinks unless every removed byte reappears, which
rewording never satisfies, so the files could only grow. 51 entries are
RSI removing its own duplicates by hand.

A surgical update may now shorten, but only when the replacement keeps
the original's bold lead or heading, so the rule survives identifiably
rather than being deleted. check_no_shrink caps the removal at 2048 bytes
whatever the caller claims, which bounds it to one rule's worth. The
unbounded bypass this replaces was used to delete 47% of SOUL.md.

The tool description now states the budget and the consolidation path, and
tells the agent to search what it read for the rule before appending, so
compliance does not depend on hitting the rejection first.

fix(agent): join a truncation continuation onto its partial (#859)

final_text is built from the last response only, on the assumption that
earlier text already reached the user as IntermediateText. That holds in
the TUI and stopped holding for Telegram once intermediates were gated to
deliverable rich reports (#838): a plain-prose partial is emitted, the
gate drops it, and the continuation alone becomes the answer.

A group turn answered in full, 551 output tokens, and the user received a
60-character provider refusal. The refusal was both the tail of the
partial and the whole of the continuation, so the answer was destroyed by
a path meant to repair it.

The partial is now held and joined: the continuation extends it rather
than replacing it. Joining covers the shapes that occur — the
continuation echoing the tail it was asked to continue from, the model
restarting and reproducing the partial, an empty continuation, and a cut
that landed mid-word where a separator would corrupt the word.

fix(session_context): atomic write to eliminate trailing-characters corruption (#853)

fix(session_context): write context store atomically

session_context's save() wrote the store with fs::write directly. fs::write
truncates per call, but two concurrent save() calls in one turn (e.g. several
session_context set operations fired together) do not serialize: a shorter
write landing over a longer one leaves the longer object's tail bytes in
place, producing "trailing characters" JSON parse failures on the next read.
This was the single largest source of tool failures in the feedback ledger
(~57% of all logged failures over weeks).

Fix: write to a uniquely-named temp file in the same directory, then atomically
rename it over the target. The unique temp name (pid + monotonic counter)
prevents two saves from racing on the temp file itself; rename is atomic on
the same filesystem, so the store is always either the previous complete
object or the new one -- never a mix.

Co-authored-by: Moe <moe@M.local>

docs(brain): move the anti-fabrication rules into the preamble

condensing the files removed it three days ago, and nothing noticed.
`Execute, don't narrate` sits in SOUL.md and is exposed the same way.

Brain files are agent-writable by design, which is the point of
self_improve. Anti-fabrication rules are precisely the ones with an
incentive to be trimmed as verbose, so they belong in the preamble, which
is compiled into the binary and cannot be edited at runtime.

Costs nothing extra in context: AGENTS.md is always-loaded too. The split
is by who may edit a rule, not by topic.

Adds the state case the deleted rule covered, plus claiming ABSENCE:
"I don't see it" without looking is the same fabrication as "I checked it"
without checking.

fix(channels): prefer chunk boundaries that leave no markup open (#876) split_message took the last newline near the limit with no knowledge of markup, so a boundary could land inside ... or between a pair of backticks. Chunks are sent as separate messages and parsed independently, so an unclosed start tag is a 400 and that chunk is lost, which reads as the reply simply stopping. Among the newlines already in the search window it now prefers one where nothing is open, and falls back to the previous choice when no such point exists. Strictly an improvement: when no markup spans the boundary the first candidate is already clean and the output is byte-identical, so the only case that moves is the one that was broken. The search can only move a break earlier, never past the length cap. Shared by Discord, Slack and Telegram, so tests cover the invariants that matter on all three: nothing is lost, no chunk exceeds the limit, plain text is unchanged, and degenerate input with no newline still splits.

absent — no silent no-op, since a gate with no rules looks enforced but

headers verified present in every template; no contradiction guards
ship by default because patterns on common governance words ("push",
"table") false-positive against real brain files (a bullet list is one
entry, so "never push" + "always push" in adjacent bullets trips a
guard meant for a single self-contradictory sentence). The mechanism
stays supported and unit-tested via the inline AGENTS_TOML const.

Also fixes a latent bug the gate surfaced: brain_verify_config() read
the belief base from dirs::home_dir() and cached it in a process-global
OnceLock, so switching profiles served a stale belief base and tests
under throwaway profiles validated content against the machine home.
It now resolves via resolve_profile_home() — the same home self_improve
writes to — and is no longer cached.

Tests seed brain templates into throwaway profiles so the gate verifies
appends against realistic anchors.

fix(rsi): surface raw failure totals vs surfaced opportunities in digest (#888)

The RSI digest listed tool_failure counts in Event Breakdown and per-tool
failures in Tool Performance, but nothing connected the raw total to the
filtered opportunity list. A reader sees 'tool_failure: N' and 'K
opportunities surfaced' with no bridge, which produced a false bug report
claiming RSI underreports failures ~25x (raw count vs noise-filtered

events (sentinel detectors excluded), distinct tools with failures, how
many surfaced as opportunities (with filter criteria stated: >=5 events,

Zero behavior change, clarity only.

fix(phantom): catch media-delivery claims, and the oven idiom (#891)

A turn announced a finished video with a changelog of its contents,
having run no tools and uploaded nothing. The user asked where it was.

Two gaps, and the phrase was the smaller one. file_context_words listed
only document types in ALL six languages — .md, pdf, csv, plus words for
file/document/report — with no media extension and no word for video,
audio or image. So a claimed video or audio delivery could not satisfy
the context half of the check whatever the wording. Document sending was
covered by the earlier work; media delivery never was.

Adds the "fresh out of the oven" idiom and its equivalents per language,
direct media-delivery claims, and media extensions plus video/audio/image
words to the context list, across all six files.

Tests cover the observed claim, the same claim in each language, each
extension satisfying the context check, document claims still working,
and two negatives: an offer to produce a file, and the idiom used
literally about a cake.

fix(telegram): name the member who tapped a follow-up (#895)

The recorded pick showed only the option text, so in a group it read as an
anonymous line from the bot rather than a selection someone made. The
callback query carries the tapper's identity and it was discarded.

The record now names them, and falls back to the plain record when
identity is unavailable or blank so the pick is never lost and no dangling
separator is left behind. The fallback echo, used when the block is too
old to edit, is covered too.

This is a partial step, not the finished behaviour #895 asks for: the
message is still authored by the bot with a name attached, rather than
being the member's own message. Labelling bot output is not attribution.

fix(phantom): catch colloquial delivery claims, drop a false positive (#894)

A turn insisted a video was delivered — "Tá aí em cima, dá o play" — with
one tool call that sent nothing. The formal wording was covered ("o
ficheiro está acima"); the way people actually speak was not, in any of
the six languages.

Bare extension words were missing too: the context list held ".mp4" with
a leading dot, so "o mp4" could not satisfy the context half of the check.
Prose writes extensions both ways.

Adding these surfaced a bad entry from the previous round. "mando o mp4"
had been added as a delivery claim, but Portuguese routinely uses the
present tense for a future promise: "assim que o render sair eu mando o
mp4" is a commitment to send later, and it was being flagged. Removed,
with a test asserting promises stay unflagged in each language.

Flagging a promise is worse than missing a claim, since it punishes the
behaviour the detector exists to encourage.

fix(telegram): unify rich delivery on markdown, drop the dead blocks path (#871)

Three rich modes existed and none was correct. Measured from the
telemetry now in the binary:

  native blocks   68 attempts, 68 x 400 RICH_MESSAGE_CONTENT_REQUIRED,
                  zero successes across two days
  rich markdown   carried 100% of delivered rich messages; renders tables,
                  does not render ATX headings
  rich HTML       returns 200 then renders headings inline and FLATTENS
                  tables into a run-on paragraph, logging nothing

The blocks attempt was a guaranteed round-trip and a guaranteed error
before every rich delivery, and every message already arrived via the
markdown fallback. Removed, along with its serializer, body builder and
the tests that only exercised them.

telegram_send used the HTML mode, so a table sent by the agent to a chat
silently arrived mangled with no error logged. It now calls the same
send_rich_markdown_id as the agent's own replies, so both paths behave
identically and there is one set of telemetry.

Headings still do not render under markdown; that is the remaining half
of #871 and needs converting them to bold before send.

fix(generate_image): always give a generated image an extension (#889)

A caller-supplied filename was used verbatim, so one without an extension
wrote an extensionless file into ~/.opencrabs/images/. Only the
auto-generated fallback ever got .png.

Downstream consumers identify images by extension. generate_document
later failed with "not a decodable PNG/JPEG ... The image format could
not be determined" on exactly such a path, and that counted against
generate_document in the flakiest list rather than against whatever named
the file. The tool was working: load_image exists to reject bad input
loudly instead of letting docx-rs panic.

A missing extension now defaults to .png. An explicit one is preserved,
including a dotted name the caller chose deliberately, and a blank name
still falls back to a uuid rather than producing a bare ".png".

fix(config_manager): resolve nested paths and child names to their section (#889)

Config is nested but read_config rendered only the first level, so the
paths people actually write were rejected. Every recorded failure was one
of `providers.stt`, `stt` or `telegram` — the real shapes in config.toml.
Requiring the caller to split them was the tool's problem, not theirs.

A dotted path now takes its head (`providers.custom.modelstudio` ->
providers) and a known child maps to its parent (`telegram` -> channels,
`stt` -> providers). An unknown section still fails, so resolution cannot
silently accept nonsense, and the error now explains the rule instead of
printing a bare list of names.

RSI had already tried to fix this from the other end by writing a brain
rule listing the valid sections. That is guidance papering over an
interface gap: the rule decays and costs context on every turn, while
accepting the path does not.

fix(slash_command): resolve skills and the /onboard:<topic> form (#889)

Every recorded slash_command failure was the tool being unable to see
what it was asked about, not a tool failing.

handle_user_command consulted commands.toml only, so no skill could ever
resolve. `/servers` and `/channels` are skills on disk and reached the
"Unknown command" arm for that reason alone. Skills are now looked up by
slash_name before a command is declared unknown, and the error says all
three sources were checked.

The dispatch matched the bare `/onboard`, so `/onboard:voice` and
`/onboard:channels` — the shapes actually typed — fell through. Both the
bare word and the colon form now reach the same arm, and the guard is
narrow enough that `/onboarding` is not captured by it.

`/skills` joins the guidance arm beside /plan and /cowork: a real TUI
command this tool cannot execute, which was erroring rather than saying so.

fix(background): clear the running indicator before delivering (#896)

mark_finished sat behind the enqueue callback, so the "running" badge on
the input border outlived the work by however long delivery took. On a
task killed externally the user saw the agent confirm it had stopped
while the indicator still showed it running with a climbing timer.

The task is over the moment the process exits, so the badge clears there.
mark_finished only mutates the in-memory map, so moving it ahead of the
callback cannot change what gets delivered or when.

fix(tui): keep a deliverable report visible when its turn folds (#904)

visible_when_folded kept exactly one assistant row per turn, the single
final_idx. A turn that produced a real report and then said anything after
it therefore folded the report away and exposed the trailing remark
instead, so the completion looked eaten. It was in the store the whole
time, just hidden.

Pressing Esc on a follow-up suggestion appeared to cause this. It did not;
it only revealed it, which is why the first two diagnoses of this issue
were wrong.

An assistant row carrying a GFM table and real bulk now survives the fold
alongside the final answer. Only ever shows more, never less: a row that
already qualified is unaffected, and prose without a table is untouched.
Both a separator row and 200+ characters are required, so a shell pipe in
a sentence and a two-cell scrap are both excluded.

fix(analytics): record the active model on the primary provider path (#905)

Analytics attributed tool executions and phantom detections to "unknown"
because the recording sites sourced the model from active_subprovider_model(),
which returns None while the primary provider is active. That method is a
fallback-engaged signal for the footer indicator, not the current model. With a
NULL model column, the COALESCE(model, 'unknown') queries bucketed every row
under "unknown", collapsing Model reliability into a single row and emptying the
Phantoms per-model breakdown.

Use the existing provider_model_for_session() helper, already used for the
provider name on the line above each site, at the seven recording sites: the
streaming-recovery and phantom emitters and the four tool_executions recorders
in tool_loop.rs, plus the parallel-tools recorder. It resolves the per-session
model pick, then the active sub-provider, then default_model().

active_subprovider_model() semantics are unchanged; its None-on-primary is
load-bearing for the footer indicator. Historical "unknown" rows are left as
written; new rows record the real model.

fix(phantom): catch the shipped-and-tracked completion claim (#903)

"The work is shipped and tracked" closed a turn as a summary of work
done. The completion_claims list covered the concrete forms — "fixed the
file", "changes applied" — but not the abstract summary, which is the
shape a turn reaches for when wrapping up.

Added with equivalents in all six language files, per the rule that
phrases live in every phantom_lang TOML and are scanned across all of
them rather than through language detection.

The detector still requires zero tool calls, so a turn that genuinely
shipped is unaffected.

fix(sanitize): remove reasoning blocks on delivery, not just their markers (#903)

strip_llm_artifacts handled `<!-- reasoning -->…<!-- /reasoning -->` by
delegating to strip_html_comments. Those are two SEPARATE self-closed
comments, so the markers were deleted and the prose between them survived
as ordinary message text. The agent's own deliberation shipped to
Telegram and the TUI as if it were the answer.

Worse than untidy: leaked narration is written in the past tense about
work done, so it fed claim-shaped text into the phantom detectors' input
and could get a turn flagged for narration that should never have been
delivered.

hoist_reasoning_blocks already removed the whole block correctly. It was
only ever called on the context-rebuild path (tool_loop.rs:745), never on
delivery. It now runs first in strip_llm_artifacts, ahead of the generic
comment sweep, with the hoisted text discarded: this function's contract
is text safe to show a user, and callers needing the reasoning call hoist
directly.

A stray unclosed marker still falls through to the generic sweep, so a
truncated stream cannot take the answer with it.

chore: local cross-compilation setup for unreleased dev binaries

Cross.toml and a build script so a dev drop can be produced without
spending GitHub Actions minutes. CI is unaffected: release.yml builds
natively per platform and never invokes cross, so Cross.toml is inert
there.

Records the blockers found getting it working, each solved: the cross
image has no arm64 manifest so DOCKER_DEFAULT_PLATFORM must force amd64;
libasound2-dev and libssl-dev are absent from the stock images, which the
GitHub runners already carry; and 0.2.5's default image ships an OpenSSL
that openssl-sys rejects, so the image is pinned to main.

Builds 4 of the 5 release targets. Windows needs an MSVC linker, which
does not exist on macOS.

fix(session_context): pin the concurrency fix and clean up temp files (#906)

#853 landed the atomic write and left two gaps its own review raised.

The concurrency test it proposed but did not write now exists, and it
reproduces: against the old `fs::write` it fails with "EOF while parsing
a value", against rename it passes. Payload sizes alternate deliberately,
since a shorter write must land over a longer one for the tail to survive
and the race to appear at all. A reader runs alongside the writers, which
is what catches the mixed state.

A failed rename no longer strands its temp file beside the store. Cleanup
is best-effort and never masks the rename error, which is the failure the
caller needs to see.

The comment now states what "atomic" actually guarantees: against
concurrent writers, not against power loss, since there is no fsync before
the rename. Acceptable for a transient store, worth saying so the next
reader does not assume durability.

docs(readme): document the safety gates (#907)

~/.opencrabs/safety/ shipped as a runtime-editable config surface with no
README coverage at all, while config.toml, commands.toml, tools.toml and
usage_pricing.toml each have their own section. The files were
discoverable only by reading source.

Documents all three: bash_blocklist.toml, brain_verify.toml and
ralph_loop.toml, with the real shapes taken from the files on disk rather
than invented examples.

States the governing principle once — the hardcoded Rust layer is an
immovable floor and these only ever add on top — and the sharp edges a
user will otherwise hit: overrides are the only allow-construct and are
evaluated first, substring matching has no word boundaries so a short
pattern over-blocks, and a brain-file write that violates a required rule
is rolled back rather than warned about.

Also states where the floor does NOT exist: an unparseable ralph_loop.toml
leaves completions unverified, unlike the blocklist which degrades to the
compiled-in rules.

docs(readme): document the epistemic engine and define OODA/BDI (#907)

The engine shipped with no README coverage, and the OODA/BDI vocabulary
it introduces appeared in seven source files and nowhere in the docs, so
a reader met terms like "Orient gate" with no definition anywhere.

Documents the four confidence levels, the belief store at
~/.opencrabs/brain/epistemic/beliefs.toml with its real shape taken from
disk, and the [epistemic] config section.

Leads with why it exists rather than what it stores: most agent failures
are confident claims about things never checked, and a completed task is
recorded as uncertain unless something actually verified it. "I finished
the task" and "the tests passed" are different claims.

Defines OODA and BDI once, before the gate names that assume them, and
explains the two design choices a reader would otherwise find surprising:
decay exists because an unverified assumption gets less trustworthy with
age, and contradiction detection flags both beliefs rather than letting
the last writer win.

docs(readme): document the Ralph loop, and correct an inert config key (#907)

Adds the Ralph loop subsection: the gate accepts `success` only when the
task type's verification commands exit zero, max_iterations caps retries
so an exhausted task is blocked rather than retried identically, and
criteria_policy decides what happens when declared criteria have nothing
verifying them.

Also corrects the Safety Gates section, which documented
`[forward].verification_required` as if it were live. It is not. Checking
what RalphLoopConfig actually parses shows only `[forward].max_iterations`
and the whole `[verification]` table are read; `[reverse]`, `[defaults]`
and the remaining `[forward]` keys are inert.

That distinction is called out explicitly, because the file ships with
more sections than the code consumes and the trap is specific: the gate
reads `[verification].task_type_commands`, NOT
`[forward].verification_commands`, so editing the latter does nothing.

docs(readme): refresh Mission Control, TTS and redaction sections (#907)

Mission Control's Analytics description predated the phantom-detection
panel, per-model reliability rows, stream-recovery counters and the
D/W/M/All window tabs. The tabs matter enough to say why they exist: a
fixed 30-day view hides a tool that has already recovered.

OpenAI TTS onboarding gained a voice picker and its own key field. The
precedence rule is the part users cannot guess, so it is stated plainly:
providers.tts.openai wins over providers.openai, entering a key here
writes to the TTS-specific slot and can never overwrite the chat
provider's key, and a blank field means no key is reachable rather than
one being inherited silently.

Redaction gained the provider-token shape (`<digits>:<opaque>`), quoted
values and bare sensitive names. Each says what it fixes, since "quoted
secrets are redacted" is only meaningful alongside the fact that a quote
previously terminated the match and let the commoner form through.

docs(brain): require the plan tool when exploring, and persist structured output

Three additions to the plan-mode preamble.

When to reach for the tool: exploring a codebase to decide what to change,
or planning work about to be executed, warrants the plan tool rather than
a chat summary or a mental list. The trigger is the shape of the work,
not whether the user said "plan" — multi-file changes and anything
describable in steps qualify.

Write the plan in full. A design .md is not an outline: problem, target
state, every step with the file it touches, what could break, how each
step is verified. Summarising to look concise defeats the point, since
the user is approving a design they cannot otherwise see. Vagueness is
the enemy, not length.

Structured output is a file. Any plan, PRD, report, audit or design doc
must be written to .md as well as shown, with the path given. A message
scrolls away; a file survives the session and can be re-read, diffed and
handed on. If the user will want it tomorrow, it exists as a file or it
does not exist.

fix(config): say what failed on reload, and name a write race as transient

The warning claimed config.toml failed to parse and told the user their
edits were not active. It gave no reason, and it fired when the file was
valid: opening keys.toml triggers a reload, and the actual error was
"TOML parse error at line 1, column 1" — the signature of reading an
EMPTY file, not a syntax error in the content.

Config writes are not atomic (eight fs::write call sites), so a reader
landing between truncate and write sees zero bytes. The user was being
sent to hunt a typo in a file that parses cleanly.

The load failure reason is now kept rather than logged and discarded, and
the message reports it. A "line 1, column 1" error is reported as a write
race with the file described as almost certainly fine, so it is no longer
indistinguishable from a genuine broken edit, which gets the full path and
the parse error instead.

Does not fix the race itself: that needs the atomic write pattern already
merged for the context store in 8b7f8bfe.

fix(config): make every config write atomic (#911)

fs::write truncates at open and then writes, so between those two steps
the file is zero bytes on disk. The watcher watches config.toml, keys.toml
and commands.toml, and any event on any of them triggers a full
Config::load(). A load landing in that window read nothing and reported a
perfectly valid config.toml as broken — opening keys.toml with no changes
was enough to produce the warning.

"TOML parse error at line 1, column 1" was the tell: that is an empty
read, not a syntax error in the content.

atomic_write writes a uniquely-named temp file in the same directory then
renames, so a reader sees either the old file or the new one. All 13 call
sites converted: 12 in loader.rs including write_key and write_array, 1 in
io.rs. A failed rename removes its temp file rather than stranding it
beside the config, and never masks the rename error.

Same pattern as the session context store.

A custom provider with no name silently dropped the ENTIRE provider write

while the wizard reported success. A first-time user configured a
provider, saw no error, and ended up with nothing saved.

The guard's reasoning was right: an empty name formats the section as
`providers.custom.` and would corrupt config.toml. The failure mode was
wrong. It now returns an error naming what is missing and what to do
about it, rather than discarding what was just typed and calling it

Every apply_config caller now surfaces the exact error to the user:

- the cancel path logged only, which is the worst place to stay quiet

- the brain-generation path logged only

feat(channels): add /restart and /exit

Neither existed. /exit was in one place only, the headless CLI REPL at
src/cli/commands.rs:1080, and /restart was nowhere, so a daemon could not
be stopped or cycled without shell access to the host machine.

Restarting reuses trigger_restart(), which /evolve already relies on: the
launching alias never has to be known because the shell expanded it before
the process existed, so args() holds that expansion and current_exe() holds
the binary it resolved to. exec() then replaces the process in place,
keeping the pid, descriptors, terminal and environment.

Both announce themselves and wait for the notice to flush before acting,
since once the process is gone nothing is left to report a failure. Neither
emits a separate acknowledgement, which would race the shutdown.

Windows has no exec(), so it spawns the replacement and exits rather than
logging that a restart is impossible. trigger_restart() now returns its
error instead of swallowing it, so a failed /evolve restart says so.

from another, failing on files the plan never touched.

Every other tool resolves this per session: tool_loop.rs:1065 builds the
context from a per-session handle and bash.rs:479 spawns with current_dir.
This path shelled out around ToolExecutionContext entirely, even though
context.working_dir() was already in scope at the call site.

The worse case was the quiet one: with a clean launch directory the gate
reports success for a repo it never inspected.

verify_with already takes the runner as an injected seam, so the verdict
logic is untouched.

feat(packaging): Homebrew tap

Installing meant cargo install (needs a Rust toolchain) or downloading a
release asset by hand. The release already publishes per-platform archives
containing the binary and the bundled rtk, which is the shape a formula
consumes, so nothing about the build changes.

Three pieces were missing. Releases emitted no sha256, and Homebrew
verifies every archive against one and refuses to install on a mismatch,
so a formula cannot reference an asset without it. The formula itself had
nowhere to live that would not drift from the release. And a tag changes
four URLs and four hashes, which is not something to maintain by hand: a
stale hash is a hard install failure, not a fallback.

The template in packaging/ is the source of truth and the tap repo is
generated from it. Rendering is a script rather than inline YAML so it can
be run locally against a published release, and it fails loudly on a
missing checksum or an unreplaced placeholder rather than emitting a
formula that breaks on a user's machine.

The tap job skips when HOMEBREW_TAP_TOKEN is absent, so a fork still
releases normally.

Verified against the real v0.3.78 assets: renders correctly and passes
brew style with no offenses.

fix(telegram): retry rate-limited rich sends and stop losing the error

A reply containing a table rendered in the TUI and never arrived on
Telegram. The last log entry for it was the 429 warning, with no success,
no failure and no fallback after it.

Three things combined to hide it.

The 429 path retried once. Telegram hands out multi-second waits under
load, and the observed retry_after was 25s, so a single retry lands inside
the same window it was told to wait for and the send is abandoned while
still rate limited. It now retries up to three times honouring the
server's delay, capped at 30s per wait, because blocking a delivery longer
than that is worse than falling back.

The retry rebound status, text and parsed inside the if block. Those
bindings fell out of scope at the end of it, so the bail afterwards
reported the ORIGINAL 429 rather than what the retry actually hit. The
error now always describes the last attempt.

The command reply path discarded the error with .is_ok(), leaving no trace
that rich was tried at all and making a fallback indistinguishable from a
clean rich send. Both outcomes are logged.

Nothing changes on the success path: a rich send that works behaves
exactly as before. Only the failure and retry paths differ.

fix(telegram): suppress prose on a react-only turn

A turn that answered with a reaction and no prose delivered the model's
internal deliberation as the message body, ending with its own conclusion
that react-only was correct. No completion followed because there was
never a completion to send.

This is the degenerate form of reasoning leaking into an answer. A turn
whose intended output is a reaction has no prose at all, so its content
channel holds reasoning and nothing else. There is no answer for the
reasoning to be appended to and nothing to fall back on once it is
removed, which is why the leak is total rather than partial.

The prompt tells the model to output ONLY the directive when reacting, so
a directive arriving with prose is a contract violation. That makes the
decision structural: a react directive plus no tool work is react-only,
whatever the content channel happens to contain. Nothing inspects the
prose to decide whether it reads like reasoning, because the leaked text
carries no markers and classifying it would eventually suppress a real
answer.

Work turns are untouched. A turn that ran tools and produced a summary
alongside a reaction still delivers that summary, and the existing
no-completion fallback for work turns is unchanged.

Leaked prose also suppresses the dropped-request notice: it is proof the
model reasoned its way to a deliberate react-only, so reporting the turn
as abandoned would be wrong.

This is why the local build-from-source passed and CI did not: no sandbox

fix(usage): group models by punctuation-insensitive identity

One model reported with two spellings appeared as two top-level rows, each
carrying part of its spend, so its real total was never shown in any view
that groups by model. The two differed by a single hyphen after the vendor
prefix.

The canonical form already existed. is_cosmetic_alias_of_parent reduced
names to lowercased ASCII alphanumerics, under which both spellings are
identical, but it only decided whether to hide a CHILD beneath a parent.
The group key came from normalize_model_for_grouping, which strips a .gguf
suffix and quantization suffixes and leaves punctuation alone, so the two
spellings produced two unrelated groups and neither was ever the other's
child. The alias check never ran on them.

canonical_model_key so both call sites share one definition rather than
drifting.

The key is unreadable by design, so each group remembers the spelling to
display: whichever variant carries the most tokens, i.e. the form the model
is actually known by rather than the typo that split it.

Only punctuation and case collapse. A preview suffix, a dated snapshot, a
version bump and a tier change all differ in alphanumerics and stay
separate, which the tests assert directly.

A first-time onboard landed on custom.lm_studio instead of the provider

Two causes. The shipped config.toml.example enabled providers.xiaomi and

fix(config): stop config loads from racing on shared state

Two defects made the suite order-dependent: a test asserting on its own
config load passed alone and failed when the full suite ran.

Consume-once flags. `Config::load()` recorded "I recovered from
last-known-good" in a process-wide AtomicBool that `was_recovered()` read
with `swap(false)`. Whichever thread called the accessor first took the
signal away from everyone else, so a caller could recover and be told it
had not. Replaced with `ConfigLoadStatus`, returned by value from
`load_with_status()`, so the outcome belongs to the load that produced it
and cannot be observed or cleared by anyone else. The startup notification
reads `first_load_status()`, which is a write-once latch and survives being
read. `was_recovered`, `was_autofixed` and `recovery_reason` are gone.

Reads that wrote. Schema migration ran inside `load_inner`, so every
`Config::load()` could rewrite config.toml, including loads from background
threads and from code that only wanted to look at a value. Migration is now
an explicit startup step via `migrate_config_files()`, called from the CLI
config load and from the per-profile daemon.

Tests that need their own config home now scope it with
`with_home_override`, a task-local that no other thread can see, instead of
pointing $HOME at a tempdir. $HOME is process-global: an unrelated test
loading config during that window resolved into the tempdir and repaired
and rewrote the deliberately broken fixture, which is how a test could fail
on a file it had just written itself.

The config suite ran 25 consecutive times green where it previously failed
on runs 1, 3 and 24.

fix(provider): report the models a fallback swap actually used

The swap alert in chat and the footer disagreed about the pair. The footer
reads the session's resolved provider and model and was right; the alert
was wrong.

`FallbackProvider::promote` built the event from `default_model()` on both
the outgoing and incoming provider. Neither is necessarily what ran: a
session pinned to a non-default model via the model picker keeps that model,
and a fallback that supports it receives it unremapped. So the alert could
name two models that no request ever carried, next to a footer showing the
real ones.

`promote` now takes the model the failing request carried and the model the
succeeding request was sent with, after any remap. Both call sites in
`complete` and `stream` have those exact values in hand.

`force_next_fallback` has no request in flight, so it takes the session's
current model from the caller instead of inventing one; the tool loop passes
`provider_model_for_session`. The model it moves TO is still the promoted
provider's default, which is what an unremapped request will land on, and
that is now stated in the doc comment rather than left implied.

fix(onboarding): keep asking until setup is actually finished

A user with claude-cli installed landed straight in chat with no provider
and no model. Onboarding never ran.

`is_first_time()` asked "could some provider serve a request right now?"
and treated yes as "the user completed setup". Those are different
questions. CLI providers need no API key, so a single `enabled = true`
section left by a partial run or a hand edit answered yes, and the wizard
disappeared while nothing else had been configured.

Completion is now a recorded fact rather than an inference, kept in
~/.opencrabs/onboarding.json alongside the step the user was last on and
the flow they picked. The gate reads the marker. It is written only where
`apply_config` actually succeeded, so the path that saves nothing no longer
counts as finishing.

Installs that predate the file have no marker, and sending someone who
genuinely finished back through the wizard would be its own bug. They get
one migration check, stricter than the one it replaces: an enabled provider
AND a model chosen for it. An enabled CLI provider with no model — the
reported case — does not qualify. The verdict is recorded so it is decided
once.

An interrupted run resumes at the step it left rather than restarting, and
says which steps are still outstanding, correctly for the quick or advanced
flow. Progress is recorded only during a genuine first-time run: a
`/onboard` re-run by a finished user has nothing to resume, and the gate
would never read it.

test: hold the claude-cli discovery inputs still while comparing them

`claude_cli_menu_matches_provider_supported_models` and
`claude_cli_trait_supported_models_uses_discovery` each evaluate discovery
twice and assert the two results match. `available_models()` composes from
the learned-model cache and from ~/.claude.json, both process-global, so a
`clear_learned_models()` or a $HOME override landing between the two calls
changed the answer and the test failed on a difference neither side caused.

The mutating tests already had a lock, but a lock private to their own file:
it serialised them against each other and not against anyone reading the
cache. That is the same mistake HOME_ENV_LOCK's comment documents, so the
same fix applies — promote it to a shared MODEL_CACHE_LOCK that readers take
too. The two readers also take HOME_ENV_LOCK, since discovery reads
~/.claude.json through dirs::home_dir(). Nothing else takes both, so there is
no lock ordering to deadlock on.

The invariant is unchanged: the menu and the provider must read the same
discovery function, and neither may drop a built-in model name.

test: match the empty-custom-name sentinel to the guard it protects

The sentinel greps apply_config for an empty-name guard ahead of the
`providers.custom.{}` section format. It demanded the pre-#914 shape:
`custom_name.is_empty()` followed by `write_provider = false`.

#914 replaced that with a stricter guard — `custom_name.trim().is_empty()`
and `return Err(...)` — because disabling the write and carrying on is the
exact behaviour #914 removed: the whole provider write was dropped with only
a warning while the wizard reported success, so a user configured a custom
provider, saw no error, and had nothing saved.

So the test was failing against a guard stronger than the one it asked for,
and satisfying it as written would have meant reintroducing the regression.
It now anchors on either spelling of the name check and requires the early
`return Err(`, so a revert to the silent-drop shape fails it. Production
code is unchanged.

The plan gate returns RequireApproval for bash/spawn_agent during

Both card renderers emit the checklist identically, as bare newlines. In classic ParseMode::Html that IS the line break, so the classic card was correct. sendRichMessage renders real HTML, where a newline is ordinary whitespace and collapses, so the rows ran together. da8afe5c fixed exactly this for prose by wrapping paragraphs in

for the rich target. It did not convert the other three section types, so within one rich card the prose was

-wrapped while the title separator, the checklist rows and the goal separator were still bare newlines. Half a card converted. The reason it could be half-converted is that render_plan_card chose the line-break convention in four independent places: title hardcoded, prose across four match arms split between two renderers, checklist hardcoded, goal style-dependent. Nothing made them agree. Sections now describe what they are — a Line that must occupy its own line, already block-level Block markup, or the classic-only gap before the goal — and serialize_card commits them to one target's dialect. That is the single place a convention is chosen, so a new section cannot pick the wrong one because sections no longer pick. The rich serializer wraps Line in

fix(channels): resume a background task on the surface that owns the session

A long command backgrounded from a channel finished, the agent resumed the
turn and wrote the full report, and the channel user never saw it. The
answer went to the TUI instead, so from the channel side it looked like the
agent had died mid-task.

Each surface builds its own BackgroundTaskManager from its own enqueue
callback, so a completion followed whichever service EXECUTED the command.
Channels do have a resume path that delivers properly, but a channel session
opened in the TUI runs on the TUI's service, so the TUI's callback fires and
the channel path is bypassed entirely. Logs for the reported session show the
Telegram resume producer handling it repeatedly, then the TUI producer taking
over and no channel delivery following either resume turn.

Delivery is now chosen by session rather than by executor. A channel claims
its session when it binds it, and the manager resolves that route first,
falling back to the executing surface's callback when nothing claims the
session so TUI-local and CLI-local backgrounding is untouched.

The decision is a pure resolve_route function rather than a branch inside the
spawn closure, so the property that was wrong is the thing under test.

Telegram, Discord, Slack and WhatsApp all claim their sessions on the same
inbound path that already registers the chat for approval routing.
Re-registration is idempotent, which is what a reconnect needs.

fix(agent): adopt the provider's token count on every response, not only on large drift

The context footer moved down between consecutive turns of the same session
with nothing removed from context, wandering over a ~20K band instead of
climbing as history accumulated.

base_context_tokens() returns 0 and documents the contract: real-time data
only, every footer shows the provider's reported value verbatim. The
calibration broke that. The write-back sat inside the `drift > 5000` branch
that exists for the over-reporting guard, with no else, so a report agreeing
within 5000 tokens was never adopted and the count stayed on the local
tiktoken estimate.

The displayed number therefore alternated between two measurement systems:
provider truth on big-drift turns, a drifting tiktoken estimate on the rest.
tiktoken is an OpenAI BPE and does not match other vendors' tokenizers, so
the estimate wandered in a content-dependent direction until it crossed the
threshold and snapped back. A sawtooth, which is why it could fall.

Rejecting an implausible report and declining to adopt a plausible one are
different decisions. The drift floor now gates only the rejection.

This is not display-only: context.token_count feeds the compaction budget,
so a stale count delays or triggers compaction at the wrong point.

The policy moves out of the tool loop into evaluate_token_report, a pure
function returning Adopt / RejectImplausible / BelowSanityFloor /
ImplausibleDrop. Each guard that was an unnamed inline condition is now a
named outcome that gets logged, and the property that was wrong is directly
testable.

Cost accounting was never affected: the DB input_tokens column already used
last_iter_input_tokens, the provider's real last-iteration prompt size.

fix(slack): fold between-tool narration into the collapsible step group

Slack showed the agent's thinking between tool calls as ordinary top-level
messages, sitting in the channel next to real replies. Telegram already
folds the same content into its flow block; Slack posted it outside the
group it belongs to.

Two mechanisms produced it. IntermediateText was posted with its own
chat_post_message, and GroupEntry modelled only tool rows so there was
nowhere else for a narration line to go. Separately, the empty-final guard
keeps every intermediate as the visible answer when the final response is
empty, so on those turns the narration became the reply permanently: that
path skips the delete-non-matching-intermediates step the normal path runs.

GroupEntry becomes an enum of Tool and Note, so one collapsible block
carries the interleaved sequence in the order it happened. The summary
counts steps as well as tool calls once the two differ, because "3 tool
calls" beside five folded lines does not describe what is inside. Notes
never count as running or failed; a note is a record of something already
said, and counting it would leave a finished group reporting a running step.

The post-or-update logic was inline in the ToolStarted arm and is now
sync_step_group, shared by both kinds of step, so narration and tools cannot
drift apart in how they reach the channel.

With narration no longer a standalone message the empty-final guard has
nothing stray left to promote, and the per-turn burst of chat_delete calls
that used to clean it up is gone with it.

Not addressed: whatever upstream produces a completed turn with empty final
text. That is what makes the guard fire, and it is worth its own look.

fix(tools): resolve /models target from the registry, never a hardcoded list

The agent-tool `/models` picked its write target from a hand-written chain of
six provider names, then fell through to "first enabled custom provider". The
registry knows twenty-two. So a user on any of the other sixteen had
default_model written into an unrelated section, and an explicit
`<provider>/<model>` prefix was ignored entirely — including between two
custom providers, which is what #939 reported.

The chain also tested `enabled` alone, never the API key, so an
enabled-but-keyless section outranked a fully configured one.

Resolution now goes through the same helpers the channel path uses:
parse_pair for the prefix, is_known_provider_name to decide whether the
prefix is real, active_provider_and_model otherwise, and config_section for
the section to write. One implementation of one decision instead of two, and
the surviving one is the tested one.

A slash alone still cannot mean a prefix, because OpenRouter model ids are
vendor/model. A prefix counts only when it names a provider the registry
knows. Where a vendor and a provider share a name the prefix wins, matching
the channel path exactly; the escape hatch is to name the provider
explicitly, openrouter/anthropic/claude-x.

When no target resolves the tool now returns an error naming what it could
not place, instead of writing the model somewhere and reporting success.

The user-facing /models on channels was never affected: it goes through
direct_model_switch, which already parsed the pair correctly. Only the
agent-tool path was wrong.

fix(models): a provider prefix must name a section the user declared

`/models <provider>/<model>` decided whether the prefix was a provider by
asking the registry of everything this software supports. That is the wrong
question. `anthropic` is a provider id AND an OpenRouter vendor, so
`anthropic/claude-sonnet-4` was read as a provider prefix whether or not the
user had an Anthropic section, and the channel path then failed later inside
create_provider_by_name with an error about reloading rather than about the
name.

The right question is whether THEY configured it, which both surfaces now
ask via ProviderConfigs::is_declared. The same input means the provider when
a section exists and is a clear error naming the qualified alternative when
it does not. Declared, not enabled: naming a provider explicitly is how you
point at one that is not active, so requiring enabled would break the case
the prefix exists for.

is_declared resolves aliases through the provider registry rather than
matching field names, so `claude_cli` and `claude-cli` both land and adding a
provider needs no second edit here. It also covers codex, bedrock and vertex,
which utils::providers::config_for silently misses.

The channel error text already promised "it must be a configured provider
section". This is the check finally matching what it claimed.

feat(sessions): hide and expire spawned sub-agent sessions

Every spawn_agent creates a session titled `subagent: {label}`, and nothing
ever reads it again. They accumulated forever with their messages, tool
executions and on-disk plan files, and cluttered the session list in the
meantime.

Two behaviours. They are hidden from session lists from the moment they
exist, since a sub-agent session is an implementation detail of one tool call
and a busy turn creates several. And they are purged once past
agent.subagent_session_ttl_days, default 7, where 0 keeps them forever. User
sessions are never in scope: the sweep matches the title prefix only.

The hide filter admits NULL titles explicitly. `NULL NOT LIKE 'subagent:%'`
is NULL, which SQLite treats as false, so the obvious predicate would have
made every untitled session disappear from the list.

Purge is a real delete, unlike the existing delete(), which archives the row
so usage joins still resolve. Eleven tables carry a session_id and only two
declare ON DELETE CASCADE, so the other nine are listed explicitly and
deleted in one transaction. A test seeds one of them and asserts it is gone,
so adding a table without listing it fails rather than leaking quietly.

Plan files resolve through the session's project, so each session's paths are
read before its row is deleted; afterwards the lookup would fall back to the
wrong directory and leave the files behind.

SessionListOptions gained a field rather than defaulting, so the compiler
named all eight call sites instead of letting them inherit a behaviour change
silently.

fix(telegram): follow a group that migrated to a supergroup

A basic group that upgrades to a supergroup gets a new chat id. Nothing
followed it, so the config kept the dead key and menu registration
re-hammered it once per allowed user per refresh — 364 warnings in one day
for a single group — while that group never got its menus.

migrate_to_chat_id appeared exactly once in the tree, in a list of field
names in raw_updates.rs, and was never read. The recovery needs no update
handler and no extra API call: Telegram returns the replacement inside the
failure text, "The group has been migrated to a supergroup with ID #-100…",
so the call that failed carries its own fix.

menu_scope gains migrated_to() to parse it, and the menu loop moves the
config section to the new id and skips the rest of that group, since every
member call would fail the same way on a dead id.

rename_section refuses a destination that already exists. If the supergroup
registered itself in the meantime that entry is the live one, and overwriting
it with the stale copy would undo whatever has been configured since.

Non-migration failures are unchanged: the parse returns None for them, so an
ordinary transient error can never move a live group's settings onto a
different key.

fix(onboarding): window the provider list so the fields below stay reachable

fix(agent): report retries when the turn fails, not only when it succeeds

A turn spent minutes retrying a timing-out provider and showed one folded
"Timed out" block and an error, with no retry line anywhere. From outside it
read as a single long hang rather than repeated attempts.

The retries happened and were recorded. ProviderError::Timeout is retryable
and custom_openai_compatible pushes every attempt into retry_notices for
exactly this purpose. There was one drain, and it sat below the seven
failure exits, so it was reachable only when the provider call succeeded.
The comment above it says the point is to let the user see the resilience
working; the placement showed it when it did not matter and hid it on the one
occasion someone is staring at an error wondering whether anything happened.

Draining is now emit_retry_notices, called from the success path and from
every failure exit. Putting it in a named function rather than repeating the
loop is the point: a new exit that forgets it is a visible omission, and
seven copies of the same block is how the original ended up covering only
one path.

It also drains when no progress callback is wired. The notices otherwise sat
in the provider's buffer until some later successful turn drained them and
rendered retries belonging to a turn that had already ended.

fix(telegram): join a client-split long message before answering it

A message too long for one send is split by the Telegram client into
several. Fragment one started a turn 7ms after arriving; fragment two landed
56ms later and was only queued for injection between tool rounds. By then the
agent was committed to answering text that visibly ended mid-sentence, so it
replied to half a message and told the user it had been cut off.

The album path already solves this shape: it debounces items so a multi-photo
album becomes one dispatch. Text never got the equivalent. The difference is
that an album carries media_group_id, while split text carries no grouping id
at all — nothing marks fragment two as a continuation, so length is the only
signal available.

Gating on length is what keeps this off the path of every normal message. A
message only waits if it actually reached the send limit, which an ordinary
one never does. Measured in UTF-16 code units, matching how Telegram counts
its own limit: a message of emoji hits the ceiling at half the char count.

Fragments are joined with a newline rather than nothing. Clients break long
text at a whitespace boundary, so the pieces are whole lines, and joining
with nothing would run the last word of one into the first of the next.

The buffer and the debounce are keyed by (chat, sender), so two people
pasting long text at once are never merged, and one person's fragment cannot
cut short another's wait.

fix(slack): do not swallow the answer when the final response is empty

A turn produced a full answer and Slack posted nothing. The step group
rendered and no reply followed; the same session in the TUI shows the
completion in full.

This is a regression from 8d4a98dc. Folding narration into the step group was
right, but the standalone posts it replaced were also feeding the empty-final
guard. sent_intermediate_ts is never populated now, so that guard's
"keep the intermediates as the visible answer" branch cannot fire and the
function returns having posted nothing and logged nothing.

The guard exists for a real case its own comment describes: the model emits
its answer mid-stream and the final response.content is an empty wrap-up.
That case is unhandled once the mid-stream text lives in the group instead of
in messages.

The step buffer is now declared outside the progress callback so the delivery
path can reach it. When the final is empty the folded narration is posted as
the answer, with the context footer, since it is the only answer there is.
Tool rows are excluded — they record what ran, not something to say back —
and whitespace-only notes yield nothing rather than a blank reply.

A turn that produces neither a final nor narration now warns. Posting nothing
silently is what let this go unnoticed.

Narration still folds whenever the final is non-empty, so the behaviour
8d4a98dc fixed is unchanged.

fix(tools): refuse a whole-file write that would clobber a concurrent edit

Several agents share one working directory by design. Every channel gets its
own service, spawn_agent hands children the parent's directory, team_create
launches a whole team into it, and agent.max_concurrent defaults to 4 — so
four writers in one tree is the shipped default before anyone opens a second
pane.

write_file replaces a file wholesale with content the agent composed from a
read in an EARLIER tool call. Anything written between that read and the
write was destroyed, silently, with nothing reported to either agent. That is
the whole of the reported failure.

edit_file was never the problem: it re-reads inside the call, so it either
applies on top of the newer content or fails to match it. Only write_file
carries stale content across tool calls.

The guard records what a session last saw for a path, on read and after its
own write, and refuses a whole-file write when the file no longer matches.
The agent re-reads and redoes the change, which it can do; what it cannot do
is notice that its write erased someone else's.

Narrow on purpose. A session that never read the file is allowed through:
write_file is documented as create-or-replace and is legitimately used to
generate a file outright. Refusing there broke test_overwrite_existing_file,
which was right to fail — that would have changed the tool's contract to
guard a case nobody reported. An agent rewriting existing source reads it
first, and that read is what arms this.

No lock, no serialisation, no worktree. The agents still run concurrently;
they just stop losing each other's work.

fix(agent): stop delivering a truncated answer as if it were finished

A turn ended mid-sentence on "Closing #947 with the full remarks:" — a colon
introducing a list that never came — and was reported as complete. The issue
was closed hours later by a different turn, so nothing was lost; the turn that
promised it simply stopped and claimed success.

The logs name the failure exactly:

  Truncation continue: joined 452 char partial with 35 char continuation
  into 452 chars

452 + 35 gave back 452. The model was asked to continue from a tail and
echoed that tail instead. join_continuation detects the echo and declines to
append it, which is right — and then returned the truncated partial, which
the caller had no way to tell apart from a successful join.

join_continuation now returns Extended or Echoed. An echo, or an empty
continuation, is a FAILED recovery: only one attempt is ever made
(truncated_mid_sentence_retry_used), so the answer is as complete as it will
get, and it is delivered with a marker saying it was cut off and asking the
user to have it finished. A warn names the sizes so the failure is
distinguishable in logs from "no continuation needed".

A restatement that reproduces the partial in full still counts as progress,
not an echo: the restart carries the whole answer rather than just the tail.

Existing behaviour is otherwise unchanged — the echo is still not appended,
and a genuine continuation still joins exactly as before.

Why no other guard caught it: the turn-end phantom verdict is gated on
tool_calls_completed_this_turn == 0, and this turn ran four iterations. A turn
that does real work and then stops mid-promise passed every check.

fix(evolve): let Homebrew upgrade a Homebrew install

opencrabs landed in homebrew-core with v0.3.79, so brew now owns the binary
for anyone who installed that way. InstallMethod had no Homebrew variant, so
a brew install fell through to PrebuiltBinary.

That path renames a downloaded GitHub asset over the running binary. In a
Cellar it SUCCEEDS, because the prefix is user-owned, which is worse than
failing: brew keeps reporting the version it installed while the file on disk
is newer, and the next unrelated brew upgrade overwrites the evolved binary
and silently puts the user back. The revert happens during some other command
days later, so nobody connects it to evolve.

InstallMethod gains Homebrew, tested before the PrebuiltBinary fallback since
a brew install is a pre-built binary in every respect except who owns it.
Detection is path-based: brew --prefix needs brew on PATH, which it often is
not in a spawned process, and costs a subprocess to answer what the path
already answers. It keys on the Cellar component rather than the prefix, so
the many hand-installed binaries in /usr/local/bin stay loose binaries.

Crash recovery had the same gap at both its branches: it offered a brew user
a raw asset download into the Cellar. Homebrew installs now decline the
per-version list, since brew serves whatever its formula points at, and the
unreachable arm is spelled out rather than folded into a catch-all so a future
variant is a compile error instead of another silent overwrite.

The new strategy lives in its own module rather than being added to a
1642-line file, and the self-contained systemd command builders moved out with
it. evolve.rs is now evolve/mod.rs at 1461 lines, with homebrew.rs and
systemd.rs beside it. The user-facing messages are pure functions so their
wording is tested without needing Homebrew installed.

feat(prompt): tell agents how to share a repo with other sessions

not do has no rule and improvises: reverting someone else's commit,

Four lines: do not rewrite commits you did not write, stage named paths,

feat(doc_parser): extract VBA macro source from macro-enabled workbooks

parse_document dumped sheet values and stopped, so the VBA project inside
an .xlsm/.xlsb/.xls was invisible: the agent could not review what a
workbook automates, nor triage a suspicious macro, which is the classic
document-malware vector. calamine already parses the CFB container behind
Reader::vba_project, so this needed no new dependency and no parser work.

Extraction lives in its own module rather than in doc_parser, which is
already 773 lines. The three macro-capable arms gain one line each; ODS
is deliberately left out because OpenDocument carries Basic, not VBA, and
calamine's Ods::vba_project is a hardcoded Ok(None).

Output is capped at 32 KB per module and 128 KB per workbook so a
macro-heavy file cannot flood the agent's context, with explicit
[truncated] and [omitted] markers rather than a silent cut. Clipping
steps back to a char boundary. An unreadable project or a module that
will not decompress is logged and skipped, never fatal: a locked VBA
project must not cost the caller the sheet data it asked for.

A macro-free workbook renders nothing at all, so its output is
byte-identical to before.

Tests build the .xlsm at run time from a vbaProject.bin vendored out of
rust_xlsxwriter's examples (MIT OR Apache-2.0, already a dependency).
calamine parses real CFB streams, so a synthetic blob will not do, and
this keeps the only committed binary to 17 KB.

fix(tui): keep the turn duration after the turn settles

While a turn streamed, the header showed a live clock. The moment it
settled the duration disappeared, so the one place a user could see how
long the work took was also the place that forgot it. Telegram never had
this: its settled tool block keeps the time, so channel users kept
information the TUI threw away.

Two unrelated sources were at play. The live header read a monotonic
Instant; the settled header re-derived the duration by subtracting the
turn's first and last message timestamps. That subtraction almost always
returns zero, because the assistant row is created at turn START and
updated in place, so it carries the same created_at as the user message
that opened the turn. Measured across the local history: 14,796 of
15,658 assistant turns share their user message's timestamp, 94.5%. The
header suppresses the field on zero, hence the vanishing act, and hence
why the ~5% that survived made it look intermittent rather than broken.

The elapsed time was already known at exactly the right moment and simply
discarded, so it is now stamped onto the assistant row at turn end and
persisted, surviving reload instead of being reconstructed from
timestamps that cannot express it. The TUI also stamps it in memory
before clearing its clock, so the duration stays put without waiting for
a reload. Timestamp subtraction remains as the fallback for rows written
before the column existed.

feat(channels,tui): honour a spoken stop, not just the bare word

Telling a running agent to stop in plain language did nothing. Every
channel gated its fast-cancel on an exact, case-insensitive match of the
bare word, so STOP with exclamation marks missed, a trailing full stop
missed, hold on and wait a sec were not vocabulary at all, and no
non-English form worked. A miss fell through to normal dispatch and
became ordinary mid-turn input, leaving it to the model to notice while
tools kept executing. The TUI had no text stop whatsoever: cancelling was
key-driven, so typing stop only added to the pile.

Detection moves into one shared module so the four channels and the TUI
cannot drift apart again. Vocabulary lives in the same six per-language
TOML tables the rest of the phrase matching uses and is scanned across
ALL of them, never behind a language guess: users are worldwide and
code-switch, and a wrong guess disarms the kill switch for exactly the
person it guessed wrong about.

The risk worth engineering around is the false positive, not the miss.
Cancelling stop the docker container would silently drop requested work,
which is worse than the bug being fixed. So single-word entries match
only a whole message while multi-word entries may also open one, since
nobody begins an instruction with hold on. Trailing address terms are
stripped first, so stop crab and hold on crabs reduce to the interrupt
while stop the bot container keeps its object and is left alone.

The TUI's 163-line cancel sequence becomes abort_active_turn, shared by
double-Escape and the typed path rather than copied, so streamed text and
tool groups still reach history before the task dies.

feat(agent): cap reasoning per turn with a token budget

A turn spent 900+ seconds and 30k+ tokens producing nothing but
reasoning. It ended with the reasoned-without-answering nudge, and the
nudge fixed it on the FIRST attempt. So the nudge is the cure, and the
defect is that we wait out an unbounded reasoning stream before applying
it. Every one of those minutes was spent travelling to a remedy that
then took one round.

thinking_loop_timeout_secs already existed at a 600s default and did not
save it. It is far above what healthy reasoning uses, it latches off for
the rest of a stream once any tool call lands, and it is armed per
request, so a turn reasoning a little under the ceiling on each of
several iterations never reaches it. That last point is why this budget
is scoped to the turn: a per-stream cap inherits the same hole. Tokens
rather than seconds because tokens describe the runaway itself, are what
providers already report, and do not punish a slow provider doing
correct work.

Default 16000, enforced when absent from config exactly as the timeout
is, overridable per provider so the one model family that runs away can
be tightened without penalising every other model. The same struct backs
the named providers and providers.custom, so one field covers both.

Enforced in the reasoning and thinking stream arms beside the repetition
guard, exiting the way that guard already does, which hands control back
to the loop and fires the existing nudge. No new escalation path and no
fallback change: walking the chain would discard a model that recovers on
the first nudge.

Scoped through a session-keyed registry rather than a task-local. The
task-local version required wrapping the turn future in a scope future,
and nesting run_tool_loop_inner one frame deeper overflowed the worker
stack in the approval tests. Keying on the session id stream_complete
already receives leaves the future shape untouched.

Documents both this and thinking_loop_timeout_secs in the README, which
described neither.

fix(agent): nudge an empty answer even when the model reasoned nothing

Turns were ending with no answer at all: the channel showed the nudge at
1/5, then a Finished card with no content and no tool calls, repeatedly,
and the counter never reached 2/5.

The trigger required an empty answer AND 40+ characters of reasoning, so
the worst response shape was the one shape that escaped it. The first
empty-with-reasoning reply nudged (1/5), the retry came back completely
silent, that reply failed the reasoning half of the check, nothing fired,
and the turn fell through and ended delivering nothing. Going quieter was
a way out of the guard.

Two things followed from that. The counter could not climb unless the
model kept reasoning verbosely on every attempt, so 1/5 was the effective
ceiling. And because the budget was never exhausted, the budget-exhausted
branch never ran, so the fallback chain was never walked either. Neither
the five retries nor the provider walk were reachable in the failing case.

The trigger is now an empty answer, full stop. CLI providers stay excluded
because they run their own loop internally, and iteration 0 stays excluded
because the opening call has not had a chance to act yet.

testable instead of buried mid-way through a very large async fn.

empty. Four independent vendors failing at once is not credible; what
they had in common was the conversation they were all sent.

The stub appended before each nudge returned a bare empty assistant
message whenever there was no reasoning to preserve. That was harmless
while only one nudge could ever fire. Once the escalation actually
reached 5/5 it left five [empty assistant] [nudge] pairs on the context,
and every fallback request was built from that same object, so all of
them answered a conversation full of empty assistant turns and failure
notices.

Both halves of never happened before follow from that. Previously the
counter was capped at 1/5, so at most one stub was appended and the
fallback chain was unreachable. Now the silent case nudges, the
escalation runs to completion for the first time, and the poisoned
context reaches every provider.

Two changes. The stub returns Option and appends nothing when there is
no reasoning, since an empty assistant message carries no information
and only corrupts the conversation. And a fallback is given the
conversation as it stood before the first nudge, because it is a fresh
attempt at the user request rather than a continuation of the dialogue
that just failed.

Both sit behind named helpers so the invariants are testable rather than
buried in the loop. Only the empty-reasoning fallback site is touched;
the four other fallback paths in this file are left alone.

sharpened instruction, while every fallback got one bare attempt and no
nudge at all. The nudge is the part that demonstrably works, and it was
the one thing fallbacks never received, so a provider that would have
answered after a single nudge was discarded on its first silent reply.

sharpened nudge between attempts and stopping the moment one produces
visible text. A hard error still abandons that provider immediately
rather than burning retries on a dead endpoint, and the quota breaker
still marks it.

Cost only lands on genuinely failing turns: the walk exits on the first
provider that answers, so a fallback that succeeds immediately still
costs exactly one call.

an incident where all four providers returned empty. That was wrong. The
cause was the per-turn reasoning budget cutting every attempt at one to

cause that outage.

since a stale name is worse than none: it labels the wrong room.

- The value is display metadata. A group title is chosen by whoever

  never reads the name. Covered by a test.

characters dropped, length bounded, truncation by character so a

nothing printable is skipped rather than written as junk.
