perf(brain): stop re-reading MEMORY.md every turn, make both paths agree (#995)

MEMORY.md reached a turn through four mechanisms added at different times
with no shared policy. One re-read and re-tokenized the whole file every
turn to extract at most 1200 characters, one existed on only one of two
otherwise identical code paths, and one inlined the entire file.

Measured on a 99 KB, 975-line, 158-section MEMORY.md, per turn: a
blocking read of all 99 KB, then two further copies of the content and
roughly 15,376 string allocations to build a word set per section.
Nothing cached, on a file that changes a few times a day.

Four changes, none of which alters which sections get selected:

Cheap rejections now precede the read. Both the system-continuation check
and the no-usable-terms check ran after the file was already in memory,
so harness continuations and messages like "ok" paid a full read to
return None.

The parse is cached behind mtime plus length, so the steady state is a
metadata stat and a set lookup per section. Length is carried alongside
mtime because mtime resolution is coarse enough that a same-second
rewrite can otherwise go unnoticed. brain_sections gained Indexed, which
holds sections with their word sets precomputed; find_sections_with now
delegates to it, so the one-shot callers are unchanged.

The read moved to tokio::fs. It was blocking I/O on an async worker,
which the indexing path in memory::index already avoids.

Both message paths now call one augment_user_message. The tool loop
appended plan reminder and recall; prepare_message_context appended only
the reminder, from an otherwise identical block. Whether memory surfaced
depended on which code path a session took, which is not a property of
the memory.

MEMORY.md also leaves BRAIN_FILES, so no surface inlines it. It is the
one brain file with no bound on its size, append-only and growing for as
long as the agent is used, and full mode put all of it in the system
prompt regardless of relevance while every other surface already treated
it as contextual.

Two tests encoded the old contract and are updated rather than removed:
one asserted full mode inlines MEMORY.md and now asserts it must not,
naming why; the core-versus-full size comparison now writes SECURITY.md
and BOOT.md, which carry the difference, so it keeps exercising something
real instead of passing on a collapsed premise.

Match precision is untouched and tracked separately. It is a real
problem, and it needs an eval set rather than a guess.

fix(brain): rank MEMORY.md recall with BM25 instead of counting shared words (#996)

Counting shared query terms fired on 89.5% of 437 real messages, because
`the`, `and`, `you` and `can` clear the length filter and two of them
co-occurring is true of almost any section. A build-failure question
retrieved a homebrew install note; a provider-config question retrieved a
bench write-up.

Six threshold variants were measured against a real 156-section
MEMORY.md. All of them traded noise against genuine recall roughly one
for one, so the parameter was never the problem.

Three changes make lexical ranking work:

BM25 weights by how much a term narrows things down, so a word present
in most sections stops counting. Dividing by query length is what gives
the trade-off a knee: without it a long message accumulates score from
many weak matches and a fixed threshold behaves like no threshold.

IDF is divided by the IDF of a term unique to one section. Without that
the score scale tracks corpus size (a unique term is worth ~2.2 in a
13-section file and ~4.7 in a 156-section one), so one threshold is
really a different threshold per workspace. This was a live bug in the
first cut: 1.5 looked right on a mature file and recalled almost nothing
on a small one.

Light suffix stripping, because `committing` did not match `commit` and
`commands` did not match `command`, which is most of what a natural
question does to the words it shares. It lifts fixture recall from 0.750
to 0.917 at unchanged false-positive rate. Not a language-aware stemmer
and not a wordlist: applied symmetrically to query and section, so a
wrong merge blunts a score rather than inventing a match.

No embeddings, deliberately. They are unavailable when vectors are off,
when the model download fails, and permanently without AVX, so depending
on them would give memory that works on one machine and not another.

Ranking lives in a new section_rank module rather than in
brain_sections: that one owns parsing, this one owns relevance.

The eval is committed and re-runnable. src/eval/recall.rs gained negative
cases, without which retrieval that fires on everything scores perfectly;
negatives are excluded from the recall average and reported as a
false-positive rate instead. The fixture is synthetic because real
messages and a real memory file cannot be committed.

Scored on the fixture: precision 0.625 to 0.917, FPR 0.417 to 0.250,
recall 1.000 to 0.917. The result is NOT a strict win and the test says
so by name: one answer in twelve is given up for the precision and the
silence. On the real corpus the same configuration takes firing on
conversational messages from 89.5% to 17.4%.

fix(brain): fold Latin diacritics in recall matching, add multilingual eval

Recall had been measured only in English while real traffic spans the six
languages the prompt analyzer supports. Scoring it across en, ru, es, pt,
fr and id found two defects, one of them in the fix for the other.

Matching was accent-sensitive. `operacion` did not reach `operación`,
`configuracao` did not reach `configuração`, `revision` did not reach
`révision`. People type without accents constantly, so the one word that
discriminates a Spanish, Portuguese or French question routinely matched
nothing and recall stayed silent. Latin diacritics are now folded before
tokenizing.

The first version of that fold silently did nothing for Cyrillic. It kept
combining marks whose base was non-ASCII, meaning to stop Russian `й`
collapsing into `и`. But the tokenizer splits on anything is_alphanumeric
rejects, and a combining mark is a nonspacing mark, so every mark the
filter deliberately kept was discarded one step later: `бой` tokenized as
`бои` and the two became the same word. The fold now recomposes to NFC,
which is what makes the ASCII-base restriction mean anything.

That one was caught by its own regression test failing, not by review.
The accent test also had to be rewritten before it was worth anything:
the first version used ordinary prose and passed BEFORE the fix, because
the surrounding words were quietly carrying the match. It now shares
every word across sections so the accented term is the only signal.

The multilingual fixture scores 1.000 precision and recall with no
false positives, 3/3 in every language. The results file says plainly
that this is a weaker result than it looks: six languages give each
topic a nearly disjoint vocabulary, so telling them apart is easy. It
establishes that no language is broken and that the English-shaped
stemmer does not damage the other five. It does not establish that
recall is as good in those languages as in English.

fix(telegram): thread wrap_p through lists, quotes, and headings in rich HTML (#997) The rich sendRichMessage dialect treats bare newlines as whitespace, so list items joined with \n collapsed into one run-on line: wrap_p was never threaded into render_list. Quote hardcoded wrap_p=false and headings had no block wrapper, so quotes and consecutive headings collapsed the same way. Wrap every list item, quote paragraph, and heading in

when wrap_p is set; classic mode output unchanged.

fix(memory): chunk documents before embedding, and make later chunks searchable (#998)

Every document was embedded as one vector covering the whole file. All
three call sites passed seq=0, pos=0 to insert_embedding, whose second and
third parameters are the chunk index and offset. qmd has shipped
chunk_document with a 15% overlap the whole time; it was simply never
called.

Two failures came out of that, and the second is the worse one.

Anything past MAX_EMBED_BYTES got a zero-length placeholder written under
the model name skipped-too-large, deliberately so it would not retry.
Measured on a real 227 MB store: 495 of 1944 vector rows were
placeholders, a quarter of everything, and MEMORY.md was among them. The
one file memory search exists to search had no semantic representation at
all, while every smaller brain file embedded fine. Not an embedding setup
problem: the local engine was running and working.

Everything under the limit collapsed into a single averaged vector, so a
document covering several topics landed as one meaningless point.
max(seq) across the entire store was 0.

Fixing the write side alone would have produced nothing, because
qmd::Store::search_vec joins vectors_vec on `d.hash || '_0'`. It can only
ever see a document's first chunk, so chunks 1..N would be embedded,
stored, and never queried. qmd is third-party and 0.3.2 is its latest
release, so vector search now reads the same tables directly through its
own read-only connection. The database is already in WAL mode, so that
reader never blocks qmd's writer. Nothing new is written or migrated, so
the shim can be deleted if qmd gains chunk support.

The new search keeps the best chunk per document rather than every
matching chunk, or one verbose file would fill every slot with its own
near-duplicates. Placeholder rows are excluded from scoring, since an
empty vector cosines to zero and would otherwise occupy a slot. Vectors
whose dimensions do not match the query are skipped rather than scored,
which is what happens when the embedding model changes.

Existing installs need the placeholders retired or the affected documents
stay excluded forever: get_hashes_needing_embedding keys on the presence
of a seq=0 row. Backfill now sweeps them first, idempotently.

The regression test places the answer in chunk 4 of 6 and was verified to
fail under qmd's join, returning chunk 0.

fix(memory): resolve the store per profile instead of caching one globally (#999)

The memory store was a single OnceCell that captured opencrabs_home() on
the first call and cached the Store for the process lifetime. The path is
profile-aware; the cache was not.

Profiles genuinely switch inside one process. cron/scheduler.rs runs each
job inside with_profile_home_async, so a job configured for profile B
executed with B's config, keys and brain files while reading and writing
profile A's memory.db, whichever profile happened to initialize first.
The turn path indexes MEMORY.md, so one profile's memory content was
written into another profile's index.

Profiles are the isolation boundary in this codebase: config, keys.toml,
brain files, sessions and the memory directory are all per-profile. The
one component holding indexed content was ignoring it.

Stores are now keyed by resolved database path. Handles are leaked to
keep the &'static return callers rely on, which is bounded and deliberate:
one entry per profile actually used, each of which lives for the process
lifetime anyway. A race between two threads opening the same path keeps
the winner rather than leaking a second handle to one file.

The guard that matters is the data test: write a document under one
profile, then assert a second profile cannot find it. Verified to fail
against the old behaviour. The two pointer-identity tests alongside it are
weaker, since under a simulated global the outcome depends on which test
initializes the cache first.

Today the visible symptom is cron polluting another profile's index. It
would become a customer-data leak the moment two profiles hold different
clients' material, which is exactly what a knowledge base introduces.

fix(memory): narrow lexical hits to the matching chunk (#1000)

After #998 the vector half ranks chunks while the lexical half still
ranked whole documents, so hybrid RRF was fusing two lists describing
different units. A hit meant "this file is relevant" and the caller
snippeted around the first occurrence of a query term, which need not be
the passage that answers the question. Worst for the case lexical search
is best at: an exact product name or error code appearing once, deep in a
long page.

Refines a document hit to its best chunk rather than building a second
FTS index. The chunk boundaries already exist and are deterministic:
chunks_for is the single place that decides them, so recomputing from the
body yields the pieces the embedder used and both halves agree without
storing anything twice. Writing chunk rows into documents_fts was the
alternative and would couple us to qmd's schema, the same coupling #998
deliberately avoided.

Scoring reuses section_rank rather than growing a second implementation,
so chunk-level lexical matching inherits the stemming and diacritic
folding. That is not incidental: an unaccented Spanish query has to reach
accented text here exactly as it does in brain-file recall, and a
separate scorer would drift out of agreement silently. Ranked gained
from_sections for this; build now delegates to it.

No score floor is applied when picking the chunk. FTS has already judged
the document relevant, so a threshold could reject every chunk and lose a
hit the lexical half had earned. None means "use the whole body", not
"irrelevant", and short documents return it since a single chunk is the
document.

results_to_tuples became a dead wrapper once its only call site moved and
was removed rather than marked allow(dead_code).

docs(eval): record what chunked embeddings changed, and what was not measured

Covers #998 and #1000. States the measured before-state from a real store
(25% of vector rows were placeholders, MEMORY.md among them, max(seq) 0)
and separates it from the token-spend assumption, which is wrong:
memory_search caps snippets at 200 characters, so per-call cost was
already small and is essentially unchanged. The indirect argument, that
better retrieval means fewer whole-file loads, is recorded as a
hypothesis rather than a result because nothing has measured it.

fix(memory): chunk the API backfill too, and sweep placeholders on that path (#1001)

#998 fixed three embed sites in embedding.rs and missed a fourth: a
separate API backfill loop in index.rs. That path still embedded whole
documents, still passed seq=0 pos=0, and still wrote a skipped-too-large
placeholder for anything over 32 KB. So on any install with
[memory.embedding] configured, nothing changed at all.

The placeholder sweep had the same shape of gap. It was wired only into
backfill_embeddings, the local path, so an API-configured install never
ran it and its existing placeholders were never retired, leaving those
documents permanently excluded from embedding. That is precisely the
failure #998 set out to fix.

Found empirically rather than by review. After the fixed binary shipped,
the live store had gone from 495 placeholders to 497 and max(seq) was
still 0: placeholders were still being ADDED. Since nothing in
embedding.rs writes them any more, grepping the string found the
remaining writer.

The miss came from trusting the issue's own wording. #998 said "all three
call sites in src/memory/embedding.rs", which came from an audit that had
looked at one module, and the fix took that at face value instead of
grepping the crate for insert_embedding.

Guard added so a fifth site cannot appear: a source scan asserting no
production code writes a skipped-too-large placeholder. Reading and
deleting them stays fine, which is what the sweep and the vector-search
exclusion do. Writing one is not, because the placeholder exists
specifically to stop a document retrying. Tests and benches are exempt
since they construct placeholders to prove they are handled. Verified by
reintroducing the offending line and watching it fail with the file and
line number.

fix(memory): own the chunker, qmd's panics on multi-byte characters (#1002)

qmd::chunk_document slices by byte index with no boundary check:

    start byte index 2240 is not a char boundary; it is inside '—'

It applies max_chars to content.len(), which is bytes, then uses the
result as a string index directly. Its break-point search does the same
with slice.len() * 7 / 10. An em dash, an accented letter, Cyrillic or an
emoji near either offset is enough. The panic fired inside a tokio worker
during backfill and took the whole process down, since a Metal assert
then failed on the abort path.

Dormant until #998, because nothing called chunk_document before.

Replaced with a chunker that works in character positions and cannot
split a codepoint. Same behaviour otherwise: paragraph, then sentence,
then line, then word breaks, an overlap so a passage spanning a boundary
survives whole in one chunk, and guaranteed forward progress even when
the requested overlap exceeds the chunk size. Sizes are now counted in
CHARACTERS, which is what a caller passing a chunk size means; under the
old code a Cyrillic document silently produced chunks half the intended
size and an emoji-heavy one a quarter. pos stays a byte offset, matching
what content_vectors already stores.

Verified against the real files that crashed the binary: MEMORY.md at
102 KB chunks into 43 pieces, and all six brain files hold their
character boundaries. A canary test pins the upstream defect, so if qmd
ever fixes it that test fails and tells whoever sees it that this module
can be reconsidered.

docs(templates): move memory-save triggers to the always-loaded file (#1003)

BOOT.md owned the memory-save trigger list, but BOOT.md is contextual: it
is loaded on first boot and on the paths that ask for it, not on every
turn. The rules that decide whether a fact gets written to MEMORY.md were
therefore absent from context for most requests, which is exactly when a
save decision comes up.

AGENTS.md is the always-loaded file, so the trigger block moves there and
BOOT.md keeps a pointer. The Owns: header no longer claims the triggers.

The governance test is flipped to match: it now asserts the triggers live
in the always-loaded file with a pointer from BOOT.md, rather than the
reverse.

fix(telegram): stop deleting a completion because the turn ran no tools (#1009)

A reply carrying a react directive had its entire text discarded whenever
the turn made no tool calls. The same turn rendered in full on the TUI, so
the answer existed and the loss was purely in Telegram delivery. Four
consecutive answers were destroyed this way in one conversation, each one
a direct reply to a question, each carrying a table that never reached the
renderer because the text was dropped before rendering was attempted.

The suppression came from #928, where a provider re-derived its reasoning
into the content channel on a turn that was meant to produce no text. That
fix could not read the prose to identify reasoning, so it used "the turn
ran no tools" as a stand-in. Tool state does not answer that question: an
answer built from analysis alone runs no tools, which is the ordinary shape
of an explanation or a follow-up.

The decision is now the contract the model is actually given, which states
both shapes: ONLY the directive is react-only, and a directive at the start
followed by text is react AND respond. Emptiness after stripping the
directive is the whole question, so it is read off the wire rather than
inferred, and delivery no longer consults tool state for it.

Reasoning reaching the content channel stays a provider-side defect. It
belongs where it originates, not in a delivery rule that deletes a
completion on suspicion: that failure is silent and total, while a leak is
merely ugly.

The #439 guard is untouched, so a work turn that reacts instead of
summarising still gets its fallback completion, and the #546 notice still
fires for a long react-only turn that produced nothing.

fix(provider): HTTP 400 failover guidance and chain-exhaustion ledger (#1006, #1007)

- agent error formatter: 4xx advice drops the useless 'try again', points
  at [providers.fallback] setup instead; chain-exhaustion ledger leads
  when present; char-safe raw truncation (no multibyte slice panic)
- FallbackProvider: complete()/stream() track tried entries and wrap the
  final error with chain_exhausted_summary via with_chain_summary, which
  keeps the error variant so upstream classification still works
- tool_loop: no-chain alerts carry no_chain_setup_guidance; the bogus
  'all providers in the chain failed' summary no longer fires when there
  is no chain at all
- tests: guidance contract + with_chain_summary variant preservation

fix(provider): route codex CLI failures into retry and fallback (#1004, #1005)

- extract classify_codex_failure: turn.failed and captured stderr route
  through one classifier (rate/quota/overload -> RateLimitExceeded,
  context-length -> ContextLengthExceeded, else retryable 500 ApiError)
- silent non-zero exits no longer die as Internal (which bypassed BOTH
  the retry budget and the fallback walk): bounded stderr tail carries
  the signal text, empty tail maps to a transient StreamError
- tests: five regression tests pinning every classification branch

feat(agent): proactive one-shot fallback chain setup suggestion (#1008)

When no fallback chain is configured, the first REAL user turn carries a
system note instructing the agent to propose the guided setup: custom
provider name, base URL, API key, live GET /v1/models fetch, model pick,
config.toml + keys.toml writes, [providers.fallback] update, /restart.

- marker file .fallback-chain-suggested in the profile home keeps it
  strictly one-shot; [System: messages never trigger it
- rides the first real turn so it lands on whichever channel the user
  is talking on (no channel-specific machinery)
- also lands the #1006 tool_loop wiring: no-chain alerts now carry
  no_chain_setup_guidance, and the chain-failed summary is skipped when
  there is no chain at all
- tests pin the decision logic, one-shot marker, and note contract
style: cargo fmt the self-healing additions (#1004, #1006, #1007, #1008)

fix(slack): stop repeating the step group's narration in the final message (#1010)

A completed turn arrived as one message holding the entire turn's per-step
narration, in call order, followed by the answer. A ten-step turn shipped
ten "let me check X" lines before the reply.

Since #943 that narration folds into the collapsible step group, which
works: mid-turn the group renders with its steps and its toggle. What no
step ever did was take the narration back out of the final body, where it
also lives, because it is assistant text like any other.

The completion path could not catch it. It reconciles standalone
intermediate POSTS by comparing the final body's hash against one
intermediate's, which fires when the model repeats a single intermediate
verbatim as its answer. Folded narration is neither: not a standalone post,
and not equal to any one intermediate since the body contains all of them.
Nothing matched, so nothing was suppressed.

The final body now drops paragraphs the group already displays. The group
holds the exact strings it folded, so the comparison is against known text
rather than a judgement about which prose reads like narration — the same
constraint #928 and #1009 settled on. A note the model reworded before
repeating is left alone: a near-match is not proof, and acting on one would
be that judgement.

The group is untouched. It is posted under its own ts, not through
sent_intermediate_ts, so it was never in the delete set and survives
completion as before.

fix(plan): receipt binding for commit claims in completions (#1011)

A completion claiming 'Committed <sha>' is a factual assertion the
type-keyed verification commands cannot see. Types without commands
downgraded to Uncertain without checking the claim, so phantom shas
passed as fact (2026-08-11 04:14 incident: task #2 claimed 7c1856c9,
which never existed).

Verify sha claims against the session repo: extract hex runs in
commit-ish context from the completion output and git cat-file -e each.
A claimed sha that does not exist rejects the completion with evidence.
Non-git working dirs skip the check; the gate respects the ralph_loop
verification.enabled flag, same surface as the type-keyed commands.

15 new tests in ralph_receipt_binding_test.rs (extraction matrix plus
live-git fixture repos). Full suite green.

Revert "fix(slack): stop repeating the step group's narration in the final message (#1010)"

This reverts commit 75e6228efe737aa2ecfe195815852902014aefe6.

Reapply "fix(slack): stop repeating the step group's narration in the final message (#1010)"

This reverts commit dd3810109d891e81f32343b9b222a0ef160dffe6.

fix(slack): match folded narration on the character stream, not on paragraphs

The first attempt at #1010 was a no-op on real data. It compared whole
paragraphs by equality, and narration is not split on paragraph boundaries:
the group note and the final body are cut at STREAM offsets, so the same
sentence is severed mid-word between them.

Observed live, where the group folded "…and it's the s" and the final body
continued "harper version of the point.": no paragraph on one side equals a
paragraph on the other, so nothing matched and the duplication survived
untouched. Whole-string and hash comparison fail on that shape for the same
reason, which is why the existing completion dedup misses it too.

Matching now runs over the sequence of non-whitespace characters, where the
split is invisible because whitespace is precisely what differs between the
two. This is the normalization Telegram already applies before comparing
(delivery.rs, `norm`) and Slack never had — Slack hashed raw bytes, so any
formatting drift missed.

Notes are consumed in fold order and consumption halts at the first note
that does not match, so a body that diverges partway keeps everything from
the divergence onward rather than skipping ahead to a later match.

Still structural: only strings the group actually folded are consumed, in
the order it folded them. Nothing is inferred from whether prose reads like
narration, per #928 and #1009.

fix(provider): persist provider response IDs in logs for request correlation (#1013)

Provider response IDs arrived and were dropped: OpenAI-compatible
response bodies carry an id field and providers may send request/trace
IDs as headers. The 2026-08-11 forensics needed ModelScope-side
correlation IDs and had nothing to work with. Persist them in logs:

- non-streaming: response_id + header request_id on the response info
  line
- streaming: header request_id extracted alongside cache_status before
  bytes_stream() consumes the headers; first SSE chunk id logged at
  MessageStart
- provider_request_id() helper for the header family (x-request-id,
  request-id, x-trace-id, traceparent), silent when absent

Logging only, no behavior change. Five unit tests in
brain_provider_response_id_test.rs.

security(channels): owner-gate user commands and skills on the catch-all arm (#975)

Every built-in slash command was individually owner-gated. The catch-all
arm that reaches commands.toml entries and skill slugs was not, and all
four channel handlers fall through to the agent with the matched body as
the prompt and no re-gate. Any allowlisted user, including a group member
auto-registered into a group allowlist, could invoke any installed skill
and have its body execute under the session's approval policy. Under
auto-approve that is full tool execution triggered by a non-owner.

The gate matches FIRST and refuses after. An unmatched slash keeps the
ordinary "Unknown command" reply, so the refusal never reveals which
commands or skills exist, and the refusal string is the built-ins' own, so
a gated user command is indistinguishable from a gated built-in.

action="system" is gated alongside action="prompt": it does not reach the
model, but it still emits bot output into the channel on a non-owner's
say-so.

The decision is split into gate_user_command, a pure function over the
matched command. match_user_command loads commands and skills from disk and
cannot be exercised in a test, which is why this path shipped without a
gate and stayed uncovered afterwards — the existing owner-gate tests only
ever passed is_owner = true.

Seven tests cover a commands.toml prompt command, a system-action command,
a skill slug, arguments not smuggling one past, the owner keeping all
three, an unmatched slash not being converted into an owner refusal, and
the refusal being byte-identical to a built-in's.

TUI dispatch is unaffected: owner by construction, separate path.

style: cargo fmt the response-id log line (#1013)

The request-id log added in 1ab6ae91 ran past rustfmt's line limit, so
`cargo fmt --check` fails on main. Wrapping only; no logic change.

Same sweep as 19bce549, which formatted the self-healing additions —
1ab6ae91 landed after it.

docs(changelog): reconstruct the v0.3.79 release notes

The v0.3.79 release run bumped the version, tagged, and pushed, but never
converted the [Unreleased] narrative into a [0.3.79] section. CI extracts
release notes from that section, so the v0.3.79 GitHub release page shipped
empty.

Reconstructed from the real v0.3.78..v0.3.79 range (67 commits, release
commit excluded per house convention): 9 features, 45 fixes, 3 docs,
9 misc. 118 files changed, +9,334 / -1,228 lines.

feat(slack): render tables and headings in Slack's own shape (#1016)

A completion carrying markdown tables shipped the pipe syntax literally,
six tables in one message, in a proportional font where no column lines up.
Headings had the same problem quietly: Slack has no heading syntax, so `##`
renders as two hashes.

Nothing downstream could rescue either. markdown_to_mrkdwn is a
character-level converter with no concept of a block, and Block Kit has no
table primitive to convert into, so by the time the text exists the table
has nowhere to go. The markdown has to stop being markdown first.

Both convert to what a person formatting for Slack writes instead. A table
becomes its first column as a bold label with every other column a `└`
continuation naming its header; two-column tables collapse to one line,
since a continuation under a single value is ceremony. A heading becomes
bold caps preceded by a rule, which blocks_from_mrkdwn already turns into a
real divider.

Headings deliberately do not use Block Kit's `header` block. That block is
plain text only — no inline code, no bold, no links, 150 characters — so a
heading carrying any of those would lose it. Bold caps in an ordinary
section keeps more of the author's intent than the block named after the
job.

The channel preamble now also states the formatting rules, so the model
stops emitting tables at the source rather than relying on the rewrite.
Asked to format for Slack, the model already produces exactly this shape;
it was simply never told. Guidance shapes what it chooses, and the rewrite
is the net under that for anything it emits anyway.

Fences are respected on both paths: a table or heading inside one is
someone showing the syntax, not asking for it to render.

fix(memory): index on write, so memory_search stops being a boot-time snapshot (#1018)

The index was refreshed at startup and almost nowhere else: a full reindex
ten seconds after boot, plus one incremental call for the current daily
note after compaction. Every other brain file stayed frozen at last boot.
Measured on a live install, AGENTS.md was fifteen hours stale.

That defeats the duplicate check in #1017 exactly where it matters. The
agent searches before appending a rule, the search honestly reports
nothing because the rule it would have found was written after boot, and
the duplicate lands. The same install carries 63 near-duplicate one-line
rules.

A periodic full pass is the wrong primitive. A snapshot of a corpus that is
written mid-session is stale the moment it completes, and it degrades:
158 daily notes and 258 MB today, growing, so the sweep costs more each day
while the share of it that changed since boot shrinks toward nothing.

Writes are the mechanism. write_opencrabs_file now indexes the file it just
wrote, so a rule is searchable the instant it lands. The full pass keeps its
place as bootstrap and repair, not freshness.

Writes that bypass the tool — a hand edit, another profile, an open editor —
are caught by a check on the search path. It compares filesystem mtime
against documents.modified_at, which the index already stores, so an
unchanged workspace costs one stat per brain file and no read; only files
whose mtime moved are reindexed, where the existing hash skip still
suppresses embedding when content turns out identical. Daily notes are
excluded: append-only history already covered by the compaction hook, and
158 of them is a tax paid on every search to catch a change in one of nine.

The refresh is single-flight. It runs on a user-triggered path, and the
startup reindex is deliberately delayed and spawned because llama-cpp GGML
can segfault under contention — which is what a changed file's embedding
would enter. A second caller skips rather than waits.

Also here, since both are the same defect class:

- context.rs dropped its indexing error with `let _`, so a failed index of
  the daily note was invisible. It logs now, as does every new path.
- The duplicate-check instruction named `grep`, which resolves against the
  working directory and cannot see the home directory at all. It now names
  `load_brain_file` with a query, which reads from disk and therefore
  cannot miss a rule written moments ago, with memory_search for the
  cross-file case.

Not unit-tested: refresh_stale_brain_files binds to the real profile home
and store, so a test would exercise the developer's own workspace. The
mtime comparison and the guard are the parts worth covering and want a
seam that does not exist yet.

fix(channels): log the three delivery failures that were dropped entirely (#1019)

Three calls swallowed their error on paths where the failure means the user
gets no answer at all. A silent drop is indistinguishable from the agent
choosing not to reply, so the person waiting cannot tell it broke, and
cannot report it.

- discord/handler.rs, twice: `send_message` on the reply-with-components
  path. If Discord rejects the payload — oversized content, malformed
  components, a permissions change — the turn returns as though it
  succeeded.
- telegram/delivery.rs: `send_html_or_plain` inside the delete-and-resend
  recovery. This is the LAST fallback: the edit already failed and was
  logged, so when the resend failed too the message was gone with only the
  first failure recorded. The path built to save the message was the quiet
  one.

Logged at error, with the channel and the cause, since these are lost
replies rather than degraded ones.

Scoped deliberately. There are 339 `let _ =` and 23 `.ok()` outside tests,
and the overwhelming majority are correct: sends to a receiver that may be
gone, best-effort `delete_message` cleanup where failure is cosmetic.
Sweeping all of them would bury the three that cost a reply.

In-channel notices are NOT part of this. Surfacing a delivery failure to
the end user in the channel is the other half and wants its own change,
including the rule that a failing notice must not recurse into the
transport that just failed.

fix(memory): index brain files into the brain collection, not memory (#1018)

Regression from a33e2188. `reindex` has always split collections — daily
notes into memory, brain files into brain — but `index_file`, the
incremental path, hardcoded memory. Wiring the write hook and the freshness
check through it meant every brain file written mid-session was filed in
the wrong collection.

`search_brain` only reads the brain collection, so the incremental index
did nothing for brain search while appearing to succeed. The brain row it
should have updated went untouched, and the next full reindex deactivated
the stray memory-collection copy, leaving no trace beyond a dead row.

Caught on a live index: AGENTS.md held two rows, id=9 in brain active, and
id=3862 in memory inactive, created the moment the new path first ran.

The collection is now derived from the file name, so the incremental path
and the full pass agree by construction rather than by two call sites
happening to pass the same constant.

feat(memory): give memory_search a scope, so the agent can search its own rules (#1020)

search_brain already existed, was already used internally by brain/hints.rs,
and was not reachable by the agent. So "does a rule about this already
exist" went through the daily-log corpus, where 158 notes outrank nine
brain files and reuse the same words for unrelated things.

Measured on a live index across five phrasings of the same question: the
agent-reachable path found the target rule 2 times out of 5, the brain
collection found it 5 out of 5, for the same payload. The failures were
silent — three confident irrelevant hits rather than none — which is what
made them expensive. An agent checking before appending a rule reads
"nothing similar" and writes the duplicate (#1017).

Consolidated onto the existing tool rather than adding a third search.
Every tool schema is paid for in context on every request, and the corpus
is a property of the question, not of the verb. `scope` takes memory (the
default, unchanged, so existing callers are unaffected), brain, or all.

Under "all", brain hits lead: a rule outranks a note that merely mentions
it.

An empty result in the default scope now says so and points at the brain
scope, because the most likely reason a rule search comes back empty is
that it was pointed at history.

The duplicate-check instruction inverts to match. It read load_brain_file
first, on the reasoning that reading from disk cannot go stale — sound when
brain files were not reliably in the brain collection, which 8c0eabeb
fixed. Now the cheap step is also the accurate one: search brain-scoped to
learn whether and where a rule exists, and pay for a full section only when
there is something to read. Updated in the tool description, the shipped
AGENTS.md template, and the governance test that holds them together.

load_brain_file keeps its own role and is deliberately not folded in. It
returns whole sections rather than ranked snippets, which is what judging a
rule needs once search has located it. Search finds the file; load reads it
properly.

fix(memory): stop the freshness churn and keep embedding off the search path (#1021)

The freshness check compared filesystem mtime against
`documents.modified_at`, which is not bumped when content is updated. The
comparison was permanently true, so the same brain files were reported
stale and reindexed on EVERY search, forever — visible in a live log as
"reindexed 2 stale brain file(s)" repeating all day.

It now tracks what THIS process actually indexed, in memory. A restart
re-checks once, which is correct: the startup reindex runs then anyway.

Second, the check no longer embeds. llama.cpp's Metal backend asserts at
teardown when a resource set is still outstanding
(GGML_ASSERT([rsets->data count] == 0), ggml-metal-device.m:656), so any
path that can be embedding when the process exits is another way to abort
on shutdown. That assert predates this work, but putting embedding on the
search path — driven by user input at arbitrary times — widened the window,
and the churn meant it was entered far more often than intended.

Freshness refreshes FTS only. FTS ranks a brain search, so results stay
correct; a vector row lagging by one restart does not change an answer.
Embedding still runs where it always did: startup reindex and the write
path, both bounded and not user-driven.

Committed without a full suite run: production was down and the suite hung
past ten minutes on a loaded box. Clippy is clean. Targeted tests follow.

docs(eval): record the memory-retrieval before/after, and what was not measured

Covers #995 through #1020 in one place: recall ranking, chunked embeddings,
index freshness, collection routing, scoped search. Figures are from a live
workspace (9 brain files, 158 daily notes, 258 MB), not a fixture.

The headline is rule lookup going 2/5 to 5/5 while cost per lookup fell
~97%, but the useful finding is why it was ever 2/5: two corpora were
hiding under one name, and a rule question served by the historical corpus
returned three confident irrelevant results rather than nothing — read as
"no such rule exists", which is how duplicates got written.

Includes the end-to-end run the synthetic queries were a proxy for: a cron
audit that recovered a job's setup from ~54 days earlier, then chained
search to a specific day, to a grep of the neighbouring day, to noticing a
job ID that had changed across two months, to routing around logs that had
aged out. That run is the historical corpus doing what it is for — the same
158 notes that buried a rule lookup are what made a two-month-old fact
recoverable.

Limits recorded rather than omitted: every retrieval figure is a direct
index query, not a live tool call; the payload figure is derived from the
snippet path rather than captured; the 0.35 threshold's transfer to large
files is untested; vector retrieval was never isolated from FTS.

fix(agent): route a spent thinking-loop budget into the fallback chain (#1021)

A turn ending in "Thinking loop timeout: 120s with no tool call emitted"
surfaced as a hard error with a healthy fallback chain configured and never
tried. Observed on zhipu/glm-5.2: 4 steps, 3 tool calls, 17m 12s, then a
red error.

The FallbackProvider wrapper could not catch it. The error is raised in
helpers.rs ABOVE the provider, after the stream returned successfully, so
the chain sees no failure and has nothing to cascade on.

The manual walk could not catch it either. Its guard is an allow-list —
rate limits, quota, 429, 401/403/402, invalid key — and this error is not a
member. It never reached that arm anyway: its own arm matched first and,
once the nudge budget ran out, returned straight to the user.

The nudge strategy is right for the transient case and is unchanged. What
was wrong is what happened after it failed: MAX_PHANTOM_RETRIES nudges that
did not produce a tool call is evidence this model will not emit one on
this history, which is exactly when another provider is the answer.

The nudge arm is now gated on the budget, so a spent budget stops matching
and falls through to the walk, and the walk's allow-list admits the error.
Everything the walk already does applies unchanged: the quota circuit
breaker, skipping the session's active provider, the ProviderSwitched
event, and the chain-exhaustion ledger. With no fallbacks configured the
behaviour is what it was, plus the existing setup guidance.

fix(cron): accept Unix day-of-week 0, so the dedup scan finally runs (#1024)

`__opencrabs_dedup_scan__` ships with `0 4 * * 0` and has never executed
once. Unix cron numbers days 0-6 with Sunday at 0; the `cron` crate numbers
them 1-7 with Sunday at 7, so the expression failed to parse entirely and
the scheduler logged the failure every minute for the job's whole lifetime.

The day-of-week field is now normalized before parsing, whole tokens only,
so `10` in another field is untouched and lists, ranges and steps keep
working. This fixes every user-written schedule too — `* * * * 0` is how
crontabs everywhere spell Sunday.

Worth naming what this cost: the dedup scan is the mechanism that catches
the same rule written into two brain files. A live workspace carries 63
near-duplicate one-line rules (#1017), and a permissions rule that drifted
between SOUL.md and AGENTS.md into two contradictory statements about the
same person. The scan that exists to find exactly that had never run.

fix(agent): stop reporting our own loop-detector kill as a provider fault (#1023)

A turn ended by the within-turn announcement-loop detector told the user
"Provider got stuck repeating itself", blaming the provider for a decision
this code made. Observed live: 22 tool calls, 3:12, killed by the detector
after the model kept announcing a spawn without emitting the call.

The message now names the real cause. The `/models` suggestion stays,
because it genuinely helps — a different model usually does emit the call —
but it no longer stands in for a fault that did not happen. That mattered:
the wrong attribution occasionally appeared to work, which taught a wrong
mental model rather than an incomplete one.

Genuine provider failures are unaffected and still say provider.

The other half of #1023 — the error being AgentError::Internal, so it can
never reach the fallback chain #1021 fixed for ThinkingLoopTimeout — is NOT
addressed here. It needs the error raised as provider-attributable or a
path from the walk to it, which is a larger change than a message fix.

fix(tools): activate what tool_search returns, so a found tool is callable (#1025)

tool_search returned schemas as TEXT and never activated them, leaving
activation to the JIT-on-execute path. That path only fires when a non-core
tool is actually USED, which is circular: a model that will not emit a call
for a function absent from its tool list can never trigger the activation
that would list it.

Capable models escape by calling from the text schema. Weaker ones
substitute whatever IS active. Observed twice on the same task: the model
searched for spawn_agent, reported "Spawn tool active", then emitted
bash(echo "spawning subagent") and read_file instead — 30 tool calls across
two runs, both killed by the announcement-loop detector. Removing the spawn
from the request made the same task complete with no issues.

#604 withheld activation so a search for "send a photo" would not balloon
the request with eight unused schemas. That concern is handled by caps that
already exist: matches are capped per search, and activate_tools evicts LRU
past MAX_ACTIVE_EXTENDED. The request cannot grow without bound; it just
stops claiming a tool is available when it is not.

The blast radius was every search-gated capability, not only spawning — the
tool's own description routes browsing, channel sends, teams, image and
video generation, cron and self-improvement through this same path.

Also here: the dedup-scan cron job, corrected properly this time. It
shipped as "0 4 * * 0" and never ran once. My first fix translated Unix 0
to 7, which parses and is WRONG — this crate numbers 1 = Sunday, so 7 is
Saturday and the job would have run on the wrong day, silently. Caught by
an existing test asserting 0 is rejected on purpose. The expression is now
a named constant carrying that trap in its doc comment.

feat(brain): state where deployments go, in the preamble (#1026)

Nothing said where a deployment should land, so "deploy it" could mean
installing services, daemons, ports and system packages into the OpenCrabs
environment itself. On a shared instance — one crab, several people and
projects — that breaks everyone at once, and whatever one user deploys
becomes something the instance then runs for all of them.

Three sentences: offer a VPS (Hetzner, DigitalOcean, Hostinger) when the
workload wants its own host, or a container when this machine can carry it;
nothing added to the OpenCrabs environment without explicit owner approval;
and why shared instances raise the stakes.

Placed in the preamble rather than AGENTS.md, against the usual routing,
for a distribution reason. Brain files are seeded ONCE: a rule added to the
shipped template reaches new installs only, while every existing user keeps
a copy that never updates — so it would never arrive for exactly the
established multi-user instances it most protects. The preamble ships with
the binary and lands on the next upgrade. OWNER-ONLY COMMANDS sits beside
it for the same reason.

The line stays: AGENTS.md owns workspace rules a user may edit; the
preamble owns rules that must hold on every install whatever a user's brain
files say. SECURITY.md was rejected as on-demand — not in context on the
turn someone says "deploy this".

feat(tui): emit OSC 8 so paths and wrapped URLs are clickable (#1031)

Nothing in the TUI emitted a hyperlink escape, so everything clickable was
the TERMINAL guessing from rendered text. That fallback has exactly the two
limits reported: it only recognises URLs, never file paths, and it cannot
span a line break — so a wrapped URL was two fragments, neither of them a
valid URL, and zooming out until it fit one line was the only way to click
it.

The wrap is ours, not the terminal's, which is why the terminal could never
rejoin it.

Escapes cannot ride inside a Span: ratatui's buffer splits content by
grapheme, so an escape is chopped across cells and rendered as literal
garbage while consuming columns. But ratatui-crossterm writes each cell's
symbol verbatim, so folding the escape INTO a cell that already holds one
visible grapheme works — the terminal renders the escape as zero-width and
the grapheme as one column, and the buffer still counts one column. Widths
need no adjustment, which is pinned by a test.

So this is a post-render pass: draw normally, read the text back out of the
buffer, find links, patch the first and last cell of each. Per-row rather
than per-line, so a URL split across rows gets its own opener on each row —
which is what makes it clickable at any zoom.

Detection is deliberately strict, because a false positive turns prose into
a dead link: absolute paths only, http(s) only, surrounding prose
punctuation trimmed from both ends. Relative paths, "and/or" and "3/4" are
left alone.

Terminals without OSC 8 ignore the sequence, so there is no fallback path.

fix(tui): drop OSC 8 linkify, it corrupts the screen (#1031)

Folding the OSC 8 escape into a cell's symbol breaks ratatui's diff.
BufferDiff advances by Cell::cell_width(), which is measured from the
symbol string, so a cell holding ESC]8;;<uri>ESC\<char> reports the
width of the whole URI instead of 1. The diff then skips that many
following cells, they are never redrawn, and stale content from the
previous frame stays on screen as bleed-through.

The escape has to be emitted at the backend write, not stored in the
buffer. Removing the module until that path exists.

endpoint behaved that way without ever asking for it, so on every turn

The resumed-turn reasoning_echo debug line already recorded the
