factory injected it through a body transform, and to_openai_request set
reasoning_effort separately from config. A user on the tiered-effort
family with an effort configured shipped both knobs in one request.

The body transform could never have got this right: it takes a serialized
body and never sees the model, so it cannot tell qwen3.8-max from
qwen3.7-plus. Resolution moves to a per-request module beside
kimi_reasoning, which already solves the same per-family problem for the
Kimi models.

Rules, matching what the models actually read:

- Tiered family reads reasoning_effort. The tier ships alone; a co-present
  enable_thinking is dropped rather than sent as a competing knob. An
  explicit enable_thinking = false becomes reasoning_effort = none, since
  dropping it would turn the user's off into server-default.
- Hybrids read enable_thinking, defaulting on. A configured effort still
  passes through untouched: they treat it as an opaque override, and
  dropping it would restore the bug where a tier never reached Model
  Studio at all (#691).
- Non-qwen models are untouched.

No default tier is invented for the tiered family. Thinking is mandatory
there, so an absent tier still thinks, and picking a value would override
the model's own choice with a guess.

The onboarding write stays: it is a user preference, visible and editable
in config.toml. Which knob it turns into is now decided per model.

feat(qwen): default the tiered family to the recommended effort tier (#1034)

An unconfigured install sent no tier at all and took whatever the endpoint
fell back to. Default to the top of the ladder, which is the vendor's
recommended setting for this family.

Only fills a gap: a reasoning_effort set in config wins, and an explicit
enable_thinking = false still resolves to the none tier ahead of this.
Scoped to the tiered family, since a tier is opaque to the hybrids and
defaulting one in would put an inert field on every request.

fix(subagent): reconcile orphaned status files at startup (#1038)

A sub-agent runs inside a tokio::spawn'd task and dies with the process.
Its status file does not, so a killed agent left a file reading Running
forever and anything consulting it saw an agent that no longer existed.

The sweep the module documented was never wired: cleanup_stale had no
caller outside tests, so the directory grew without bound while the doc
claimed a 7-day startup cleanup.

New reconcile pass, run once at startup before any agent is spawned.
Every non-terminal file belongs to a dead process by definition, so each
moves to a new Interrupted state and is returned to the caller, which
will report it into the originating session. Interrupted is distinct from
Failed on purpose: the work did not fail, it never finished, and nothing
knows how far it got. It stamps completed_at so the file ages out on the
same schedule as any other terminal state, and carries the reason so a
restart is distinguishable from a genuine error.

Reconciliation runs before the sweep, so an interrupted file gets its
stamp before anything tries to age it.

Also replaces the two dropped writes in the spawn completion path. Both
sat on the exact failure they were meant to record: a lost mark_failed
loses the record of an error that already happened, and either one leaves
the agent reading as running with nothing logged.

Startup wiring is the TUI path for now, which is where the existing
background-task accounting lives. Moving both onto a shared path every
surface runs is #1037.

fix(restart): route recovery reports by session, not by whoever booted (#1037)

The completion path picks its destination by session (#940), because a
channel-bound session driven from another surface otherwise reports to
the wrong place. The restart path never got that fix: it called the
booting surface's callback directly, so a channel session's interruption
notice landed locally.

Swapping in the route map alone does not work. Recovery runs during
startup, before any channel has registered a route, so the map is empty
at the moment the report is produced. Reports now park when no route
claims their session, leave the instant one appears, and flush to the
booting surface after a grace period so a channel that never comes up in
this run cannot strand them. Nothing is dropped on either branch.

Rows are cleared per row after being accounted for. clear_all() ran
unconditionally, so a row whose report was never produced was dropped
from the table anyway and its session heard nothing.

Sub-agent interruptions now report too, reusing the status files
reconciled in #1038. They are framed like the command case: state that it
did not finish and hand the decision back, rather than letting an absent
result read as success or failure.

Recovery moves behind one entry point covering both kinds, so a surface
wires up restart accounting with a single call instead of knowing which
stores exist.

feat(subagent): report a finished agent's result to the session that spawned it (#1036)

The tool advertises fire-and-forget: spawn, get an agent_id, carry on.
Taking that offer lost the work. On completion the output went into the
manager's HashMap and the status file, and nothing read either at a loop
boundary, so a parent whose turn had already ended never saw it.

wait_agent was never broken and is untouched. Spawn-then-wait in the same
turn returns the output as that tool's result exactly as before.

A push would duplicate that result for a parent already blocked on
wait_agent, so the agent tracks how many waits are outstanding. The count
is read under the same write lock as the terminal transition, so a
wait_agent racing a completion either registers first, and the push is
skipped, or arrives after and reads the finished state directly. A RAII
guard releases the registration, since the wait has several early returns
and a leaked count would suppress the push permanently.

Failures push too. A parent that is not told has no way to distinguish
work that failed from work still running.

Delivery goes through the session route, so a channel-bound session gets
its result rather than whichever surface executed the spawn (#940). A
sub-agent is reached from a tool with no service context, so unlike a
detached command it has no callback of its own to fall back on; the
booting surface registers one at startup and the resolver uses it when no
channel claims the session.

Output is tail-truncated into the pushed message so a long transcript
cannot flood the parent's context. The child's own session keeps the
full text.

fix(tui): stop the voice dialog hiding stored keys and overwriting them (#1039)

The key inputs are seeded with EXISTING_KEY_SENTINEL when a key is
already on disk, so the secret is never rendered. The two halves of the
dialog read that marker in opposite ways.

The renderer treated it as no key, so a configured provider displayed as
empty and offered its "API key is optional" hint. The save path guarded
only on emptiness, and the marker is not empty, so opening the dialog and
saving without retyping persisted the literal string over the real key.
Not a failure to persist: it destroyed what was there. Every other
consumer of the sentinel already guards against exactly this.

New key_field module holds the semantics once, so display and persistence
cannot drift apart again: is_configured for "is a key set", is_new_secret
for "is there something to write", masked for what the field shows. They
differ on the sentinel and nowhere else, which a test pins.

A stored key now renders as saved rather than blank, so the field stops
claiming a configured provider has nothing.

providers.tts.openai is no longer written from groq_key. That section is
real OpenAI, no base_url, so another provider's credential could only
ever produce a 401 there. The dialog has no OpenAI TTS key input to put
in its place, so it writes nothing rather than something that cannot
work; the slash command already sets that key properly.

fix(qwen): reach hosted qwen outside Alibaba and vendor-prefixed model ids (#1040)

The thinking knobs were inert on every qwen deployment that is not an
official Alibaba host with a bare model id. Two gates each excluded it,
and both were written against qwen-code's assumptions without checking a
real third-party deployment.

The host allowlist matched dashscope/aliyun/aliyuncs/bailian/dialagram.
The same models are served by ModelScope, NVIDIA NIM, OpenRouter and any
OpenAI-compatible gateway, and none of those got preserve_thinking or the
family gate. The allowlist was protecting a locally served qwen GGUF,
which takes thinking through chat_template_kwargs; "is a local server" is
what it needed to say, not "is an Alibaba host". Now it says that.

Model classification prefix-matched the raw id, but these hosts namespace
their catalogue: Qwen-Ambassador/Qwen3.8-Max, Qwen/Qwen3.5-397B-A17B. A
tiered-effort model failed the tiered prefix and fell through to the qwen
arm, so it was classified as a hybrid and given the switch it does not
read while the effort tier went unset. Silent misclassification rather
than a clean miss, because the vendor segment often begins with qwen too.

Matching now runs on the vendor-stripped, lowercased id, shared by every
qwen check rather than reimplemented per call site. That also fixes
looks_like_qwen_target, which only recognised namespaced ids when the
vendor happened to start with qwen: a vendor named anything else failed
it outright.

A remote host that does not read these fields ignores them per the
chat-completions spec, which is the same reasoning looks_like_qwen_target
already documents for its cache_control markers.

provider_without_reasoning_setting_sends_none used a qwen id to assert a
generic property, and the tiered default now legitimately fires for it.
Split: the generic case keeps a non-qwen model, and a new test pins the
tiered default, the tier shipping alone, and preserve_thinking.

feat(loop): notice a repeating tool round before the provider rejects it (#1030)

Nothing detected the agent re-running an identical tool round. An
identical call returns an identical result, so it is never productive,
and undetected it ran until the PROVIDER objected: DashScope-style
backends reject the conversation with a 500 and the history stays
poisoned. repetition.rs recovers from that; this notices first.

The turn is untouched. On the threshold round a correction is appended
after the tool results and the loop continues, which is the same shape
the phantom nudges already use. Nothing ends, nothing retries differently,
and the fallback ladder is unchanged. The reference implementation halts
the turn and offers a disable dialog; that remedy is deliberately not
copied, only the detection.

The repeated call still executes and its result still reaches the model.
Suppressing it would silently change what the agent did, and a detector
is not entitled to that.

Rounds are compared as a unit, so a parallel batch is one identity rather
than several, and the tracker resets on a fallback swap. A swap replays
the turn against another provider, and without the reset those replayed
calls stack onto the run and trip the threshold on calls the model made
once.

The threshold sits one below qwen-code's, which is itself documented as
below the server-side limit, leaving a round of headroom for the
correction to change course before the guardrail fires.

No canonicalization pass was needed for the argument hash. This crate's
serde_json has no preserve_order feature, so its Map is a BTreeMap and
object keys already serialize sorted; a test pins that, since enabling
the feature later would silently reopen the evasion.

docs(telegram): ground the owner-gate claim in the fix that made it true (#975)

The comment above the ephemeral delivery of slash-command output claimed
"Every slash command is owner-gated" before that was actually enforced:
skills and commands.toml entries bypassed the gate until #975. Name what
the gate now covers, built-ins individually and user commands and skills
through the catch-all gate, so the claim reads as verified, not asserted.

fix(telegram): tell being added apart from another bot arriving (#1041)

One notice served both events, so they were indistinguishable in the
owner's DM and half of them carried the wrong advice: being told to add
OpenCrabs' own id to allowed_users is not an action anyone should take.

Split by case. Being added says so and drops the allowlist advice
entirely; another bot arriving says the chat is one we are already in,
which is the missing sentence that explains why the owner is hearing
about it at all, and keeps the allowlist advice with the id to actually
add.

Both now name who performed the add. It was already in scope, used a few
lines below for the cowork check, and it is the one field that answers
how this happened.

Both also carry a reachable handle. A numeric chat_id left the owner
unable to find the group they were being told about; a public chat now
gets its t.me link, and a private one says it is private rather than
leaving the absence unexplained.

The notification send no longer discards its error. A failed owner DM
meant the join went entirely unreported with nothing logged.

fix(telegram): only the owner may add the bot to a group (#1042)

Nothing checked who performed the add. Telegram does not gate it either:
any member with invite rights can add a public bot. A production instance
was added to an unrecognised group and was answering there sixteen
seconds later, staying over a day before anyone noticed.

Commands are already owner-gated. Being added to a group is a strictly
larger grant than any single command, since it exposes the whole agent,
its tools and its credentials to everyone in the chat, and it was the one
thing left ungated. It now uses the same is_owner predicate, so there is
one definition of authority rather than two that can drift.

On an unauthorised add the bot leaves and the owner is told who tried,
with the id needed to act on it. Leaving comes first and the decision
fails closed: an owner DM that cannot be delivered must not leave the bot
sitting in a chat it was never authorised to join. A leave that fails is
reported as such, with the BotFather lever that works when it does not,
rather than reading as handled.

The adder is now logged on every join. It was already in scope and simply
unused, which is why the add that prompted this could not be traced to
anyone afterwards.

fix(telegram): stop recording chats that were never authorised (#1043)

Passive capture exists so the bot holds context in a chat it belongs to.
It ran for every undirected message regardless of whether the chat was
ever authorised, so a group nobody approved still had its members'
messages and media written to the database and disk. Refusing to answer
someone never stopped us recording them.

New retains_history predicate: a chat qualifies when it has its own
groups entry, which is what the owner adding the bot creates, or when the
sender is someone we answer anywhere. Computed once and applied at all
four drop sites, so the attachment download is skipped too — that is the
half that writes to disk.

The directed path is untouched: a message addressed to us is still stored
with its attachment.

Also corrects the doc on TelegramConfig::is_owner. It claimed an empty
allowed_users means everyone is treated as owner; config::owner::is_owner
does the opposite and denies everyone when both lists are empty. The
stale claim misled the first version of these tests into asserting an
unconfigured channel retains everything, which is the opposite of what it
should do.

feat(telegram): render mermaid fences as images in rich messages (#1044) Mermaid diagrams in model output are pre-validated against mermaid.ink and embedded as inside the Telegram rich-HTML message; a diagram the renderer rejects degrades to a legible failure block (error note + original source) instead of failing the whole send with RICH_MESSAGE_PHOTO_NO_MEDIA_FOUND. Messages without a mermaid fence are byte-identical to the existing markdown path. - rich/mermaid.rs: base64url, fence detection, config gate, async pre-validation (bounded timeout, never panics), recursive block resolution, image/failure HTML builders - ast/render_html/render_json: Block::Mermaid + MermaidResult - mod.rs: markdown_to_html_mermaid + unified mermaid-aware senders - config: channels.telegram.mermaid_render (default true, opt-out; diagram source is sent to third-party mermaid.ink) - wired into delivery (streaming + fallback), handler command replies, telegram_send tool, cron scheduler Known limitation: a mermaid+table message routes through the HTML path, so the table renders as a 
 grid rather than a native rich table.

Tests: 20 new telegram_mermaid_test + 2 render_json mermaid tests; full
gate green (6492 passed, clippy clean, fmt clean).

feat(telegram): mermaid via markdown+media keeps tables native (#1044)

The mermaid routing now prefers the markdown dialect with the Bot API
10.2 media field (tg://photo?id= references + InputRichMessageMedia),
validated live in prototype message 1073: the diagram renders and pipe
tables stay native rich tables. The HTML dialect is demoted to a
fallback for Bot API < 10.2 servers. Pre-validation against mermaid.ink
is unchanged, so RICH_MESSAGE_PHOTO_NO_MEDIA_FOUND still cannot fire.

- mermaid.rs: MediaEntry, find_mermaid_fences (byte-range scanner),
  replacement_for (pure, unit-tested), markdown_failure_block,
  resolve_markdown_media (async, last-to-first replacement)
- api.rs: build_body_markdown_media + send_rich_markdown_media_id
  (body shape identical to validated prototype 1073)
- mod.rs: unified sender rewritten to resolve-once -> markdown+media
  primary -> HTML fallback on transport error; orphaned non-id
  send_rich_markdown removed; stale doc reference fixed
- 10 new network-free tests (30 mermaid tests total)

fix(telegram): decode rich message blocks as typed AST (#1058)

Incoming rich messages with summary+blocks content went through lossy
text extraction, dropping structure entirely: headings lost their
markers, bullet nesting flattened, table rows fused, media file_ids
discarded. Replace the text-scrape fallback with a typed renderer that
walks RichBlock/RichText nodes per the official Bot API schema and
falls back to structural text matching for unknown tags. Wire shape
verified against a real Raw Bot capture (details fixture included).

- rich_decode.rs: typed RichBlock/RichText renderer, inline spans
  concatenate directly (no separator space), let-chain collapse for
  embed blocks
- telegram_rich_decode_official_test.rs: 14 official-schema fixtures
  incl. the details-loss repro from the raw capture
- telegram_rich_decode_test.rs: heading expectations bumped to render
  "## " markers (the point of the fix)

fix(agent): gate the RSI autonomous engine behind rsi_enabled (#1063)

The RSI engine spawned unconditionally on every boot, including headless
daemons, and no config key gated it. On an unattended Telegram daemon that
meant hourly autonomous agent cycles with auto-approved tools: provider
quota burn, brain-file appends every hour, and 7-9h spans of activity that
read as write_opencrabs_file hangs (the diagnosis that opened this issue).

[agent].rsi_enabled is an Option<bool> so an absent key can default by run
mode rather than being indistinguishable from an explicit true: ON for the
interactive TUI (the feature users expect), OFF for headless daemons.
Explicit true/false always wins, so a daemon operator who wants RSI opts
in knowingly. The engine task still always spawns and re-reads the live
config mirror every cycle, so flipping the key hot-reloads on the next
cycle boundary in both directions, no restart.

- config/types.rs: rsi_enabled Option<bool> field, mode-based default doc
- brain/rsi.rs: rsi_effectively_enabled(); boot gate around template sync
  + startup digest; per-cycle re-check with transition logging
- cli/ui.rs: headless flag threaded into spawn_rsi_engine
- config.toml.example: key documented under [agent]
- tests: 5 pins on the resolution matrix (None-parse, explicit wins both
  directions, TUI-on/daemon-off defaults, example config ships mode-based)

fix(memory): embedding API calls get timeouts, a vector gate, and stop blocking writes (#1062)

A daemon's write_opencrabs_file could hang forever: the embedding API
client was the lone reqwest::Client::new() in the codebase (no timeout;
reqwest default is wait forever), one sequential HTTP call per chunk, and
the write path awaited the whole index inline. One blackholed endpoint
wedged the tool call permanently.

Three changes:

- embedding.rs: embed_via_api builds a 10s-connect / 60s-total client
  (house pattern from local_engine.rs, exa_search.rs, a2a_send.rs)
- index.rs: Phase 2 embedding is detached into tokio::spawn. FTS (Phase 1,
  the searchable index) completes and the write tool returns; embeddings
  are enhancement and always terminate now via the timeout
- mod.rs: embedding_api_configured folds in vector_enabled, and
  embed_content_api early-returns on it, giving the API path the same gate
  the local path always had. vector_enabled = false with a leftover
  [memory.embedding] section used to still fire one HTTP call per chunk on
  every write

Tests: 5 pins including the regression itself: index_file returns in
0.02s against a blackhole endpoint (accepts TCP, never responds), embed
gated off is a no-op, connection-refused surfaces as Err fast.

Fixes #1062

fix(telegram): cap inline rate-limit waits at 30s (#1064)

A 429 with a large RetryAfter window slept the FULL window inline before
retrying, so one rate-limited send could park an entire agent turn for
hours (observed: 8288s = 2h18m on a live daemon, the log's last line
ever). The turn looked hung while it was actually queued behind a sleep.

Inline waits are now clamped to 30s (the post_rich precedent), capped
retries log the true window so forensics shows a flood ban instead of a
mystery hang, and typical short windows keep full #297 semantics: command
replies are delayed, never silently dropped.

- rate_limit.rs: clamp_inline_wait() helper, MAX_INLINE_RATE_LIMIT_WAIT 30s
- intermediates.rs: both send paths clamp (send_retrying_rate_limit 3 attempts,
  send_html_or_plain 1)
- delivery.rs: placeholder-edit fallback clamp
- flow.rs: refresh_flow clamp
- tests: 3 regression pins, paused clock, incl. 8288s window to 90s inline

fix(tui): order the model picker newest-first (#1057)

The picker rendered the model list in insertion order, and a newly
discovered model is appended, so every new release landed at the bottom.
That put the entry the user is most likely reaching for in the position
hardest to find, and it got worse with each release.

Alphabetical would not have fixed it. Ascending text order puts glm-5.3s
after glm-4.5 anyway, and glm-5.10 sorts before glm-5.2 as text while
being the newer model. Ordering is natural and descending: digit runs
compare as numbers, everything else as text.

Two things the first attempt got wrong, both caught by tests:

Separators were compared as text, so a catalogue display name and a raw
id differing only in ' ' versus '-' let the separator outrank the version
number. Separators are dropped now.

Dropping them then emitted an empty text token where the other id had its
next version digit, so glm-5-turbo beat glm-5.3s on "turbo" versus "".
Empty tokens are skipped, which is what lets the number-outranks-text rule
compare 3 against turbo — the comparison that decides which is newer.

Sorting sits on filtered_model_names, not all_model_names: the latter's
fetched-then-config insertion order is a contract other callers rely on,
and an existing test asserts it. Ordering is only what the picker shows
and never touches config.models on disk.

Two selection tests asserted a name at a fixed index, which held only
under insertion order. Their real property is that selection indexes the
displayed list, so they now resolve through it rather than assuming the
order.

fix(agent): stop delivering the same answer twice in one turn (#1070)

accumulated_text deliberately collects text from every loop iteration,
which is right for a model that narrates as it works. It also means a
model that RESTATES its whole answer after a tool round gets that answer
delivered twice, concatenated into one message.

CLI providers make this the common case rather than the corner case:
they are stateless per invocation, so each iteration replays the full
prompt including the model's own previous answer, and restating beats
continuing. One turn on the claude-cli fallback path spawned three
subprocesses and shipped three copies of the same reply.

Only one of the append sites checked whether the text was already there.
Extract that check into is_duplicate_iteration_text and apply it at
every site, including two the issue did not list: the second cancel
variant and the give-up path.

- streaming and CLI segment loops skip a duplicate segment but still
  flush pending tool markers first, so tool chrome survives the skip
- the normal path skips the DB append with it, so a resumed session
  does not surface the duplicate either
- whitespace-only candidates are never duplicates: "".contains("") is
  trivially true and would swallow the separator bookkeeping

Containment catches verbatim re-emission only. A reworded restatement
still gets through; that needs similarity scoring, and a false positive
there would silently delete content the user is waiting on.

fix(sanitize): stop reasoning-tag stripping from eating message text

Three defects in strip_llm_artifacts, all on the delivery path:

1. An unclosed opener set `remaining = ""`, discarding every character
   after it. Mentioning a reasoning tag in prose silently truncated the
   rest of the message with no error and no log line.
2. The 10-character thinking form was never stripped. The gate checked
   only the 7-character form, and the two do not substring-match (the
   byte after `k` is `i`, not `>`), so the stripper never ran.
3. The reasoning stripper advanced 13 bytes past a 12-byte close tag,
   swallowing the first character after every block it stripped.

Collapsed the three near-duplicate strippers into strip_tag_block(text,
open, close). Taking the close tag as a parameter removes the
hand-counted length behind defect 3.

Unclosed openers are now handled by position: an opener that leads the
text still strips the remainder (a genuinely truncated reasoning
stream), while an opener that follows real text drops only the token and
keeps what the user wrote. This matches the policy the marker path
already settled on in sanitize_reasoning_leak_test.rs.

Two existing tests changed. One pinned the destructive behaviour as
intended; the other expected a single space where two is correct, and
had been passing because of defect 3.

Full lib suite 6549 passed, 0 failed. Clippy clean.

fix(phantom): let fact-based detectors fire the self-heal, not just gate it (#1073)

`claims_uncalled_commands` (#789) and `claims_unbacked_evidence` (#785)
were listed in `phantom_eligible` but absent from the trigger, whose six
branches all read the wording for a signal. A turn could be ruled
eligible on fact-based evidence, miss every wording branch, and ship the
fabrication with no nudge and no log line: the detectors ran, were
correct, and had no path to the correction they were computed for.

Add both to the trigger OR-list. Neither is gated on
`tool_calls_completed_this_turn == 0`, because #785 and #825 exist
precisely because a turn that did run tools can still fabricate a
separate claim alongside them.

False-positive risk differs in kind from the regression e843f405
addressed. That one came from wording heuristics misreading legitimate
completion acknowledgements after real work. These two compare claims
against `turn_tool_input` / `turn_tool_output` directly: a command
appearing in no tool input was not run, in any language, under any
phrasing.

Tests pin the asymmetry itself. A past-tense claim naming a command that
never ran is caught by the fact-based check while all six wording checks
miss it, stays clean when the command really ran, and a genuine
completion acknowledgement after real work fires nothing.
style: format test files left unformatted by 921cb9cf and b1d1994f

fix(phantom): widen the command allowlist so inspection claims are checkable

`claims_uncalled_commands` is the only phantom detector that checks fact
instead of wording, and its reach is bounded by a 28 program allowlist.
That list carried `psql` but not `ps`, and `sha256sum` but not `stat` or
`date`, so the commands that produce the small verifiable facts a turn is
most tempted to invent were exactly the ones it could not see. A claimed
build timestamp sourced from a `stat` that never ran passed untouched.

Adds the inspection, hashing, network, service and toolchain programs
that were missing, grouped by family. `env`, `file` and `test` stay out
on purpose: they are also ordinary English nouns, and a backticked noun
phrase inside an executed framing would fire a false self heal.

Regression tests in src/tests/phantom_allowlist_test.rs cover the caught
case, the honest case, one fixture per added family, the prose noun
exclusions, proposals, and a non English framing.

fix(phantom): stop the sentence split from tearing dotted commands in half (#1074)

The uncalled-command check split the turn text on '.' before extracting
backticked spans, and the span parser needs an opening and a closing
backtick in the same fragment. Any command naming a dotted path, a file
extension or a domain was cut in two, so the span was never parsed and
the allowlist never consulted.

That is the majority shape of a real inspection claim, because the
invented fact is normally about one specific file. Widening the
allowlist in b343f8e9 could not surface it: those fixtures were
deliberately dot-free, and the pre-existing extra-flags test asserted
is_empty() on a dotted fixture, passing for the wrong reason.

Backticks are now paired over the whole text first, and only delimiters
outside a closed pair split a sentence. Pairing up front rather than
toggling statefully keeps a stray unmatched backtick from swallowing the
remainder into one pseudo-sentence, which would let a framing in one
paragraph vouch for a command three paragraphs down.

fix(config): stop keys.toml dropping four provider API keys at runtime (#1066)

merge_provider_keys copies api_key one explicit arm per provider, and four
sections had no arm: providers.ollama, providers.stt.openai_compatible,
providers.tts.openai_compatible and providers.memory_embedding. The file
parsed, the key sat on disk, and the runtime never saw it, so the failure
was a bare 401 indistinguishable from a bad credential.

This is not a hand-edit-only footgun. /onboard writes the two voice keys
to exactly those paths via try_write_keys!, so two of its four voice-key
writes landed in a section that was never merged.

memory_embedding needed a different fix. ProviderConfigs has no field for
it, so serde discarded the section, and adding one would not have helped
either: src/memory/mod.rs parses config.toml directly and never passes
through Config::load() where the merge runs. The key is now resolved from
keys.toml at that one consuming site, and an explicit key in
[memory.embedding] keeps priority.

The stt/tts arms also gained the is_real_key guard the other arms already
had, so the __EXISTING_KEY__ sentinel /models writes internally can no

fix(config): one owner for the stored-key marker, and heal keys already poisoned by it

The '\''a key is already stored'\'' marker was spelled out at eight call sites,
each with its own equality test against the literal. Equality is the
wrong test. Three secret inputs in the voice step routed typing and
paste through handlers that never cleared the seeded marker, so a
pre-filled field that was edited held __EXISTING_KEY__<typed>, and every
one of those equality checks read that as an ordinary credential. A real
key reached keys.toml with the marker glued to its front, a value that
401s exactly like a wrong key with nothing on screen to explain it.

per-field paste arms now clear the marker before the first edit, which
is what every other secret input in the wizard already did. Backspace
clears the marker whole rather than a character at a time, since
__EXISTING_KEY_ no longer reads as seeded and would be saved as a key.

keys.toml already carrying __EXISTING_KEY__sk-... heals on the next load
instead of needing a hand edit. merge_provider_keys, the custom-provider
and channel key checks, the provider factory'\''s key_status, the memory

fix(rsi): split environmental bash failures out of the tool-defect count (#1068)

is_recoverable_tool_failure had no bash arm, so every failed bash call
fell through to a hard tool_failure. That put two unrelated populations
in one bucket: a command the model got wrong, which is agent behaviour
RSI should act on, and a well-formed command that met a missing file, a
closed port or a dead service, which says nothing about the tool. The
result was tool_failure|bash as the ledger's loudest signal, pointing
RSI at 'bash is broken'.

Classification lives in the new brain::bash_failure so it can be
exercised on real snippet shapes without going through the ledger. Model
markers are checked first and win: a script that touches a missing path
and then dies on bad syntax would otherwise be laundered into
environmental by the first message. An unmatched snippet stays Unknown
and therefore a failure, because guessing environmental would drop real
defects out of the denominator, which is the failure mode #236 already
paid for once.

The marker list is deliberately specific rather than the shorthand first
sketched on the issue. Bare 'not found' would swallow 'command not
found', the most common model error in the ledger and a string #236's
regression test has pinned as a genuine defect. 'unbound variable' moved
to the model side for the same reason: it is a shell scripting mistake,
not an environment.

Scanning is stderr-only when the snippet has a stderr section. Captured
stdout routinely contains these phrases as ordinary content, and a match
there would exempt a real defect on the strength of a filename.

Metadata for a bash failure now leads with class= and exit= and ends
with the head of stderr. Ordering is load-bearing and fixes a second
defect found on the way: the row was built as <snippet> | cmd=<cmd> and
then capped at 500 chars, while the snippet carries up to 8000 chars of
captured output, so any failure with real output silently lost the cmd=
that #132 added the enricher to provide.

fix(memory): sweep for unembedded documents, and show embedding health in doctor (#1069, #1067)

Embedding ran in exactly two places: once at startup inside reindex, and
on the write path for the one document being written. Neither retries. A
backfill that failed for a transient reason left every document
unembedded until someone restarted the process, and nothing said so:
search falls back to keyword-only FTS and keeps answering, so the only
symptom is results that feel slightly worse. One install ran 94 days
with a single vectorised chunk out of 589 with every diagnostic green.

Landed as one commit because the two halves are the same mechanism. The
sweep is what feeds the health entry doctor reads, and neither module
compiles without the other.

The API backfill moved out of the indexer into embedding.rs first. It
sat in index.rs as the twin of backfill_embeddings, and keeping the two
apart is exactly what let them drift: #998 and #1001 were both 'the
placeholder sweep was wired into the local path only', filed weeks
apart, because nobody editing the embedder ever saw the API copy. Two
defects went with the move: a spawn_blocking that queried the store,
logged the count and dropped it (its own comment said 'for now, just
log'), and clear_skipped_placeholders called twice in a row with the
second always returning 0.

backfill_sweep re-runs it on [memory] backfill_interval_secs, default
300, 0 to disable. read_memory_config parses config.toml on every call,
so a key fixed mid-session takes effect on the next tick with no cache
to invalidate and no reload plumbing. A tick landing on a running sweep
skips rather than stacking, which is not politeness: freshness.rs
documents that llama-cpp GGML can segfault under contention.

For doctor, there is no live probe and deliberately so. Nothing in this
codebase probes a provider; the CLI doctor's provider check constructs
the client and never calls it. What every provider gets is passive
health recorded from real traffic, and the embedding endpoint now feeds
that same table from the sweep. That costs no API call, says since when
rather than right now, and refreshes every tick instead of only when
someone runs doctor.

Both doctors call one builder, because they share no code today and
have already drifted. The key is resolved through read_memory_config,
the same function the embed path calls: reporting a key from a
different code path than the one that consumes it is how #1066 stayed
invisible.

Tests: 6 sweep cases, 9 doctor cases. Each was checked against a

missing key as OK) to confirm it is not vacuous.

fix(boot): claim the profile before any startup work (#1072)

A second instance of the same profile used to boot all the way through:
two full memory reindexes over one memory.db, two provider factories,
two sets of channel connect attempts. The scheduler lock and the channel
token locks caught it later and only partially, by which point the
duplicate work was already done and the process stayed up serving
nothing.

acquire_instance_lock is now the first thing cmd_chat_inner does, ahead
of the database, the provider, the tool registry and the reindex. Same
mechanics as the scheduler lock: an advisory flock the kernel releases
when the fd closes, so a crashed instance never wedges a profile. It
lives in its own locks/instance/ subdirectory rather than beside the
channel token locks, because foreign_lock_owners scans that directory
and SIGTERMs what it finds, and a lock file dropped there would make the
TUI kill the process that is starting up.

The daemon path exits 1 naming the holding PID. The TUI does not, and
that is the one deviation from the issue: BOOT.md documents that the TUI
takes priority and shuts down a running daemon, so a blanket exit would
mean the TUI refuses to start whenever systemd has the daemon up, which
is the normal state on a daemonised box. It preempts first and gives up
only if the lock survives that. The preemption call moved up from just
before channel start, which is the real ordering bug: it used to fire
after the database, the provider and the reindex had already been set up
alongside the daemon's. Its user-facing message stays where it was,
since it needs a TUI event channel that does not exist that early.

An unusable lock directory degrades to unguarded rather than to
refused. Turning an environment problem into a machine that will not
start is a worse failure than the duplicate work this prevents.

The token-lock denial is now an error naming the cause, not a warn, but
still not an exit. With the instance lock above it a same-profile
duplicate never reaches channel start at all, so what remains is the
cross-profile case: a daemon running three channels where one token
collides with another profile is still useful for the other two plus
cron, and killing it turns a config mistake in one channel into total
downtime.

Item 3 of the issue, skipping the reindex when the lock is held, is
moot: the guard sits above the reindex, so a duplicate exits before
reaching it. No second guard written.

Tests: 6 cases, all against a TempDir. The real locks directory is off
limits here because preempt_instances_in SIGTERMs the PIDs it finds
under it. Each was checked against a deliberate mutation (never taking
the flock) to confirm it is not vacuous.

fix(tools): reap the child process when a tool future is dropped (#1046)

A tool that timed out left its OS process running. tokio drops the
Child when the future is dropped, but does not kill the process unless
kill_on_drop is set, and the flag appeared nowhere in the repository. So
a grep that hit its timeout kept running after its turn had settled and
reported an answer produced without it.

kill_on_drop(true) on the eleven tokio spawns that execute work on the
agent's behalf: bash (all four), code_exec, dynamic tool, analyze_video
(both), doc_gen pptx, and the two evolve probes.

Three groups are deliberately left alone.

std::process sites (plan_tool, evolve/systemd, browser/manager) run
synchronously, so no dropped future can orphan them and the flag does
not exist on that type.

brew update/upgrade and cargo install --force are self-update paths.
Killing a package manager midway leaves a broken install, which is worse
than an orphaned process, so they keep running if their future goes.

The parallel batch executor already handled this: it selects on the
cancel token and drops the stream, and those are buffered futures rather
than spawned tasks, so dropping genuinely cancels them.

Tests pin the tokio semantics the fix depends on rather than asserting
the flag is present, so a tokio behaviour change would surface as a
failure instead of a silent return to leaking processes.

fix(provider): recognise every wording of a token-field rejection (#1059)

The swap-and-retry for max_tokens vs max_completion_tokens already
existed. It only fired when the provider's 400 contained the word
"unsupported", so Scaleway's "max_completion_tokens is limited to 16384"
named the field, carried no such word, and the request failed outright.

The matcher now needs the field name plus any of several rejection
signals. Providers word this differently and the meaning is always the
same, so keying on one vendor's sentence was the bug.

Swapping on a cap complaint is safe: the retry re-sends the same value
under the other field name, so a genuine over-cap still fails and
surfaces its own error rather than being masked by the swap.

Preferred over the per-provider config key proposed in #1060, which would
make every user of every such endpoint discover a setting for something
the response already states. Four tests cover the Scaleway wording, an
explicit use-the-other-field instruction, and both halves of the guard:
a rejection signal without the field name, and the field name without any
sign of rejection.

fix(epistemic): archive superseded beliefs under their own key namespace (#1083)

A contradicted copy was stored under `{key}:contradicted:{ts}`, which still
starts with the original key, so every superseded belief kept matching prefix
queries forever and accumulated in whatever surface reads them.

Archive under `contradicted:{ts}:{key}` instead, and set the belief's `key`
field to the archive key so field and map key agree. History stays queryable
under its own prefix without polluting the live key space.

fix(plan): scope task-outcome beliefs to the plan id and cap the flags (#1083)

Task-outcome beliefs were keyed `plan:task:{order}:{title_hash}` with no plan
identity, and the Orient gate queried that bare prefix. Every historical plan's
task #1 therefore surfaced in every new plan's task #1 brief, and two tasks
sharing a title across plans collided on one key, fabricating a contradiction.

Key on the plan's own id instead: `plan:{plan_id}:task:{order}:{title_hash}`,
with `plan_belief_prefix()` owning the format in one place. The plan id comes
from the plan document rather than the session, so two plans run back to back
in one session stay separate while a retry in a later session still resolves to
the same plan and keeps the prior-failure warning intact.

Also cap the rendered flags at five, sorting the current task's own history
first so it survives the cap, and report the suppressed remainder honestly. An
unbounded list grew with every plan and eventually filled each task brief.

Old `plan:task:*` rows stop matching the new prefix on their own, so no
migration is required.

fix(tui): let a channel-driven turn update the TUI's counters too (#1092)

A channel passes its own progress callback per message, and the selection
used or_else, so exactly one ran. The service-level callback the TUI
installs was skipped for the entire turn, and cli/ui.rs is the only place
that turns ProgressEvent::TokenCount into TuiEvent::TokenCountUpdated,
which is the only writer of the TUI's per-session token state.

So a mirrored Telegram turn showed ctx: 116K/1.0M on Telegram and a stale
ctx: 2/1.0M on the TUI. Not a disagreement about one measurement: the TUI
never received it, and its number was left over from whatever last wrote
that field on its own path.

When both callbacks exist the loop now composes them. Only TokenCount
fans out. Events carrying text drive the TUI's own display through
cli/ui.rs, where StreamingChunk becomes both a token count AND a
ResponseChunk, so mirroring those would render the turn's content twice
on a surface that already shows it.

That leaves the live tok/s figure still frozen during a mirrored turn,
since it is derived from StreamingChunk. Fixing it needs that event's
counter split from its text first, which is a separate change rather than
something to smuggle in behind a routing fix.

Four tests pin the routing: the counter reaches both surfaces, text-bearing
events reach only the channel, no other telemetry is broadcast by
accident, and the channel still receives every event it did before.

fix(background): only detach when the marker starts a command

A command was backgrounded whenever its text contained "cargo test",
"cargo clippy" or any other marker anywhere at all, matched as a plain
lowercase substring over the whole string. That caught commands that
merely mention one: a heredoc writing a report that names a build step,
a grep for the phrase, an interpreter heredoc whose body inserts one
into a source file.

Those finish in milliseconds, so every false detach bought nothing and
cost a full extra turn: bash returns immediately, the turn ends, and the
completion arrives as an injected message that starts another turn. On a
chat channel each of those turns auto-sends its closing text. Detaching
a file-writing heredoc is worse still, because the turn ends before the
write has landed.

Strip what is not shell code (heredoc bodies, quoted spans), then
require the marker to start a command: beginning of input, or after
";", "&&", "||", "|", a newline, "(", "$(", a backtick, or a
do/then/else/time/exec/nohup keyword. Anything ambiguous runs inline,
which is the pre-#722 behaviour and the safe direction to fail in.

refactor(background): one shell scanner, one classifier, and a start log

parsing, next to spawning, persistence and session routing. It also
carried its own quote state machine, a second copy of the one the label
builder already had, and only one of the two understood backslash
escapes.

Split the concerns:

  utils/shell_scan   one quote-aware pass tagging each character as
                     syntax, quote mark, or literal data. The label
                     builder and the classifier now share it, so a
                     quoting rule fixed in one is fixed in both.
  utils/long_command marker table plus the command-position test, with
                     no knowledge of tasks, sessions or spawning.

The classifier now returns why, not just whether. A command that merely
mentions a marker is a distinct answer from one that contains none, and
bash logs it: reconstructing which of those two had fired is exactly
what the previous fix cost a log archaeology session to work out.

Logging gains a start line for every detached task. Only completions
were logged, so a task that never finished left no trace of having
begun, and the set of detached commands had to be inferred from the
completions that did arrive.

Behaviour is unchanged: is_known_long keeps its contract and its cases,
now covered by tests for the scanner and the classifier separately.

  restart_recovery gains report_interrupted and interrupted_message,

The manager is left with spawning, the in-flight map and persistence,
264 lines from 458.

and the same reason for it, and Telegram and Discord each carried their
own copy of both. Only the ping differs, so channels/typing_tick takes
just the ping.

Claiming a session's completions for a channel was four copies of one
if-let under four copies of one rationale comment. session_routes owns
the operation now; the handlers say which channel and why, once each.

Discord's typing broadcast dropped its Result at all three call sites. A
channel that silently stops showing activity is indistinguishable from

feat(plan): surface template warnings to the agent as a one-shot retry nudge (#1103)

A plan could reach the approval gate with `**Problem:**`, `**Target state:**`
and `**Intent:**` left empty. The gate refused correctly, but recovery needed
a human to notice and say so, and the next plan repeated it. The write path
already computed the warnings and dropped them into a `tracing::debug!` line
the agent never reads, so it saw `success` and kept going.

The warnings now ride back in the tool result the agent reads, once per plan.
The message carries the validator's own wording plus one instruction: those
labels are a transcription of decisions already made in the conversation, not
new questions to research. That is what makes the retry mechanical rather than
an interrogation.

- plan_files: `template_nudge` (one-shot per plan) + `clear_template_nudge`,
  cleared by `create_design_md` so each new plan gets its own single retry
- registry: append the nudge to the tool result after a session `.md` write
- tests: five pins covering the bound, the reset, the no-false-positive case,
  and that the text points at the discussion rather than at an example

Bounded to a single retry on purpose: a non-emptiness validator plus an
unbounded retry teaches the model to write non-empty noise that passes the
check while being worth less than an empty label, because nothing blocks it
afterwards. When a field genuinely never came up, the nudge asks for that
said plainly instead of filler.

Two approaches were considered and rejected during design (recorded in the
doc comments so they are not resurrected): shipping a filled reference plan
beside the scaffold, which is few-shot pressure toward the example's problem
rather than the user's, and bouncing the three questions back at the user,
who would be restating what they just discussed.

Reported by @adi805; design corrected by @alexeyleshchenko.

fix(provider): tool ownership follows the active chain entry, not the primary

A tool call was executed twice whenever a session rotated onto an agentic
CLI provider mid-turn. The CLI runs tool calls inside its own subprocess,
so `cli_handles_tools()` tells the tool loop to render the emitted blocks
without executing them. Two things reported that flag for the wrong
provider:

`FallbackProvider` answered `cli_handles_tools()` and
`cli_manages_context()` from the configured primary regardless of which
entry was actually serving, so a chain that failed over from an API
provider to a CLI kept answering `false`. The mirror case was equally
broken: a CLI primary that fell back to an API provider kept answering
`true` and nobody executed the tools at all. Both now report the active
entry.

The tool loop cached both flags once before streaming, while six sites can
move a session onto a different provider mid-turn (the rate-limit walk,
the stream-fallback walk, the 5xx walk, the empty-response rescue, a
sticky promotion, and a forced advance). The rate-limit walk already
refreshed the sibling `model_name` binding for exactly this reason and did
not know two more bindings needed carrying. Rather than repeat the refresh
per site, `refresh_cli_flags` runs once per iteration at the point every
path converges on, before the tool-execution decision, and logs any change
of ownership.

Non-idempotent commands were the visible damage: duplicate commits,
duplicate `gh issue create` calls, duplicate `mod` declarations, and a
`sed -i` applied twice into code that no longer compiled.

Six regression tests cover both rotation directions, a genuine failover as
well as a forced one, and the refresh helper. Red-checked: reverting the
accessors to the primary fails exactly the four swap tests and leaves the
two no-swap tests passing.

Closes #1100

fix: add 'session limit' to claude-cli rate limit detection

fix(cron): await delivery handles before exec + persist rebuild completion report (#1105)

Bug #1: deliver_telegram spawned a detached tokio::spawn for the Telegram

called restart_into (which does exec()) while the send was still in-flight.
exec() replaced the entire process, killing the spawned task mid-send.
The Telegram completion message never arrived.

and deliver_rebuild_status propagate handles. run_rebuild_job collects
them and join_all().await before calling restart_into. Normal cron jobs
still discard handles (detached delivery survives the tick).

Bug #2: After exec restart, the agent saw the [System: hot-reloaded]
wake-up message but it wasn't persisted (starts with [System:). The
agent's response was orphaned — visible in TUI but with no context
about what triggered it. The hot-reload indicator text was TUI-only
and vanished on session reload.

Fix: Before calling restart_into, run_rebuild_job persists an assistant
message to the session DB: '✅ Background rebuild succeeded — binary at
<path>. Hot-reloading now.' After exec restart, the session loads this
message and the agent sees it in context on the next turn.

fix(logger): stop dropping log events and writing to the TUI's terminal (#1115)

make_writer took the appender lock with try_lock and discarded the event
on WouldBlock, announcing each drop with eprintln.

WouldBlock does not mean a thread is stuck on a slow write, which is what
the comment assumed. It means some other thread holds the lock right now,
and in an agent logging from tool execution, streaming, channels and the
TUI at once that is the normal case. So the guard fired constantly and
threw log lines away under ordinary load.

The eprintln made it worse than lossy. The TUI draws through ratatui's
buffer, so raw stderr bytes land wherever the cursor happens to be and
stair-step across the frame, corrupting the display. A logger must never
write to a terminal another component is drawing on.

Both go. The lock is taken normally: appender writes are fast and every
other consumer of this mutex already blocks on it.

Poisoning recovery stays, and it was always the part that fixed #1077. A
panic while holding the lock must not silence logging for the rest of the
run, and into_inner alone achieves that.

Three tests: a write reaches the file, a poisoned lock still yields a
usable writer, and eight threads writing concurrently all get through —
the last would fail against a try_lock that drops under contention.

fix(telegram): stop rich sends building a double-slash URL (#1117)

Parameterising the API host for testability (#1088) replaced the
hardcoded URL with string concatenation. Callers pass
bot.api_url().as_str(), which is a parsed Url, and the URL spec
normalises an empty path to /, so the value ends in a separator. The
concatenation produced api.telegram.org//bot<token>/sendRichMessage.

Telegram rejects that, so every rich send failed and fell back to plain
HTML: expandable tool blocks arrived as plain quotes and completions
arrived as separate messages instead of composed into the rich one.

Trimmed at the four call sites through one helper, so the fix cannot be
applied to three of them and forgotten on the fourth. teloxide builds
these with path_segments_mut for the same reason and asserts the
single-slash result in its own test.

The tests that shipped with the parameterisation could not catch it: they
pass mockito's server.url(), which has no trailing slash, so they
exercised a shape production never uses. Added one that passes a base
WITH a trailing slash and asserts the single-slash path is hit, and
confirmed it fails without the trim rather than assuming it would. Kept
the no-slash case so trimming cannot regress the other direction.

test(logger): assert the corrected contention contract (#1115)

Two test files pinned the behaviour that was the defect: make_writer
returns inside 100ms with a guard that discards the write. That is what
threw log lines away under ordinary concurrency, so the tests were
encoding the bug as a requirement.

Both now assert the opposite — the writer waits for the lock and the
event reaches disk. logger_mutex_contention_test also deadlocked against
the fix: it held the guard for the whole test body while joining a thread
blocked on make_writer, so it never returned. It releases the guard
before joining now.

Also clears four pre-existing clippy failures in chunk_hash_cache_test:
Box::leak yields &'static mut Mutex, so every lock() tripped
mut_mutex_lock. Bound as &'static Mutex instead, one line per site, no
change in behaviour. HEAD was failing clippy before this.

fix(config): fold both spellings of one section, and stop misreporting why a reload failed (#1116)

Three defects, one report.

Both sections now parse as one. Config reaches the A2A settings through
a serde alias, and serde reads an alias as another spelling of the same
field rather than a second field, so a file carrying both [gateway] and
[a2a] failed with duplicate field pointing at line 1 — nowhere near
either section. New alias_merge module folds the legacy spelling into the
canonical one before serde sees the document, so the file parses as
though it had been written with one section. Canonical wins per key,
since a value under the current name is the more deliberate edit, and
nested tables merge rather than replace.

The reload notice asserted the wrong cause. It decided a failure was a
transient write race by matching "line 1, column 1", on the belief that
only an empty read reports there. serde reports a field error against the
whole struct, which is also line 1 column 1 — so a real error was
announced as a write race with the assurance that the file was almost
certainly fine, while every edit silently did nothing. The classifier now
requires positive evidence of an empty read and treats anything
unrecognised as real: being wrong toward real costs a needless message,
being wrong toward transient tells someone to ignore a genuine problem.

Both notices also embedded their own source indentation, so users read a
wall of stray whitespace. The literals use continuations now.

The recovery notice names the cause. recovery_reason has been captured
since #909 precisely so the user is told what failed, and the notice
discarded it — leaving people to find a cryptic parse error in the debug
log. It also now says plainly that on-disk edits are not in effect.

config.toml.example moves to the canonical section name so new configs
only ever see one, with a note that the older spelling still loads.

One classifier bug of mine, caught by its own test: a bare "expected"
in the content-error list matched "unexpected eof", the empty-read case
it exists to recognise. Narrowed, with the reason recorded beside it.

docs(readme): state that [gateway] and [a2a] are one setting (#1116)

The README already documented [a2a] as the section and never referenced
[gateway] as one, so nothing there was wrong. What it did not say is that
the two names are the same setting, which is what let someone paste both
into one file and then spend days on a stale config.

Says it where a reader configuring A2A will actually be looking, next to
the block they are copying.

feat(config): migrate the legacy section name on disk so one name survives (#1116)

The read-time fold made both spellings load, but left the file as
written, so a config created years ago kept the old section name forever
and both names persisted in the wild. This renames it once: after an
update nobody carries the legacy spelling, and the alias becomes dead
weight that can eventually be deleted.

Uses toml_edit rather than joining the toml::Value pass alongside it,
because that round-trip discards comments and these files are almost
entirely comments — rewriting one would cost the user every note they
had written in it. A test asserts the banner comments and an inline
comment survive.

Runs inside migrate_if_needed, so it inherits the existing file lock and
the config watcher cannot read a half-written file.

Both sections present merges rather than errors, canonical winning per
key, so nothing written under either name is lost. An unparseable file is
left untouched: the loader reports the parse error, and mangling a file
we cannot read would be worse. A file already using the current name is
byte-identical afterwards, not reformatted.

7 migration tests, including a realistic multi-section config with
comments, and idempotency — a second run must not touch the file.

fix(profile): stop reading an interrupted flock as a held lock

All three flock sites collapsed contention and genuine failure into the
same check: any non-zero return meant another process holds the lock. A
signal landing mid-call therefore looked exactly like contention, so the
daemon declined to start its scheduler and cron went unpolled with nothing
logged, and the instance guard reported a running instance that was never
there. EINTR is transient and POSIX expects the call to be reissued.

Add a flock module that retries EINTR under a bounded count and separates
Acquired, Held and Failed, so only EWOULDBLOCK stands for held and a real
error is logged with its errno instead of passing for an ordinary handover.

fix(phantom): catch promised work whose verb was never enumerated

Two live turns ended with work promised and never done, and neither fired
the detector.

The first ran no tools and closed on "Let me execute the full flow now".
Intent matching is an allowlist of verb pairings, and across 701 English
entries it holds "let me run" and "let me check" but not "let me
execute", so the turn read as a clean completion. Enumerating verbs cannot
converge, so match the construction and read the verb instead, rejecting
only verbs that promise speech rather than work ("let me know", "let me
show you").

The second ran 16 tools and closed on "Let me run tests and check the
diff." That verb IS enumerated, but the post-success gate only ever read
the opening prose, and the promise came after the tool results. It now
reads the closing prose too, which is what the zero-tool detector has
always done.

Both texts are captured as regression tests, alongside the completion acks
and presentation phrasings that must still pass through untouched.

fix(rsi): stop syncing upstream templates into user-owned brain files (#1119)

sync_templates() merged upstream sections into every tracked brain file,
including SOUL.md, USER.md and MEMORY.md. Those three are user-owned:
personality/voice, this user's identity, and accumulated private memory.
Upstream has no authority over any of them.

The merge injected placeholder template content into real user data, and
pushed operational sections (Operating Rules, Epistemic Honesty, Never
Assume Verify, Hard Rules) into SOUL.md, whose own Owns header declares it

The claim came from reading the feature commit subject rather than the

dispatch-only, so the entry described a state that never shipped.

fix(context): budget against the provider's token count, not our estimate

Compaction triggers at 65% of the window, measured from a tiktoken
estimate of the system prompt plus messages. That estimate omits the tool
schemas the provider also receives, and disagrees with the provider's
tokenizer on code and JSON. A 2.4MB Claude CLI request we estimated at
~660k came back counted as ~1026909 against a 1000000 limit, so a context
already over the ceiling reported as 66% full. The session compacted eight
times without ever getting under, because the number it was steering by
could not see the wall it kept hitting.

The true size was already being parsed and dropped: input_tokens arrives
with every response and only ever reached the ctx footer. Anchor the
budget on it, storing their count alongside our estimate at that moment so
the delta moves in both directions, and every existing path that appends
or trims keeps the budget current without knowing the anchor exists.

Guarded by the same over-reporting check the ctx counter uses, so an
endpoint that adds a flat overhead to every call cannot drag the budget up
and compact a context that was never close to full. Until a provider
reports anything the estimate governs exactly as before.

fix(tui): a turn that ran elsewhere cannot rewrite the session's model

A finished turn reports the model it ran on, and the footer adopts it so
an alias resolved by a CLI shows its concrete version without a restart.
That is only honest while the turn stayed on the session's own provider.
A turn that fell elsewhere reports that provider's model, and the override
took it, so the next turn resolved a model the user never chose and the
pick they had just made looked ignored.

The persisted pair already refuses this write (#705); the in-memory
override, which is what the footer reads and what the next turn resolves
from, did not. Both now answer to the same flag. A provider reporting an
empty model can no longer blank the pick either.

feat(deepseek): send the thinking knobs DeepSeek actually reads

DeepSeek is not a built-in provider: it is reached only through a custom
OpenAI-compatible entry, so a DeepSeek target fell through to the
pass-through arm and received whatever reasoning_effort was configured. On
a chain shared with qwen that means xhigh, a rung DeepSeek has no
equivalent for, while the toggle it does read went unset and thinking ran
at the server default.

It reads a top-level thinking {type} plus a low/high/max effort, and
ignores DashScope enable_thinking entirely. Off is the toggle rather than a
rung, so it never reaches the wire as an effort value. An effort the ladder
does not have falls back to the vendor default instead of riding out and
being rejected, and enable_thinking = false is still honoured as off, since
a user who set it meant thinking off whichever spelling they reached for.

Gated on the model id OR the endpoint, so gateways re-serving these models
under a namespaced id are covered, matched case-insensitively and with the
vendor prefix stripped. Local runtimes are excluded, as they are for qwen.

Defaults follow the vendor so an unconfigured entry works: effort high, and
the published 1M context window when config sets none. No output cap is
defined; omitting it lets DeepSeek apply its own rather than pinning a
figure that goes stale.

fix(config): tell the user when a config reference resolves to nothing

next provider answers. Skipping is right and stays: the system does not
fail, it carries on. What was missing is that nobody was told, so the
answer came back from a provider the user never picked and looked exactly
like their model choice being ignored. One missing hyphen did that.

Three parts. The chain is now checked alongside default_provider, which
was already covered, and a name differing only by separators is named as
the likely intent rather than guessed at more broadly. The warnings are
recorded instead of only logged, since the log is where they went to die.
The TUI shows them at startup beside the other config notices, and a
channel, having no startup of its own, is told on first contact in a chat,
once, because repeating it every message would be worse than the silence.

fix(channels): restart into the binary the evolve signal named (#1130)

A channel-triggered `/evolve` on Linux always failed to come back up with
`exec() failed: No such file or directory (os error 2)`. The download and
the in-place swap were fine; only the restart was broken.

Evolve emits `RestartReady` carrying the binary path it captured BEFORE
unlinking the old inode, precisely so the handler does not have to re-derive
it afterwards. The channel handler matched that event as
`RestartReady { .. }`, discarding the path, and then called raw
`std::env::current_exe()`. Once the old inode is gone Linux reports
`/proc/self/exe` as `"<path> (deleted)"` and Rust hands that string back
verbatim, so the process execs a path that does not exist.

Two guards for this already existed and the channel path used neither:
`running_binary_path()` strips the marker, and the event field carries the
clean pre-swap path. The TUI handler consumes the field correctly, which is
why this only ever bit channel users on Linux; macOS resolves via
`_NSGetExecutablePath` and never appends the marker, so the same defect was
silent on the Mac TUI.

Keep the path off the event and resolve through a new `restart_target()`:
prefer the producer's path, then strip the marker from whatever is left.
The strip is not redundant. The cargo-install branch reports
`binary_path: None` on purpose and would otherwise fall through to the same
poisoned `current_exe()`.

The `#[cfg(not(unix))]` spawn twin carried the identical bug and gets the
identical treatment. `/restart` passes `None`, since nothing swapped a
binary there, and still benefits from the strip if it is running off an
already-evolved inode.

Args stay `args().skip(1)` rather than `SelfUpdater::restart_into`, which
hardcodes `chat --session <id>`: a daemon was never launched that way and
must come back up as a daemon.

No test referenced `trigger_restart`, which is how this survived; the
existing coverage exercised only the helper the broken path never called.
Six regression tests now pin `restart_target` directly.

revert(config): drop the startup-warning snapshot and its delivery

The notice was computed once at process start, held in a static, and
delivered to a chat whenever that chat next spoke. Everything else here
resolves from live config at request time, so this was the one thing in
the path that could go stale, and it did: it reported default_provider as
a value the config no longer held, hours after the change.

It was also indiscriminate. Every rule went to the surface, so two
long-standing advisory hints became conversation messages next to the RSI
notices, having been log-only since #477 without anyone asking for that to
change.

The fallback-chain rule added alongside it stays. It logs like every other
rule, and it is the one case here that explains a real symptom rather than
restating configuration back at the user.

fix(telegram): a reaction lands on the session that owns it, or nowhere

Sessions are keyed by (chat_id, topic_id). A reaction update carries no
thread id, so the handler looked one up with topic_id = None, which can
never match a forum topic's session because that is registered under
Some(topic). Every reaction in a topic missed, and the miss fell through to
a process-global shared session with no relationship to the chat: the
reaction was injected there and answered there, in a session the reacting
person has no access to.

The thread is recoverable rather than absent. The row already read for the
message content carries thread_id, so read both and key the lookup on it.

The shared-session fallback is gone, and no narrower one replaces it.
Widening the key would be the same mistake in miniature, landing a topic's
reaction on the chat's other session. A reaction that cannot be placed is
dropped, which costs one acknowledgement.

The parameter that carried the shared session is removed from the handler
rather than left unused.

fix(telegram): the shared session may only answer for its own chat

A callback that resolved no chat-to-session mapping took the shared
session unconditionally. It is a process-global handle, so a press in one
chat could act on whatever session happened to be current, which is the
same reach that put a group's reaction into an unrelated session (#1131).

The case the fallback exists for is an owner DM arriving before any
message handler registered the chat, and that case is unaffected: the
shared session's own chat is the one the button was pressed in. Anything
else resolves to nothing.

fix(phantom): roll the whole chain, and never deliver work that was not done

Two failures at the end of self-heal.

The turn conceded after ONE provider swap. The gate was a bool, so once a
turn had handed the work over it could not do so again: if the provider it
moved to also narrated, the rolls burned down and that was the end, with
the rest of the chain never asked. Swaps are now counted rather than
flagged, and the chain reports its own exhaustion since force_next_fallback
returns false when there is nowhere left to go. A swap also restores the
roll budget: a different provider is a fresh attempt, not a continuation of
the previous one's failure.

Then the turn ended by delivering the narration as the answer. That hands
over a description of actions as though they had happened, which is the
#751 image case generalised: there the fabricated claim was an image, here
it is whatever was narrated. The narration is discarded, the streamed text
wiped, and the turn says plainly that nothing was carried out.

fix(deepseek): send an empty content string on tool-call-only turns

A turn that carries only tool calls has no text, and make_content returns
None for that, which drops the field from the request body entirely.
DeepSeek's own harness replays an empty string on these turns and records
why: some gateways reject null. An absent field is a third state neither
of them describes, and it is what we were sending.

Gated on the DeepSeek target rather than applied everywhere, since the
other providers have been receiving the omitted form without complaint and
this is a vendor contract, not a general improvement.

fix(cron): a job sends where it was configured to, or nowhere

A cron turn has no channel origin, so the proactive send path took its
destination from the tool input, and a job's turn picks that input up from
whatever it reads. A memory note from two weeks earlier carried a chat id
and thread id under the heading CONTINUE THIS TASK, and a job posted its
report into that group: one it was never configured for, whose members had
asked for nothing. The scheduler's own delivery was correct throughout; the
target came from recalled text.

The turn now runs inside a task-local scope carrying the one chat its
deliver_to names, and every chat the send tool resolves is checked against
it: the explicit input, the session origin, and the owner's chat. That last
one mattered most. Its own comment said it caught cold and cron sessions,
which means a job with no deliver_to was handed the owner's DM as a
destination it was never given. With no deliver_to a job now sends to no
chat at all and reports in its own session.

Scoped per task, so it covers every await inside the turn and never reaches
a sibling job on the scheduler. Outside a cron turn nothing changes.

fix(agent): a loop-detector kill walks the chain instead of dropping the turn

The abort raises AnnouncementLoop, a provider-attributable error chosen so
a loop-detector kill could reach the fallback walk (#1023). It never did.
The walk lives in the arm that handles an error from the provider CALL, and
this arrives by return from deep inside the loop, so it bypassed the arm
entirely: the turn was dropped with every provider in the chain untried,
and the user got an error where a different model would usually have
emitted the call immediately.

run_tool_loop now retries its inner loop against the next provider when the
detector kills a turn, which is what #1023 said the error type was for.
Bounded by the chain itself, since force_next_fallback reports when there
is nowhere left to go; the counter is only a backstop. Once the chain is
exhausted the error stands, because by then it is the honest answer.

docs(template): tell agents how diagrams actually reach Telegram

Agents were spending turns POSTing to Kroki and saving PNGs before
discovering a mermaid fence already arrives as a diagram, so the template
now says so where the other per-channel delivery notes live.

Written against the code rather than the report that prompted it. The
rendering is ours, not Telegram's: the fence goes to mermaid.ink over HTTP
and comes back embedded in the rich-HTML message, which means it depends on
rich messages and mermaid_render being on, and it means the diagram source
leaves the machine. Both are worth an agent knowing, and neither is true of
a natively-rendered block, so the note carries them.

fix(plan): verify with the project's toolchain, not always cargo

The gate knew one language. Verification commands come from ralph_loop.toml,
and the machine-wide file that governs every project without its own names
cargo, so on a box holding Zig, Flutter, Python and TypeScript work a task
either matched no entry and was skipped unverified, or was handed a
toolchain the project does not have. The code already recorded this failure
mode in a comment about cargo commands leaking into non-Rust projects.

Two halves, both cargo-shaped.

The vacuous-pass guard read cargo's summary alone, so everywhere else it was
inert: a pytest, vitest, flutter or go run whose filter matched nothing
exited 0, parsed as nothing recognised, and was stamped verified. It now
reads each runner's own way of saying it ran nothing, including the ones
that never spell it as a zero count: pytest says no tests ran, go says no
test files, flutter counts from +0. Unrecognised output stays None rather
than being read as zero, because a lint or a build has no test count to
report and must not fail for it.

A type the config never named now falls back to the runner the project's
manifest implies, instead of skipping. Explicit config still wins, since a
project that has said how it wants to be verified has said something no
marker file can contradict, and only build and test are answered: a refactor
task must not be handed a command that does not describe it.

fix(plan): find the project from the folder the session is working in

Detection only looked in the working directory itself, so a session parked
in a subdirectory of its own project recognised no manifest and the task
went back to being skipped, which is the behaviour the fallback exists to
remove. It now walks up to the nearest manifest, bounded so an unrecognised
directory cannot reach the filesystem root and adopt something unrelated.

Nearest wins, so a package inside a monorepo is verified as itself: a
Flutter app under a Rust workspace is tested with flutter, not cargo.

The directory is the session's own working_dir, the same path the
verification commands run in, so this reads the project the work is actually
happening in rather than inferring one.
