fix(telegram): page and filter the model picker instead of sending it whole

Choosing OpenRouter did nothing at all: no list, no error, no timeout. The
picker sent the catalogue twice, enumerated in the message text and again as
one button per model, so with several hundred models the text alone passed
Telegram's 4096 characters. editMessageText answered MESSAGE_TOO_LONG three
times over, and the only trace was a log line, which is why it read as still
loading rather than broken.

Paged rather than capped, so the rest of the catalogue stays reachable:
twenty per page with a prev/next row, and a case-insensitive substring
filter with the match count shown, so a name can be narrowed to instead of
scrolled to. A filter matching nothing says so rather than drawing an empty
list.

Each page records its own models as the rendered list. Long names travel as
positions and are resolved when tapped, so catalogue positions would have
made a tap on page three select a model from page one. An overlong filter is
dropped from the navigation payload rather than truncated, because
callback_data caps at 64 bytes and a truncated filter selects the wrong
models while a missing one merely shows more than intended.

A render that still fails now says so in the chat. Reporting it only to the
log is what turned a rejected request into an endless spinner.

feat(subagent): give each child its own worktree so a fan-out stops colliding

Children inherited the parent's directory, so several spawned at once wrote
the same bytes with no arbitration. The collision was by construction, not
by coincidence: a parallel fan-out is designed to run them together.

Each child now gets a git worktree on a subagent/<id> branch, and works
there. Isolation is affordable because .git is shared: a checkout is ~20MB
of source against a 39GB target/, and that build cache is cloned
copy-on-write where the filesystem supports it, which costs no disk and no
time. A child on a filesystem without clonefile simply builds cold.

Nothing here is load-bearing. Outside a repository, or if git refuses, the
child works in the parent's directory exactly as before, and a tree left by
a crashed run is cleared rather than being allowed to refuse isolation to
every later child.

On completion a tree that holds nothing is returned and never mentioned.
One that holds a commit or an uncommitted edit is kept, and the result the
parent reads names the branch, the path and the merge that lands it.
Reporting that only to the log is how isolation turns a clobbering problem
into a stranded-work problem.

Work is judged by HEAD having moved off the commit the tree was cut from,
not by asking git what is absent from a remote: in a repository with no
remote that calls every commit work, so every tree would be kept forever.

Merge feat/subagent-worktree: a private checkout per sub-agent

A fan-out spawns several children against one tree, so they collided by
construction. Each now works in its own git worktree on a subagent/<id>
branch, at ~20MB of source since .git is shared and the build cache is
cloned copy-on-write.

A tree holding nothing is returned silently; one holding work is kept and
named in the result the parent reads, with the branch and the merge that
lands it.

feat(tools): one writer at a time per path

Agents sharing a working tree write the same bytes with no arbitration.
Sub-agents have their own checkout now, but that isolation degrades to the
parent's directory outside a repository or when git refuses, and the
collision returns with it. Nothing else here guards a file: every lock in
the tree is process- or session-scoped.

The write tools take the lock themselves rather than agents being asked to
check first. A prompt-layer rule cannot reach the case that matters most,
since two children colliding in the degraded path never read the parent's
instructions, and nothing would reveal that one had skipped the check.

Deliberately weak in three ways, because a lock that can block real work is
worse than the collision it prevents. A contended write waits briefly and
then proceeds, reporting the overlap so the file's contents are known to be
suspect rather than silently wrong. Every failure to lock degrades to
writing anyway. The guard releases on drop, including on a panic, so a
writer that dies mid-write costs a pause rather than a wedged file.

Lock files live under the profile home keyed by a hash of the absolute
path. Beside the target would litter the user's tree, and a repository
would see them as untracked additions the agent then tries to explain.

does not serve, and when its own /v1/models fetch had not landed yet the

already uses elsewhere. A provider with no entry yet now contributes

ci: refuse to administer the host's rustup

dtolnay/rust-toolchain manages rustup on whatever machine it runs on, and
defaults CARGO_HOME to ~/.cargo when it is unset. On a self-hosted runner
that is somebody's workstation, so CI was installing toolchains into their
installation: twenty rustup toolchain install calls in one release, and the
rustup binary itself gone afterwards, leaving all thirteen shims in
~/.cargo/bin dangling and no working cargo for the machine owner.

Isolating the runner's environment fixes it, but a launchd plist on one
machine is not something the repository can enforce, and the first repair
held only until the next release. Every toolchain step now fails the job
when CARGO_HOME or RUSTUP_HOME is unset or points at the host's own
installation, so the isolation cannot silently lapse.

Scoped to self-hosted runners, where the directories belong to a person. A
hosted runner is a disposable VM and is unaffected. The publish job is
guarded too: it runs hosted today, but it is the job most likely to move.

fix(subagent): re-bind tool_search to each child registry (#1210)

build_child_registry copied the parent's ToolSearchTool instance as-is; that instance captured the PARENT registry Arc at construction (tool_setup binds it once at startup). A child's tool_search therefore activated discovered schemas into the parent's registry under the CHILD's session id, while the child's request builder read active tools from its OWN registry — the discovered schema never rode on a child request, and well-behaved models looped re-searching instead of emitting calls for undeclared tools (observed live: deepseek-v4-flash and kimi-k2.7-code across two providers; child registry count stayed 61 through every search).

Fix: build_child_registry skips the inherited search-tool instance and registers a FRESH ToolSearchTool bound to the child's own Arc. Return type becomes Arc<ToolRegistry> so callers hand the same Arc to both the re-bound tool and AgentService::with_tool_registry; the three callers (spawn, resume, team_create) drop their redundant Arc::new wrap. Re-binding per level keeps nested spawns correct — each generation's search tool points at its own registry.

Three independent token buckets keyed by chat id, layered BESIDE the

concurrent sessions in several topics split one Telegram budget — the
Aug-25 logs showed 391 chat-action 429s (worst second: 36 attempts),
while edits sailed at 32/min with a single 429, proving limits are
per-method-family.

- G1 typing (admit_chat_action): ~1 sendChatAction / 3s per forum,
  burst 8; concurrent sessions in a topic coalesce into that refresh;
  hold-and-release under pressure, drop past typing_max_hold_secs.

- G3 sends (pace_send): ~1/s spacing under an 18/min group ceiling;

Scope is forums-only: negative chat ids arm governance on the first

fix(tool_search): bind to the registry whose active set is actually read (#1210)

The tool captured an Arc to the registry it was constructed against. A
sub-agent's registry is a copy holding the same Arc<dyn Tool> values, so
the copied tool_search kept pointing at the PARENT: in a child session
it activated there under the child's session id, while the child's
request builder read the child's own active set. The schema never rode
on the child's next request, so the model could not call what it had
just been told was callable.

a registry -> tool -> registry cycle. Survivable for one long-lived
parent, not for a child per spawn. An upgrade failure says so plainly
rather than returning an empty result the model would read as 'no such
tool exists'.

fix(tg): token-keyed suggestion stash - each tap resolves its own keyboard (#1217)

Reconciles #1217's resolve-vs-reject directive with #1226-H2's strip
semantics, which turned out to be two halves of one design:

The stash was one slot per session UUID, so consecutive turns' keyboards
overwrote each other and every callback trusted whichever set landed
last - wrong-text injection by construction under overlap. Keyboards now
register up front and receive an opaque 8-char token that rides in every
callback payload (followup:<token>:<idx>, well inside Telegram's 64-byte
budget). The tap takes the entry BY TOKEN, and the serving session comes
back from the stash entry instead of client-supplied data, so a stale or
forged id can no longer pull another turn's options (#1217 correct
resolution).

Unknown tokens hit the existing #1226 stale-shell arm unchanged: dead
keyboards still strip themselves and toast, which IS H2's reject-and-
strip applied to per-keyboard identity. set_pending_followups splits
into register / attach_followup_host / drop_pending_followup;
clear_pending_followups sweeps all of a session's sets when the user
types instead of just the newest.

Callback-data cap test updated to token form and pinned at the worst
index.

fix(tg): route inline-button callbacks to the session that serves the chat (#1248)

Message ingress composed the session's topic id as
normalize_topic(topic_session_id(..), known_forum); resolve_callback_session
called topic_session_id alone. In a known forum the General topic therefore
resolved to Some(GENERAL_TOPIC_ID) for messages and None for button presses,
so a /models tap looked up the pre-#1220 base session and wrote the provider
and model pick into a row that serves no messages. The picker confirmed the
switch, the chat kept answering on the old pair, and the user had no way to
see why.

Both paths now go through session_resolve::session_topic_for_event, which
performs the whole two-step composition, so ingress and callbacks cannot
disagree about which bucket a topic belongs to.

fallback_providers was built once in AgentService::new and never replaced, so
editing fallback_chain in config.toml had no effect until a restart. The
ConfigWatcher hot-swapped the primary provider and refreshed tools, commands,
approval policy and the context budget; the chain, the other half of the same
config block, was not among its callbacks. A provider deleted from the chain
kept receiving live traffic for hours, which is what made the reload look
broken from the outside when in fact five of six things were reloading fine.

The list moves behind an RwLock, readers take fallback_chain_snapshot() (a
cloned Vec of Arcs, since every caller walks the chain across await points and
a live guard would pin a stale list and make the future non-Send), and the
watcher calls reload_fallback_providers next to the existing swap_provider.
The rebuild runs even when the primary rebuild failed, because the two are
independent and a stale chain is the exact state being fixed. An empty result
is applied as-is: clearing fallback_chain has to clear the runtime chain, or
removal is unrepresentable.

fix(compaction): walk the fallback chain instead of dying on the primary (#1247)

compact_context called provider.complete() once and surfaced whatever came
back, while every other request path in the process walks [providers.fallback].
A session whose primary was rate-limited or out of credit therefore kept
chatting normally through a fallback and failed /compact every single time on
the dead primary. That is the worst pairing available: the session that most
needs compacting is the one whose window is full, and a session that cannot
compact cannot recover.

complete_compaction_request mirrors the tool loop's walk: skip the primary's
own name, skip providers the #952 quota breaker has marked exhausted, remap the
model to each fallback's default when it does not publish the requested one,
honour cancellation between hops, and report the full ledger when everything
dies.

The fall-through policy also moves into provider::error::should_try_next_provider,
shared by the chain, the tool loop and compaction. FallbackProvider gated on
is_retryable alone, and is_retryable deliberately answers false for a hard
quota (#952: do not burn backoff against a wall), so chain traversal read that
as fatal and aborted on the one error class a chain exists to survive. The next
provider bills a different account and would have answered fine.

fix(provider): never remove a provider from the fallback walk (#1251)

The quota circuit breaker from #952 was a process-global quarantine
table: a provider whose API reported a hard quota was marked exhausted
for an hour and every fallback walk skipped it. It was keyed by provider
name with no model dimension, so one dead model blacked out every model
on that provider, for every session in the process, off a single error.
It also marked the session's own active pick, which is how a user's
explicit selection ended up looking ignored.

That single routing decision is the parent of a long fallout list
(#981, #1084, #1100, #1101, #1104, #1108, #1124, #1140, #1247, #1249),
each patched around the table rather than at it. health.rs itself was
never revisited after the commit that introduced it.

Providers and models the user configured are now never removed from
consideration. Failure is reported with provider, model and reason; the
human decides whether to switch.

- delete provider::health and its five skip filters in the tool loop
  plus the sixth in compaction, and the seven mark sites feeding them
- delete compute_health_start_index, which read persisted failure
  counts and started the chain on a fallback so the configured primary
  was never attempted at all
- drop the skipped parameter from chain_exhausted_summary: with nothing
  ever skipped, the "Skipped (quota-exhausted)" line could only be a lie

Quota classification stays. is_quota_exhausted still makes a hard quota
non-retryable so the chain advances immediately instead of burning
three in-place retries, and still shapes the reason text.
Classification informs the human; it does not route.

Sticky promotion is untouched: a chain that swapped after a failure
stays on the provider that answered, as before.

Verified: cargo fmt clean, clippy --locked --lib --bins --tests
--all-features -D warnings clean, 7227 passed / 0 failed.

fix(tg): never reclaim system chrome as the turn's answer (#1253)

A group turn whose completion was exactly `<<react:emoji>>` arrived right
after a provider switch, and the user got the self-healing banner as the
reply plus no reaction at all. Twice in a row, reading exactly like a
dropped request. The chain was healthy throughout: it failed over in 0ms
and the fallback answered in under four seconds.

Cause was type-level. `FlowEntry` had `Tool` and `Text` only, and system
chrome shared `Text` with model narration: SelfHealingAlert, RetryAttempt
and ProviderSwitched all entered as `DisplayItem::Intermediate`. With an
empty final, the #478 reclaim pops the trailing text run and promotes it
to the answer, on the documented assumption that a trailing run after the
last tool IS the answer. True for narration, false for scaffolding. On a
react-only turn the only trailing entries were the banner, so the banner
became the reply, and because that made the final read as non-empty the
react-only path never ran and the reaction was dropped with it.

Provenance is now carried in the type:

- `DisplayItem::System` / `FlowEntry::System` for chrome, rendered exactly
  like `Text` and produced by the three chrome arms in progress.rs and
  resume.rs
- `pop_trailing_folded_texts` pops only model `Text` and leaves chrome in
  the block, so an empty final stays empty
- `last_folded_text` looks past trailing chrome for the delivery duplicate
  check, so a late banner cannot hide a folded answer and make it render
  twice
- supersession (#982) is same-kind only, so a retry counter still collapses
  in place while chrome and narration never overwrite each other

Chrome skips the model pipeline on the way in: no artifact stripping, no
rich-report promotion, no react extraction, since it is our own text.
Secret redaction stays, because the alert embeds a raw upstream error.

Verified: cargo fmt clean, clippy --locked --lib --bins --tests
--all-features -D warnings clean, 7241 passed / 0 failed.

fix(provider): a balance 429 stops telling the user to retry later (#1254)

A provider with an empty account answers HTTP 429 with code 1113,
"Insufficient balance or no resource package. Please recharge.", and the
agent appended "(rate limited, please retry later)" to it. The advice
contradicts the sentence it is attached to: a billing state does not clear
on any retry timescale. The text is not internal either, the self-healing
banner embeds it verbatim, so a whole group chat was told to wait for
something only money or a different provider fixes.

Routing was already correct and is untouched: "insufficient balance" is in
the quota phrase list, so the chain advanced with zero in-place retries.
The defect was that the advice suffix was chosen from the HTTP status
alone and never consulted the classifier the router already trusts.

`rate_limit_message` now builds that text from the upstream message: a
recognised quota or balance wording gets remedy-oriented advice and drops
any Retry-After countdown, everything else keeps the retry advice, since
treating an unknown throttle as terminal is the more expensive mistake.
Both the OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic error paths route through it.

Second defect in the same failure, one line away: "Streaming call served"
logged the requested model while the fallback had remapped to its own
default, so the log answered "what actually ran" with a model that never
ran. `Provider::served_model` reports the model of the entry that served,
mirroring the remap rule the chain applies, and both call sites use it.

Verified: cargo fmt clean, clippy --locked --lib --bins --tests

fix(phantom): catch a sequenced plan announcement in a zero-tool turn (#1261)

A turn handed a multi-step implementation task answered with one sentence
of intent, "Setting up the plan, then mapping every call site before
touching anything.", emitted zero tool calls, and that sentence was
delivered as the answer. 39 output tokens, over in 13 seconds, none of the
work done. The log for the turn reads `Found 0 tool uses to execute`
followed immediately by `Agent completed after 1 tool iterations`: the
harness already knew nothing had run and let the announcement through.

Checked against every regex and phrase list in all six phantom_lang files:
zero matches in all six. Two independent gaps.

- work_announcement_re enumerates EXECUTION verbs (running, checking,
  pushing, committing). The PREPARATION verbs a plan is announced with
  (mapping, planning, drafting, listing, outlining, tracing) appear in no
  list. Announcing the run-up to work is as empty as announcing the work.
- Both that pattern and gerund_re key on an imminence marker: a trailing
  now / ... / :, or a leading "Now". A clause sequenced with then / before
  reads as a plan rather than as something imminent and carries neither, so
  it never reached either check. #1193 widened the compound-gerund case
  inside the marker requirement; this shape is outside it.

New plan_announcement_re in all six language files, scanned across
all_langs() like the other tells, matching a gerund-led clause sequenced
with then / before / after that / next and each language's equivalents.

Read by the zero-tool gate only, deliberately not by
has_forward_intent_post_success: after a successful tool call the same
shape is also a legitimate recap ("Updating the config fixed it, then the
build passed"), and the zero-tool count that disambiguates it is gone. In
the zero-tool path there is no ambiguity left to lose.

Verified: cargo fmt clean, clippy --locked --lib --bins --tests
--all-features -D warnings clean, 7251 passed / 0 failed.

fix(phantom): a bare tool name counts when the model claims to have used it (#1262)

Asked to use the plan feature and execute, a turn answered "Setting up the
plan, then mapping every call site before touching anything.", called
nothing, and closed. The session then stayed silent for over two hours
until a human nudged it, at which point the same request ran normally.

mentions_registered_tool is the check written for exactly that claim: a
zero-tool turn whose text NAMES a registered tool is narrating usage that
never happened. `plan` is a registered tool. It could not fire, because
the function skipped every name without an underscore, on the grounds that
bare names like `bash` and `plan` are ordinary prose words.

Right about the risk, wrong about the remedy. What separates a claim from
a coincidence is not the length of the name, it is whether the text makes
the name the object of an action the model attributes to itself. The skip
blanked a whole class of tools at once: plan, bash, grep, ls, evolve,
rebuild. Naming any of them while calling nothing was invisible to the one
detector built to catch it.

A bare name now counts in a tool-use frame, and only there:

- a use marker immediately before it, across at most one determiner
  ("setting up the plan", "running bash", "usando a ferramenta")
- a tool noun immediately after it ("the plan tool")
- backticked or slash-prefixed, written as a name rather than as a word

The one-determiner limit preserves what the original skip protected: in
"run it in bash", `it in` sits between the marker and the name, so the name
is not the marker's object and the text is left alone. Markers, determiners
and tool nouns live in all six phantom_lang files and are read across
all_langs(), never from a detected language. Multi-word names keep matching
unconditionally.

Distinct from #1261, which added a wording pattern for the same incident.
This is the fact-based check: it does not care how the sentence is phrased,
only that a real tool was named and never called, and it is the one that
should have fired first.

fix(recovery): capture push-initiated turns for restart recovery (#12)

A push wake (session_notify / background-task completion) entered the
agent through resume_interrupted_turn, which passes track_pending=false
by design (#729): a resume must not re-insert its own pending row. That
left push-initiated turns invisible to boot recovery — a kill mid-tool
(a binary swap restarting the daemon under the swap-performing session,
like the Compiler's) left zero pending_requests rows and the turn was
never resumed.

Capture: pending_requests gains an origin column (user|system, default
user for legacy rows). run_tool_loop's track_pending: bool becomes
track_origin: Option<PendingOrigin>; new send_push_turn() drives push
turns with Some(System) so they are tracked while running and deleted at
exit. Telegram wake plumbing threads a track_push_turn flag through
resume_session/resume_session_inner: bg-resume enqueue wakes, the
end-of-turn detached flush and the stranded-reaction flush track (true);
user buttons (followup tap, plan approval, callback routing) stay
untracked (false); boot replay of an EXISTING row stays untracked (false,
the #729 guard). bg_resume::run_resume_turn now uses send_push_turn so
slack/wa/discord completions track as system too.

Boot pass: system-origin rows are NOT replayed as an LLM turn (re-running
an interrupted tool call could double-execute side effects such as
installs or binary swaps). Boot re-delivers the original push text via
restart_recovery::deliver_or_park (origin=Recovery), which re-drives the
intent through the normal wake path — captured again if killed, deleted
at exit, never perpetual (#729 holds). Summary now counts by origin:
interrupted=N (user=U system=S).

Tests: PendingProbeTool also captures the row's origin mid-turn; new
push_turn_is_tracked_with_system_origin asserts the row exists while
running with origin 'system', and push_turn_row_deleted_at_exit asserts
it is gone after completion. The existing #729 test (normal tracked,
resume untracked) is untouched.

fix(notify): refuse delivery into a channel a newer session now owns (#17)

A channel session can be REPLACED on its chat/topic — the idle-timeout
reset archives the old session and creates a successor for the same
topic — while its delivery route stays registered (routes are UUID-keyed
and never evicted). Without a gate, session_notify and background-task
completions wake the replaced session, which posts into a conversation
the successor now owns: two sessions writing one channel.

Gate: every push to a session with a registered channel-ownership probe
is refused when the probe reports the channel Occupied by another
session. Runs OUTERMOST in deliver_to_session — interrupt does NOT
override it; a replaced session must never be woken into its successor's
conversation. The bg-resume choke point (build_enqueue_callback) guards
too, since background completions resolve their route directly,
bypassing deliver_to_session. Unknown ownership fails open — the gate
never makes a surface unnotifyable.

Ownership is tracked in TelegramState.channel_ownership, a sync mirror
maintained ONLY at register_session_chat (the single write site of the
async maps), because the delivery gate's probe is a sync closure that
cannot take tokio mutexes. The refusal names the occupying session so a
sender can redirect without a discovery round.

Tests: 8 new — occupied refuses (with and without interrupt), ownership
gate outranks turn gate, owned/unknown pass, tool refusal text names the
occupant, mirror tracks replacement (incl. DM vs general bucket keys).

fix(notify): refuse delivery into a channel a newer session now owns (#17) (#1267)

A channel session can be REPLACED on its chat/topic — the idle-timeout
reset archives the old session and creates a successor for the same
topic — while its delivery route stays registered (routes are UUID-keyed
and never evicted). Without a gate, session_notify and background-task
completions wake the replaced session, which posts into a conversation
the successor now owns: two sessions writing one channel.

Gate: every push to a session with a registered channel-ownership probe
is refused when the probe reports the channel Occupied by another
session. Runs OUTERMOST in deliver_to_session — interrupt does NOT
override it; a replaced session must never be woken into its successor's
conversation. The bg-resume choke point (build_enqueue_callback) guards
too, since background completions resolve their route directly,
bypassing deliver_to_session. Unknown ownership fails open — the gate
never makes a surface unnotifyable.

Ownership is tracked in TelegramState.channel_ownership, a sync mirror
maintained ONLY at register_session_chat (the single write site of the
async maps), because the delivery gate's probe is a sync closure that
cannot take tokio mutexes. The refusal names the occupying session so a
sender can redirect without a discovery round.

Tests: 8 new — occupied refuses (with and without interrupt), ownership
gate outranks turn gate, owned/unknown pass, tool refusal text names the
occupant, mirror tracks replacement (incl. DM vs general bucket keys).

feat(tui): resolve a dropped path by its extension, not by word boundaries (#1288)

A dropped path can contain spaces and macOS names every screenshot that
way, so scanning by whitespace can never find one. Anchors on the known
extension instead: each occurrence is a candidate end, the start is the
longest plausible beginning that resolves to a real file.

Longest-match matters. Resolving the fragment after the last space would
attach File.png from the working directory instead of /dir/My File.png.
Bare filenames are refused for the same reason.

Also distinguishes a path that is absolute but absent, which is a drop
from another machine into a session running over SSH.

split_whitespace, so a spaced path shattered and the only fragment
carrying the extension was tested as a relative path and failed.

Measured before the fix, with the file present on disk: path alone
attached, path plus one typed word attached nothing.

An unreachable absolute path is now replaced with an explicit marker
rather than forwarded as prose. Left as prose it sent the agent hunting

The guard is the load-bearing half. The agent serves the client's

The classic HTML ladder promoted any line starting with '#' to a bold
header and stripped the hash run doing it, so a receipt line opening
with an issue reference lost the number it existed to carry. The rich
gate had always required ATX semantics: one to six hashes, then a space.
Two parsers, two answers, and which one a message got depended on the
route it happened to take.

The ladder now calls the same is_atx_heading the gate uses, so the
predicate has one definition. Tests assert the agreement itself across
every line shape rather than sampling a few, since agreement is what
broke.

fix(compaction): a context that shrank always leaves a marker

Truncation moved the live context and told the database nothing. The
loader kept anchoring on the previous marker, so a restart reloaded the
history that had just overflowed and overflowed again on the first turn.
Two sessions died that way: 397% and 372% full, 793k tokens still on
disk, a fresh loop on every message. The 90% floor was the worst case,
since it can drop messages and then hand a context back under 65% that
returns before any summariser runs.

enforce_context_budget now reports what it did rather than only what it
summarised, and every branch that drops messages says so. A marker with
no summary is lossy and says as much in its own text; no marker at all
is unrecoverable. The four call sites build their row from the outcome
instead of each keeping a copy of the marker string.

feat(compaction): summarise in the background instead of stopping the turn

Auto-compaction held the turn for the whole summariser call, which is
anywhere from ten seconds to twenty-nine minutes of a session that looks
hung. The call now runs against a snapshot while the turn carries on,
and the summary is swapped in on a later budget check, so compaction is
something the session reports afterwards rather than a wait the user
sits through.

Two rules keep that honest. A turn about to answer waits for an
in-flight summary first: a reply composed against a context one swap
away from replacement is answering from history that is about to stop
existing. And a context reaching 80% waits too, because there is no
longer enough headroom to be sure the next call fits.

Neither ever cancels the summary to reclaim room. Cancelling is what
truncated a context, discarded the summary that would have justified the
truncation, and left no marker, so two sessions replayed the overflow on
every restart. Waiting degrades to exactly the behaviour we had before,
which is the worst it can get.

The swap keeps whatever arrived while the summariser was thinking. A
blocking compaction could not miss anything; a backgrounded one leaves a
gap, and that gap holds the most recent work the agent did. Orphaned
tool results at the head of it go, since the summary now sits where
their tool call used to.

A synchronous compaction aborts any background one first: it replaces
the context that summary describes, so the result could only overwrite
fresher state. That covers /compact, which stays blocking and visible
because the user asked for it.

fix(compaction): bound a summariser attempt so a wedged one hands the work on (#1255)

Every HTTP provider caps a single request at 300 seconds. CLI providers
carry no timeout at all, so a summariser that stopped answering held
compaction for as long as its process felt like living, and the fallback
chain underneath was never reached: walking it requires the first
attempt to return, and it never did.

Each attempt now gets a deadline, and a provider that blows it is handed
on rather than waited out. Timeout is already retryable, so the existing
walk picks up from there without new plumbing.

The deadline is scaled from what this session's compactions actually
cost, tripled, so a conversation that habitually takes four minutes is
not declared hung at five. A session with no history has nothing to
scale from and gets the floor, which is the same 300 seconds every HTTP
provider already enforces rather than a number picked to sound right.

fix(channels): wait for a channel's transport instead of dropping the wake (#1242)

At boot the wake pass and a channel's own connect run concurrently with
nothing ordering them, so a wake regularly asked for a transport seconds
before it existed. Every adapter answered the same way, with a warn and a
return, which is a permanent loss: nothing retries, and the session stays
silent until its owner happens to send a message. Observed across ~21
daemon restarts in 48h; in one case a background result was never
delivered at all.

The wake now waits for the transport, bounded, and only gives up when the
channel is genuinely not coming up in this run. Slack and WhatsApp were
the worse two: their readiness check sits after the resume turn, so
returning threw away a finished answer and the provider call behind it.

The window is the same one a parked restart report waits for a route,
by construction rather than by coincidence. That is what makes the
ordering between the two startup flush paths deterministic: they raced
because each had its own unstated idea of ready.

The recovery pass at boot dispatches replayable pending requests and
resume dispatches but reported nothing: an operator restarting into a
pile of interrupted work saw requests fly by with no count of what the
boot actually recovered. boot_report.rs keeps a ledger of dispatches
(telegram transport-gone, resume ok/err, generic ok/err, dedup) and
schedules one summary message a grace window past the last dispatch,
so it lands after the replay dust settles instead of racing it.

fix(tg): bg-echo bubble rides the markdown dialect so tables stay native (#1234)

The rich echo bubble pre-converted its body through the fallback
markdown_to_html before send_rich_html_id, collapsing pipe tables into
static markup at build time — the server-side rich parser never saw
table source, so cron results (the table-heaviest payload class on this
path) rendered flat. New markdown-dialect envelope keeps the body as raw
source up to the wire in the block form the rich markdown parser accepts
(<details> and </details> on their own lines, inline <summary>), sent
first via the #1230 markdown variants (mermaid-aware). The HTML-dialect
envelope survives as the fallback rung; the classic blockquote stays the
last resort. Titles carrying angle brackets route straight to the HTML
dialect — the markdown dialect has no escape for them and a hostile chat
name could break the envelope open.

feat(telegram): one boundary between a topic key and a wire address (#1319)

GENERAL_TOPIC_ID is a session-scoping key. #1220 invented it so a forum's
General topic would not collide with a DM on the same chat, which is
right. It is not an address: General messages carry no
message_thread_id, so putting 1 on the wire asks for a thread that does
not exist and every message-CREATING call is refused.

Edits hid it. They address a message_id and never consult a thread, so a
General-bound session kept updating its status cards in place and failed
only when it had something new to say.

Every sender goes through delivery_thread_id rather than converting the
stored topic itself. Six call sites were each doing the conversion by
hand, and patching six invites a seventh.

fix(telegram): resolve General to no thread on every delivery path (#1319)

Five of the six conversion sites: both resume paths, the startup
crash-recovery resume, inline keyboards, and the chat-wide latest-thread
lookup.

The two arms of the resume match mean different things and stay
separate: a session bound to General has a KNOWN address of 'no thread',
while an unbound one falls back to the chat-wide lookup. Collapsing them
would post a General session's message into whichever topic spoke last.

fix(telegram_send): make 'no thread' expressible, and stop re-injecting one (#1319)

The precedence had two states, so omitting thread_id meant 'unspecified,
go resolve' rather than 'General', and the session topic put the
synthetic 1 back. General was therefore unreachable by any input: naming
thread 1 was refused on the wire, and omitting it was overridden. A live
differential test confirmed both paths failing identically.

Three states now. Explicit null is General; an explicit number goes
through the boundary, so naming thread 1 resolves to no thread; absence
still resolves from the session. A bound session returns even when the
boundary yields None, because 'no thread' is an answer, not a miss.

through a custom endpoint since it has no first-class provider.

contract per host. z.ai additionally gets Accept-Language, which its docs

A 4xx carrying HTML is retried on purpose: a CDN or load-balancer error page

backoff is futile and risks extending the block. Observed when an account
already taking 429s all week, peaking at 76 in one day, drew an Aliyun block

those made up 150 of the 151 retries in three days of logs.

their retry budget. The block wording sits about a kilobyte into the page,
past the prefix the HTML sniff scans, so the check reads further.

fix(logging): redact the Telegram bot token before anything is written (#1322)

The Bot API carries the token in the URL path and reqwest's error Display
includes the failing URL, so logging a transport error wrote the token to
disk in plaintext. Anyone with read access to the log directory had the bot,
as did anyone handed a log excerpt in a bug report, which is how this was
found. Three days of logs carried 42 such lines from four sites.

Nothing at those sites was doing anything unusual: logging a transport error
is right, and the token rode along invisibly. That is what makes a per-site
fix unreliable, and there are over a hundred sites formatting an error this
way, so the leak is the default behaviour rather than a mistake in four
places. Redact at the writer instead, where every event has to pass through
whatever its origin, so a new call site is covered the day it is written.

Only the secret half is replaced; the numeric bot id is public and stays, so
a redacted line still says which bot failed. Lines with no token borrow
through untouched behind a substring check, and the writer reports the
caller's byte count rather than the shorter redacted one, or write_all would
resend the tail and duplicate part of the line.

The exposed token still needs rotating: this stops new leaks, it cannot
unpublish the old ones.

streamed text is deliberately not gated, only the spinner: hiding the text

z.ai buffers a tool call's arguments and emits them as one chunk after
the whole call is generated. A 40 KB write_file argument at ~75 tok/s is
minutes of SSE silence, which the 90s idle timer reads as a dead
connection; the retry re-sends the same request and dies the same way.
OpenAIRequest gains tool_stream, sent as true on streamed requests to
either documented z.ai host and omitted everywhere else. The gate is the
host via identity::Vendor, never the model id, because glm-* is re-served
by gateways that do not read z.ai fields. The stream reader already
accumulates fragmented arguments, so nothing changes on the read side.

GLM-5.x is always-on thinking, and z.ai's clear_thinking defaults to true
on the standard endpoint, so every tool step in an agentic loop re-derived
the whole reasoning chain from scratch. The request now carries
thinking: {type: enabled, clear_thinking: false} for a GLM-5.x model on
either z.ai host, which keeps prior turns' reasoning server-side and makes
it cacheable. enable_thinking = false is still honoured on 5.0 to 5.2,
which accept disabled; on 5.3+ it is logged as ignored instead of sent,
because the endpoint rejects it. Other hosts and GLM-4.x are untouched.

fix(provider): map reasoning_effort onto the GLM-5.3 ladder instead of letting the endpoint silently pick max (#1349)

GLM-5.3 accepts low, high and max. Any other value returns 200 and falls
back to max, the deepest setting, so an xhigh copied from a qwen config
was the slowest possible thinking on every step with no warning.
glm_reasoning::effort_for maps foreign rungs to the nearest one (xhigh to
max, medium to high, minimal/none/off to low, unknown to max) and the
builder logs the mapping once per request; wire rungs pass through
unnoted. Applies only to GLM-5.3+ on z.ai; 5.2 still accepts xhigh and
other hosts read their own knobs. README zhipu section documents the
three rungs, recommends high for agentic sessions, and describes the

fix(provider): a fallback runs its own configured default_model, not the model the failed request carried (#1374)

The remap was a validity guard: it consulted default_model only when the

entries all listed Qwen3.8-Max, so three 300s attempts went to the same
host with a byte-identical request while the Qwen3.7 models configured
for those entries were never tried. models[] is capability, default_model
is intent. substitute_request() in fallback.rs now runs the substitute on

fix(provider): a context-length rejection walks the fallback chain (#1379)

should_try_next_provider ended in a catch-all false, and
ContextLengthExceeded matched nothing above it, so a summariser request
the primary refused on size was retried three times against the one
provider that had already refused while eleven fallbacks stood idle.
Windows differ by an order of magnitude across a chain, so which provider
is asked changes the answer, and the caller rebuilds the request for
whoever receives it. with_chain_summary already passes this variant
through unchanged, so an exhausted chain still reaches the tool loop's
emergency compaction. Two tests: the walk, and the policy plus the
variant-preservation the chat path depends on.

fix(agent): an overflow walks the compaction chain widest window first (#1379)

Handing a context-length rejection to the chain is only half the fix if
the next entry is narrower than the one that refused: that is a refusal
spent before the answer. chain_order::widest_first sorts the fallbacks by
the window each offers its own default model (the model a substitute
runs, #1374), stable so ties and unknown windows keep the configured
order. Compaction applies it for ContextLengthExceeded only; every other
failure keeps the configured order, pinned by a test.

fix(sessions): scope-all model writes preserve recency order (#1367)

set_provider_model_all_sessions and apply_force_default looped
update_session() per row, which stamps updated_at on every call.
One scope-all run restamped every session with the same fresh
timestamp: /sessions recency ordering destroyed and title-suffix
lookups (updated_at DESC LIMIT 1) nondeterministic until the next
real interaction.

Both callers now use a single bulk UPDATE that touches only
provider_name/model, leaving updated_at untouched by construction:

  UPDATE sessions SET provider_name=?1, model=?2
  WHERE archived_at IS NULL
    AND (provider_name IS NOT ?1 OR model IS NOT ?2)

IS NOT keeps NULL pairs safe and preserves the rows-changed count;
archived rows stay excluded as before.

Regression suite scope_all_recency_test.rs pins the #1367 property:
pairs change, every updated_at byte-identical across staggered rows,
idempotent no-op on re-run, archived rows keep their archive-time
stamp (archive() legitimately restamps updated_at, repo:444), and
config-reload force-default preserves recency too.

fix(loop-guard): rotate the fallback chain on a loop break instead of dropping the turn (#1397)

The three tool-call loop guards (consecutive modification calls, the
near-match guard, the identical-call dominance guard) ended the turn on
a break: breadcrumb appended, partial response returned, pending call
discarded, fallback chain never consulted. Every sibling failure already
walks that chain before the turn may end: stream drops retry five times
then fall back, phantom calls nudge five times then swap providers,
announcement loops rotate through the #1023 wrapper. A model that loops
on one provider usually does not on the next, which is the whole reason
the chain exists.

Each break now returns the provider-attributable AnnouncementLoop error
that the run_tool_loop rotation wrapper already matches: it promotes the
next provider with force_next_fallback and replays the turn, and only
when the chain is exhausted does the error reach the user. The message
carries the raw pending call (name plus compact JSON arguments), which
the stripped signature could never show, so a break is never silent
about what did not run; the exhausted-chain message adds how many
providers were tried and that nothing is queued. The unused breadcrumb
helper and its two tests are removed.

Tests: src/tests/loop_break_test.rs (10). Pure: pending-call rendering,
truncation by chars, error variant and message, exhausted-chain rewrite.
Turn-level: a provider that re-issues one call forever behind a
FallbackProvider yields an Ok turn with the fallback promoted; the same
provider alone yields the loop error naming the dropped call verbatim.

build(release): ship the default feature set, not --all-features (#1402)

Release binaries were built with --all-features on every platform, which
ignores the default set. Two consequences, both wrong.

It shipped eval and profiling, which are development-only. The README states
the eval harness is compiled under cfg(test) and never ships in a release
binary; with --all-features it shipped in every one of them, on every
platform. Building the default set makes the shipped binary and the
documented feature list agree.

It also meant a feature could not be made opt-in by editing the default set
at all: the prebuilt binary, which is the install path the crate description
recommends, would have carried it regardless.

local-stt stays a default deliberately. Running voice fully on-device is a
headline capability, not an add-on, so it works on a fresh install. It brings
the rwhisper tree and a low-severity h2 advisory with it, and the README now
says so next to the feature rather than leaving it in a CI ignore list: the
vulnerable client is reached only through kalosm-common and hf-hub, whose job
is downloading models from Hugging Face over TLS, so nothing a session does
touches it.

Windows is unaffected. Features are additive, so the default set is a subset
of what --all-features already compiled there.

docs: state what the version number covers before 1.0 freezes it (#1403)

The crate is published so the binary can be installed with cargo install, and
its pub modules are internals: they are public because the binary and the
integration tests need them across module boundaries, not because they are an
API to build against. Tagging 1.0 without saying so would freeze seventeen
modules nobody intends to support, and the first internal rename after it
would technically require 2.0.

So state it. The CLI commands and flags, the config.toml format, and the
on-disk layout of ~/.opencrabs/ are covered by the version number. Every Rust
item may be renamed, moved or removed in any release, including a patch.

Written in both places a reader might look: the crate docs, which is what
docs.rs renders for anyone considering a dependency, and the README for
anyone reading the repository. Both say why the modules are pub rather than
only that they are unstable, since without that the surface looks deliberate.

Neither closes the door: if a real library consumer appears, carving out a
supported surface is worth doing deliberately, and an issue describing the
use case is the way to start that.

docs: add a vulnerability-disclosure policy (#1406)

The repository had no way to report a security bug privately. A finder's only
options were a public issue or nothing, which for a project holding provider
keys, bot tokens and channel credentials is the wrong default, and #1322 was
exactly that class of bug.

Routes reports through GitHub's private advisory flow, and says what is in
scope. The scope section is the part worth getting right: credential leaks
into logs or chat, approval-gate escapes, session and channel boundary
crossings, remote input reaching local execution, path escapes in the file
and drop-transfer paths. Explicitly out of scope is anything that needs the
operator to point the agent at a hostile endpoint or tools.toml, because
those are trusted by design, and the model merely doing something disagreeable
when no gate was bypassed.

Also names the advisories already suppressed in CI, so a reporter is not
re-filing what is tracked, while inviting the report that one of them is
reachable in a way we have not accounted for.

Kept distinct from src/docs/reference/templates/SECURITY.md, which shares the
filename and nothing else: that one is a brain file instructing the agent
about its own conduct, seeded into ~/.opencrabs/ on install. Both files say
which is which, and the README link to the template now spells out the
difference.

The PR added the detector and the corrective-retry path with no tests of its

test(tui): move the theme picker and user-theme tests out of their source files

Twenty tests lived in `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` blocks inside
tui/render/theme_picker.rs and tui/render/user_themes.rs. Every test in this
repository belongs in src/tests/ as its own file registered in mod.rs, and
these were the only two places that still did otherwise.

Moving them exposed what `use super::*` had been hiding. Inline tests inherit
the source file's whole scope for free, so nothing had to be written down:
KeyEvent, Theme, theme, presets, user_themes and Color are now imported
explicitly, and build_items, build_theme, contrast, CONTRAST_PAIRS and
CONTRAST_FLOOR are pub(crate) because a test outside the file cannot reach a
private item. Each carries a comment saying it is widened for the tests,
matching how the rest of the codebase already handles this.

That widening is the real cost of the convention and also the argument for it:
five items were only testable by virtue of sitting in the same file.

Swept the rest of the tree rather than assume these were the only two. What
remains is lib.rs declaring the src/tests module itself, which is required,
and an example inside a markdown doc.

fix(brain): log backup-prune failures instead of printing them (#1413)

Two eprintln! calls on the backup-pruning path wrote straight to the
terminal. That path runs whenever a protected brain file is written, which
happens mid-turn while ratatui owns the screen, so the output landed outside
the frame and left the render holding characters it never drew.

It also bypassed redaction. The scrubber added in #1322 wraps the tracing
layers, so anything routed through tracing has its secrets removed before it
reaches a writer; direct printing never touches that. Both sites interpolate
a path and an error Display, which is the exact shape that leaked a bot token
in the first place. Nothing sensitive went through them, but the guarantee
did not cover them.

Both are now tracing::warn!, which the console layer already sinks while the
TUI is up and which passes through the scrubber on the way out.

The guard test scans the directories whose code can run inside a turn and
fails on any direct print, so this cannot come back quietly. It was verified
by reintroducing one eprintln! and confirming the test names the file and
line. src/cli/ and the userbot login command are exempt on purpose: they run
with no TUI and their output is the interface, and routing the login QR
through tracing would send it to io::sink exactly when a user needs to scan
it. A second test pins that exemption to a file that still exists, so it gets
re-examined rather than silently widening.

fix(tui): keep a running session marked processing when it regains focus (#1420)

load_session sets is_processing from processing_sessions, then twenty-eight
lines later promote_to_foreground overwrote it with bg.is_processing, a
snapshot taken whenever that session was last demoted. A stale false clobbered
the correct true, leaving a session that was still working marked idle.

The desync is older than the symptom. Before #1342 the thinking block rendered
on streaming_reasoning alone, so the flag being wrong changed nothing on
screen. #1342 added the is_processing guard to stop a cancelled turn claiming
to think, which was right, and turned the latent desync into a visible wipe on
the exact case reported: switching to a session that is mid-turn.

processing_sessions is the cross-session source of truth and everything else
derives from it, including the pane renderer, which is why panes were
unaffected and only the focused session went quiet. Promotion now derives from
it too instead of restoring a snapshot of a value whose authority lives
elsewhere.

fix(session): persist a live turn before switching away from it (#1421)

Content produced during a turn lives in the sidecar's pending_messages until a
focus switch merges it back. When that session finishes while it is not
focused, ResponseComplete drops the sidecar entry on the grounds that the DB
has the content. That is only true if something wrote it, and the switch never
did, so a turn could look truncated on return.

persist_streaming_state already exists for exactly this and is called on both
paths that end a turn early, abort and /stop. Session switch was the one way
to leave a live turn without flushing it, which made the same output durable
if you cancelled and lost if you merely looked at another session.

Flush before demoting, and only when the session is actually running, so an
idle switch still writes nothing. Dropping the sidecar on background
completion can then stay as it is: once the switch has persisted, re-reading
from the DB is a true statement rather than an assumption.

fix(brain): catch fabricated facts in post-success wrap-ups (#1423)

The post-success exemption treated any text-only iteration as a completion
acknowledgement once the turn had a successful tool call, so a 4,664-char
report of invented counts and commit shas shipped undetected (log
2026-09-07 01:35:59, tools_completed=24).

Length cannot separate an ack from a report: across 128 exempted iterations
over three days the median is 968 chars and p90 is 2,563, so most exempted
text is legitimately long and a size bound would re-break what the exemption
exists for. The check is therefore fact-based, per #1073: extract git shas
and result tallies from the iteration text, and if any appears nowhere in
the conversation's evidence, the exemption does not apply.

Evidence means what tools printed, what was actually run, and the user's own
words. The model's own text and thinking are excluded, so an earlier
fabrication cannot vouch for the next one.

fix(memory): load the embedding model on CPU so a Metal assert cannot abort us (#1432)

A user on macOS lost the whole application while OpenCrabs was loading the
local GGUF embedding model: GGML_ASSERT(buf_src) failed in
ggml-metal-device.m, then SIGABRT. The TUI had already begun drawing, so from
outside it looked like the app failing to start, and it was first reported as
onboarding never appearing.

Nothing in Rust can catch it. GGML_ASSERT calls abort(), so there is no
unwinding and the map_err on load_from_file is unreachable for this class of
failure. That is how an optional index takes down the entire process.

LlamaModelParams::default() offloads to the GPU, which on macOS routes the
load through Metal into a known llama.cpp defect. Requesting zero GPU layers
keeps us off that code path, removing the crash class rather than one
assertion.

The workload argues for CPU regardless: small embedding models over short
chunks, batched, off the interactive path, so offload buys little here and
costs the process on an affected machine. It is also strictly better than the
workaround the user found, which was to disable vector search entirely to get
the app to start.

The params are split into their own function so a test can assert the offload
is off. The crash itself cannot be reproduced in a test, because abort() would
take the runner with it, so the assertion is on the parameter that keeps us
away from it, which is what a later change could silently undo. Verified by
reverting to default() and watching the test fail.

fix(config): stop materialising an enabled xiaomi section in configs that never named it

`ProviderConfigs::xiaomi` was the only one of nineteen provider fields
carrying a `#[serde(default = "...")]` constructor, and that constructor
produced an enabled section with a default model, vision model and context
window. Any config whose `[providers]` table omitted xiaomi therefore parsed
as though the user had enabled it.

That default dates from the window when MiMo shipped as the keyless default
provider, where a populated section with no config block was the whole point.
The commit that converted xiaomi into a normal keyed provider retired the
status and left the default in place.

Reading it was survivable, because the registry marks xiaomi
`requires_api_key` and the keyless phantom is skipped when resolving an
active provider. Writing it was not: `Config::save` serialises the struct
with `to_string_pretty`, TOML has no null, and serde drops the eighteen
`None` providers on the way out. A parse-then-save cycle turns the providers
a user configured into a single section they never chose.

The picker never needed it. `load_default_models` reads every provider's
catalogue from the embedded `config.toml.example`, which ships xiaomi
disabled, so the default was also contradicting the example it sat beside.

Drop the constructor and the metadata block it wrapped, both unreferenced
once the attribute goes, and give xiaomi the plain `#[serde(default)]` every
other provider has. Repin the test that asserted the old behaviour, keeping
the two assertions that were always correct.

fix(config): seed the shipped example from whatever first needs config.toml to exist

`config.toml.example` carries a section for every provider, disabled, with its
options documented inline. That file is how a provider setting gets changed by
hand: find the section, edit the value, save. It only serves that purpose if it
reaches disk.

It reached disk from exactly one place, `ensure_config_files`, called from a
single onboarding step and guarded on `config.toml` not already existing.
Two other paths created the file without it. `write_item` built its document
from `DocumentMut::new()` when the file was missing, so one `write_key` for any
section at all produced a config holding that key and nothing else. The startup
auto-generate in `args.rs` called `Config::save`, which serialises the struct
with `toml::to_string_pretty`, and since TOML has no null representation that
wrote only the providers that happened to be set, with no comments.

Whichever path ran first won permanently, because the seeding guard only fires
while the file is absent. A user who lost that race was left with a config
carrying no provider sections, and no way to hand-edit a provider short of
knowing the exact section and key names.

Seeding is not a wizard step. It is what the file needs before anyone writes to
it, so it moves to `config::seed` and every creator goes through it:

- `write_item` and `write_keys_key` seed before falling back to an empty
  document. keys.toml had the identical hole.
- `ensure_config_files` delegates instead of doing its own `fs::write`. It
  targeted `workspace_path` while all of its actual writes go through
  `write_key` to `opencrabs_home()`; those agree by default, so routing
  seeding to the same place also closes a latent mismatch.
- the auto-generate seeds and then flips `enabled = true` per provider that
  holds a key, rather than serialising the whole struct over the path. Its
  purpose is preserved: a user arriving with keys set still is not asked to
  choose a provider, since the example ships a `default_model` for each of
  them and `setup_looks_finished` resolves a provider and model as before.

Seeding goes through `atomic_write`, so it inherits the guard that stops a test
build rewriting the live config. An existing file is never touched: this
supplies a starting point, it does not restore one.

fix(tui): persist the theme name itself, not a name wrapped in quotes

`/theme set <name>` applied the palette live, said it had persisted, and came
back as the default on the next boot with no error and nothing in the log. That
reads as a theme being randomly forgotten rather than one that was never stored
in a form the lookup could match.

Both write sites handed `write_key_string` a value they had already wrapped in
quotes, and `write_key_string` builds the TOML string itself, so the quote
characters ended up inside the value:

    [tui]
    theme = '"dracula"'

The boot lookup is exact, so it matched no preset and fell through. The picker's
Apply path had the same bug. `/theme reset` had it too, writing a two-character
string of quotes where it meant to write an empty value; that fell through to
the default by accident rather than by intent, and left the key behind.

Pass the bare name at all three sites. `group_name.rs` was already using
`write_key_string` correctly and is unchanged.

Fixing the write alone would leave anyone who already hit this stuck, since
their stored value stays unmatched forever and fails silently. `configured_name`
strips a matching surrounding quote pair on the way in, so a poisoned config
recovers on the next boot. Only a matching pair is stripped: a name that merely
contains a quote is a lookup miss rather than this bug, and is left alone.

fix(config): never promote a template placeholder to bot_owner

config.toml.example shipped four live allow-lists carrying documentation ids,
and that file is written verbatim into a real config. On the next load the
bot_owner seed migration promoted the first entry of each to an explicit owner.

An explicit bot_owner IS the owner set, so the positional fallback that makes
the first real user the owner could never fire. The operator was silently not
the owner of their own bot and hit refusals from owner-gated commands with no
indication why, while anyone holding an account matching a placeholder held
owner rights over channels the operator never configured.

Four changes, the reporter's own list:

- The four allow-lists in the template are commented out, matching the
  bot_owner lines already commented directly beneath them. An empty allow-list
  is the secure default the code already handles.
- The migration refuses to seed a value in OWNER_SEED_PLACEHOLDERS, and warns
  with what to do instead rather than silently doing nothing.
- It does not seed a channel that is not enabled. A channel nobody has turned
  on has no operator to pin yet, and every channel ships disabled, so this was
  the path by which placeholders became owners of unconfigured channels.
- It logs at INFO when it does seed, naming the channel and value. This
  happened with no trace at all, so a seeded owner was indistinguishable on
  disk from one the operator set.

The placeholder list is pinned against the template by a test that parses every
allow-list out of the shipped file, commented lines included, and requires each
id to be refused. It immediately found two the report did not list, the
per-group example pair, which are now covered.

Worth recording that the previous commit widened this. Before seeding moved to
config::seed, a config created by write_key held only the key written and no
channels tables, so the migration had nothing to promote. Every creator path
now seeds the full template, so every install reached the armed allow-lists
rather than only those that ran onboarding.

Three migration tests encoded the old behaviour and are updated rather than
worked around: they now enable the channel they expect seeding for, and the
whatsapp case uses an id that is not one of the template's own.

fix(telegram): stop asking Telegram to replace a rich message with itself

The rich edit path re-sent identical content on every refresh. Telegram
answered `400: message is not modified`, and `post_rich` ran that through the
generic failure branch: logged as a send failure at WARN, returned as an error.
An evening of ordinary group use produced dozens of them, every one a round
trip whose only purpose was to be told nothing had changed, spent against the
same budget that was already backing off elsewhere in the session, and every
one a line of noise in the log people read when something is genuinely broken.

Two halves, and both are needed. `edit_dedup` remembers what each message was
last edited to and skips an edit whose content and markup already match, before
the pacing gate as well as the request. If one slips through anyway, the
`not modified` answer is treated as the success it is: the message is in the
state we asked for, so it returns Ok and records the fingerprint instead of
logging a failure. The other edit paths in this crate have always read it that
way; this one had not.

The fingerprint spans the rich payload and the reply markup together, because
that pair is what Telegram compares. Hashing the text alone would skip an edit
that only swaps a keyboard, which is a real change.

A fingerprint is recorded only once an edit has landed. Recording at attempt
time would let a failed edit convince the next identical attempt that it was
redundant, and the message would keep whatever it had.

Tracking is capped, and the cap clears rather than evicting: a miss costs one
edit that Telegram answers `not modified`, which is what every edit cost
before this change.

feat(sessions): link a session to its project on the first turn

Sessions were titled automatically on their first turn but never linked to a
project at that moment. The only path that created the link was the `/cd`
handler, so unless a user happened to change directory by hand, a session
carried a correct working_directory and a project_id of NULL forever, and every
per-project view, filter and cost rollup under-reported by however many
sessions that was.

The link now happens at the same first-turn trigger that titles the session,
and deliberately not inside the spawned title future. The title is an LLM call
that can fail, time out, or hit a rate-limited provider; the link is a string
match and one UPDATE. Nesting it would mean a provider outage leaves sessions
unlinked, which is the failure being fixed. A test pins that ordering, since
nothing else would notice it being moved.

The matching rule moves to `services::project_match` rather than staying inside
the `/cd` handler, and `/cd` now calls it too, so the two cannot answer the same
question differently.

`backfill_unassigned_sessions` sweeps existing rows with the same rule for
sessions that predate the project they belong to. It runs once at startup, off
the critical path since nothing there waits on the answer, and is idempotent so
a later run picks up only what the earlier one could not. One session failing
to link logs and continues rather than abandoning the sweep.

An explicitly assigned session is never reassigned, and a session with no
working directory is skipped: channel sessions carry no path, so no
directory-based rule can classify them.

Matching on a basename is knowingly imprecise. Two unrelated directories
sharing a basename collapse onto one project, and a checkout under an unrelated
directory name is unreachable. That is a property of the schema, which has only
a name to compare against, and fixing it means a migration that is deliberately
not part of this change.

fix(claude-cli): surface silent turns instead of faking success (#1441)

A rate-limited or crashed CLI turn ended with nothing on the channel. The
user saw silence, not an error, and the fallback chain never ran.

Three shapes produced it, all in the stream translator:

- rate_limit_event sent a Ping and recorded nothing, so a limit that never
  recovered was indistinguishable from a healthy pause.
- EOF without a Result synthesised MessageDelta{EndTurn} + MessageStop, ie
  a successful empty turn.
- A clean exit having emitted zero events only logged a warning.

Nothing downstream caught any of them. CLI providers are deliberately
exempt from should_nudge_empty_answer because they run their own inner
loop, so the retry/fallback ladder never ran and the placeholder was
deleted. The logs show which shape dominates: "CLI EOF without Result"
appears 54 times against 2 for the working error path.

The turn now fails when it ends with no Result and no content:
RateLimitExceeded when a rate_limit_event was seen, so the fallback chain
is walked, Internal otherwise. The stream is still kept alive through a
rate-limit pause, since the CLI resumes on its own when the window rolls
over; the flag only matters if it never comes back. Both exit-status
branches respect a failure_reported flag so a turn already failed at EOF
does not get a second error on top.

The fix is in the provider, not the guard: removing the CLI exemption
would nudge on every legitimate mid-loop iteration.

Five source-level sentinels pin it (the stream runs in a spawned task over
a live child process, so it has no in-process seam). Four are behavioural
and were verified to fail with the fix reverted; the fifth pins the CLI
exemption that forced the fix location.

fix(agent): keep the recovery row when shutdown cancels a turn (#1462)

A turn in flight when the app quit was never resumed on the next boot,
while sessions interrupted by a hard kill came back fine.

Quitting with Ctrl+C twice cancels the in-flight token before setting
should_quit (tui/app/state.rs). The cancelled turn then unwound through
the normal return path in run_tool_loop and deleted its own
pending_requests row, so the next boot had nothing to resume. A hard kill
never reaches that code, which is why only the graceful path lost work.
Confirmed in the incident logs:

  00:05:12.960  Stream cancelled by user
  00:05:12.960  Stream aborted by cancellation
  00:05:16.027  OpenCrabs debug logging enabled   <- the relaunch
  00:05:19.369  Found 1 interrupted request(s)    <- a different session

The delete is correct for a turn the user deliberately stopped: Esc
twice, /stop, /discard and stop words all abandon the work and must not
have it replayed. Both meanings arrive as AgentError::Cancelled and
CancellationToken carries no reason, so the shutdown paths raise a flag
before cancelling and the cleanup reads it. Ordering matters: raising it
after the cancel races the unwinding turn, which may already have
deleted the row.

The flag is process-global because the tool loop reads it several layers
below the TUI that sets it. /restart, /exit, /quit and TuiEvent::Quit end
the process without cancelling, so their rows already survived; they set
the flag anyway so it means "this process is going down" rather than
naming one key combination.

Not claude-cli specific: is_cli_provider is not in scope at the delete,
and the CLI touch_session is UPDATE-only. The CLI session was simply the
one holding a long turn when the quit landed.

Seven tests. Five drive keeps_recovery_row directly (shutdown cancel
keeps, user stop deletes, completion during shutdown deletes, other
errors delete, flag latches). Two are source sentinels for the wiring the
unit cases cannot reach: that the delete consults the decision, and that
the flag is raised before the cancel. Verified by reverting both halves;
the first pass caught that the unit cases alone were vacuous, since a
correct helper nobody calls fixes nothing. The flag cases share a mutex
because libtest runs them as parallel threads of one process.

The /sessions dialog printed created_at while list_sessions orders by
updated_at DESC, so the column and the position disagreed on every row
that had been opened long ago and used recently. A session created in

single activity bump and its use of the message timestamp, and the set of
files allowed to write sessions.updated_at, so a future touch-on-open
cannot be added silently.

fix(projects): linking a session to a project no longer restamps recency (#1460)

assign_session and unassign_session stamped updated_at = now on every
write. The startup backfill added in 3b03ab70 sweeps unassigned sessions
and links each one whose working directory names a project, so the first
boot after that change restamped 60 sessions with the boot second,

learned in #1367. Two regression tests pin it: the backfill sweep and the

fix(db): stamp past a migration that already ran under an older list order

Startup failed outright with "duplicate column name: channel_thread_id". Not
one migration failing, the binary refusing to launch.

Migrations apply by list INDEX. `pending_requests_thread_id` sat at index 40
and was applied there, stamping user_version 40. Merging the notify-queue
migration, whose filename date is earlier, re-sorted the list and pushed
thread-id to 41. On the next boot `to_latest` replays index 41 against a table
that already has the column, and SQLite rejects it.

This is the mirror of what migration_heal was written for. The heals there
repair a migration that was SKIPPED, and can run after `to_latest`. This one
has to run before it: the crash happens inside `to_latest`, so there is no
"after" to heal from. That is also why the notify_queue heal never helped
despite this being the same event that broke both, the boot died two lines
earlier.

The guard fires only when the stamp is exactly one behind AND the column is
genuinely present, so it can never skip an unapplied migration; a database
missing the column still runs it normally. The migration this database really
was missing, notify_queue, is created by the existing post-pass heal once
`to_latest` stops throwing.

Tests reproduce the exact broken shape (stamped 40, column present,
notify_queue absent) and assert startup completes with both healed, that a
healthy database is untouched across repeat boots, and that a stamp one behind
WITHOUT the column is refused rather than silently skipped.

fix(a2a): refuse an unauthenticated non-loopback bind, and compare the token in constant time

The bearer token is the only authorization boundary in front of the a2a
gateway: send/stream run the agent with its full tool surface for any caller
that clears require_bearer, and that middleware lets everyone through when no
key is set. On loopback that is fine, only same-box callers reach the port. On
any other bind it is an open, unauthenticated, tool-capable gate.

start_server now refuses to come up when the gateway is enabled, the bind is
not loopback, and no api_key is set, naming the fix (set a key, or bind to
127.0.0.1). The safe default (disabled, loopback) is unchanged; a silently open
gate becomes a startup that will not proceed without a key. The decision is a
pure helper so the whole matrix is tested: loopback and keyed binds pass, a
wildcard or public bind without a key is refused, and a non-IP bind fails safe.

The token comparison used `token == expected`, which short-circuits at the
first differing byte and leaks the token one byte at a time through response
timing. It now hashes both sides to a fixed-length SHA-256 digest and compares
those, the standard hash-then-compare mitigation, no new dependency.

Reported as OC-07 in a product security evaluation by Abraxas Labs
(abraxaslabs.tech, @abraxas_null), who recommended exactly this fix: require a
key unless the bind is loopback, and compare the token in constant time.

fix(evolve): verify the release SHA256SUMS before swapping the binary, pin the download host (OC-03)

The auto-updater downloaded a release asset and renamed it over the running
process after a single `--version` health probe, which a hostile binary passes.
The release publishes SHA256SUMS on every build, and the updater never read it,
so a compromised release, a stolen release token, or a browser_download_url
pointing off-GitHub became code execution on the next auto-update.

Now, before the archive is extracted or swapped:

- the download host is pinned to github.com / objects.githubusercontent.com over
  https; a release JSON whose asset URL points elsewhere is refused before the
  fetch happens;
- the archive is hashed and checked against the release's SHA256SUMS entry for
  that asset. A missing SHA256SUMS, a missing entry, or a mismatch fails closed
  and aborts the swap, pointing the user at /rebuild.

auto_update stays true by default; the checksum is what makes that safe now.

Root swaps are not blocked by default: an existing root daemon must keep
updating, and a forgotten flag must never silently break updates. A new
`[agent] evolve_allow_root` (default true) lets a security-conscious operator
refuse a root swap, and the refusal explains what to do. The checksum
verification is the real integrity gate and runs regardless of this flag.

The verify helpers are pure and unit-tested: host allow/deny incl. suffix
lookalikes and plaintext http, SHA256SUMS parse incl. binary-mode `*` prefix
and malformed digests, and asset-name extraction.

fix(config): write config files owner-only, move daemon logs off /tmp, scrub all secrets from logs (OC-05)

Three credential leaks, all confirmed at source.

through atomic_write, which wrote at the process umask (0644) with no chmod.

now sets 0600 on the temp file before the rename, so the file is never visible
at its final name in a readable state; config.toml is tightened the same way. A
chmod failure removes the temp file rather than publishing a secret it could not
lock down.

The macOS LaunchAgent wrote daemon stdout/stderr to /tmp, which is
world-readable, and daemon stderr carries URLs, tracing events, and
chat-adjacent text. Both now go to the same private log directory as every other
log (logging::log_dir(), ~/.opencrabs/logs by default), created 0700.

The log-writer scrub matched only Telegram bot tokens, so any other secret that
rode a provider error's Display (sk- keys, Slack/Discord tokens, Bearer headers,
PEM blocks) landed in the daily log in plaintext. The writer now runs the same
broad secret patterns the channel-output redactor uses, unconditionally, since a
log on disk is a credential regardless of the display redaction flag. Telegram
tokens are scrubbed first so their bot-id-preserving shape is unchanged, then
the broad pass runs on top.
