fix(tools): one SSRF guard for every fetch tool, DNS-resolved and redirect-checked (OC-04)

web_scrape had an SSRF guard with holes and http_request had none at all, so a
channel-influenced URL could reach cloud metadata, LAN admin panels, or RFC1918
hosts and return the result to chat.

The guard moves to a shared brain::tools::ssrf used by web_scrape, http_request,
and their redirect policies, so they cannot disagree, and it closes the reported
bypasses:

- IPv4-mapped IPv6 (::ffff:a.b.c.d) is unmapped and re-checked as IPv4, so a
  mapped metadata address cannot dodge the v4 rules;
- IPv6 link-local (fe80::/10) and unspecified (::) are blocked;
- IPv4 unspecified (0.0.0.0) and CGNAT (100.64.0.0/10) are blocked, with the /10
  mask verified not to over-block public 100.x;
- the cloud metadata host is blocked by name (metadata.google.internal), not
  only by IP;
- a domain is DNS-resolved and every resolved address is checked, so a
  public-looking name that resolves internally (nip.io tricks,
  metadata.google.internal) is refused before the request goes out;
- every redirect hop is re-validated, so a public URL that 302s to an internal
  one is stopped;
- http_request now runs the guard at all, on the initial URL and on redirects.

Loopback (127.0.0.0/8, ::1, localhost) is deliberately allowed per maintainer
decision: a local-first agent legitimately reaches the operator's own machine,
and the guest-driver path that made localhost debug ports an exfil target is
already closed by OC-01 (approval owner-gating) and OC-02 (deny-by-default
ingest). The SSRF teeth here are reaching OTHER hosts' internal networks.

fix(tools): route execute_code and dynamic shell through the bash blocklist, reserve core tool names (OC-06)

bash documents check_blocked_command as the immovable floor that applies even
under approval, but execute_code and dynamic shell executors ran their commands
without it, so `rm -rf ~` (and fork bombs, /etc/shadow reads, …) through those

runtime-TOML blocklists that bash itself uses:

- execute_code checks the code body before writing or running it, for every

  or node as from a bash body;
- the dynamic shell executor checks its rendered command, after parameter
  substitution, so a `{{param}}` expanded into a blocklisted command is caught;
- add_tool refuses a dynamic tool whose name is a core tool (bash, execute_code,
  read_file, evolve, …), so a model-authored, unguarded stand-in can no longer
  unregister and replace the real, blocklist-enforcing one.

feat(memory): depth-2 impact chains over call_edges (#89)

"impact of X" / "who calls X transitively" / "what breaks if I change X"
now walk call_edges transitively (recursive CTE, depth-capped at 2) and
render indented chains, breadth-capped at 50 rows:

  mid calls leaf at line 42 (depth 1)
    top calls leaf at line 7 (depth 2)

Each caller appears once at its shallowest depth, ordered by
(depth, caller, file, line). The transitive pattern MUST precede the plain
"who calls X" pattern in detect_structural_query — the plain pattern would
otherwise swallow the query and answer depth-0 only.

Cycle guard: the recursive member increments depth and stops at the cap, so
an A→B→A cycle in corrupt data terminates bounded instead of walking the
96k-edge table forever; UNION (not UNION ALL) keeps identical rows from
fanning out. Pinned by a dedicated A→B→A fixture test — 96k real edges
should not contain cycles, so the guard exists precisely for corrupt data

fix(tui): keep the background-task manager across a provider-switch rebuild

Long commands (cargo test/build/clippy, docker build, gh run watch, …) stopped
detaching to the background after a provider switch. The detach gate in bash
requires context.background_manager to be Some, and that is copied unconditionally
from the AgentService's background_manager.

rebuild_agent_service rebuilds the whole service when the provider changes and
carried over the approval, progress, queue, sudo, ssh, subagent and
session-update wiring, but not the enqueue callback. The enqueue callback is
what creates the background manager, so the rebuilt service had
background_manager == None and every session after the switch ran long commands
inline. A session on a non-default provider triggers this rebuild the moment it
is loaded or resumed, which is why a resumed non-default-provider session never
detached while a fresh one on the startup provider did.

The rebuild now carries the EXISTING manager and its enqueue route across via a
new with_existing_background_manager, reusing the same Arc rather than building a
fresh one, so detachment keeps working and any in-flight detached task stays
tracked by the one manager instead of being orphaned.

across keeps background_manager Some, reuses the same Arc, and preserves the
enqueue route.

feat(channels/whatsapp): edit-in-place streaming instead of chunk-spam (#1408)

Streaming posted every intermediate chunk as its own message, on the
strength of a comment claiming the protocol has no message editing. It
does: Client::edit_message exists and its window covers 15 minutes,
longer than virtually every turn.

A streamed turn now grows ONE message, and the final answer edits that
same message up to the finished text, so the turn ends as exactly one
message. An edit the server refuses clears the tracked message and the
rest of the turn appends instead, posting the triggering chunk right
away, so no content is ever dropped.

Chunks go down one channel to a single consumer task rather than one
spawned task each, which is what let two fast chunks race for the same
edit. Whatever is already queued is drained and merged into one edit, so
a burst of five chunks costs one stanza, and every edit is still paced
through the #1407 limiter.

outbox.rs holds the last editable message per session. SendResult's
message_id was discarded at all 33 send sites; it is now captured once,
which is the plumbing #1409, #1482 and #1484 each named as a dependency.

feat(channels/whatsapp): acknowledge finished turns with a reaction (#1409)

The react action has built a full ReactionMessage since 41e8e5b7, but the
channel never reacted on its own: on Telegram the crab acknowledges a
finished task with an emoji and WhatsApp stayed silent. What was missing
was knowing which message to react to, which the #1408 outbox provides.

Only streamed turns are acknowledged. Those ran tools and took long
enough that an acknowledgement means something; a plain chat reply needs
no tick on itself. A failed reaction is a warning and nothing more, since
the answer was already delivered.

feat(channels/whatsapp): publish presence and recover expired media (#1488)

A WhatsApp media URL is not permanent. Asking about a photo from a
conversation a few weeks old failed the download, and the channel said
"failed to download image" and nothing else - from the user's side,
indistinguishable from the bot being broken. The protocol has a recovery
path for exactly this and nothing here had ever called it.

The downloaders now go through one helper: on a failed download it asks
the server to re-upload the blob, patches the fresh directPath onto a
local clone of the media proto, and downloads again. A NotFound answer
means the blob is genuinely gone rather than stale and is logged as such.
Unencrypted newsletter media has no media key and the reupload path does
not serve it, so that case is reported instead of retried.

set_available is now published once per connection. Without it the paired
account reads as permanently offline to everyone it talks to, and
WhatsApp withholds contact presence from a client that never publishes
its own.

feat(channels/whatsapp): handle inbound video, sticker, location, contact, reactions and poll votes (#1410, #1482, #1483)

The inbound arms matched image, audio and document only. Everything else
fell through to a bare return, so sending the bot a location pin or
voting in its own poll produced nothing at all. One condition decides
what the handler admits, so widening it is one change even though three
issues each asked for a slice.

Video and sticker are downloaded and pushed through the same vision and
file funnel as an inbound image. WhatsApp does not name video blobs, so
the filename is built from the mimetype: the funnel keys off the
extension and a nameless "file" lands in the wrong branch.

Location, live location, contact card and inbound reactions carry no blob
and turn straight into a line of text. A reaction with an empty emoji
produces nothing, because that is how WhatsApp encodes a reaction being
removed and reporting it would read as approval that was taken back.

Poll votes are the odd one out: the crypto was never the gap, since
wacore::poll implements the vote path and MsgSecretStore already persists
the secret. A vote names its options by SHA-256 hash and never by label,
so a decrypted vote is a list of hashes unless the poll's own option list
is at hand, and nothing kept it. poll.rs now remembers the options of
every poll the bot sends, bounded to the last 100, and resolution follows
the poll's order rather than the vote's so two people who picked the same
pair read identically. A hash matching no option is dropped rather than
printed as hex: it means the voter used "add option" on a poll we did not
author.

inbound.rs and poll.rs keep their extractors pure, so the exact shape the
agent sees is pinned by tests rather than by a live account.

feat(channels/whatsapp): send audio as a native voice note (#1486)

WhatsApp draws a tap-to-play bubble only when the message carries ptt.
The channel TTS reply already set it, but the send_audio tool action did
not, so audio the agent sent on purpose arrived as an unstyled file.

send_audio now flags ptt by default; a caller that wants a plain
attachment passes voice_note: false. A bare audio/ogg mimetype is
upgraded to audio/ogg with the opus codec named, since the client wants
it spelled out. Other containers are passed through untouched, because
relabelling mp3 bytes as Opus would break playback outright.

send_recording had no call sites anywhere. The recording indicator now
shows while audio is prepared and clears afterwards on both the tool path
and the channel TTS path, including the failure paths, so a chat is never
left stuck showing "recording...".

feat(channels/whatsapp): block contacts and send disappearing messages (#1487)

The channel exposed no privacy or safety controls: it could not block a
spamming number and could not send a message that expires.

block_contact, unblock_contact and list_blocked are new actions. The
resolved JID is logged on every block so the owner can audit it later.
list_blocked reads the server rather than the local mirror, because the
owner may have blocked someone from their phone and reporting a stale
local set as fact would be worse than one round trip.

blocklist.rs mirrors the server list so the inbound guard can drop a
blocked sender with a set lookup instead of the server query
Blocking::is_blocked needs. It is refreshed once per connection and
updated on every block the bot performs. The key is the JID user part,
never the full JID, or the same contact walks past the guard from a
second device.

ephemeral.rs resolves the per-message TTL against the new
channels.whatsapp.ephemeral_ttl default. An explicit 0 means "this one
does not expire" and beats the default, so a channel that expires by
default can still send something permanent. A value over the 90 day
maximum is clamped rather than refused.

fix(channels/whatsapp): charge every message-delivering action to the send budget (#1407)

The limiter shipped covering send and reply only. Every media send, poll,
reaction and forward went straight to the wire, so the budget
under-counted by however many of those a turn made - the exact
never-rate-limited failure mode the issue was opened for, minus two
actions.

They cannot reuse gate: it parks an over-cap send in a queue holding
{ jid, text } and the drainer replays it as plain text, so a queued photo
would deliver its caption as a bare message and drop the image. The new
gate_action paces on the same bucket and, under a saturated daily cap,
refuses and tells the agent instead of pretending to have sent.

Gating covers the actions that deliver a message. Receipts, presence and
account operations are not messages and are not charged to a message
budget.

feat(channels/whatsapp): pin, forward and programmatic profile (#1484)

pin and unpin act on a chat, not a message: chat_actions exposes pin_chat
and unpin_chat, and the chat_id plus message_id shape the issue proposed
does not exist in the protocol.

Client::forward_message does exist as a one-call API, contrary to the
issue, but it takes the original message proto rather than an id: it
rebuilds the body with the forward flags and relays media from the same
CDN blob instead of re-uploading. The channel kept no protos, so
recent.rs keeps the last 200 inbound messages. Media protos carry URLs
and keys, never the blob, so entries stay small. Re-seeing an id
refreshes it and moves it to newest, so a message still being referenced
does not age out mid conversation, and a forward past the window is
reported as out of window instead of silently sending nothing.

set_profile_name and set_profile_status ship as actions here rather than
a separate whatsapp_profile tool: the channel already routes every
WhatsApp operation through one tool.

feat(channels/whatsapp): status updates, newsletter discovery and labels (#1485)

Three surfaces no other channel here can reach at all. They are also the
highest-signal spam pattern Meta watches, and on this channel the phone
number IS the bot: there is no token to rotate if it gets banned. So the
rails are config rather than a convention the caller is trusted to keep.

A status target must appear on channels.whatsapp.broadcast.allowed_targets,
and an EMPTY allowlist allows nobody - the opposite of the usual "empty
means everyone", because an unconfigured install must not be one tool call
away from messaging strangers. A refusal names the numbers, and if any
target is refused nothing is sent at all. Matching normalises to digits so
an allowlist is not defeated by formatting.

Sends are paced at a deliberately slow 5s by default, and a configured 0
falls back to that rather than disabling pacing: turning the rail off is
not a knob this offers, because a config typo must not become a
mass-send. The result states the wall-clock floor up front.

Newsletter posting is not included: it needs newsletter message reception,
which this channel does not do. list_newsletters gives the discovery half.
Labels are private organisation on the owner's own account, so they carry
no rails and are not charged to the send budget.

docs(readme): describe the WhatsApp channel's new surface

Covers edit-in-place streaming and completion reactions, the inbound
types now handled including poll votes, expired-media recovery, native
voice notes with the recording indicator, the ephemeral_ttl and broadcast
settings, and the widened whatsapp_send action list.

Refs #1408, #1409, #1410, #1482, #1483, #1484, #1485, #1486, #1487, #1488.

fix(channels/whatsapp): create polls through the lib so votes can be decrypted (#1482)

The send_poll action built the poll proto by hand and never set
MessageContextInfo.message_secret. Voters derive their vote-encryption
key from that secret, so every vote on a bot-created poll was
undecryptable by construction - the decode path added alongside it would
have shipped looking correct and doing nothing.

polls().create mints the secret, persists it where the decode path looks
for it, and picks the proto version WhatsApp Web uses for the select
count (v3 single, v1 multi) rather than the v1-with-count-zero the
hand-rolled version always sent. A multi_select option comes with it,
since the count is now meaningful.

The secret lookup also normalises both halves of its key the way the
store writes them. Comparing a device-suffixed JID would have missed a
secret that was present.

feat(channels/whatsapp): try the native-flow path for interactive buttons (#1411)

This channel shipped buttons once and removed them: 2f15f1d1 tore
ButtonsMessage out of the approval flow because modern clients silently
never render it, and the comment saying so was still in handler.rs. So
the bar for putting buttons back is higher than "the field exists".

NativeFlowMessage is a genuinely different path. Three details are
load-bearing and none of them are visible in the proto: the card rides
inside viewOnceMessage, which is the envelope clients expect rather than
anything to do with disappearing media; the wrapper carries
deviceListMetadataVersion 2, which multi-device clients want before they
render anything inside it; and each button's params are a JSON blob, not
fields, built with serde_json because a label is user text and a quote in
it would otherwise produce JSON the client cannot parse.

It also fixes a latent bug. The tap parser read only
buttonsResponseMessage, but a native-flow tap answers as an
interactiveResponseMessage with the id inside that JSON blob, so even a
card that DID render would have had its tap parsed as nothing and the
approval would have sat there until it timed out. Both shapes are read
now, and parsing stays on whatever the config says: it costs nothing, and
a tap that arrived is itself evidence the card rendered.

Wired to tool approvals behind channels.whatsapp.interactive_buttons,
default off. An approval prompt that does not render is the one message
an owner cannot answer, so this does not default to an unproven path, and
either way the same instructions ride in the body text so a card that
renders without its buttons still tells the reader what to type.

send_buttons exists so the card can be tried against a real phone without
handing the approval flow over to it first. Its result says plainly that
a successful send is not proof, because WhatsApp drops a card it dislikes
silently rather than erroring.

docs(readme): correct the WhatsApp surface and add a check so it stops drifting (#1526)

The whatsapp_send row said 26 actions when 27 ship, missing send_buttons,
and the telegram_send row beside it said 19 when 20 ship. A count in a
table that nobody re-derives while adding an action is a count that goes
stale, and a reader cannot tell a stale one from a true one.

interactive_buttons was undocumented entirely. Of the nine keys on
WhatsAppConfig it was the only one absent, and it is the one that gates
whether a safety-critical approval prompt takes an unproven render path.
A config key nobody can find is a decision nobody can review, so the
example now carries it, off, with the reason and with the way to test it
before turning it on.

The channel row described about half of what shipped: no blocking, no
disappearing messages, no pin or forward or profile setters, no status,
newsletters or labels, no send budget, no buttons. WhatsApp now has the
largest action surface of any channel here and had close to the least
prose.

readme_channel_surface_test re-derives the counts from the tool schemas
at test time, asserts every schema action has a match arm, and asserts
every WhatsApp config key appears in the README. session_idle_hours is
exempted by name rather than skipped silently: it exists on all eight
channel config structs and is documented for none of them, so it belongs
to a cross-channel pass instead of this one.
fix(whatsapp): route whatsapp_send to session chat before owner fallback and resolve LID sender_alt

perf(tui): stop re-reading every skill and commands.toml per help frame (#1530)

render_help built its command list inside the draw call, so each frame ran
load_all_skills() — a walk of every project's skills directory, reading and
frontmatter-parsing each SKILL.md — plus a read and TOML parse of
commands.toml. On this machine that is 15 read_dir calls and 20 file reads,
and the event loop ticks at 100ms, so holding the help screen open cost
roughly 200 file reads a second for a list that cannot change while you are
looking at it.

Nothing was dropped and nothing was logged, so the only symptom was a warm
laptop on a screen rendering static text. It also scaled with the user's own
content: every skill anyone added made the help screen more expensive to
look at.

help_catalog collects the rows once, on entering the screen, which still
picks up a skill added mid-session. It has a second effect worth naming: the
rows now exist outside the draw call, so their count is available to the key
handler. Nothing could know how many rows the screen had, which is why its
scroll offset has no ceiling.

fix(tui): clamp Help and Settings scroll to the end of the content (#1527)

The down and page-down keys called saturating_add with no upper bound.
saturating_add stops at usize::MAX, not at the end of the content, and
Paragraph::scroll renders blank rows past the end rather than refusing. So
holding the key wound the help screen into empty space with no cue for how
far back to scroll; the only recovery was Esc and reopen.

The renderer records what it drew and the height it had to draw into, the
way render_chat already does with chat_area_height, and the key handler
clamps against that. This needs the row count to exist outside the draw
call, which is what #1530 made possible.

Settings is fixed in the same commit because it is the same bug: it shares
help_scroll_offset AND the key-handler arm, so clamping only the help screen
would have clamped Settings against whatever help last drew — or against 0
and 0 when help was never opened, where max_scroll is 0 and Settings would
have refused to scroll at all. A test asserts no screen in the file renders
that offset unclamped, since the next screen to share it will hit this too.

feat(tui): search the help screen with / (#1527)

The help screen listed every command in one scrolling column with five keys
to navigate it and no way to search. That was fine when the list was short.
On this machine it is 69 command rows across four sections plus headers and
a keybinding reference, in a column showing about 30 at a time, ordered by
section rather than by anything a reader can predict.

The irony is that autocomplete already filters: typing /mis in chat finds
the match instantly. The help screen, which you open precisely because you
do not know the command's name, was the one place you could not search.

/ opens a filter, matching case-insensitively on name AND description, so
someone searching "deploy" finds /release if its description mentions
deploying. Matching the name alone would only help people who already knew
the answer. Esc clears the filter and stays; a second Esc leaves, so a
mistyped filter costs one key rather than the screen. A filter matching
nothing says so, since falling through would blank the pane and read as a
crash, and the scroll offset resets whenever the result set changes under
it.

The pattern mirrors the sessions screen so this is not a new interaction to
learn.

feat(tui): log viewer in Mission Control, opened with L (#1528)

Logs were write-only from the app's side: logging/logger.rs writes a daily
file and nothing in the codebase ever read one back, so debugging meant
leaving the TUI to grep — at exactly the moment you wanted the context the
TUI had.

Two things on disk shaped this rather than the format on paper. A day's file
here reached 106 MB and 331k lines, so the reader seeks from the end and
parses a bounded tail instead of loading a file to display it. And the
format is one entry per line only until a logged message contains a newline:
those spill onto following lines with no timestamp and no level. A
line-based parser gives them a made-up level and a level filter then drops
them, which is precisely backwards — multi-line messages are JSON payloads,
stack traces and captured output, the things you opened the log for. Worse,
the entry's first line survives, so the filter looks like it worked. A line
with no parseable header therefore belongs to the entry above it.

L, not l: lowercase l is the vim-right panel cycle and taking it would break
panel navigation. MC already distinguishes case, with G for End beside g for
Home.

The viewer opens on the newest file scrolled to the tail, filters by minimum
level and by text across target, message and body, and steps between days
with [ and ]. Level colour comes from theme::Role rather than raw ANSI, so
it follows the user's theme. A failed read says why instead of rendering as
though the log were empty.

Live tailing is deliberately out of scope: it needs a watcher and a redraw
cadence, and adding it later does not invalidate any of this.

test(telegram): run the rate-limit retry tests on a paused clock (#1532)

Both retrying tests slept 90 seconds of real time each: the ladder waits
MAX_INLINE_RATE_LIMIT_WAIT (30s) per retry, three times. Both tripped the
harness 60-second warning on every run.

start_paused makes tokio auto-advance whenever nothing is runnable, so the
waits resolve instantly while Instant::elapsed still reports the virtual
90s. telegram_send_retry_test.rs already tested this same function that
way and asserted elapsed was zero; this file simply never got the
attribute.

The elapsed assertion matters more than the speed. Attempt counts alone
cannot tell a capped 30s wait from the full uncapped window, so a
regression that removed the #1064 clamp would have kept these tests green
while the bot sat on a flood-banned chat for hours. Measuring the wait is
what turns it from a cost into coverage.

Wall clock: the saving is smaller than the sleep suggests, because the
tests ran in parallel with the rest of the suite rather than in series.
The 90s overlapped most of the other work, so the full run went 103.10s to
95.34s across the two runs, not to ~15s.

Merge PR #1531: route whatsapp_send to the session chat before the owner fallback

From adi805. A whatsapp_send call with no `phone` argument fell back to the
owner's number rather than the chat the turn came from, so a tool reply in
someone else's conversation was delivered to the owner instead. Telegram
already did this correctly through session_chat(); WhatsApp did not.

The fix threads session_id into resolve_jid so it can look up the session's
own JID first, and keeps the owner number as the last resort rather than the
first. It also resolves LID senders through sender_alt: a modern 1:1 DM
arrives addressed by the opaque LID, so session_phone and the owner check
both have to read the PN that rides alongside it, or every allowlisted
contact looks like a stranger.

Conflict resolution, all in whatsapp_send.rs: the PR was written against a
tree with 15 resolve_jid call sites, and #1485 had since added the broadcast,
label and blocking actions, bringing it to 20. Every one of them now passes
session_id; the PR's signature change is kept intact and none of the newer
actions were dropped.

fix(channels/whatsapp): a blocked contact could walk past the guard from a LID

The inbound blocklist guard from #1487 matched only `info.source.sender`.
A modern 1:1 DM is addressed by the opaque LID, while the mirror holds
phone numbers - the server blocklist and `block_contact` both key on the
PN. So a blocked contact messaging from a LID matched nothing and was
handled normally, past the one guard whose whole job is stopping them.

Surfaced by the LID routing work in #1531, which established that
`sender_alt` carries the other identity for exactly this reason.

`blocks_either` checks both addresses, since they are two names for one
account. It lives on the blocklist rather than at the call site because
the normalisation that strips a device suffix has to apply to both halves,
and duplicating that at the guard is how the two would drift apart.

An absent `sender_alt` is not a miss: group stanzas and older clients
carry none, and the guard still has to work on the address it does have.

test(subagent): run worktree tests against an overridden profile home (#1535)

create() does not derive the worktree path from the parent repo it is
handed - it takes it from the profile home:

    worktree_root() -> resolve_profile_home().join("worktrees")

So passing an isolated TempDir as the parent read as isolation and was
not. Every run wrote its checkouts into the developer's real
~/.opencrabs/worktrees/, and two of the tests keep their tree on purpose,
so the leak was the assertion succeeding rather than an escaped edge
case. Five hardcoded fixture ids were sitting in a live home.

It was also self-perpetuating. On the next run create() found
path.exists() and took the stale-path branch, which tries to unregister
the tree from the parent repo it was given - a fresh TempDir that has
never heard of it. A clean run was green and re-armed the next one to
fail, which is why these passed in isolation and failed in a suite.

with_home_override is task-local, so unlike pointing $HOME at a tempdir
it cannot leak to a sibling thread under a parallel run (#912).

The added test asserts where the checkout landed. Nothing in the other
eight would notice losing the isolation: they check the returned tree and
every one of those assertions passes just as well when it sits in the
real home, which is exactly why the leak went unseen.

test(brain): resolve the seed home once per test instead of twice (#1536)

Each test resolved $HOME twice and independently: home_for_profile() to
build the path the assertions read, then with_profile_home() recomputing
it inside ensure_brain_seeded(). Both reads end at dirs::home_dir(), so a
$HOME swap landing between them seeded one directory while the assertion
checked another - the failure reads as "first open must seed SOUL.md"
when SOUL.md was in fact written, just somewhere else.

The home is now resolved once into a TempDir and handed to both the
seeding call and the assertions, so there is no second read to disagree
with the first.

That also stops the tests writing into the developer's real profile home.
The old helper built ~/.opencrabs/profiles/brain-seed-test-* and removed
it at the end, which leaves the directory behind on any panic - the same
mistake #1535 fixed next door. ensure_brain_seeded() resolves through
opencrabs_home() alone and never consults the profile NAME, so the home
override is the whole requirement; scoping a name as well would imply a
dependency that does not exist.

seeding_lands_under_the_overridden_home_and_not_the_real_one pins both
halves: the seed follows the override, and the live home is unchanged
across the call. A developer's real home legitimately holds a SOUL.md, so
its presence proves nothing either way - the state is sampled before and
compared after.

fix(channels/whatsapp): accept either identity when gating an approval reply (#1533)

An approval reply was gated on is_owner(&phone) alone. `phone` is whichever
address the stanza arrived on, and a modern 1:1 DM is addressed by the
opaque LID, so an owner replying "yes" arrived as digits that are not
their phone number and the gate refused them:

  WhatsApp: non-owner 83911178752119 replied approval Yes - refused (OC-01)

The tool call then sat unanswered until it timed out five minutes later,
which reads to the owner as the agent ignoring them.

The gate further down the same function already checks both identities;
this one is now the same shape. Nothing is canonicalized here on purpose:
the question is whether this person is the owner, not which of their two
names to file them under, and narrowing to one value would lock out
whichever half they did not arrive on.

fix(channels/whatsapp): key sessions and buffers on the canonical identity (#1533)

A 1:1 message carries two addresses: the one it was sent to and the one
riding alongside it in sender_alt. sender_alt is not "the phone number",
it is whichever identity the sender is not, so a PN sender carries their
LID there and a LID sender carries their PN. Preferring one field or the
other gets exactly half the senders wrong.

canonical_user picks by server family instead: the PN when either address
is one, the LID only when nothing better exists. The approval key, both
photo debounce buffers and the session key now resolve through it, so the
same contact lands on the same key whichever address a stanza arrives
with.

This also restores the pre-#1531 session key for PN contacts. #1531 fixed
LID senders by preferring sender_alt, which inverted the bug for PN
senders and rendered their session label as a bare LID.

test(read): buffer the fixture writes instead of one syscall per line (#1534)

The four fixture loops in the read_file tests wrote with writeln! straight

fix(138): persist seen-skills to DB and register filename-form load_brain_file

Gap 1: the seen_skills registry was in-memory only, so every daemon
restart made skill-consuming sessions look skill-less to the
post-compaction inventory stamp (#125/#131). mark_seen now best-effort
persists each (session, slug, epoch) row to a new session_seen_skills
table (detached task, WARN-only on failure), and AgentService::new fires
a once-per-process hydrate at boot that reloads rows and prunes rows for
deleted sessions. Slash invocation (register_active_skill) also marks
seen so the stamp's union covers slash-invoked skills across restarts.

Gap 2: load_brain_file's filename form ('<slug>.md') resolved nothing —
skills live in skills/<slug>/SKILL.md — so query-filtered loads
registered no consumption (live-observed 2026-09-08: Suggest options
lane's only skill-adjacent call registered nothing). The filename form
now resolves through the skill registry exactly like the bare slug form
(mark + body + query filter included).

Scope: the seen (durability) half only. Upstream already performs the
union at src/brain/agent/service/tool_loop.rs (active.union(&seen)), so
the active-registry half needs no port and is scoped out here — issue
#138's own solution text permits this ("or is explicitly scoped out
with a stated reason").

The epoch column is folded into the CREATE because upstream's registry
value IS the epoch (HashMap<(Uuid, String), u64>); persisting the key
while dropping the value would not persist the registry. The migration
appends LAST in the include_str! list because user_version is a list
INDEX, not a count — inserting mid-list would re-run already-applied
migrations on existing databases.

fix(138): explicit Result typing in SessionSkillsRepository::all()

The collect() into a bare Vec left the interact closure's error
parameter uninferable — three E0282/E0283 diagnostics at
session_skills.rs:79, because anyhow::Result is in scope alongside
several From<rusqlite::Error> impls (rusqlite_migration's Error,
HookError). CI gate run 34746172253 went RED at the Clippy step on
exactly this.

Mirror the fork's own fix (bdac0282): collect into an explicit
rusqlite::Result<Vec<...>> as the closure's final expression. The
turbofish pins the Ok type, and the error parameter resolves from
query_map's concrete closure return type instead of staying open.

Side effect, intended and matching the fork: a malformed row now
surfaces as an error rather than being silently dropped by
filter_map(Result::ok).

Also removes an unnecessary_sort_by shape from the new round-trip test
(clippy runs with -D warnings), replacing the sort with direct row
lookups.

  grows, an oversized frame answers a parse error and resyncs at the next
  newline instead of killing the session. Generous by design; the bound
  exists for runaway streams, not to reject large legitimate prompts.
- The dead `SessionState.cwd` field is deleted, not masked: the resolver
  never consults it, so the session/new signature now documents cwd as
  accepted-and-ignored.

fix(rsi): classify permanent cap-bails and dedup their reporting

sync_templates bailed every cycle when a brain file exceeded its
[brain.caps] line cap on its own (AGENTS.md: 531 local lines vs the 500
default), because the merged-size check can never pass while local > cap
- 126 identical [Bailed] entries accumulated in rsi/improvements.md and
the activity feed, while new upstream sections were withheld forever
with no way for the listed levers (prune, pruned.toml) to unstick the
state.

Classify the bail into two states: Permanent (local_lines > cap,
deadlocked regardless of merge size) vs Transient (local <= cap <
merged, resolvable by ordinary means). Transient keeps per-cycle
reporting. Permanent is reported once per state fingerprint - filename +
cap + a 25-line local-size bucket, hashed - persisted in a new sidecar
rsi/cap_bail_state.toml so dedup survives process boundaries; identical
re-observations drop to debug level, and a bucket or cap change re-arms
the gate. The Permanent entry says plainly that the file is over the cap
on its own, sync cannot fix it, and the only real levers are raising
[brain.caps].<file> or an owner-approved cleanup pass
(write_opencrabs_file cleanup_intent / a /compact-style prune) - pruning
upstream headers will NOT unstick it.

Regression tests in src/tests/rsi_stale_regression_test.rs pin the
classifier (both states + boundaries), the fingerprint (bucketing,
cap/file binding), the gate (emit once, suppress repeats, re-emit on
change, per-file independence), the sidecar round-trip, and the
Permanent wording.

feat(session): /clear starts the agent fresh at the current point without a summariser call (#1585)

A failed manual /compact on a large context is expensive: the whole
post-marker snapshot goes to the summariser, and on failure the walk sends
it again to every provider in the chain. There was no LLM-free way to move
on; /new starts a different session row and takes the visible history and
the title with it.

/clear appends one user row starting with the compaction-marker prefix.
The context loader already cuts at the last such row and the TUI already
hides it on reload, so history stays on screen and in the database, the
session keeps its id and title, and the next turn loads only the marker
body. The body says the user cleared the context, names the session title
and points the agent at session_search (tail on this session, or search
with the title), so it is not blind. An in-flight background compaction
is aborted first, as compact_context does, or its summary of the old
context would be applied over the cleared one on a later visit.

TUI: /clear in the command table; refused while a turn runs with a note
to cancel first; the ctx footer drops to the baseline a new session starts
at. Channels: owner-gated like /new, handled without an agent turn on
Telegram, Discord, Slack and WhatsApp, listed in /help and the Telegram
menu. A failed manual compaction now ends with the way out: cancel if it
is still running, then /clear.

Tests cover the marker prefix the loader and the TUI key on, the body,
the untitled case, the banner strip, the receipt line, a real clear on an
in-memory database (history kept, loader cuts at the marker, a second
clear works), the abort-before-write order, the owner gate, every surface
handling the command without an agent turn, and the failure hint.

fix(tui): treat a marker the model quoted mid-line as text on reload, not as a cut point (#1587)

The model, reading its own history through session_search, quoted an old
row's reasoning markers and a ledger opener cut off by an ellipsis inside
its reasoning. The reload splitter took the quoted ledger opener as real,
walked prose looking for the closing bracket, failed, and pushed
everything after it as the answer: the ledger head, the rest of the
reasoning, an orphaned close marker and the real ledger raw. The reasoning
splitter had the same blind spot, taking the quoted close as the end of
the real block. Live view never parses the row, so the same turn had
rendered collapsed until the double-Escape reload.

Real markers start a line, always: the persist path writes them that way,
and on a live database 109,369 of 109,755 reasoning openers and 122,582
of 122,715 ledger openers sit at a line start, every sampled mid-line one
a quote. The new ledger_scan module finds the next ledger that both starts
a line and parses, skipping any candidate that does not instead of ending
the scan; expand_message runs on it. The reasoning and phantom markers
follow the same line-start rule, and a line that is nothing but a marker
is dropped from visible text.

Tests are built from the row shape: the quoted opener is skipped and the
real ledger found at its offset, the text before it is one collapsed
reasoning block with nothing visible, a quoted close does not end the
real block, orphaned marker lines are dropped, a line-start opener with
broken JSON is skipped rather than fatal, v1 ledgers and inner arrows
still parse, and the line-start search itself.

feat(browser): composed-tree JS helpers for shadow-DOM traversal

Every selector path in the browser module resolved against the light DOM
only: document.querySelectorAll never enters a shadow root, so controls
rendered inside a custom element were invisible to the agent.

Adds shadow.rs, a pure JS-source builder module: a preamble of helpers
that walk the composed tree (document plus every OPEN shadow root)
instead of a single document. Root collection is cycle-guarded by a Set
and capped, and the walk is iteration-capped, so a pathological page
cannot hang Runtime.evaluate. Helpers are scoped consts, not globals, so
nothing is left behind on the page.

A CLOSED root stays out of reach here by construction — el.shadowRoot is
null for one by spec. Reaching those is the CDP path's job.

fix(browser): browser_find enumerates and keeps shadow-root elements

Routes css / aria / text search and the interactive inventory through
the composed-tree helpers, and makes the stale-stamp cleanup deep: once
we stamp inside a shadow root, a flat cleanup would leave stamps rotting
there and a stale [data-opencrabs-match="3"] could resolve to a node
from a previous page state.

Two inventory heuristics would otherwise have eaten every newly-visible
element:

- Occlusion hit-test: document.elementFromPoint retargets to the shadow
  host and Node.contains does not cross a boundary, so every pierced
  element compared as occluded and was dropped. Now hit-tests inside the
  element's own root and compares ancestry along the composed tree.
- Dup-collapse: rect containment alone would fold a shadow-inner control
  into an unrelated light-DOM wrapper that merely overlaps it. The
  collapse now also requires composed-tree ancestry, so it still fires
  for a real nested wrapper and never for a coincidental overlap.

Matches carry a shadow flag, surfaced as [shadow] in the report, so the
model can see why a hand-written selector for one would not resolve.
XPath stays main-document: the XPath spec has no notion of a shadow
boundary, and the tool description now says so.

fix(browser): resolve selectors across shadow roots in click/wait/screenshot/act

Fixing enumeration alone would have produced a selector that lists fine
and then fails to click, which is strictly worse than today's honest
"not found" — the round trip is the actual defect, so both halves land
together.

Page::find_element issues DOM.querySelector rooted at the document node,
and CDP's querySelector does not cross a shadow boundary; the pierce
flag on the underlying getDocument buys nothing there. Adds
manager::resolve_element, plain lookup first and pierced only on
failure, so a page with no shadow DOM pays zero extra round-trips and
there is no regression surface on the common case.

That fallback is also the only path that reaches a CLOSED shadow root:
JS sees el.shadowRoot as null for one by spec, while
DOM.getDocument { pierce: true } returns it. Uses find_elements_pierced
and takes the first match rather than find_element_pierced, which pops
the LAST one and would disagree with plain find_element.

browser_act's pre-flight, fill and select move to the deep JS helpers so
what pre-flight validates is what execution resolves; its xpath branch
keeps the documented spec limit. Source-scan sentinels pin both the
no-bypass rule and the plain-before-pierced ordering.

fix(browser): browser_type and scoped browser_content resolve inside shadow roots

Both went through document.querySelector, so an input or a region a
browser_find call had just handed back resolved to nothing. Swapped for
the deep helper; outcome strings (no_element / not_input) and the
native-setter dance for controlled React/Vue inputs are unchanged.
content.rs also JSON-encodes the selector now instead of escaping single
quotes by hand.

Full-page browser_content deliberately keeps page.content() rather than
chromey's outer_html_full: that path applies no output cap at all, so
serializing every shadow tree would be an output-sizing change wearing a
shadow-DOM costume. The reason is a comment at the call site and a
sentinel test, not a silent omission.

test(browser): e2e fixture for the shadow-DOM round trip

Local fixture page with an open root, a root nested two levels deep, a
closed root, and a shadow-inner button under a pointer-events:none
overlay. Asserts the inventory surfaces the open roots and marks them
[shadow], that the selector it returns clicks and types, that the
overlaid button is not reported occluded (the elementFromPoint retarget
fix), and that the closed root resolves through browser_click while
staying absent from the inventory.

Also pins the two behaviours the design did not assume: that
document.body.innerText already includes shadow-rendered text, and that
the CDP pierced lookup really does reach a closed root. Ignored like its
neighbours — run with
cargo test --features browser --lib browser_e2e -- --ignored

is what the caller asked for, and each root contributes its own tree

fix(whatsapp): release the outbox at turn start so a follow-up never edits the previous answer

`Outbox` keeps one entry per session and `OutboxEntry::editable` stays true
for 15 minutes, but nothing ever released the entry at a turn boundary: the
doc comment claimed `clear` was "called when a turn ends" while the only call
sites were the two edit-failure paths in `stream.rs`. So a follow-up sent
inside the window found the previous turn's message still tracked, and the
first streamed chunk edited the answer the user had already read instead of
posting a new one.

The entry cannot be dropped when a turn ends: `stream::finalize` edits it up
to the finished answer and the completion reaction targets it, both after the
agent call returns. It is released when the next turn begins instead, via
`WhatsAppState::begin_turn`, called in `handle_message` right after the
session resolves and before the stream task spawns. This also stops a
completion reaction from landing on the previous turn's message when the
current turn tracked nothing.

Covered by turn-boundary tests on the live state plus a source-scan sentinel
pinning the release ahead of `stream::spawn`, since `handle_message` needs a
live client and cannot be unit tested.

fix(notify_queue): reap stale rows after the redelivery pass, not before

reap_stale_unclaimed deletes on `WHERE created_at < ?1` and nothing else:
its SQL carries no claim or route predicate, so a row is only "unclaimed"
because the caller has already offered it to a live route and kept what
re-parked. Running it before the offer made the age the sole test, so any
long downtime (a sleeping laptop, a machine off over a holiday) deleted
every parked push past the ceiling for perfectly live sessions with
working routes. That is the one outcome this module's own contract
forbids: "a DUPLICATE after restart, never a lost message".

The call now sits at the end of redeliver_persisted, extracted into
reap_stale_after_redelivery so the entry point stays thin. Every row it
sees has been through deliver_or_park and come back re-parked; anything a
route could take was delivered and cleared moments before. now_unix() is
snapshotted once instead of re-read per logged row.

clear_dead_sessions keeps its place before the read, which is correct:
a row whose session is gone can never be claimed, so offering it only
re-parks a push nobody can receive.

Pinned by src/tests/notify_queue_reap_order_test.rs, three ways: all() is
age-blind at the data layer, so nothing below the caller protects an old
row for a live session; the reap call sits after deliver_or_park; the
dead-session reap stays before the read. Source sentinels for the two
ordering pins because redeliver_persisted resolves its pool through the
process-wide global_pool() OnceLock that only a real Database::connect
sets.

Refs #1617.

The dedup, framing, sender-label and render helpers lived inside
telegram/handler.rs, so Discord, WhatsApp and Slack each grew their own
copy of the fetch-and-inject block with no dedup and no #682 framing
(#1618, #1619, #1620).

Moves the four helpers verbatim into src/channels/group_history.rs and
generalizes two parameters: frame_history takes a room noun ("group" vs
"channel") and current_sender_label takes the surface string. Adds
build_preamble, which runs the whole fetch, dedup, render and frame pass
and returns None when nothing survives dedup.

Telegram's own output is unchanged: its call sites pass "group" and
"Telegram group", reproducing the previous strings byte for byte.

test(group_history): pin the lifted helpers against the legacy strings

Seven tests over the shared module. Two of them are the byte-identity
bar for the lift: frame_history with the "group" noun and
current_sender_label with the "Telegram group" surface are asserted
against the exact strings telegram/handler.rs emitted before the move,
so any drift in the Telegram prompt fails here instead of shipping.

The rest cover the new noun parameter, oldest-first render order, the
empty-input case and the dedup helpers.

fix(discord): dedup channel history and label the current sender (#1619)

Guild turns prepended the last 30 stored channel messages unconditionally,
with no check against what the live session already held. After a compaction
those same messages are still in front of the model, so the block was re-sent
on every turn until the next compaction, which it also pulls forward.

Routes the fetch through channels::group_history::build_preamble, which
filters rows already present in the live context and skips the block entirely
when nothing survives. Same path Telegram has used since #133.

Also adds the #682 framing Discord never received: guild turns now carry the
current-sender label, even for the owner, so the model does not address the
speaker by a name that only appears in the injected history. DMs keep their
old shape since no other member's name is in play there.

test(discord): pin the history wiring against a silent fallback (#1619)

The dedup and framing behaviour is covered in group_history_test. What can rot
independently here is the wiring: the handler drifting back to a hand-rolled
block, or losing the sender label. The handler needs a live gateway to
exercise, so these are source-level sentinels.

fix(slack): record the thread a channel message belongs to (#1620)

ChannelMessage::new() hardcodes thread_id: None and only .with_thread() sets
it. Slack called neither, so every stored row landed with a NULL thread_id
across all three write sites: the inbound capture closure and both bot-reply
inserts.

Harmless while every history fetch is channel-wide, and fatal the moment one
is scoped to a thread: recent() filters with strict equality and SQL NULL
never equals a value, so a scoped lookup over NULL rows returns nothing at
all. This has to land before the fetch is scoped, not with it.

test(slack): pin thread persistence and the NULL-scoping trap (#1620)

Two live-DB cases: a thread-scoped fetch must see only its own thread while a
top-level turn keeps the channel-wide view, and a row stored without a
thread_id is invisible to any scoped lookup. The second documents the
transitional cost, rows written before the fix stay NULL.

The third counts write sites against .with_thread() calls, so a fourth insert
added later cannot quietly skip it.

fix(slack): dedup channel history, scope it to the thread, label the sender (#1620)

Three defects in one block. Channel turns prepended the last 30 stored
messages unconditionally, with no check against what the live session already
held, so after a compaction the same messages were re-sent every turn. The
fetch was channel-wide, so parallel threads all saw each other's messages, the
bleed #226 fixed for Telegram forum topics. And the #682 framing was missing
entirely, so the model could address the current speaker by a name that only
appeared in the injected history.

Routes the fetch through channels::group_history::build_preamble with the
thread key derived from thread_ts exactly as the write path stores it, and
labels the current sender on every channel turn including the owner's. DMs
keep their old shape since no other member's name is in play there.

Transitional note: rows written before the persistence fix carry a NULL
thread_id and stay invisible to the scoped fetch, so a thread regains history
only as new messages land in it.

test(slack): pin the history wiring against a silent fallback (#1620)

Dedup lives in group_history_test and thread scoping in

to a hand-rolled block, dropping the sender label, or passing None where the
thread key belongs. The handler needs a live socket to exercise, so they are
source-level sentinels.

feat(whatsapp): render suggestion sets past the button cap as a poll (#1616)

Native-flow cards cap at three buttons, so a four-to-eight option set fell
straight to the numbered list and the user had to type a number on a phone.
A single-choice poll is the only other one-tap surface WhatsApp offers.

The routing itself moves into a pure suggestion_surface() so it is testable
without a socket: the card keeps everything it can take, since it carries the
body text and the typed instructions and so degrades better on a client that
renders nothing; the poll claims only what the card cannot. A failed poll send
falls through to the numbered list rather than losing the suggestions, and an
owner who never opted into interactive_buttons still gets text.

feat(whatsapp): select a follow-up suggestion from a poll vote (#1616)

Rendering the poll is only half of it. A vote names its option by LABEL, so
the numeric selector could never match one: the vote arrived as a
'[poll vote] X chose: Y' line, failed to parse as a number, and fell into the
branch that clears the pending set. The poll rendered and then killed the
suggestions it was offering.

decode_vote now returns the chosen labels alongside the line it renders,
rather than having the caller split the prose back apart, and a label selector
consumes the set on a match. Matching is trimmed and case-insensitive because
the label makes a round trip through WhatsApp's poll proto. A multi-select
vote selects nothing, since these polls are single-choice by construction and
a two-option vote is not a pick.

test(whatsapp): pin suggestion-poll routing and vote selection (#1616)

Whether a phone draws the poll cannot be tested here and nothing below
pretends otherwise. What is pinned is which surface a given set picks, that an
opted-out owner still gets text, and that a vote consumes the pending set
exactly once and only for a label that was actually on offer.

feat(telegram): process-wide rate limiter and global 429 cooldown lock

Add a process-wide token-bucket pacer and a global 429 cooldown lock so the
bot stays below Telegram's global request limit instead of discovering the
limit by being flood-banned.

- `rate_limit`: `GLOBAL_COOLDOWN` holds the server-declared retry window
  (plus a margin) after ANY endpoint sees a 429. `record_global_429`,
  `is_global_cooldown_active`, `wait_global_cooldown` and
  `reset_global_cooldown` expose it, and `wait_out` records the window so
  every send site feeds the same lock. `parse_retry_after` now matches the
  retry-after header case-insensitively.
- `governor`: `GLOBAL_PACER` (25 req/s, burst 25, 5s max hold) is acquired by
  `pace_send` and `pace_rich`; `admit_chat_action` and
  `edit_admission_media_kb` drop drop-eligible work (typing indicators,
  cosmetic intermediate edits) immediately while a global cooldown is active,
  instead of spending retry attempts into an active flood window.
- Unit tests live under `src/tests/` (`governor_internals_test.rs`,
  `rate_limit_global_cooldown_test.rs`), registered in `src/tests/mod.rs`,
  per the upstream test-isolation rule.

ci(windows): raise build timeout to 60m and drop dead save-if

The first CI run of the windows-build job died at its own 40-minute cap
mid-link: cold cache, llama compiled clean, root lib compiled with
warnings only, and the thin-LTO link (the 4-vCPU hosted-runner tail)
never got to finish. The build was minutes from done.

  warm rust-cache runs land near 10. Cap stays so a true hang cannot

on the previous palette until an unrelated resize happened to clear the
cache, which is most of why switching themes looked like it changed

foreground, which no palette can move, so body text rendered identically
under crab-dark, dracula, alucard and every imported pack theme.

Seeding the fold with Role::TextPrimary fixes it without touching the
tags: patch leaves an inner colour alone, so links, inline code and
headings still win, while modifier-only tags such as bold now inherit the
prose colour instead of the terminal's. Inline HTML, the one other text
site rendering at Style::default(), takes the same seed.

That also retires the force-white branch on user messages: it existed
because default-fg prose could land unreadable on the message
background, and with an explicit foreground every preset already pairs a
legible text_primary with its surface_code_alt. Forcing white was itself
wrong on the light themes it claimed to protect.

fix(usage): net the cached prefix out of input_tokens on compat providers (#1636)

`prompt_tokens` on an OpenAI-compatible API is the gross prompt, cached
prefix included, but `TokenUsage::input_tokens` is documented non-cached
and `pricing.rs` bills `cache_read_tokens` separately on top of it. All
four assignment sites handed the gross value straight through, so every
cached token was charged twice, at the full input rate and again at the
cache-read rate, and counted twice in the token total.

The netting happens at the provider boundary, where the contract is
documented, via `OpenAIUsage::net_input_tokens()`. Only the cache-read
prefix is subtracted: nothing shows a compat provider folding
`cache_creation_input_tokens` into `prompt_tokens`.

The `[STREAM_USAGE]` receipt lines keep reporting the gross `input=`
value unchanged and gain an `input_net=` field, so past and future logs
stay comparable.

Anthropic and Gemini are unaffected: both report `input_tokens`
natively non-cached.

test(usage): guard the cached-prefix netting on every compat usage path (#1636)

Nine tests, seven of which fail on the pre-fix provider code.

Each assignment site is driven end to end against a local socket rather
than asserted on a parser in isolation: usage inlined on the finish
chunk, the usage-only final chunk, the non-streaming response, and the
`nonstream_compat` synthesizer. Both cache-field spellings are covered,
`prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens` and `cache_read_input_tokens`.

Three edges that a naive netting would break: a cache read larger than
the prompt must clamp instead of wrapping, a provider reporting no cache
split must pass its prompt through untouched, and `net + cache_read`
must always reassemble the provider's gross prompt exactly.

The cost guard replays the real GLM-5.3-Flash bench run against the
published card and asserts both the corrected bill and the inflated one
the defect produced, so the gap itself is what a regression has to move.

fix(usage): anchor the ctx meter and compaction budget on the gross prompt (#1636)

One usage report carries two different numbers and the tool loop was
reading one of them for both jobs.

`input_tokens` is the billing input, non-cached, because the pricing
table charges cache_read and cache_creation on top of it. The prompt the
model actually saw is `context_input()`, cached prefix included. Once the
compat providers stopped reporting the gross prompt in the billing field,
reading it for the context budget would have anchored a 35k prompt at a
few hundred tokens on a 98% cache hit, and compaction would never fire
again. Anthropic already had this: it marks the system prompt and tools
with cache_control, so its `input_tokens` has always been the uncached
remainder and the ctx meter has always under-read it.

The ctx meter, the `record_provider_reported_tokens` anchor and the
token calibration now read `context_input()`. Billing keeps reading
`input_tokens`. The "provider reported nothing" guard moves to
`context_input() > 0`, because a fully cached prefix is a legitimate zero
in the billing field and that is not the same as silence.

test(usage): correct the compat cache test that asserted the double count (#1636)

`nonstream_with_cache_usage` fed a 1000-token prompt with a 900-token
cached prefix and asserted `input_tokens == 1000` alongside
`cache_read_tokens == 900`, pinning the defect in place. It now asserts
the netted 100, plus that net + cache reassembles the gross prompt.

fix(provider): stop the DONE-stream estimate from outranking reported usage (#1636)

The `[DONE]` branch emits a MessageDelta on every compat stream carrying
a local estimate of the prompt, message tokens plus tool schemas. It
fires after the real usage delta, and the consumer reconciles the two
with `max()`.

That was harmless while `input_tokens` held the gross prompt: the
provider's own number was always the larger one. Netting the cached
prefix out inverts it. On a 98% cache hit the reported input is a few
hundred tokens against an estimate of the whole prompt, so the estimate
wins every time and the prefix lands back in the bill, now as a guess
rather than a reported figure.

The estimate is a last resort, not a second opinion: once the provider
has reported real counts the fallback delta exists only to carry
stop_reason, and reports zero tokens. When the provider reported nothing
at all the estimate still stands, unchanged.

test(usage): guard the DONE-fallback against outranking reported usage (#1636)

Asserts the invariant over the raw event sequence rather than replaying
the consumer's reconciliation: no delta in a compat stream may report
more input than the provider reported uncached.

The prompt is deliberately large. A one-word request estimates below the
netted input, so the assertion would hold with or without the fix and
the test would prove nothing. At this size the unguarded code reports
[474, 4005] and fails.

fix(logging): install a crash-signal diagnostic handler for SIGBUS/SIGSEGV (#352)

A fatal fault signal is delivered to the kernel's default disposition, so the
daemon dies silently — recording neither the signal nor the faulting address.
A production instance was killed by SIGBUS under host memory pressure and left
no panic, no backtrace and no log line behind; that blind spot is what this
closes. The kernel OOM-killer was separately observed reaping children inside
the unit cgroup rather than the daemon itself, so the faulting signal is not
attributable from the journal alone.

Install a handler for SIGSEGV, SIGBUS, SIGILL, SIGFPE and SIGABRT that renders
a one-line crash record (signal name, signo, si_code, faulting address, tid,
pid) plus a backtrace, writes it to both stderr and a crash log, and re-raises
the original signal so the process still dies by the true signal and the exit
status stays honest.

The handler is async-signal-safe: it runs on a dedicated 64 KiB alternate
signal stack (sigaltstack), performs no allocation, and uses raw
non-allocating direct writes. The crash-log path is resolved and leaked as a
CString at install time, because the handler may not allocate.

The record renderer truncates as a true prefix rather than a fragment: when
the buffer fills, the cursor is sealed at capacity so every later push fails
its bounds check. A spliced record — si_addr=0x7fpid=1234 — reads as data when
it is garbage; in the last thing a dying process emits, a short prefix is
strictly better than a corrupted one.

Installation happens in main; a failure to install is logged and never fatal,
so a box where the handler cannot be installed still starts.

Merge PR #1637: crash-signal diagnostic handler for SIGBUS/SIGSEGV

A daemon killed by SIGBUS or SIGSEGV left nothing behind but the exit
status. This installs an async-signal-safe handler that writes a decoded

Merge PR #1630: process-wide proactive rate limiter and global 429 cooldown lock

The per-chat pacer cannot see a process-wide ceiling, and a 429 learned in
one chat was information every other chat never got. Adds a global permit
every outbound Telegram send takes, plus a shared cooldown deadline that a
429 extends monotonically as max(existing, now + retry_after + margin), so
concurrent 429s cannot shorten each other. Fails open at GLOBAL_MAX_HOLD so
the pacer can never hang a turn, and typing refreshes and non-final edits
drop through a non-blocking check instead of queueing.

Author: leshchenko1979

fix(telegram): take the global permit before the per-chat pacing gate (#1630)

Both pacers called `acquire_global_permit()` after `if !lim.enabled
{ return; }`, so turning the per-chat limiter off also removed the
process-wide ceiling and the wait on an active 429 cooldown.

Those are different policies. `limits.enabled` governs how a single chat
is paced; the global permit is the safety floor for the whole process and
the only thing that stops every chat firing straight through a throttle
another chat already discovered.

fix(telegram): record 429s discovered outside wait_out (#1630)

`record_global_429` was armed from `wait_out` alone, so a throttle found
on any path that handles its own retry stayed private to that path and
the global cooldown never saw it. Three such paths:

- the plan card's edit and create failures parse a real retry-after,
  suppress this session's card writes, and return;
- a queued final that comes back 429 feeds the per-peer requeue maths
  only;
- the raw HTTP send retry sleeps on its own timer.

All four now record the wait before acting locally. The deadline extends
monotonically, so recording a wait another path already recorded is a
no-op rather than a double penalty.

path drops the guard before it awaits — but this is the one lock where
getting it wrong later stalls every outbound Telegram send in the
process, so the constraint is written at the lock rather than left to be
rediscovered.

Merge PR #1629: trigger-gated cron pipeline with mechanical pre-flight

Gates a cron job's execution on a cheap shell probe, so a polling job
becomes an event job: the trigger runs first and the agent only fires when
the condition holds. Conditions cover exit status, output presence and a
regex, threaded through CronJobPatch so partial updates behave, with a
migration appended last per the list invariant and defaults in from_row so

A skipped run is still recorded rather than silently doing nothing, so the
job's history shows it ran and decided not to fire.

fix(cron): kill a timed-out trigger's shell instead of orphaning it (#1629)

`TriggerRunner::run` wraps `wait_with_output()` in a timeout. On expiry

drop, so the shell kept running unsupervised. A trigger that hangs does

outlive it; taking the whole tree would need a process group and is not
this fix.

Merge PR #1632: Windows reliability (shell spawning, cwd, encoding, search fallback)

From moneyacademyKE. Ten Windows-surfaced fixes plus a Windows CI job:
platform shell pair instead of hardcoded sh -c, MSVC verbatim args,
timeout tree-kill, system-directory cwd fallback, BOM/UTF-16 aware
read_file, session_search empty-query fallback, backslash tilde.

Follow-up commits on top address the lossy-read overwrite hole, the
CI gate cost, and the gh routing text.

fix(tools): a transformed read must not arm a whole-file overwrite

read_file now decodes BOM-aware and falls back to lossy so a binary or a
PowerShell UTF-16 log does not hard-fail the read (#1632). That tolerance
leaked straight into write_file: the same path calls mark_fully_read and
file_versions::record, which is exactly what unlocks a wholesale
overwrite (#1168, #954).

Both guards then pass on a binary. The partial-view guard is satisfied by
the read itself, and the staleness guard cannot help: write_file reads the
current file with read_to_string, which yields None on those bytes, and
is_stale_write treats None as "not stale". A model that reads
opencrabs.db and later writes that path replaces the database with U+FFFD
soup, with nothing reported.

The decoded text is not a byte-faithful view of the file, so it is not a
basis for replacing it: writing it back re-encodes UTF-16 as UTF-8 at
best. Arm the overwrite only when no transform was applied. The read
still succeeds, and its warning now names overwrite_read_confirm so the
later refusal is anticipated rather than mysterious.

No behaviour change. Five files arrived unformatted with #1632 and three

ci: keep windows-build out of the required gate and path-filter it

#1632 put the Windows build back into ci-gate.needs, reversing #627. The
measurements from that PR's own runs say why #627 removed it: 51m09s for
the one successful cold build, the gate going from ~43m to ~65m, and at
roughly 160 PR-triggered runs a fortnight that is ~136h of GitHub-hosted
runner time against the 3 Windows builds release.yml actually ran in the
same window. It is also the only job here not on the self-hosted Mac, and
the new 60m cap leaves 15% headroom over the measured 51m, so one
cache-busting dependency bump reproduces the #627 failure exactly: every
check green except Windows timing out mid-compile.

The bug class it protects against is real (the hardcoded `sh -c` spawns
survived months of green CI because the gate never compiled Windows), so
the job stays. It is advisory rather than blocking, and its expensive
steps only run when the PR touches a path that has actually produced
Windows-only breakage: the dependency graph, the toolchain, the platform
abstraction, the spawn and read paths, or this workflow. The filter fails
open, and a `windows` label forces a build for what the list misses.

Known gap, stated rather than papered over: a new cfg(windows) block in
an unlisted file is not caught at PR time. release.yml's matrix still
builds Windows before any tag ships, which is the coverage #627 relied

Both UTF-16 paths from #1632 built their code units with

One `decode_utf16_payload` helper now serves both and reports the odd

and whole-file paths cannot describe the same decode differently. A
truncated file still reads, it just says it is truncated.

produces is the orphan the sweep exists to kill — a timed-out `cargo

Best-effort is a decision about whether to abort, not a licence to say

fix(provider): sticky fallback counts rescues in a window, not in a row (#1667)

fix(provider): streams must not inherit the transport total wall clock (#1687) (#1692)

* fix(provider): streams must not inherit the transport total wall clock (#1687)

reqwest's `.timeout()` covers the response body read, so the client carrying it put a
hard wall-clock ceiling on every SSE body it served, however healthily chunks arrived.
`complete()` and `stream()` shared one client per provider family, so `timeout_secs`
was simultaneously the non-streaming ceiling and the stream guillotine — and with the
flag unset, as on the reporting host, the family's hardcoded default governed (300s
today, 60s from #217 until #1635 raised it).

Split the client in all three families: a stream client with connect_timeout, pool and
tcp_keepalive but no total timeout, and the existing timed client for `complete()`,
`/models` and every buffered path. `stream()` and its in-function retry sites move to
the stream client; `with_timeout` now rebuilds only the non-streaming client, and
AnthropicProvider::with_client can no longer reintroduce a ceiling on the stream path.

Inter-chunk silence remains the only stream timer (`stream_idle_timeout_secs`: 3600s
CLI/local, 45s z.ai, 20s other remote), the correct detector for a dead stream. No new
clock is introduced, so no new disagreement.

Tests:
- stream_total_wall_clock_test.rs: 12 frames at 120ms against a 250ms total ceiling.
  Pre-fix on 0b6cf46cb it died with `Streaming error: error decoding response body`,
  the #1687 defect reproduced; post-fix every fragment is delivered.
- the same file proves the ceiling still bounds non-streaming calls (retries disabled so
  the assertion measures the clock, not complete()'s 4-attempt ~15s budget) and that a
  buffered response inside the ceiling still succeeds.
- provider_stream_total_timeout_test.rs: #1635's idle-adjacency guard compared two
  constants that no longer share a path, and the value was never the defect — #1635
  raised it 60s to 300s and the mechanism survived. Replaced with a source scan of all
  three families: no `.timeout(` in the stream builders, `stream()` on `stream_client`.
  #1635's cross-family floor and retry-log-budget scans kept.
- README and config/types.rs corrected: `timeout_secs` is the non-streaming ceiling, has
  never touched streams, and the default it overrides has been 300s since #1635.

* test(stream): drop the unreferenced hangup recorder

serve_hanging_json was written to prove the transport ceiling from the server
side, then superseded when the non-streaming test pinned complete()'s retry
ladder to a single attempt, which measures the same thing directly. Nothing
called it, so CI's Lint job failed on `function serve_hanging_json is never

fix(agent): thinking-loop guard stands down on a delivering stream and is per-provider scopable (#1690) (#1699)

The guard raced the stream against [agent] thinking_loop_timeout_secs and, on
expiry with no tool call, returned Err(ThinkingLoopTimeout) unconditionally.
tool_loop then stripped everything the stream had delivered (bytes: usize::MAX)
and re-sent the whole conversation for phantom enforcement, so a healthy turn
that simply answered in prose lost ten minutes of work. After #1687 removed the
transport total ceiling, this guard became the first wall such a stream meets.

Contract change, two parts:

- The guard disarms instead of killing when the stream has delivered content
  (last_delta_at is set): the answer survives, the post-success phantom path in
  tool_loop still nudges narrated tool intent, and stream_idle_timeout_secs
  still bounds silence. A stream that delivered NOTHING still returns the
  error, because there is nothing to lose and the retry exists for exactly that
  shape. The issue's wording asked for a nudge message on a delivering stream;
  standing the clock down is the deliberate deviation, argued in the PR body.
- thinking_loop_timeout_secs is now resolvable per provider:
  [providers.<name>] overrides [agent] (default 600), and Some(0) disables the
  guard for that provider - 0 is a value here, unlike the transport clocks
  where 0 is skipped as a typo, because a provider that legitimately never
  needs the guard (long local reasoning models, CLI backends) had no way to
  say so. Resolved via resolve_thinking_loop in config/timeout.rs, carried by
  the Provider trait's new thinking_loop_timeout() accessor (default None),
  implemented on all three families plus fallback delegation, and applied by
  the factory's report_timeout_chain (now a 3-tuple).

Tests: thinking_loop_nudge_test drives the real agent service with a mock
provider - a delivering stream survives the 1s threshold with every chunk
intact, a silent stream still errors so phantom enforcement runs, Some(0)
disables, per-provider beats [agent], and the factory wiring is asserted.
Docs: README gains a thinking-loop guard section; config.toml.example
documents the new key and its 0-means-disabled semantics; a witness test pins
both. AgentConfig's stale 'stream is killed and retried' doc is corrected.

fix(phantom): score fact detectors on mixed iterations (#1693) (#1709)

Every fact detector in phantom.rs sat behind `tool_uses.is_empty()`, so a
response that fabricated a claim AND emitted a real tool call in the same
iteration bypassed all of them: the call made the turn look like work, and
the claim rode it out to the user. Observed on 2026-09-22 — "Gate died on
2× E0603 \"this item is private\"" was delivered inside an iteration that
did dispatch a tool, so no detector ever evaluated the sentence.

Opening the gate alone would have been half a fix: no existing extractor
pulls a rustc diagnostic code out of prose. `asserted_shas` needs seven
hex characters and E0603 is five; `asserted_tallies` knows only
passed/failed/ignored. So `asserted_diagnostics` admits a standalone
Eddddd token, refusing one glued to a longer word on either side
(1a2b3E0603ff, src/E0603.rs, E06031, 0xE0603) to keep identifiers and
hex runs out of the fact set.

`mixed_iteration_facts` evaluates the three command/fact/evidence branches
together and returns a verdict carrying its own branch names and the
structured-report flag, so the injection point never needs the iteration
text alive. Executed commands are the union of prior inputs and this
iteration's own calls — otherwise "Running `gh pr list`" plus a
`gh pr list` call would flag the work it is about to do — while tool
outputs stay prior-only, because an in-flight call has produced nothing
and cannot vouch for a past-tense claim.

The correction lands after the tool results, mirroring the repeat-correction
